The UKIRT Infrared Deep Sky Survey (UKIDSS; Lucas et al. 2008) uses the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope (UKIRT) to survey the whole sky visible from Mauna Kea , Hawaii, in two optical bands and two infrared bands. In April 2010, UKIDSS completed its Early Data Release (EDR), including images of some areas that had not been observed by the UKIRT Wide Field Survey (uwfS; Collins et al. 2010). In this paper we present a new method of searching for distant galaxies by using these new UKIDSS EDR images of the Galactic Plane. We use the UKIDSS Galactic Plane Survey (GPLS; Hambly et al. 2008) to identify two stellar populations, A and B, with different colours and redshifts. We then apply a colour-colour diagram, constructed using these two stellar populations and star-forming galaxies with known redshifts, to find regions in colour space where the distant galaxies can be found. We apply this technique to two separate areas of the sky, labelled L7 and L11, and find a total of 66 galaxies at redshifts greater than z = 1.5, with a mean distance of 92.2 ± 5.4 million light-years. We conclude that this new technique is a potentially useful method of selecting distant galaxies, and discuss the implications of this result for studies of the epoch of reionisation.' — RMCGP Team

A surprising variety of celestial objects have been discovered orbiting around the center of the galaxy IC342. This includes at least 15 dark galaxies, up to 750 globular clusters and a large number of highly unusual x-ray sources. An x-ray survey of the central square kiloparsec of this galaxy has been performed using the Chandra X-ray Observatory at a resolution of 20 pc. A total of twenty-two point-like x-ray sources are resolved by Chandra, the vast majority of which are likely low-mass x-ray binary systems (LMXRBS). A globular cluster appears to be powered by a bright ultraluminous x-ray source, several other globular clusters appear to possess faint x-ray sources, and two newly discovered dwarf galaxies appear to be entirely powered by x-ray emission from stellar black holes. The presence of a large number of highly unusual x-ray sources is quite remarkable, and no other galaxy centers has shown such a diverse population of anomalous objects. The large number of these objects over 10 Gyr shows that some of the dark galaxies may be viable candidates to form new galaxies.

We consider a generalised model for time-dependent variance, with a short-term memory. This model can be used to describe some empirical economic time series, including the volatility of commodity prices, interest rates and equity prices. We use estimates of this model to fit several of these time series and show that this improves the quality of the fit compared to more common functional forms. We fit this model to the S&P 500 and NASDAQ 100 stock indices , as well as the US 10-year treasury bond yields and the 10-year UK government bond yields. We also use this model to fit the historical volatility of the S&P 500. We find that this improves the fit over the standard Black-Scholes model for the historical volatility. We also study the short-term memory of this model. We simulate a fluctuating variance with this model and show that the variance quickly forgets its previous values. We also show that if this model was used to simulate the S&P 500, then the simulated S&P 500 would quickly forget the experienced variance. We also consider a generalised CIR model for the short-term memory. We show that if the short-term memory of this model is governed by a generalised CIR model, then the long-term memory of this model is governed by a generalised CIR model. We also find that this model can be used to describe some nonlinear relationships between time-dependent variables and covariates. We also apply machine learning methods to the task of learning the parameters of this model from historical data. We find that the quality of the fit of the model to the data can be significantly increased by using this parameter learning method. Finally, we consider several robust fitting methods and find that these do not significantly degrade the quality of the parameter fit. We investigate the applicability of this model to other economic time series by fitting it to commodity prices, interest rates and equity prices. We find that this model significantly improves the quality of the fit over more common models. We also study the long-term memory of this model by fitting it to a time series with long-term autocorrelations. We find that the long-term memory of this model implies long-term correlations in the error terms of this model. Finally, we apply this model to the historical volatility of the S&P 500. We find that this model improves the fit over the standard Black-Scholes model for this volatility. We also find that this model is used to describe the short-term memory of the historical volatility. We find that this model significantly improves the quality of the fit of this model over the standard Black-Scholes model. Finally, we apply machine learning methods to the task of learning the parameters of this model from historical data. We find that the quality of the fit of the model to the data can be significantly increased by using this parameter learning method. We investigate the applicability of this model to other economic time series by fitting it to commodity prices

The bound on the curvature of the universe, as inferred from the propagation of light emitted at the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) epoch, is equivalent to that of a flat universe, σ ≤ 10 -5. This is assuming the universe is well described by a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric, with σ = 0 one order of magnitude higher than the bound on the Hubble parameter, H ≤ 10 -5 (Planck 2013), seven orders of magnitude more stringent than the direct bound, suggesting that the true bound is significantly non-zero. It has been suggested that this significant disagreement may be an indication of new gravitational physics, such as new theories or deviations from General Relativity (GR). We present a simple extension of the Friedmann equations that increases the allowed bound of the curvature from zero, and examine the impact of this extension on current cosmological datasets. We find that while this extension relaxes the bound on the Hubble parameter to H ≤ 10 -5, the bound on the curvature remains at σ = 0 with 95% confidence. We conclude that current cosmological data do not require the curvature of the universe to be non-zero at the 95% confidence level.

A weak MgII absorption at z=0.45 is discovered in the QSO J2228+0154 spectrum obtained with the Keck telescope. This system has a complex Voigt profile with five absorption components, one of which is due to high ionization species like SiI, SiII, SiI and FeI. The total column density of this complex is (2.3+/-0.4)x1020 cm-2 which implies a very weak neutral hydrogen column density of (2.8+/-0.5)x1020 cm-2. The metallicity of this system is very low with a 12+log(O/H) of 7.1 and a metallicity of 1/100th the solar value. This system is a very faint metal-poor galaxy at the peak epoch of star formation. The first star forming episode in the universe was likely triggered by a small MgII halo merging with a more massive one at z=0.5.

In the standard model (SM), top -antitop production is described by seven penguin diagrams at the Tevatron, and nine at the LHC. For LHC energies, higher-order corrections are large and uncertainties from other sources, such as intrinsic theoretical uncertainties in the leading-order calculations, as well as experimental uncertainties in the knowledge of the jet energy and the momentum of the initial state particles, grow due to increased higher-order corrections. While the total top quark cross section has been measured in both experiments to be consistent with the SM expectation, with a global significance of 2.9 standard deviations, there are several anomalous observations which have been reported: the measurement of the forward-backward asymmetry by both CDF and D0, the total cross section for top-antitop production, and the production of a single top quark in association with a W boson. While the measured forward-backward asymmetry is consistent with the SM expectation, all other measurements are 2.5-3.6 sigma deviations from the SM predictions. It is currently hypothesized that these deviations may be the result of the production of new, strongly-interacting particles which decay to top quarks, and thus the search for these particles has been the focus of recent studies. In this work, we perform a global fit to all anomalous measurements, including the production of nonstandard spin one particles, which decay to top quarks and a new, heavy, neutral scalar or vector spin one particle. We find regions of the parameter space of the new physics model, compatible with all observations, and present the corresponding expected signatures at collider experiments.

The symmetries of Anti-de Sitter (AdS) and asymptotically flat spacetimes imply that their conserved charges should satisfy certain linearly independent differential equations. In particular, the conserved charges in three and higher dimensional AdS should satisfy a system of first order differential equations with constraints, and for asymptotically flat spacetimes in four and higher dimensions, they should satisfy a second order differential equation with constraints. In this short note, we prove a couple of identities relating the conserved charges of these spacetimes that satisfy either a first order or a second order differential equation with constraints. Our identities don't seem to have been discussed before in the existing literature. This note is an extension of our earlier work [1], where we dealt with the case of three dimensional Anti-de Sitter space (AdS$_3$) in (3+1)D and the case of four and higher dimensional asymptotically flat spacetime in (4+1)D. The main motivation for writing this short note was to have a single document which contains all the results. [1] G. Chakraborty and S. Deshmukh, "Identities for conserved charges in (n + 1) dimensional spacetimes with (n - 1) dimensional horizons", arXiv:1910.06501 [hep-th] *This work was done when the author was with: Center for High Energy Physics, Institute of Engineering Sciences, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, Karnataka 560012, India *The note can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.06501

The fine structure of solar prominences was observed by the Extreme ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (EIT) on board the SOlar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO). Prominences are the coronal extensions of the Sun formed by the release of magnetically stored energy. EIT observations showed that their structure is composed of stacked faculae. Faculae are magnetic bright points visible in the solar photosphere. The prominence fine structure was visible only over a narrow range of heliocentric distances, from 0.95 to 1.07 solar radii. The appearance of the fine structure is strongly dependent on the local orientation of the prominence with respect to the observer. The prominence fine structure was not visible when the observer was looking along the long axis of the structure; when the observer was looking along the short axis the appearance of the structure was that of a coronal arcade; finally, when the long axis of the fine structure was inclined by 55 degrees with respect to the radial direction, the appearance of the fine structure was like a “ coronal leg ”.' This observation clearly shows that the fine structure of solar prominences is not purely composed of plasma flowing along structures similar to those of coronal arcades; the appearance of the fine structure changes strongly depending on the local orientation of the structure with respect to the observer. It is likely that the prominence fine structure is the footprint of a current sheet embedded in the prominence.

I present a new analysis of the proper motions and radial velocities of F and G dwarfs in the Milky Way neighborhood. This sample, obtained from the Spectroscopic Properties of Nearby F and G Dwarfs (SPONGES) survey, is restricted to stars with a diameter of 7.5 kpc < rho < 22.5 kpc and |z| < 1 kpc and a color, (G* - r* - r), that places them between 1.5 and 3.5 mag below the main sequence. By statistically comparing the heliocentric radial velocities to their respective absolute visual magnitudes, I infer the full 3D kinematics of this sample. In agreement with previous analyses, I find that the tangential velocity, Vt, increases with median Galactocentric radius, Rv. I additionally find that Vt and Rv are correlated at a significance of 4.2σ, meaning the velocity field of F and G dwarfs cannot be explained by a simple Galactocentric radial dependence. I attribute this velocity covariance to the complex evolution of the Milky Way, which likely included a early heliocentric migration period and subsequent accretion of satellite galaxies. I also analyze the individual proper motions and do not find evidence of a kinematically anomalous population. This work shows that a broad sample of local F and G dwarfs can be used to study the 3D kinematics of the Milky Way as a function of age and provides valuable constraints for future simulations of the Milky Way’s formation and evolution.

Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs), like their two-dimensional counterparts, such as graphene, are atomically thin structures with fascinating properties. Due to the edge state characteristics, GNR field effect transistors (GFETs) exhibit quite different scaling behaviors compared to conventional two-dimensional field effect transistors. In this work, using first-principles quantum transport simulations based on three-dimensional (3D) quantum mechanical tunneling, we investigate the scaling behaviors of GFETs with different widths. By varying the channel width W, we find a scaling law consistent with W3/2, which agrees with prior two-dimensional scaling analyses. Further, we identify the evolution of scaling regimes with W: within the narrow width range (W < 10 nm), W2 scaling, which corresponds to single channel transport, is observed; above this range (W > 10 nm), W scaling, corresponding to parallel conduction, is observed. The observed W2 and W scaling regions correspond to channel resistance contributed from conduction and from disorder, respectively. Furthermore, we uncover interesting non-monotonic behavior in the evolution of scaling behavior, with an inflection point occurring at W ≈ 20 nm. With our findings, we establish a framework to study GFET scaling and offer design guidelines for high -performance GNR FETs.

A hypercontractive inequality for matrix-valued functions, with applications to quantum computing and LDCs. Given a probability measure space, a random function, and a -dimensional random variable, the goal is to bound the norm of the random variable, where is the expected value. This quantity is known as the quadratic form associated with, and has numerous applications in analysis, probability, and physics. The best known bound on the quadratic form of a -dimensional random variable is where is the second smallest eigenvalue of the conjugate -transpose. This bound is typically weak when the random variable is allowed to grow and can be improved using convex analysis. Using this technique, we prove a general hypercontractive inequality for quadratic forms that applies to any function that can be expressed as an algebraic polynomial of. This inequality has numerous applications, and in particular yields optimal hypercontractive inequalities for matrix-valued functions that are polynomial to several matrix arguments or that satisfy a matrix form of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. In addition to free probability and linear differential geometry, this inequality has applications to the Kadison–Singer problem for LDCs, local covariance testing, and compressed sensing. This is a new proof of the hypercontractive inequality for quadratic forms, and as such, it extends the scope of the theorem to functions that are algebraic polynomials of the conjugate -transpose. This is the first time that this broad class of functions has been shown to satisfy a hypercontractive inequality. The resulting bounds have numerous applications and are optimal up to a logarithmic factor in several interesting cases. For example, they yield optimal hypercontractive inequalities for matrix-valued functions that are polynomial to several matrix arguments or that satisfy a matrix form of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

Using millimeter emission from dust, A.B. Shrestha et al. have resolved the circumstellar disk around HD 163296 into multiple distinct annular structures. The authors determine the disk structure and kinematics by modeling the visibilities from mm continuum observations at 880 micrometers, sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths, and short-spacing (0.2-2 mm) measurements at880 micrometers. The authors find the disk to be most likely composed of at least four components: a narrow outer disk located at 3.2±0.2 au with an inclination of 18.3±3.1°; an outer disk located at 20-50 au with an inclination of 4.5<unk>3.2°; an inner disk with an inner radius of 30-45 au and an inclination of 44.8±3.2°; and an outer radius of 180 au with an inclination of 17.7±2.5°. The authors also find the disk to be infalling with an estimated mass accretion rate of 4.3×10−8 M⊙ yr−1, and with a total radial disk mass of 13.3 M⊙. The authors suggest these structures may result from a recent radial flux event, and may provide an excellent target for future studies of planet formation.

MCHIT (Monte Carlo model for proton and heavy-ion therapy) is a user-friendly code for the calculation of hadrontherapy treatments. MCHIT solves the anisotropic Boltzmann transport equation, using advanced sampling methods and Monte Carlo models to compute the dose deposited by particles in the monitor chamber. The code can be used to simulate treatments with protons or heavy ions and it has been recently extended to GPUs to allow fast calculation of treatments with large numbers of beams. MCHIT can be freely downloaded from www.magicsaming.info/MCHIT.html. Authors: I. P. Goncalves, S. R. de Souza, D. K. Atmore, S. G. Mallat, J. F. Jesus, and A. L. The Lasso method has been very popular for regularized regression analysis due to its good performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model selection. However, in many applications the choice of the tuning parameter (the penalty term) is not data-driven but instead based on other prior knowledge, leading to biased estimates if this prior information is incorrect. In this paper we propose a method that adaptively chooses the tuning parameter using a combination of a classical Lasso estimate and a Group Lasso estimate, both of which take into account prior information. We derive the resulting criterion and show that it leads to consistent variable selection and parameter estimation, even if the prior information is incorrect. We establish oracle inequalities and suggest a data-driven choice for the smoothing parameter in the Group Lasso. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method via extensive simulations and an empirical analysis in a real data example. In this work we revisit the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger spin-fermion model [1] in the limit of weak electron-phonon coupling, using methods that are extensions of those employed in the treatment of the classical O(3) spin-wave model [2]. We show that, in this limit, the spectrum of spin-wave excitations of the polaron has a fermionic form in terms of a path integral, just as the spectrum of spin-wave excitations of the antiferromagnet does. We compute the one-loop quantum corrections to the dispersion of the polaron spin wave along symmetry-breaking directions, and show that they have the same form as the one-loop correction to the antiferromagnetic mass. We also study the interactions between two spin waves, and show that the leading non-linear correction has the same form as the coupling between fluctuations of the magnetization in the antiferromagnetic linear spin wave theory. Finally, we describe how to renormalize the polaron spin wave in the model that underlies the spin-wave theory, and discuss how the spin wave interaction enters into the antiferromagnetic spin wave model. The computation of the one-loop quantum corrections gives concrete support to a recently proposed effective field theory of the spin-fermion model [3].

Tests of Bayesian model selection techniques for gravitational wave (GW) astronomy are presented using simulated data. These techniques are used to compare two models of gravitational wave (GW) astronomy for data containing both signals and non-gravitational noise. These techniques are then applied to published LIGO and Virgo data from the initial LIGO and Virgo observing runs, respectively. The first model contains a single black hole (BH) signal while the second model contains two BH signals, the signal representing the largest possible gravitational wave. Both models were derived from binary black holes and first discovered by the LIGO-India observing runs. The results of these analyses indicate that these model selection techniques provide very good evidence in support of the two-signal model over the single-signal model. Additionally, a technique for approximating the evidence for more complicated models, such as models containing three or more signals, is also presented. This technique is applied to the two-signal model to determine the evidence in support of the two-signal model over the three-signal model. This evidence is approximately 0.3% of the evidence in support of the two-signal model over the single-signal model, indicating that the three-signal model provides a very small improvement to the model selection goodness of fit. These results indicate that even the most sophisticated gravitational wave observatories, such as LIGO and Virgo, are not well suited to distinguishing between more complex gravitational wave signals. Bayesian model selection is an important technique for future gravitational wave observatories, such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO-India), to employ in order to simplify the data analysis process by reducing the number of signals that must be considered, thereby reducing the data volume and the computational cost of the analysis.

Recent optical and near-infrared images have revealed a thin, comet-like extension around several young stars, dubbed supernoave ejecta with double tails. Observations of the 126my-old V4046 star showed a double-tailed morphology with a separation of ˜0.5″, similar to that of comets. Subsequent studies have revealed that this is a very common phenomena in young stars, found in roughly 30% of the investigated young stars. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the observations, including close encounters with terrestrial planet-mass objects, loss of kinetic energy from the cometary-like extension, or jet-related feedback from the central star. However, direct observational evidence is still sparse. Here, we report on the ALMA observations of a transitional disk around the young star HD163296, with corresponding HST observations at optical wavelengths. We have identified distinct Na I absorption lines corresponding to the star, the disk and the halo of the transitional disk around HD163296. The observed spatial distribution and velocity structure of the Na I lines are well matched with the predictions of hydrodynamical simulations of the interaction between the stellar ejecta and the disk. The observed absorption lines are consistent with the ejecta having a cometary morphology with a highly significant double tail. This is the first observational evidence for the interaction of supernoave ejecta with a protoplanetary disk.

Non-Metric Gravity (NMG) is a scalar-tensor theory that generalizes the Einstein-Hilbert action in a highly nontrivial way. In particular, NMG introduces a fundamental length scale L in such a way that gravity is always weaker than what would be expected from Einstein’s theory of general relativity (GR). By matching the weak-field limit of NMG to the solar system ’s dark matter and to gravitational wave observations, bounds on the characteristic length scale L of the order of the GUT scale can be derived. However, these bounds can be significantly violated when the Lorentz symmetry and local gravitational invariance are both violated, as has recently been found to be possible in a wide class of nonlinear modified dispersion relations. In this paper, we investigate this possibility and obtain the spherically symmetric solution of NMG with nonlinear dispersion. We show that this solution describes a compact object with a nonzero gravitational mass, whose strength is set by the coupling parameter λ of the nonlinear dispersion relation. We further show that for sufficiently strong coupling λ, these objects are good candidates for the dark matter. Finally, we show that the nonlinear dispersion also causes gravitational redshifts that are stronger than those predicted by GR.

Isotropically cross-linked actin networks are composed of filamentous actin molecules aligned along the filament long axis and joined together by complex bonds that form rings. These networks present solid-like behavior at the macroscopic scale and liquid-like behavior at the microscopic scale. In this paper, we study the rheological behavior of such actin networks at different length scales. Microscopic techniques were used to characterize the linear and nonlinear mechanical response of single actin networks and the slow dynamics of ActinDenaturedFlexibleDrop. Macroscopic experiments were conducted on packed actin networks flowing between two different length scales. We found that the linear modulus of an actin network increases with the force applied to stretch it, showing that actin networks are solid-like at the macroscopic scale. However, at very low frequencies, we found that the complex modulus decreases with the frequency, which indicates that the actin networks are more liquid-like at the microscopic scale. Finally, we demonstrated that ActinDenaturedFlexibleDrop, which is a polymer model based on actin networks, presents similar rheological behavior as its biological counterpart.

Soft Constraint Logic Programming is used to implement Unicast and Multicast Qos routing. This allows the traffic to reach the desired QoS level without the need of intermediate routers, thus reducing the overall network footprint and the required infrastructure. Numerical simulations show the effectiveness of the approach in terms of QoS delivered to the desired traffic, reduction of the overall network footprint and energy consumption.' This work extends our previous paper [1] by also supporting multicast sessions. First, a background on Soft Constraint Programming is presented to provide the reader with the basic concepts on which Soft Constraint Logic Programming is based. Next, the approach used in [1] is extended to support Unicast as well as Multicast Qos traffic. A numerical example is used to show the effectiveness of the approach in terms of QoS delivered to the desired traffic, reduction of the overall network footprint and energy consumption.' This work was partially supported by Spanish project CONACYT and Mexican SEP projects with awards CONACYT 74598 and SNI 74598.

A long paper with many sections. Here is a high-level paper with some important points highlighted. First, we consider a regression problem where the input space is high-dimensional. For example, pixels of images are often used as input to machine learning models. In such settings, standard approaches such as decision trees or linear regression fail to capture high-level structure in the data. For example, when fitting a linear model to images of fruits and vegetables, the size and shape alone are not sufficient to determine whether a given image contains beets. Second, we consider a setting where the number of examples is much larger than the available training data, a setting known as small N large P (NLP). For example, face detection in photos of people with unconstrained facial expressions and expressions is a challenging NLP problem. Other large N problems include drug discovery and computational biology, in which the search for chemical compounds and protein structures that bind to a drug or protein, respectively, can be modeled as a huge-dimensional regression task. Third, we develop a framework for regularized empirical risk minimization that allows us to capture the structure in the input. This framework, called optimal transport with linear separation (OTLS), learns a mapping from the input space to a lower-dimensional space called the weight space, in which the examples are separated into clusters by solving an optimal transport with linear separation problem. The features of the input space are thereby embedded in the weight space, allowing the resulting models to simultaneously capture the structure in the input space and perform dense prediction in the weight space. We then apply a standard optimization technique called projected gradient descent to learn the model parameters. Our method is computationally efficient because the optimization problem is convex and the objective is strongly convex with parameter s 2. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on synthetic and real-world data sets.

Recently, we presented c2d Spitzer IRS spectra of disks around T Tauri stars (TTSs) in the embedded phase, also known as the T Tauri phase. In these papers, we modeled these data with a Dusty disk plus photosphere model, finding that typical TTSs have envelope mass fractions of a few percent at disk radii of a few tens of AU. In this paper, we extend the Dusty disk plus photosphere model to include nine additional gas-phase lines from atomic species and H_2. We find that these additional lines can significantly improve the quality of the fits. We also test whether two-layer models, with inner and outer disk radii, improve the quality of the fits. We find that for [Ne II], [Ne I], and H_2, the two-layer models do not significantly improve the quality of the fits. However, for the [Si II], [S I], [Fe II], and [Si III] lines, the two-layer models do significantly improve the quality of the fits. We conclude that the gas in TTSs' disks likely has a significant component in the molecular form, e.g., H_2. This conclusion is consistent with previous models of planet formation, which predict that most dust will grow into larger bodies before collapsing into molecules. Finally, we note that the quality of the fits is similar in the embedded and disk phases, suggesting that the gas-phase composition does not evolve significantly during the embedded phase.

Globular clusters are populous systems of hundreds to thousands of gravitationally-bound stars. These clusters are usually spherical and co-spatial with their host galaxy, but deviations from spherical symmetry are frequently observed. One such deviation is the presence of non-point-like objects, commonly referred to as dark matter sub-halos. The dark matter hypothesis suggests that these sub-halos are the source of occasional disruptions of star clusters, resulting in extended stellar structure. The extent and morphology of these extended stellar structures are dependent on the inner and outer properties of the cluster, which are in turn dependent on its formation history and the properties of its host galaxy. Here, we report the discovery of three globular clusters with extended horizontal-branch stellar populations. The clusters exhibit a kinematic decoupling from their host galaxies, with substantial kinematic offsets between the positions of the clusters and their host galaxies’dark-matter distributions. These structural and kinematic discrepancies are not naturally explained by current sub-halo-based cluster dynamics models, indicating that current models of globular cluster dynamics and stellar evolution may be incomplete.

In this paper, we propose and implement a method to control a flashing ratchet by using time-delayed feedback. In contrast to most previous realizations of flashing ratchets, our ratchet is fully deterministic, in the sense that all the particles of the ratchet follow the same trajectories. This is achieved using near-concentric circular tracks , in which the particles, confined by a harmonic potential, undergo small amplitude fluctuations. These fluctuations are accompanied by a periodic modulation of the harmonic potential, causing the particles to perform small circular orbits with a constant motion along the circumference. By appropriately choosing the frequency and amplitude of these additional oscillations, we can arrange for a given particle to switch between a clockwise and a counterclockwise orbit with a time delay. In this way, we can implement control protocols that are formally equivalent to traditional feedback control systems. We analyze our ratchet both theoretically and experimentally. The theoretical analysis provides design guidelines for the system parameters, while the experimental analysis verifies the expected equations of motion as well as the ability of the system to implement a variety of more complicated control protocols.

Li and Rb are two alkali metal isotopes that exhibit a multitude of temperatures when exposed to thermal radiation from a reservoir. The two isotopes, when isolated from the reservoir of radiation, reach an effective quantum ground state corresponding to a single collective state. We demonstrate thermalization of both isotopes to their effective ground state at finite temperature, via a combination of photon scattering and magnetic field control of population and internal temperature. We also extend the method to atoms with multiple ground states, in this case $^7$Li and $^{87}$Rb, achieving quantum ground state temperatures by coupling to a single phonon mode in each case. Our results represent a landmark in sympathetic cooling of atoms to temperatures far below the typical modes of a single phonon, and a path to reaching the quantum ground state of multiple species of atoms via a combination of laser cooling and magnetic control. Our two-photon Raman scheme allows for efficient, on-demand coupling of Li and Rb atoms to the deep vacuum of molasses (Doppler) state atoms. First, we address cooling to the ground state by coupling to a single phonon mode, the scissors mode, using a pair of Raman lasers tuned to the $2\,^2S_{1/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{3/2}$ and $2\,^2P_{1/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2S_{1/2}$ transitions. The scissors mode is a mode of motion of the Li and Rb atoms with zero point energy equal to $k_B\times$288nK, where nK is the temperature in units of 0.1K. We characterize the temperature of the scissors mode by coupling population to this mode and measuring the change in momentum distribution of the atoms, finding the mode to be $288\pm29$nK. We then achieve quantum ground state temperatures of Li and Rb by transferring population to the quantum ground state using three Raman lasers and an adiabatic rapid passage (ARap) technique. We measure the final state purity, which approaches unity, as well as the entropy of the system, which we calculate to be equivalent to the zero-point energy of the scissors mode. Finally, we cool $^{87}$Rb to the zero-point energy of the scissors mode by repeating the process starting from the ground state. We find a total entropy reduction of $21.4\pm0.8$nK in three successive stages. We use a reservoir of thermal radiation to set the atoms’ temperature. We demonstrate that Li and Rb reach their effective quantum ground state at finite temperature through scattering of thermal radiation. We isolate Li in the $2\,^2S_{1/2}$ ground state and Rb in $2\,^2P_{1/2}$ and $2\,^2P_{3/2}$ ground states, and couple the atoms to the vacuum of a cavity via a dipole coupling to a mechanically compliant rod near the cavity

In this work, the effects of turbulent diffusion on the chemistry of diffuse molecular clouds are examined. In particular, the effects of weak turbulent diffusion on the radiative transfer and chemical enrichment of carbon and silicon are considered. Turbulent diffusion acts to spread material over larger spatial scales and, in the case of carbon, enhance its overall rate of depletion relative to the case without diffusion. Thus, while the total amount of carbon remains unchanged, turbulent diffusion increases the temporal contrast of carbon abundances within a diffuse molecular cloud, thus accelerating its chemical evolution. Carbon depletion by catalyzed reactions is also accelerated due to the increasing spatial contrast of carbon abundances. Silicon is substantially less impacted by turbulent diffusion. Both the neutral and ion silicon abundances increase with time, but the increase is less than that of carbon. Overall, the presence of weak turbulent diffusion may have an appreciable impact on the chemical enrichment of carbon and silicon within a diffuse molecular cloud.

On 12 February 2023, the potentially hazardous asteroid (144898) 2004 VD17 was identified by the Mount Lemmon Tenerife Observatory (MLAST) as it travelled around the Sun. This near-Earth object (NEO) is approximately 1-kilometre in diameter and has a minimum orbit intersection distance (MOID) of 0.0435 AU with Earth. If (144898) 2004 VD17 had an equivalent radius of 1 km when it passed through a distance of 0.0435 AU from Earth, it would have a probability of approximately 7.2 × 10−13 of making a close approach to the Earth and a 0.033% chance of impact. Here we report the results of a study carried out to better understand the physical properties of (144898) 2004 VD17 and determine its potential threat to Earth. To achieve this, observations of 2004 VD17 were acquired over two days using high-resolution astrometry from the Siding Springs Observatory, complemented by Earth-based radar observations from the Arecibo and Goldstone Observatory, and high-resolution asteroid observations from the Uppsala Astronomical Observatory (UAO). These observations showed that (144898) 2004 VD17 is unlikely to impact Earth in 2023. Furthermore, it is likely to be a captured NEO, with a low probability of posing a significant threat to Earth in the future. Observations of (144898) 2004 VD17 suggest that it is most likely a captured asteroid whose orbit becomes unstable and cross that of Earth every few hundred years. The identification of 2004 VD17 only twelve months prior to its next near-Earth pass in 2023 suggests that it may not be stable in its current orbit. This study highlights the utility of wide area surveys in the discovery of potentially hazardous objects. While the value of a rapid response search for near-Earth objects cannot be understated, high-precision astrometry with a wide field of view can find objects like (144898) 2004 VD17 well in advance of potential hazard determination. The use of additional data sources, such as radar data, in the discovery process can provide valuable information for characterizing potential hazards to improve the efficiency of response and mitigation efforts.

Recent observations suggest that coronal mass ejections (CMEs) may possess two different energy release processes. The first involves the magnetic field divergence that occurs as the CME moves through the interplanetary medium, giving rise to the ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) catastrophe. This results in an expansion of the CME leading edge (demarcated by the theta effect) that can lead to a thin shell or partial shell collapse. The second release mechanism involves the fast moving magnetic field lines interacting with ambient magnetic field lines, which may lead to the invocation of magnetic reconnection. Reconnection has been implicated by many in-situ and remote-sensing observations as leading to the accelerated acceleration of CME leading edges and to shock brightenings and outer atmosphere shocks associated with CME deceleration regions. In this article we present results from the development and testing of a physical model that describes these two release processes. We discuss our findings in the context of the slowly-varying-parameter and adiabatic invariants methods of solution. We also compare the results obtained using this model with recent observations of two distinct CME acceleration regions and three shock brightenings. Finally, we present results of a direct model comparison, using several forward-modeling codes and adiabatic invariants, with recent observations of similar CME acceleration and outer-atmosphere shock events. We find that the two-release-process model provides the best explanation for these observations.

Using data from the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, we describe the spectral and timing properties of the low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1728-34. We fit the continuum as well as photoelectric absorption edges of helium, ionized helium, and nitrogen using interstellar medium (ISM) models to better account for background emission and absorption. We model the reflection component using smeared edge functions to determine the global broadband continuum and other parameters. During the first three observations the source exhibited pulsations at a pulse period of 6.67 hr, confirming its neutron star nature. We find the surface gravity of the neutron star is high, and the mass of the compact object is at least 1.6 solar masses. The source exhibited high levels of absorption as well as localized regions of high absorption near 21.0 and 0.25 keV, which we ascribe to the edge absorption of ionized helium and neutral nitrogen, respectively. Using our new spectral results, we discuss previous observations and provide updated interpretations of these observations.

Humans exhibit complex temporal variability in their physiological signals, e.g., electrocardiograms (ECG) and blood pressure (BP). While time domain analysis can provide useful information about regular patterns in such signals, a more sophisticated approach is needed to fully capture their complexity. Recently, high dimensional measures of heart beat dynamics (HRV) such as detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) and multi-fractal spectrum (MFS) have emerged as powerful tools to quantify the long-term correlations as well as multifractality in time series. Although MFS characterizes temporal correlations along different time scales, its computation is computationally intensive and expensive. Thus, the use of MFS has been limited to short data records. In this work, we propose a computationally efficient approximation to MFS called approximate multifractal spectrum (AMS) which allows us to characterize the complexity of human heartbeat dynamics over long data records. We perform heartbeat dynamics analysis on a database containing 5-min data records from 300 human subjects aged between 8 and 77. We find that both DFA and MFS characterize heartbeat dynamics as multifractal, i.e., they display power-law scaling in the dependence of fluctuation amplitude on time scale. However, MFS provides more accurate information about the multi-fractal spectrum while DFA is a better metric to quantify the long-term correlations in time series. In addition, we find that AMS yields a good approximation to MFS. Thus, AMS provides a good compromise between efficiency and accuracy that is suitable for analyzing large data records.

The article determines cosmological parameters \Omega_\Lambda and H_0 by modeling the gravitational lensing signal from a sample of radio galaxies. The study uses the photometry from the telescope Pan-STARRS1 and the radio galaxy catalogue from the luminosity-distance sample, generated by Bob Hartmann. The data was reduced using the MOCASSIN simulation code, to generate models that fit for cosmological parameters. The study calculates theevidence based on a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. The results show that \Omega_\Lambda is 0.64 and H_0 is 73.5kms-1 Mpc-1. The results are consistent with aLambdaCDM model and H0 measurement from the Planck satellite. The results show that the evidence supports aLambdaCDM model with a \Omega_\Lambda of 0.64 and a H_0 of 73.5 km s-1 Mpc-1. In this paper we determine the most common indices of fixed points of maps on the space of rational functions, which are used to describe dynamical systems. We determine these common indices and express the number of rational functions with these common indices in terms of generalized Fibonacci numbers. We apply our results to give explicit formulas for the indices of fixed points of maps that generate cat maps and logistic maps. Finally, we give a method to determine these common indices for a wide class of maps on the space of rational functions. This method can be used to find indices of fixed points of rational functions that are not discussed in this paper. Indexes of fixed points of maps on the space of rational functions describe dynamical systems. These indices appear in asymptotic formulas for the number of rational functions that satisfy certain fixed point properties. In this paper, the number of rational functions that have n fixed points (indices) is equal to the generalized Fibonacci numbers. These asymptotic results are useful in applications, for example, in modeling of dynamical systems. In this paper, we determine the most common indices of fixed points of maps on the space of rational functions. We express the number of rational functions with these common indices in terms of generalized Fibonacci numbers. We apply our results to give explicit formulas for the indices of fixed points of maps that generate cat maps and logistic maps. We also apply our results to give a method to determine these common indices for a wide class of maps on the space of rational functions. This method can be used to find indices of fixed points of rational functions that are not discussed in this paper. This paper is part of my PhD thesis at the University of Agriculture in Budapest, Hungary. It is a part of my PhD thesis at the University of Agriculture in Budapest.

Long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are one of the most extreme forms of death in the universe. Understanding their origin and their rate in the early universe have important implications for the enrichment of the early metals and neutrinos production, which in turn affect the reionization process. Finding the progenitors of LGRBs can also help us understand the nature of these explosions, potentially providing information on the Equation of State (EOS) of neutron star (NS) matter at supranuclear densities. Although there have been many attempts to find their progenitors, no satisfactory explanation has been found. One promising finding is that some long gamma-ray bursts seem to have associated with peculiar supernovae, whose progenitors have been found to be very massive stars (20-25 M⊙). Here we show that the population of the extremely low metallicity long gamma-ray burst progenitors consistent with the origin of the associated peculiar supernovae at z ~ 2-4 can be reproduced with binary systems in which the initially more massive star forms a compact companion via merger with a neutron star or a black hole via dynamical capture in a close orbit, with the initially less massive star in the range 8-20 M⊙. Such stars can form a formation channel with very low metallicity , even if they have initial mass exceeding 40 M⊙. Such massive stars have not been observed in the local universe, thus this formation channel could have contributed to the formation of the population of long gamma-ray burst progenitors at high redshifts. This formation channel for the long gamma-ray burst progenitors can provide a clue to the origin of association between some long gamma-ray bursts and peculiar supernovae.

In this paper, we reconstruct the scalar-tensor (ST) Lagrangian with a spatially-flat LCDM background and Noether symmetry. The reconstruction is carried out by starting with a generic ST Lagrangian and then obtaining the corresponding ST Lagrangian equations. For a general ST Lagrangian, this reconstruction is carried out by obtaining a fourth-order PDE for the metric. We show that if the ST Lagrangian belongs to a particular family with a different dynamics for each value of a an arbitrary coupling function Λ(ϕ), then this fourth-order PDE can be reduced to a second-order one that can be solved in closed form. We carry this out in the specific case where Λ(ϕ) corresponds to the function Λ model. We illustrate our method with this model and show that the model can give a good fit to current cosmological data. This work was done in collaboration with Richard A. Daviltt and Michael B. Muhleman.

A new class of quantum photonic molecules composed of resonant microcavities of matching and mismatching frequencies is proposed and investigated. We demonstrate that such composite structures may provide new functionalities of microlasers and optoelectronic components, such as: 1) enhancement and suppression of spontaneous emission channels enabled by the dark and bright modes of the cavities forming the molecule; 2) independent tuning of bright and dark modes over a broad wavelength range by changing the size and refractive index of the molecule's constituents; 3) remote control of the molecule's optical properties via Förster resonant energy transfer across the composite structure; 4) efficient coupling of quantum emitters, such as atoms and molecules, to the molecule's bright modes. The proposed photonic molecules have potential applications in all-optical signal processing, communication, and quantum information processing. Methods: Theory and simulations are presented for a specific example of the proposed photonic molecules composed of resonant microcavities with matching frequencies and different sizes and refractive indices. This example is chosen to demonstrate the ability to control spontaneous emission channels, dark and bright modes, Förster energy transfer between bright modes, as well as possible applications to all-optical signal processing, communication, and quantum information processing.

The existence of dark matter is established by the gravitational effects it has on visible matter in galaxies. The nature of dark matter, however, is unknown. The most popular theory regarding its nature, the cold dark matter theory, states that it is comprised of elementary particles which neither give off nor receive electromagnetic radiation. Observational evidence has established that dark matter exists in clusters, or aggregates, large enough to be observed in both particles and galaxies. These clusters are believed to evolve via the mutual ly beneficial interaction of their constituent particles and galaxies. Since the constituents of dark matter do not give off or absorb light, their direct observation has been challenging. Understanding the dynamics of these clusters can therefore aid in understanding the properties of dark matter. B514 is a globular cluster located in the M31 galaxy approximately 25,000 light-years from Earth. Using the Hubble Space Telescope, I have determined that B514 has an additional extended halo which, based on its structural and dynamical characteristics, is most likely comprised of dark matter. I have determined that this dark matter cluster has a mean density of 0.105 halo particles per cubic light-year and a diameter of 1.33 kpc or 17,650 light-years.

The Costas property (CP) in the unit circle, also known as the circular rotation property, states that the complex exponential function Θ(t)=e^{it}, where i is the imaginary unit and e is the real number, rotates through 2π radians or 360 degrees when operated on around the unit circle. This article generalizes CP in the following way: let f be a differentiable function that is injective on an open interval I with endpoints a and b such that f'[a]≠0 and f'[b]≠0. Then, for all t in I, the equation f(x)=t has at most two solutions. The authors call a function that satisfies the preceding conditions CP-generalizing. A number of properties of CP are inherited by this general definition. In particular, the constant function f(x)=c is CP-generalizing for any real number c. The authors give a number of examples of Costas functions that are CP-generalizing but do not share any other properties of Costas functions. The article concludes with several open questions.

A well -known fact in the design and analysis of distributed algorithms is that the performance of a protocol may degrade drastically in the presence of a Byzantine faulty process. In order to ensure progress and prevent faulty processes from acting in a malicious manner, many conventional algorithms and protocols make the shared assumption that all processes are perfectly trusted and will never misbehave. However, this assumption is rarely realistic , and thus there is a significant need for mechanisms that allow distributed protocols to deal with the presence of faulty processes. In this regard,fault-tolerant distributed computing can be thought of as an error management system, where correct processes must be able to detect and subsequently recover from faulty processes that behave in an arbitrary and unpredictable manner. A number of protocols have been developed to deal with the presence of faulty processes in the standard model, where the faults are assumed to occur only in processes and not in the communication channels. However, most of the available fault-tolerant algorithms and protocols are designed to achieve highly optimistic fault-tolerance bounds, where each process executes an exact copy of the original protocol and all processes synchronize at the end to determine the outcome of the operation. Such strong consistency cannot be guaranteed in the presence of lighter faults where processes may crash and restart but still return an incorrect result. In this regard, we propose a fault-tolerant distributed algorithm for a set of standard computation tasks (including averaging, max, and min) that is able to tolerate up to ε-faults, i.e., a faulty process crashes with probability ε and returns an incorrect result with probability at most ε. We achieve resilience against Byzantine faults even when the underlying network is subjected to skewed link failures and the adversary has complete knowledge of the system. The algorithm enjoys good correctness and communication overhead, and offers an exponential improvement over the state-of-the-art in terms of the number of processes. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm via simulations. We have implemented our algorithm in the SAFE network, which consists of a total of 2036 processes, and we report the evaluation results on a large network with a varying number of faulty processes. Our simulation results show that our protocol can tolerate up to ε-faults, and can achieve good reliability even when as many as 23% of processes may be faulty.

One of the most surprising results from the early years of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey was the discovery of a population of close galaxy pairs, showing a substantial population of "asymmetric" galaxies (those with morphological disturbances). Given the apparent prominence of these disturbances in gas-rich galaxies, it has been hypothesized that the asymmetry observed could be associated with recent or ongoing galaxy mergers. In this paper, we test this hypothesis using a sample of 106 close pairs from the Million galaxy catalogue. We find that the close pairs show significant evidence of having undergone a recent merger, with the fraction of galaxies showing such disturbances correlating strongly with the size of the separation. For separations of less than 5Mpc, 65% of galaxies show some form of disturbance (typically distorted isophotes and/or asymmetries), compared to only 29% for larger separations. The disturbed fraction for close pairs is consistent with that seen in strong lensing studies of the Cosmic Microwave Background, and suggests that the disturbance signal is not induced by the tidal forces experienced in recent mergers. Based on these results, we present a revised merger history for the Universe, finding a substantial increase in the merger rate at the redshift. We suggest that this high merger rate, and the accompanying perturbations of the dark matter potential, may help to explain the spatial distribution of galaxies in larger clusters in cosmological N-body simulations.

Simulations of the large-scale structure of the universe require significant computational resources, which have led to an explosion of studies in the last decade. Although recent efforts have employed sophisticated techniques to increase the dynamical range and precision of these simulations, they have been performed in periodic boxes with idealized cosmological initial conditions. Here, we present the first large cosmological simulation that follows the growth of both black holes and galaxies self-consistently from the early universe to the present day. Our simulation volume comprises a billion co-moving cubic megaparsecs and is comparable in size to the Millennium simulation used to model the growth of supermassive black holes in the local universe. The simulation accurately models the growth of structure, quasars and galaxies, and employs a novel technique for including black hole growth, interaction, and feedback in a fully cosmological context. We find that, at high-redshifts, supermassive black holes reside in all major galaxy mass halos, but only grow to a fraction of a billion solar masses by $z=0$. In contrast, at low redshifts, galaxies in the simulation possess a broad spectrum of black hole masses, with nearly half growing to a quarter of a billion solar masses by $z=0$. We present results comparing our simulation to observations of quasars, galaxies, and black hole-galaxy scaling relations and find excellent agreement. These results confirm that supermassive black holes and their hosts grow in a coordinated fashion, with feedback processes regulating black hole growth and the formation of large-scale galaxies.

Planets are known to occur throughout the universe, from parsec-scale disks around young stars to larger gas and ice giants in our solarsystem. Recently, the discovery of worlds within other stars’ orbits has raised questions about whether these planets could have migrated in from more distant orbits, and whether these planets were in fact born in the hot gaseous outer regions of these same stars. The retention of metals such as calcium, scandium, and titanium –produced in nature’s biggest known explosion, a Type 1a supernova– on these close-in planets provides a powerful evidence that these planets may have formed within the calcium-rich outer layer of their host stars’ protoplanetary disks. The calcium, scandium, and titanium can be clearly identified in the planet’s host star’s spectrum using high-dispersion spectroscopy due to the extreme scattering signature of these elements in the surrounding material. The presence of these elements in the planet’s host star’s spectrum then strongly implies that these planets formed from gas that was enriched in at least these three elements by their host stars’ Type 1a supernova. Additional analyses of other metal species should similarly reveal the supernova signatures present in these planets’ host stars. This provides strong evidence for their formation via core accretion, rather than gravitational instabilities, and suggests that these planets possess atmospheric compositions that differ from both “dry” Earth-like planets and “wet” water worlds. If future observations confirm the identified supernova signatures are indeed unique to calcium, scandium, and titanium, this would represent the most compelling evidence to date for the existence of extraterrestrial life and thus warrants a thorough study of these planets’ chemical compositions.

The recent detection of gravitational waves and the associated Nobel Prize awarded to the LIGO Scientific Collaboration was a landmark achievement. The detection of gravitational waves heralded a new era of observational astronomy, and heralds the discovery of numerous unknown phenomena in the universe. Over the past two decades, a large number of scientific groups have been involved in the development and operation of gravitational wave detectors. One of the main drawbacks in past searches for gravitational waves was the lack of sensitivity in theDetectors. The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) comprised of two Michelson interferometers formed in Livingston, Louisiana and Hanford, Washington and operated between 2007 and 2018. A major factor in the design of these detectors was thechoice of suspensions, which consist of long, unsupported wires, and their subsequentaranas. The LIGO Detectors wereat the limits of sensitivity for comparable massBlack Hole Binaries (MBHB). A newtemplate family was developed to improve the design and alleviate technicalissues arising from environmentalfactors, such as seismic noise and wind gusts. This led to the construction of Enhanced LIGO, which since 2018 has been operationallyCompleting the first direct observation of gravitational waves and the first observation of neutron stars merger. This article details the development of the new template family and discusses the improvements in the sensitivities of both the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) and Enhanced LIGO. The new templates were developed forcomparable massBlack Hole Binaries and heralded a new era of observational gravitational-wave astronomy.

[PEAT] provides fast, reliable and reproducible image manipulation and reconstruction in electron microscopes. This video shows the main techniques used in this technology and their applications in the biological field. [PEAT] is an image manipulation and reconstruction technique developed for electron microscopes. It provides fast and reliable image manipulation and reconstruction. This technology was developed with help from the French National Research Agency (ANR), the European Union's Framework 7 Program, and the Institute of Molecular Biology in Frankfurt (IMBF). PEAT was initially developed to help scientists study the molecular structure of crystals and see how their components fit together. Today, it is used in a variety of scientific fields, including materials research, biology, and structural biology. In materials research, PEAT can be used to rapidly screen thousands of possible chemical compounds for use in developing new materials for healthcare, energy storage, and other applications. In biology, PEAT can be used to quickly generate three-dimensional molecular models of new viruses in tissue samples. This allows scientists to understand how the virus infects cells and infects other organisms. In structural biology, PEAT can be used to solve the three-dimensional structure of large molecules, such as those found in the cells of the human body. It can also be used to determine how protein molecules work in the human body. Because PEAT uses direct electron imaging to analyze images rather than relying on iterative techniques such as image reconstruction, it is much faster than other electron microscopy methods. It is also more precise and reproducible. This video shows the main techniques used in this technology and their applications in the biological field.

Francium (Fr), radon (Ra), noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, and Xe) and halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, and I) are isoelectronic sequences. Here we present the structure calculations to predict the electron affinity (EA), excitation energies (EX), excitation spectra, polarizabilities (PA), and lifetime (τ) of the Fr+ isoelectronic sequence. We predict EA = 4.15 (4) eV and EX = 0.73 (15) eV for the anion of FrH-. The 0_00-1_00 predicted ionization potential (IP) of Fr+ is located at IP = 9.23 (3) eV. The 0_11-1_11 IP is 7.44 (3) eV. The predicted 0_00-1_00 IP-IP separation of 1.33 (9) eV is in excellent agreement with experiment. The polarizability of Fr+ is located at 155 (16) Å3, in excellent agreement with the experimental measurement of 160 (15) Å3. The predicted 0_00-1_00 τ of Fr+ is 1.48 (16) ps. This is in good agreement with the experimentally measured 1.59 (2) ps.

Distillable entanglement is a key feature of quantum many-body systems, with potential applications in quantum mechanics and information science. It describes a situation where two or more parties can distillably extract pure Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) pairs, starting from some less-entanglement meta-data and using local operations and shared randomness. So far, all distillable entanglement (DE) examples have been found in spin systems or free quantum fields. In this work, we present a universal method to distillably extract pure EPR pairs with any target DE amount. For any integer value above zero, we construct small lattices of interacting spin-1/2 or harmonic-oscillator systems, each capable of distillably generating that amount of pure DE. The existence of pure DE is shown analytically via low-entropy ground states of extended Hamiltonians. The amount of pure DE scales with system size in the large-system limit, and is bounded from above by the entanglement entropy of the subsystems. These results imply that a generic (perhaps random) quantum many-body system has no pure DE state, and that pure DE states are highly nonlocal and efficiently simulate classical mixtures of them. We provide an example in the spin 1/2 XXZ chain with exactly half of the system 's entanglement law intact. This model has previously been shown to have a pure DE state on a total of four contiguous spins (total area 2), but this is the first example with area 2.3% of the chain.

A neutron star (NS) is a celestial body composed almost entirely of the atomic nucleus of a collapsed star. A neutron star typically has a surface gravity of around 9.8 m/s² (comparable to that of a 22-story building) and a diameter of about 12 km (7 miles). The low density of a neutron star vs. a normal solid is a consequence of the very high density of its matter, with most of a neutron star's 10^{15} kg-strong mass being concentrated in just a few kilograms of material at the surface. As a result, even a small impact would be sufficient to cause dramatic damage. Neutron stars are born from nearby portions of space known as pulsars, as a result of the gravitational collapse of a neutron star at the end of its life. Once formed, the resulting mass can be estimated as two solar masses (the mass of the sun). Neutron stars are thought to be purely mechanical objects, with no active process occurring on their surface. The existence of pulsars was confirmed in 1967, when}] PSR B1919+21 was the first observed radio pulsar. This name has been assigned to more than 3,200 pulsars and other radio sources, as of June 2018. Neutron stars are among the most massive objects in the universe; the least-massive neutron stars have a maximum observable mass of approximately two solar masses. They are also some of the most dense objects in the universe, with a theoretical minimum central density of approximately 10 × 10^{17} kg/m³. Neutron stars are generally tidally locked to their companion stars, with one hemisphere permanently faced towards the companion. The companion's surface can be heated to several tens of degrees Celsius by the neutron star's rotational energy (as it slows the star's rotation with its gravitational force). Depending on the rotation rate and magnetic field, the heated surface may emit X-rays or visible light as a result of radiative levitation. Neutron stars spin incredibly fast. In this paper we review the general formalism and apply it to charged-pion photoproduction reactions at energies above the two-pion threshold, i.e. at invariant energies greater than 2 GeV. First, we present a spin-averaged amplitude, based on a Lagrangian that includes nucleons, resonances, and hyperons as explicit degrees of freedom. The excitation spectrum of the latter is consistent with the most recent experimental findings. To this we add a phenomenological Lagrangian that accounts for the known tensor-force component in the $t$-channel exchanges. Next, using the principle of maximum optical rigidity, we analyze the couplings of the resonances to the known states. We consider not only the well-established excited states, but also many resonances that have been proposed in the recent literature. We show that the large-$N_c$ approximation is violated for the exchange of the Roper and theDelta resonances. We perform a systematic study of the resonance parameters and their interference with the amplitude contributions, in order to reproduce the existing photoproduction data above 2 GeV. The results for the amplitudes are provided as computer code.

The acceleration of the universe is still unknown. One of the most popular explanations is the dark energy, described either by a cosmological constant or by a dynamical form (quintessence). A lot of people think that it is not possible to discriminate between these two scenarios with present data. We show that it is possible to make this discrimination if we have enough information about the evolution of the universe. We consider only linear cosmological perturbations and we focus on the case of a constant equation of state, W=0. We show that it is possible to discriminate between these two scenarios if W is constant with a high accuracy for a period larger than 50% of the age of the universe. If the equation of state is not constant, it is not possible to discriminate between these two scenarios. If the equation of state is constant but its accuracy is not very high, it is not possible to discriminate between these two scenarios. If the equation of state is constant but it is not constant enough, it is not possible to discriminate between these two scenarios. If the equation of state is constant but its accuracy varies a lot, it is possible to discriminate between these two scenarios, but only if the values of W are close to -1. We conclude that it is possible to discriminate between a cosmological constant and quintessence if the equation of state is constant and very different from -1. This result does not prove that the dark energy is a cosmological constant or quintessence, but it gives some constraints on these two scenarios. In general, it is not possible to discriminate between two possible dark energy scenarios if their behaviour is very similar. However, if we assume the equation of state of dark energy is constant, it is still possible to discriminate between a cosmological constant and quintessence. This discrimination can be done with current data, but we need to assume that the equation of state is constant. It would be interesting to check this with more precise data in the future, in order to understand whether this assumption is really needed or not. This research was done with Pierre Fleury, Cyril Brouder and Romain Teyssier. Astronomy and Astrophysics, article title, authors, abstract submitted to arXiv.org, date published, volume, issue, journal name, page numbers AM CVn stars are semidegenerate main sequence stars with very low masses in the range 0.8 to 1.4 M⊙ 2 and exhibit extreme radial velocity variations on time scales of hours. The compactness of these stars together with the very low masses make AM CVn stars excellent test beds for General Relativity and for theories of gravity, including dynamical general relativity. In this work, I present HST/FGS parallaxes for 12 AM CVn binaries, which represent an improvement of a factor of four in precision over the previous best HST parallax measurements. These measurements, in turn, represent the best ground-based measure of the Gravitational Red Shift due to the compactness of these stars and are the most precise test of Einstein’s General Relativity to date. Additionally, these parallaxes provide the best measurement of theabsolute luminosity of these stars to date and yield lower limits on their distance of 0.5 to 0.5 parsecs, the latter depending on the reliability of the model assumptions. These results have important astrophysical implications such as the lower bounds on the compactness ofneutron stars and the mass and radius of magnetars.

The origin of the molecular emission around the southern hemisphere Re 4 IRS - HH 188 region was studied using data from the ATCA and the SEST. Emission from molecular lines such as CS, HCN, HCO+, H21, and CH3OH was found to be associated with the shock excited by IRS 4B, and possibly IRS 4A, interacting with an inclined disk of gas and dust. The observed HCN J=3-2 and HCO+ J=3-2 spectra are characteristic of hot-core chemistry, whereas the weak CH3OH line suggests a more minor influence of thermal processing. The observed spatial distributions and velocity structures suggest that the observed emission originates from an hourglass-shaped shocked envelope with a close-to-centroid orientation, a bow-shock cavity walls and a wide redshifted component possibly arising from an externally triggered jet.
