We introduce a generic approach to implement recursive query evaluation in database and logic processing systems. The core idea is to split the evaluation into two phases: (1) a recursive query translation that produces a parametrized query that is optimized for specific evaluation context (including limiting the complexity of the query evaluation via pre-processing); (2) an evaluation phase that evaluates the parametrized query in the specific context. We demonstrate the approach with a recursive query translation in https://github.com/alyssaxo/poly API for translating recursive queries to SQL and PLS systems and for evaluating the translated queries in native DB and PLS systems respectively. We conduct experiments on two real-life dataset queries with increasing complexity in terms of depth and size. The experimental results show that the evaluation phase costs are acceptable (O(depth)) and the translation phase offers almost linear runtime improvement over brute-force method (implementing the same parametrization in native SQL/PLP).

This paper estimates the power spectrum of cosmic shear, the density distortion caused by the distorsion of the gravity field of distant galaxies by the distribution of dark matter, dark energy and baryons in the universe. We use extensive simulated convergence power , including the full distance between bins, to fit a model to the data from cluster counts and cosmic shear. The resulting constraints on the dark energy equation of state parameter, Omega_<unk> de0<unk>, are relatively small, due to the choice of data set or modeling of the covariance, but the covariance remains a significant source of uncertainty. Marginalizing over this covariance, we find the 95% confidence interval w=-1.31+/-0.19 (w=-1.04+/-0.19) for a flat -field universe with the ratio of the energy densities of dark energy and matter, Omega_{de0}, constrained, and we measure the curvature b_{space}=-0.72+/-0.16 (b_{space}=-0.53+/-0.16). We estimate the constraining power of future surveys and find that combining cosmic shear with cluster counts will lead to a tight constraint on w (with the 95% confidence interval w=-1.00+/-0.06), while adding shear information to existing cluster surveys will only weakly improve the constraint on w (with the 95% confidence interval w=-1.15+/-0.10).

A fundamental limit on the precision with which one can measure a quantum system in terms of its coupling to an external environment is articulated. Based on recent results on quantum estimation with a canonical example of an NMR quantum computer, this fundamental limit is identified in terms of the bath “inverse temperature” (or “decoherence”) and the spectral density of the bath. It is found that under standard error correction conditions the ultimate limit on precision scales inversely with the square root of the number of probes used to measure the system (i.e. as the “sample size”). The “sample size” limit is then contrasted with the “volume” or “time” limits familiar from classical statistical mechanics. It is argued that the power of quantum computation can be fully exploited only by optimizing the use of all three of these resources. In this work, we present a method to compute Yukawa potentials in a system with partial periodic boundary conditions. The method is based on an Ewald summation technique for the long-range interactions, combined with a Singular Integral Operators (SIO) technique for the short-range interactions. The method is demonstrated by means of two applications. In the first application, we consider the convergence of the three-dimensional Ewald summation for Yukawa interactions in a system with one-sided (z-periodic) boundaries. We perform numerical tests to assess the accuracy of the method, and we show the consistency and stability of the algorithm as the system size is increased. In the second application, we consider the two-dimensional Ewald summation for Yukawa interactions in a system with two-sided boundaries. We apply the method to obtain thermodynamic properties of a two-dimensional Yukawa interaction, such as the critical temperature, the internal energy and the specific heat. The results for the critical temperature are compared with available theoretical and numerical results, and a satisfactory agreement is found. The agreement is further improved by using the SIO method to accelerate the convergence of the Ewald summation for the long-range interactions.

In network science, the growth model describes how new nodes connect to existing networks. Most of the previous works focus on a single growing pattern. However, the choice of attachment s greatly affects the global evolution of networks. In this paper, we propose to study network evolution in an optimal choice space, where all possible patterns of new node attachments are considered. We find a phase transition at a critical choice space dimension, below which the resulting network is small-world and above which it is a big-bang percolation. We validate our model with static and growing real-world networks and find that most of them are fragile against reducing the choice space dimension, which means they are difficult to be preserved. Only a handful of networks, such as the Internet and the transcriptional regulatory networks, are robust against such randomizations, suggesting that they can grow in an optimal choice space. In addition, the model predicts some general rules for network growth. For example, networks are more likely to be robust if they have multiple choice patterns.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a popular algorithm for solving sequential decision-making problems. In most real-world scenarios, the amount of data required to train deep neural networks for such problems is very large. Unfortunately, collecting such large amounts of data is often impractical or impossible. Genetic algorithms (GAs) have the potential to scale well to such large problems, and to provide an effective global search approach. In this paper, we present an application of GAs to the scalable RL problem of collecting experiences from multiple simulated environments to train a deep neural network policy in the real world. We find that GAs are effective at solving this problem, and show that in some cases it is better to train multiple policies rather than using a single policy for the entire world. We also consider an alternative policy optimisation approach based on differential evolution, and show that it is generally not effective on this problem. Genetic algorithms have the potential to scale well to large problems and provide an effective search approach. We apply this approach to training a deep neural network policy using collected experience from multiple simulated environments. The policy is trained on one environment, and then tested in another. We find that in some cases it is better to train multiple policies than use a single policy for the entire world. We combine the genetic algorithm approach with a global optimisation approach based on differential evolution. We collect experience using a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach. Each agent trains a deep neural network in a simulated environment, and then queries the value function model of an opponent agent. This allows the agent to learn from the experiences of others, but without any communication or synchronisation. This multi-agent reinforcement learning approach can scale to large numbers of agents, each with relatively slow communication channels. We find that genetic algorithms are effective at solving this multi-agent reinforcement learning problem, and in some cases outperform a baseline approach based on training a single policy globally. While single-agent reinforcement learning is a very well-studied problem, multi-agent reinforcement learning is much less explored. This paper presents one approach to multi-agent reinforcement learning using genetic algorithms. The approach is tested on a multi-agent collect-experience-using-differential-evolution problem, but it can be applied more generally. We also consider the special case of a single global environment, which is not efficiently learnable by conventional methods. We show that using a committee of independent genetic algorithm agents can achieve better performance than using a single genetic algorithm agent on this problem. By combining genetic algorithm scalability with a decentralised multi-agent approach, this paper presents an approach to multi-agent reinforcement learning using genetic algorithms. The approach is tested on a multi-agent collect-experience-using-differential-evolution problem, but it can be applied more generally. We also consider the special case of a single global environment, which is not efficiently learnable by conventional methods.

We consider the motion of a viscous incompressible fluid in an open bounded domain Ω of $\mathbb R^d$, $d=2,3$, with respect to an external forces field $f$ and with temperature-dependent kinematic viscosity coefficient $\nu(u)=2\mu+\mu_s\big(\frac{1}{2}|Du|\big)^{s-1}$, and $\mu,\mu_s>0$, $s\in(1,2]$. In particular, we show that the corresponding renormalized Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation (R-HJB) admits a unique solution uniformly bounded in $L^\infty(\bar{\Omega} \times (0,T))$ and that this solution converges in the sense of G-convergence to the unique viscosity solution of the homogenized equation. Furthermore, we introduce a notion of generalized solution for the original problem, the so-called $\alpha$-limit solution, for any $0<\alpha<1$ and prove that it also converges to the unique viscosity solution of the homogenized equation in the same space of functions. We also discuss various critical problems and extend our results to the cases $s\in(0,1]$ and $d=2$ and $s\in(2,\infty)$ and $d=3$.

Is the Bardeen-Petterson effect responsible for the warping and precession in NGC 4258? This paper reports an analysis of archival Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) data that was originally presented in 2012, which shows that while the general orientation of the black hole and its accretion disk are inconsistent with the Bardeen-Petterson effect, the equatorial rotation curve of the gas and stars is not inconsistent with this phenomenon. This, combined with the fact that simulations of the BPE cannot reproduce all of the features of the gas and stars in the stellar rotation curves, casts doubt on whether the BPE is the sole responsible mechanism for the warping and precession in this galaxy. The Bardeen-Petterson effect (BPE) is a theoretical phenomenon which posits that a rotating black hole can cause gases and stars on either side of an accretion disk to undergo precession due to frame-dragging. Over the past several decades, observations of nearby galaxies have provided evidence that some of these galaxies do, in fact, possess supermassive black holes in their orbits. In some of these galaxies, gas and stars near the central black hole are observed to be in orbit about that hole, exhibiting the effect of gravitational warping. This phenomenon has been shown to be consistent with the predictions of the BPE. In 2012, observations of the nearby galaxy NGC 4258 were used to show that the BPE cannot be the only responsible mechanism for the observed warping and precession. Instead, it was suggested that other, independent forces (most likely a combination of both the BPE and non-BPE effects) are responsible for the warping and precession observed in this galaxy. Subsequent observations of this galaxy in 2019 showed that the black hole and its accretion disk had rotated into a position where the observed features of the BPE were consistent with the observations. It was concluded that while the BPE may not be the only responsible mechanism for the warping and precession in this galaxy, it is a likely contributor. In this paper, we analyze archival VLBA data from 2012 to show that the BPE cannot be the only responsible mechanism for the warping and precession observed in NGC 4258. We find that the orientation of the black hole and its accretion disk in this galaxy are inconsistent with the BPE, but that the equatorial rotation curve of the gas and stars is not inconsistent with this phenomenon. Combined, these results cast doubt on whether the BPE is the sole responsible mechanism for the warping and precession in this galaxy. The black hole at the center of NGC 4258, observed in 2019, is seen here at a position consistent with previous observations. However, the observed features of the Bardeen-Petterson effect are not consistent with the current orientation of the black hole and accretion disk. Overall, the results of this paper cast doubt on whether the Bardeen-Petterson effect is the sole responsible mechanism for the warping

A strong correlation between the intensity ratio of the maser lines at 43 and 86 GHz and the Infrared (IR) colors obtained from WISE satellite data is reported for the first time. The color analysis is carried out on a 60-day moving average . The color analysis reflects the variations in the degree of flux contribution by thermal emissions from the surrounding regions. The IR colors are found to have higher absolute values when the line ratio is low, and lower absolute values when the line ratio is high. These variations are found to be highly correlated (r=0.91). The data presented in this study suggest a possible link between the infrared and the physical conditions of the gas and the characteristics for the maser emission. The reported results provide an independent confirmation of the existence of a relation between the physical conditions of the gas and the characteristics of the mid-infrared spectrum (i.e., the Infrared Colors). The reported correlation was found for the first time for SiO maser lines. Since the mid-infrared radiation from the regions is dominated by thermal emissions from the warm dust, the results presented here can be taken as further evidence for the existence of a causal link between the physical conditions of the gas and the characteristics of the mid-infrared spectrum. A mixture of two competitive random number generators (RRGs) is used to produce large amounts of pseudo-random binary sequences with arbitrary period. A recently introduced variable, the probability filling factor (PFF), is used to quantify the statistical spread of these generated sequences. The PFF can be interpreted as a particularly fast indicator for assessing if a binary sequence contains a substantial amount of zeroes. This makes it well suited for identifying rare events in large amounts of data. In this work, the PFF is used to characterize the statistical properties of the so-called rare event sequences, i.e. the generated binary sequences with a particularly low number of zeroes. These rare event sequences occur, e.g., in cryptography, if a random key is used for encrypting a long message, where a repetition of zeroes in the key could lead to a termination of the encryption algorithm. It is shown that the generated PFF fluctuations follow a zero-range process with a power-law tail in the middle of the fluctuations. This corresponds to a strong spatial heterogeneity of the low-zero sequences and to a growth mechanism of these sequences from a few deterministically produced seeds. For certain mixtures, it is found that rare event sequences happen with a high frequency, which makes them of interest for cryptography. The manuscript is a prequel of a paper about the same topic, which has been published in the Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10955-018-1998-x).

In the last decade, the detection of the gamma radiation from the Galactic and extragalactic sources provided an opportunity to study the nature and characteristics of these sources. Based on the data from the Fermi and Planck satellites, it was found that the total energy of the gamma radiation emitted by the galaxies and contained in a sphere of 20 billion light-years radius is equal to 0.25 eV. The value of the energy density of this radiation is comparable with the density of light in this volume. The estimates of the density of the gamma radiation in the near space (at distances less than 20 billion light-years from Earth) with similar accuracy were obtained only in 1965-1970. The most precise of these estimates, based on the measurements of gamma rays from the radioactive sources (the unique method with such accuracy) was made by Robert Dicke and his collaborators in Princeton. Their results, confirmed later, show that the density of the near-space gamma radiation is equal to 0.09 mW/m2. By comparing this value with the energy density of the gamma radiation contained in the same volume we can conclude that the latter exceeds the former by several orders of magnitude. The latter result can be attributed to the emission of a large number of gammas rays by the interaction of the particles of the cosmic radiation with the matter. Thus, the results of the most precise measurements of the gamma radiation density in the near space confirmed the previous estimates and showed that the energy density of the particles of the cosmic radiation in this volume substantially exceeds the density of the electromagnetic radiation. The estimates of the total energy density of the particles of the cosmic radiation in the space of the size of the universe obtained from various sources are comparable. The most reliable information about the total energy of these particles at present day was obtained from the measurement of the energy of the particles of the lightest supersymmetric particle, the neutralino, by the CMS and ATLAS collaborations of the LHC. The masses of these particles are equal to approximately 200 GeV. The result of the CMS collaboration showing that the sum of the energies of all supersymmetric particles is equal to 22.2 +/- 0.9 + p g , where the sum is done over all supersymmetric particles and the error is stat. + syst., can be converted to the energy density of the particles of the cosmic radiation in the space of the size of the universe with the aid of the formula energy density = mass density *Speed of light cubed. The obtained result, equal to 0.1 GeV/cm3, corresponds to the energy density of the particles of the cosmic radiation many times greater than the energy density of the electromagnetic radiation. Therefore, the obtained result indicates the existence of an unknown type of interaction which greatly increases the energy of the particles of the cosmic radiation in a small volume compared with the energy of the electromagnetic radiation. Sandstone is one of the most important rock types in world with many significant economical and cultural implications. One of such implications is that of building and structure. Sandstone is used in the construction of several architectural structures such as bridges, buildings, and skyscrapers. Fontainebleau sandstone, which is one of the most well-known types of sandstone, is used in the construction of the exterior walls and staircases of the great Miami Penitentiary. Despite its significance in the construction industry, not much research has been carried out on Fontainebleau sandstone. This can largely be attributed to the complex hierarchical fracture network of the sandstone which makes it hard to study. This paper studies the fracture patterns of fractured Fontainebleau sandstone using optical microscopy and statistical analysis. The results show that the fracture pattern of the fractured sandstone follows Weibull statistics. Moreover, it was also shown that the failed surfaces are not smooth and possess non-Gaussian statistics which might have significant implications on the mechanics of fracture d Fontainebleau sandstone.

Recently, researchers have developed a class of computational games known as evolutionary games, in which a population of computer agents playing different strategies interact via direct competition for resources or cooperative behavior. One such game is the Ultimatum Game (UG), in which one agent, the Proposer, anonymously proposes a split of a monetary payment to another agent, the Receiver. If the Receiver accepts the proposal, then the split is realized; if not, the Proposer must either accept a suboptimal split or submit nothing. The motivation for the UG has traditionally been rooted in studies of Economics, specifically distributions of economic behavior. Using an evolutionary computation, the current work analyzes the long-term behaviors in the UG from the perspective of critical behavior. In particular, two Proposers' strategies which enforce either equal or proportional splits, respectively, will dominate the UG over the long term under most parameter regimes. More surprisingly, however, the long-term behavior of the population is shown to be dependent upon Proposers' initial strategies, whereby those Proposers adopting more or less the same strategy as the Receiver's initial proposals quickly go extinct. Ultimately, the current work identifies a bifurcation in the long-term behavior of the UG whereby Proposers exhibit either continuous or continuous changes in strategy with respect to the accepted split. The result is unique from the traditional notions of Economics, wherein agents typically adopt a fixed strategy and only respond to local Nash equilibria. The current work concludes by discussing these findings' applicability in the real world, limitations of the current approach, and avenues for future research.

In the past decade, many new modes of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) amplitude have been observed, most notably $B \to \pi \pi$, $B_s \to K \pi$, and $B \to K \rho$. Although $B \to \pi <unk>pi$ and $B_s \to K \pi$ can be easily accommodated in the standard model (SM) with tree contributions, the magnitude of the decay rates for these modes as well as $B \to K \rho$ require new tree or Penguin-Custodial- Symmetry breaking (Penguin-CSB) models to reach an acceptable level. In this Letter, we study the charmless strange $B^+ \to VP$ decays, where V (V = $ \rho^0, \omega, \phi$) and P denote a light vector or pseudoscalar meson, respectively. We present an updated analysis of these modes, based on both theory predictions and measurements of various model-independent parameters, such as $A_{\perp}$ and $B_s <unk> to K <unk>rho$, which can be used to suppress the huge dominant contributions from charming penguin and electroweak penguin amplitudes. We also make a preliminary study of the direct CP violation in these modes, and find that the large branching fractions and the large direct CP violations may be signals of new physics.

In the recent past, precise measurements of CP-violation parameters in the kaon system, namely the CP-violating phase in the mixing parameter $<unk>Mu$ and the direct CP-violation parameter $\Delta $, have improved our understanding of the weak scale. These parameters are well described by the Standard Model (SM) prediction with a large contribution from the flavour sector. This indicates the presence of new sources of CP-violation (CPV) beyond the SM. In this paper we investigate the supersymmetric (SUSY) parameter space of the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) in light of these new constraints. We identify several benchmark scenarios with different hypotheses on the origin of CPV, which will be tested at future collider s and low-energy experiments. We find the SUSY parameter space of the MSSM to be highly constrained, in particular for large values of the higgsino mass parameter $\mu$. Moreover, we study the impact of recent LHCb measurements on the MSSM parameter space. We show that the global fit of the SUSY spectra provides a good fit to the data under all hypotheses and that the imposition of constraints on the mass parameter $<unk>mu$ in the case of the Higgs boson, flavour physics and Electroweak precision observables tends to significantly reduce the SUSY parameter space. In this region, the CPV is dominated by phases in the sgn(mu) parameter and the corresponding complex trilinear coupling A_t, suggesting a promising avenue for experimental detection at future hadron colliders and direct detection of CPV.

In this paper, we present a construction of free fermions for supergroup WZNW models using a free fermion resolution of supergroups, along with a spectral flow that relates models with general supergroups to supergroup levels. We give a free field model of the WZNW model based on the free fermion resolution. We compute correlation functions using the operator product expansion, and show that they agree with the known results in the case of the supergroup $GL(1|1)$ and the superconformal model with central charge c=6. In particular, we confirm the correctness of the recently proposed four-point functions with general symmetry and global consistency conditions. We also discuss how to apply the method to construct free fermions for the supergroup WZNW models with other supergroups and show that the models with general supergroups can be obtained as WZNW models based on free fermions. In this paper, we propose a quantum repeater architecture capable of supporting long-distance, fault-tolerant quantum communication over broadband metropolitan networks. To accomplish this, we introduce a novel technique for combining long-distance entanglement and quantum fast forwards to scale computation. Our system design is optimized for several key metrics: entanglement generation rate, consumable resources, memory usage, and pair production . The entanglement is generated between lightmatter qubits in a quantum frequency quadpter, and a local computation of the quantum entanglement is accomplished in parallel on a cluster of nearby quantum computers, and a quantum signal reconstruction of the entanglement is completed at a metropolitan node. Through numerical simulation, we show that this system can achieve high-rates of entanglement generation and consume a small number of quantum photons and matter qubits. Introduction Quantum repeaters use quantum entanglement to enable distributed quantum communication over long distances. Entanglement is a quantum property that permits two or more particles to have correlated properties, even when separated by a large distance. Quantum repeaters use entangled quantum signals to distribute entanglement over long distances. Because of the exponential decay rate of entanglement with distance, long-distance quantum communication requires repeaters that extend the entanglement over long distance. Previous approaches to quantum repeaters use individual systems, each optimized for a specific range of distances. Systems optimized for short distances, such as quantum key distribution (QKD) systems, achieve high rates of entanglement generation through detection of either quantum side-channels or modification of qubits in transmission. These systems optimized for long distances, such as quantum memories, achieve high rates of entanglement generation through purification of largelyentangled quantum systems. Both systems require local adaptation of the transmission process, which limits the distances over which entanglement can be distributed. In this paper, we present a quantum repeater architecture that combines features from these approaches to optimize quantum repeater systems for short and long distances. The design is intended to support long-distance entanglement distribution over broadband metropolitan networks. It makes use of parallelization to scale the computation, low overhead from entanglement generation to quantum memory usage, and low-dimensional entanglement between light and matter qubits to achieve high rates of entanglement generation at low quantum resource consumption. Entanglement generation is facilitated by using light-matter entanglement, in which matter qubits interact with light in quantum frequency quadpters (QFQs). The QFQs are fully integrated on-chip networks that provide multi-user connectivity and may be instantiated using silicon photonics. These networks support entanglement distribution over long distances by enabling parallelization of purification protocols. However, the purification rates in previous approaches were limited by the need to localize the entanglement generation to the quantum purification registers. In this design, we propose a metropolitan node that combines long-distance entanglement distribution with fast forwards, a form of quantum communication that allow a quantum signal to be reconstructed despite loss. A project to build an optical/near-infrared telescope on the top of a highland in the Chilean Andes,named the Cornell Caltech Atacama Telescope (CCATA), has been proposed and is in progress. The telescope will have a large mirror with a diameter of 10.4 meters, which is much larger than any existing optical telescope. The CCATA will be able to conduct advanced optical and near infrared astronomy, such as observing exoplanets, studying the emission from circumstellar disks, and searching for nearby Earth-like planets around other stars. The telescope will be built by a joint team of researchers from Cornell University and Caltech, in collaboration with both local and international scientists and students. This will allow the Telescope to be operated in a sustainable and internationally diverse way, giving cutting-edge astronomical research while also fostering innovation in education, outreach and science technology. The Cornell Caltech Atacama Telescope (CCATA) will advance astronomy by several significant advancements. First, by building the largest optical/near-infrared telescope, the CCATA will enable the exploration of far ultraviolet and low-mass star habitable planets in the spectrum of the Earth. The CCATA will also advance studies of the circumstellar disk, the ring-shaped region of swirling dust around a young star, by enabling detailed study of the dimming of these regions as they block the light of the central star. Additionally, the CCATA will detect signs of life by searching for nearby Earth-like planets, and also will identify non-native cloud cover and analyze gases in Earth’s atmosphere for Mars analog landing sites. The telescope will allow studying many key topics in planetary astronomy, while also enabling education, outreach and enhancing science technology. The CCATA, a joint project between Cornell University and Caltech, will be an advance and transformative tool for planetary astronomy, enabling the detection and characterization of life on other worlds. A epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) medium with perfectly conducting boundaries has been introduced for the first time to our knowledge to greatly enhance the fields and decrease the dissipated energy within the material for field confinement in narrow channels and tight bends. Unlike other approaches, squeeze energy from the field to increase the voltage and current within the ENZ medium, greatly reducing the total power loss. The enhancement of the magnetic field is sufficient to trap over 90% of the incident energy. We demonstrate through simulations and experiments that the proposed device can greatly enhance the electric and magnetic fields within the material while greatly reducing the dissipated power. The ENZ mediums can be used to significantly increase the voltage and current, as well as confine energy, from the electric and magnetic field of an incident wave, enabling the conversion of wave energy to electricity with significant power savings over other methods. The conversion of wave energy to electricity has great potential to reduce the negative impact of wave action on coastal habitats and land areas impacted by current generation and other energy production mechanisms. It can also reduce the strain on the electricity grid from fluctuating power generation. However, current wave energy technologies suffer from high cost, low energy density, and inefficiencies from transferring wave action to electrical current. The proposed approach combines the high efficiency of near-zero-epsilon dielectric wave energy converters with the magnetic field enhancement capability of epsilon-near-zero materials1 to greatly improve wave to electricity conversion efficiency. We show through simulations and experiments that a wave energy converter with perfectly conducting boundaries can enhance the trapped energy level to above 90% for both linear and sinusoidal edge wave incident energy, as shown in Fig. 1a and 1b. Additionally, it is shown that the energy increase is linearly dependent on the field intensity in the epsilon-near-zero medium, as shown in Fig. 1c. The field within the ENZ medium is enhanced by decreasing the real part of the permittivity, leading to greater field localization. The imaginary part of the permittivity is decreased to near zero to minimize the power lost due to dielectric losses. To ensure the breakdown strength is not compromised, the loss tangent, 1.0, is maintained. This highly conductive medium allows almost all of the incident energy to pass through the material, as shown in Fig. 1d. This wave-to-electricity conversion approach can enable significantly lower cost devices and systems for capturing wave energy and transferring it to electricity.

High-energy cosmic rays (HECRs) offer a unique window into the highest energy processes in the universe. Most of the HECRs have been observed to reach the Earth's atmosphere without interaction with cosmic magnetic background (CMB) photons. The HECRs beyond the GZK cut-off energy are believed to be highly energetic gamma-ray bursts from neutrinos and neutrinos. These observations pose a challenge to theoretical physicists to understand the origin and transport in the galaxy of these energetic particles. In this paper, I discuss computational methods that I have developed to simulate the propagation of HECRs in the galaxy. These simulations numerically propagate the trajectories of large numbers of CRs in three-dimensional magnetic fields derived from a model of the galaxy. These simulations solve the transport equation including anisotropic diffusions, drifts, and energization by a randomly oriented magnetic field. The computational tools I have developed include efficient algorithms to integrate particle trajectories, a fixed three-dimensional grid to represent the galaxy, a fast algorithm for solving the magnetic field line equations, and a flexible algorithms for tracing individual particles. The trajectories of 1 billion protons have been simulated, including an estimate of the noise generated by the limited simulation time. The CR arrival directions from these simulations match well with the positions of prominent structures in the galaxy including the galactic plane, the bulge, and the disk. These features are generated by the magnetic field lines and their intersections. The fraction of protons reaching the Earth's atmosphere with their incoming directions within 20 degrees of the Supergalactic plane is about 1%. The galactic magnetic field model is very important in determining the trajectory of the HECRs in the simulation. This allows the propagation of the uncertainties in the model into the calculated HECR arrival directions.

The Burst Monitor (BM) on the Gamma-Ray Large Area Space Telescope (GLAST) is one of the main instruments for rapid detection and localization of gamma-ray bursts. During the operations of GLAST, several theoretical studies suggested that the number of gamma-ray bursts can be slightly overestimated by the BM, due to the interaction of electrons with the liquid Xenon (LXe) detector. In this work we perform a detailed analysis of this effect, and present new calibration constants, which can be used to correctly analyze the data from GLAST. The work is performed in the framework of the GLAST mission and the sensitivity of the instrument is not affected. We describe the BM event trigger and analysis scheme. We present and discuss results of simulations, which are used to determine the magnitude of the effect. We also describe our measurement of the two Xenon signals from gamma-ray interactions, which can be used to determine the electron background, and use it to calculate the correction coefficient.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are powered by accretion of gas and/or by supermassive black holes (SMBHs). It is believed that most of SMBHs have masses less than 10^8 solar masses in the centers of normal galaxies, but the masses of SMBHs in AGNs derived from the observed spectrum are much greater than 10^8 solar masses, which are called "massive SMBHs" (MSSMHs). The MSSMHs have larger angular momenta than the SMBHs, and their growth requires a short timescale. It is still an open question how MSSMHs are grown in the centers of normal galaxies. Suzaku performed the first large-scale survey of AGNs detected by Swift/BAT in the hard X-ray band (15-50keV), which covers a wide range of black hole mass. We found that most of AGNs detected by Suzaku have large masses of black holes and show common featureless spectra, which are different from those of normal galaxies. The estimated masses of SMBHs in AGNs detected by Suzaku are much greater than 10^9 solar masses, which are the most massive SMBHs ever found in the centers of normal galaxies. We named them "new type" SMBHs (nSMBHs). We discuss the difference of growth of nSMBHs and MSSMHs and the difference of host galaxies between nSMBHs and MSSMHs.

In this paper, we give a brief overview of discrete time linear control systems. First, the systems are described in terms of differential equations. Next, the systems are rewritten in a discrete time form. Examples are given to illustrate the concepts. Unlike continuous time systems, discrete time systems can be easily implemented. The system can be realized using a digital signal processor, or microprocessor, for example. Also, discrete time systems have a simple relationship between the input and output. Discrete time linear control systems can be described as: $$x(t+1)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)$$ where, $x(t) <unk>in \mathbb{R}^n$, $u(t) \in \mathbb{R}^m$ are the state and input vectors at time , $t=0,1,2...$ A is the system matrix, and B is the input matrix. Unlike continuous time systems, discrete time systems can be easily implemented. The system can be realized using a digital signal processor, or a microprocessor, for example. Also, discrete time systems have a simple relationship between the input and output.

The quiet sun photosphere displays small scale magnetic features that are generally below the detection limit of ground-based telescopes. These regions of small scale magnetic activity have important effects on the evolution of the solar system, including determining the source terms for energy and momentum. The Hinode satellite provided the first clear evidence for these effects in the observations of transverse structuring of small scale magnetic features. This structuring, or transverse inversion, has a clear interpretation in terms of Alfvénic waves propagating upwards and exerting a pressure that transports heat and drives the heat flow. Here we present the results of numerical simulations that include the full buffeting and tearing of magnetic fields by the Alfvénic waves. These simulations, which include many of the required physical processes, reproduce the observed structuring of the magnetic fields in the range of scales simulated. The results of numerical simulations include the full buffeting and tearing of magnetic fields by Alfvénic waves and reproduce the observed structuring of the magnetic fields in the range of scales simulated

Groups of galaxies provide an effective way of studying the large-scale structure of the universe. Over the past few years, many algorithms have been proposed to identify galaxy groups. The galaxies that form these groups can be used to trace the mass distribution of the underlying dark matter distribution and provide a powerful means of understanding the link between galaxies and their environment. Despite their utility, current group-finding algorithms have a number of limitations. In this work, we present a new, simplified algorithm for identifying galaxy groups in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 5 (SDSS DR5). We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by comparing its results with those of other group-finding algorithms. We measure the properties of galaxy groups identified using this method and present a catalogue of galaxies with halo masses above $10^{13.5} h^{-2} M_{\odot}$ ($h=0.72$). This catalogue is available electronically and can be accessed via the Durham Astronomy Centre's web interface (http://www.dur.ac.uk/Dur_Centre/Astronomy_Centre/AC_home.html).

Cache-oblivious mesh layouts aim to place the caches (processor) and memory in such a way that enables the most efficient communication. Many prior art protocols for cache-oblivious mesh layout assume a fixed number of memory blocks and aim to minimize the total communication cost over the entire network. In this work we study the problem of placing caches and memory in an ad-hoc network such that the total memory access cost is minimized. We first analyze a low-cost non-optimal algorithm and then propose a new cache-oblivious layout based on circle packing. We provide a rigorous approximation guarantee for our protocol and show that it achieves a better trade-off between memory access cost and total communication cost than the previously known protocols. We further demonstrate the applicability of our protocol through implementation on a mesh processor platform. We describe a cache-oblivious mesh layout that minimizes the total communication cost over an ad-hoc network with an arbitrary number of memory blocks. Our layout first places the caches and memory such that the nearest caches of each memory block are adjacent. We then minimize the sum ofhops to all the memories as described by Chakrabarti and Palanichamy [2]. We provide a rigorous approximation guarantee for our protocol and show that it achieves a better trade-off between memory access cost and total communication cost than the previously known protocols. We further demonstrate the applicability of our protocol through implementation on a mesh processor platform. We study the problem of placing caches and memory in an ad-hoc network such that the total memory access cost is minimized. This is related to the problem of power and thermal governor for mesh processors. We first analyze a low-cost non-optimal algorithm and then propose a new cache-oblivious layout based on circle packing. Our cache-oblivious layout first places the caches and memory such that the nearest caches of each memory block are adjacent. We then minimize the sum ofhops to all the memories. We first prove that circle packing is a good lower bound on the memory access cost. We then present an $O(n log n)$-approximation algorithm. We show that our protocol provides a rigorous approximation guarantee: the total communication cost of our protocol is at most $(1+\epsilon) \mbox{Circle PackingCost}$ for any $\epsilon>0$. We also demonstrate the appllicability of our protocol through implementation on a mesh processor platform. A coronal hole was observed by the Solar Optical Telescope on-board Hinode on 2007 March 7. EIT and base difference images showed a region of low temperatures (7000 K) in the upper gamma surrounded by a round area of reduced temperature and clear divergence pattern. The SPectrometer on-board SoHO also detected an anomalous cavity, with regions of low temperatures (7000 K) in the inner part and highest temperatures (17,000 K) near the edge. These regions of low and high temperatures were well aligned with the boundaries of the coronal hole observed in EIT and the divergence pattern. Additionally, the SoHO data showed hotter plasma (around 17,000 K) at the eastern edge of the observed hole. These observations suggest a cool, diffuse jet of material along the PIL of the upper gamma sunspot, with hotter, more tenuous plasma moving along the bottom edge of the coronal hole. The overlying field carried by the plasma appeared to be the cause of the anomalous cavity formed along the bottom boundary of the coronal hole.

We present a catalogue of nearest neighbors around a sample of isolated galaxies from the AMIGA project. The isolated galaxies catalogue was created using the Test of Isolation algorithm developed by Pimbblet (2006). The catalogue contains 651 nearby galaxies with a radial velocity difference of less than 3000 km/s and a distance of less than 0.5 Mpc from the isolated target. We calculate both the projected distance to the nearest neighbor and the real-space separation between the isolated galaxy and its nearest neighbor. In both cases we find that 27% of the isolated galaxies have a nearest neighbor within 6000 km/s and 50% have a neighbor within the first 1 Mpc. Around 45% of the isolated galaxies have a neighbor within 3 Mpc and the percentage increases to 57% when we consider a neighbor within the first 1.5 Mpc. For 30% of the isolated galaxies we find that there is no nearby neighbor within 3 Mpc. We find that larger isolated galaxies tend to have a higher probability of having a neighbor within 3 Mpc, but the probability of a neighbor within the first 1.5 Mpc remains high across all isolated galaxy sizes.

A search for thermal emission from the planet TrES-1 was conducted with the HAWAII 2.0 m telescope at the summit of Mauna Kea. Observations were conducted on March 19, 2008 during regular instrument testing that occurred nightly. Data were analyzed and no evidence of thermal emission was found at the 3.6 mum wavelength predicted for TrES-1. Results of this search are included with this submission. Abstract: We present a search for thermal emission from the exoplanet TrES-1, with the HAWAII 2.0 m telescope on the summit of Mauna Kea. Observations were conducted on March 19, 2008 during regular instrument testing that occurred nightly. Data were analyzed and no evidence of thermal emission was found at the 3.6 mum wavelength predicted for TrES-1. Results of this search are included with this submission. This null result does not prove that TrES-1 does not emit thermal radiation at 3.6 mum, only that such emission was not observed with the instrumentation and observations described here. Future observations of this kind of target are encouraged to help clarify the situation.

Finite volume methods (FVMs) are widely used to solve Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) due to their robustness and efficiency. However, model parameters (e.g., reaction rates in reaction-diffusion equations) are often difficult to infer from FVM solutions, because there is a mismatch between solution fidelity and solution regularity required for accurate identification of model parameters. This prevents the direct use of FVM solutions in, for example, real-time monitoring or uncertainty analysis, and hinders the development of methods that exploit the information carried by solution noise. In this work we develop an optimal approach to flow inversion, in which the model is inverted using a probabilistic framework in which model parameters are treated as random variables. To make the problem feasible, we make use of empirical Bayes (EB) to estimate model parameters from noisy FVM solutions. To further reduce the Bayesian inversion problem to a computational problem that is easily handled by modern large-scale computing systems, we develop a sparse formulation for the Bayesian inversion. We demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approach with several one- dimensional and two-dimensional flow inversion problems. Finally, we show that the Bayesian inversion can effectively exploit knowledge of the initial conditions to estimate model parameters accurately.

In this paper, we construct two classes of low-dimensional supersymmetric lattice models. The first class is fermion models. The lattice fermions transform in the fundamental representation of a global symmetry group G. The global symmetry group can be either a local symmetry (i.e. gauge group) or a non-local symmetry (e.g. higher spin symmetry). We show that for sufficiently large global symmetry group G and a specific choice of the background gauge field, the model has an $SO(2N+1)$ global symmetry in $N$ dimensions and $SO(2N)$ global symmetry in $(N-1)$ dimensions. The $1/N$ perturbation connects a strong-coupling phase with a Fermi liquid phase. The Fermi surface is organized into “spinons” and “spin-0 fermions”. The spinons form spin singlet bound states, and the spin-0 fermions form a Fermi sea. The second class of supersymmetric lattice models are boson models. The lattice bosons transform in the vector representation of a global symmetry group G. The global symmetry group can be either a local symmetry (i.e. gauge group) or a non-local symmetry (e.g. higher spin symmetry). For a global symmetry group G whose double cover is a semi-simple group, we show that a non-trivial two-body scattering process between the two bosons (created by the local symmetry) leads to emergent compact translational symmetries. The resulting model is an incarnation of Higher Spin Invariant Luttinger Liquids . We present a minimal lattice realization of these two classes of models using ultracold -diffusion in synthetic dimensions.

Galactic accretion is a fundamental process in the evolution of galaxies, driving both growth of their central black holes and fuelling of their prodigious energy output through active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback. Given the often low angular momentum of accreted material, most accretion occurs in the form of hot, diffuse gas that is poorly bound to the dark matter halos in which galaxies are embedded. This hot gas—which we refer to as ‘hot galactic halos’—is often observed through X-ray emission , but is also predicted to be a large, diffuse fraction of the accreted material, in the form of baryons not locked up in stars or locked in dark matter halos, which are the most abundant forms of galactic structure. Measuring this diffuse gas and understanding its distribution and fate are thus of paramount importance for constraining the rates of both black hole and galactic growth. Here we present a new suite of X-ray zoom-in simulations of Milky Way-mass dark matter halos at different resolution and with different levels of active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback. We focus on the epoch of ongoing, continuous galactic accretion and compare our results to both X-ray observations of the Milky Way in its current (post- Formation of the Inner Helmi stream) state as well as observations of galactic accretion at higher redshifts. We find good agreement between our simulated hot galactic halos and those observed, with our ‘AGN’ simulation generating far more baryons in hot galactic halos in diffuse form than in the ‘no AGN’ simulation—a behaviour that is also seen in observations of distant, high redshift galaxies. However, we do find that at low masses simulated compared to the most massive observed systems, our ‘hot galactic halos’ are too hot—we find that the fraction of baryons in the form of diffuse gas is lower than the observations by a factor of ~2, though we do find that this is largely due to our inability to resolve the most diffuse gas in low-mass halos. We show that this difference can be largely accounted for by reducing the density threshold for star-formation from the sub-grid star-formation model, consistent with expectation from gravity-only simulations. When including this sub-grid model correction, we find excellent agreement between our simulated hot galactic halos and the observations. We conclude that the inclusion of sub-grid physics may be required to produce realistic diffuse gas fractions from cosmological simulations of galaxy formation.

A light bridge is a recently discovered phenomenon in the solar photosphere. It consists of a dark band separating a light region from its surroundings. The light region consists of several bright threads emanating from the dark band. The photospheric environment of a solar pore with a light bridge is analyzed in this study. It is shown that the environment of the pore has larger granular size, lower longitudinal gradient of the inclination of the pore, and higher value of plasma-$\beta$ compared to the surroundings of the pore. The results suggest that the light bridge is formed as a result of evaporation of plasma from the dark band. Author: Dmitriy I. A bright X-ray burster KS 1741-293 was observed by Integral several times between 1996 and 1998. The instrument sensitivity increased significantly from the first to the second observation period, enabling a better understanding of the source properties. The spectrum could be well fitted by an absorbed power law with no evidence for the typical curvature in high energy spectrum of X-ray binaries. The source intensity was relatively stable within a factor of 2, and no pulsations were detected. The lower limits on the intensity and the distance were determined. The implications of the results on the source classification are discussed. Observations Integral observations of KS 1741-293 cover two separate periods, from 1996 March to 1998 December and in 1998 January. The total exposure times are 133 ks and 223 ks, respectively. The source was very bright, exceeding 10 count s$^{-1}$ in the LECS and 5 count s$^{-1}$ in the MECS. The background was negligible, and no events were detected in the hot pixels of the detectors. Data analysis Time-averaged spectra were obtained from the source-excised data of individual instruments and of the source-excised data sets. The data were fitted by an absorbed power law, and the parameters were consistent within the errors. No significant curvature was detected in the high energy part of the spectra, as expected from X-ray binaries. No pulsations were detected either. The source intensity was stable within a factor of two, and the lower limit on the intensity and the distance to the source was determined.

No model of CR acceleration, nor of CSM interaction, can account for the observed degree of bilateral symmetry, nor for the observed alignment of the non-thermal with the synchrotron emissions. A highly unusual core-collapse supernova of magnetorotational origin is proposed, where an extreme cross-field velocity dispersion of metal-rich core material during neutrino-driven wind rotarization transports much higher than average magnetic flux to the protoneutron star surface. This results in a configuration that breaks axisymmetry of the magnetar, driving non-radial stellar motions and explosive, bipolar, massive-star evolution. The polar CSM interaction induced by this magnetically driven explosion best explains the observed morphological symmetry and the spatial coincidence of non-thermal with synchrotron emissions, which are here shown to be mutually exclusive in a dipole geometry. Evidence for a magnetar-driven supernova in Kepler's Supernova Remnant. Kevin G. Denney, Alissa A. Bartels, James E. Kenworthy, Benjamin J. Shappee, Christopher A. Baty, Erik Mulligan, Jeffrey J. Green, Thomas J. W. Lazenby, James E. J. Lee, Roman J. Lee, Jon H. Groce, Henry Ioannidis, Ralf S. Dyding, Alexei V. Filippenko, and Daniel E. Reichart The bilateral structure of Kepler's Supernova Remnant (SNR) has long been a mystery. The SNR exhibits highly unusual symmetries: a strong axial alignment of the non-thermal emissions with the spin axis of the protoneutron pulsar, and the near-total lack of observed hotspots or polar asymmetries. In this paper, we present compelling evidence that the origin of these symmetries can be explained by CSM interaction following a highly magnetic, rapidly rotating star, and that the polar CSM interaction results from a highly unusual, possibly magneto-rotational core-collapse supernova. We base this interpretation on the following observations: (1) the degree of bilateral symmetry, (2) the axial alignment of the non-thermal with the spin axis, (3) the spatial coincidence of non-thermal with synchrotron emissions, and (4) the highly unusual dynamics and symmetry of the pulsar's apparent explosion breaks, as evidenced by a large misalignment between the spin and dipole axes. We find that the most likely geometry is one in which the supernova shockwave first encounters, and is propelled by, a previously existing, highly asymmetric, fossil magnetar wind. These highly unusual dynamics, enabled by extreme cross-field velocities during neutrino-driven wind rotarization, transport much higher than average magnetic flux to the protoneutron star surface, resulting in a magnetar configuration that breaks axisymmetry. This axisymmetric, fossil magnetar wind breaks the spherical symmetry of the SNR, driving non-radial stellar motions and explosive, bipolar, massive-star evolution.

Recent studies have demonstrated that apoptosis, or programmed cell death, is dysregulated in many diseases, including cancer. Thus, the identification of apoptosis regulators that have the potential to be exploited therapeutically represents an important area of ongoing research and drug discovery. In this work, we developed and implemented a generic computational framework for the systems identification and analysis of apoptosis networks at the single-cell level. Using this approach, we identified key network nodes whose activity level differs between non-apoptotic and apoptotic subpopulations of HeLa cells exposed to staurosporine, a drug that causes cell apoptosis. The proteins selected were those associated with the mitochondria and cell death receptor signaling pathways. Subsequent knockdown experiments confirmed that depletion of the selected network nodes caused a significant decrease in HeLa cell apoptosis and increased the population survival. Moreover, the identified apoptosis regulators provided insight into the drug's mechanism of action, as opposed to existing staurosporine treatments, a phosphorylated form of staurosporine selectively induced apoptosis in HeLa cells via the identified regulators. This study presents a proof of concept for the utility of systems identification to guide drug discovery, and further suggests that non-phosphorylated staurosporine and its clinical derivative have limited efficacy as apoptosis regulators. This work also provides a framework that may be applied to the identification and analysis of other signaling pathways in HeLa cells. This work will be published in the journal Nature Communications on July 28, 2022 . Galaxies in the young universe were first assembled during the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), a period of rapid reconfiguration of the intergalactic medium (IGM) driven by high energetic photons from young, highly luminous galaxies. Current observations of the Gunn-Peterson trough in the spectra of high-redshift quasars indicate that the IGM was reionized at $z = 7-8$ and that the process was largely complete by $z = 6$. Large volumes of the high-redshift universe have been observed by the HST and LSST telescopes, but our understanding of the nature of the EoR, and especially the space density of galaxies responsible for heating the IGM, has been limited by the small sample of reionization-epoch sources available for study and the large effective volume over which they are observed. This paper presents deep, wide-field observations of the SSA22 field obtained with the Mayall 4-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory that increase the number of observed high-redshift galaxies by more than an order of magnitude and improve the measurement of the volume-weighted reionization and ionizing emissivity at $z = 7-8$ by an order of magnitude. These observations demonstrate the feasibility of targeting very high-redshift Ly-alpha emitters (LAEs) with the Large Synoptic Space Telescope (LSST) and demonstrate the power of large telescopes, particularly on northern mid-latitude sites, for extending our understanding of the Epoch of Reionization through improved observations of the most luminous high-redshift galaxies.

A detailed study of the suppression of cosmic ray flux above a sharp upper energy limit, known as the GZK cutoff, requires precise measurements of the altitude of the shower maximum, which can be achieved using surface detector arrays such as the Pierre Auger Observatory. In this work we present a new analysis technique based on the distribution of distances between consecutive surface detector elements, that allows the measurement of parameters that are more sensitive to the nature and the intensity of the primary particle than the traditional lateral distribution function. We apply this method to characterize the suppression of cosmic ray flux above the so-called GZK energy limit, and compare the results with previous measurements using traditional parameterizations. We also study the sensitivity to changes in the content of primary cosmic rays and in the chemical composition by using a new composition-sensitive parameter, the spectral rigidity, which is a measure of the energy separation between adjacent energy levels of a given atom or nucleus. We find that the behavior of the measured composition-sensitive parameters above the GZK cutoff is in agreement with the observation of this feature as a result of the interaction of high energy cosmic rays with the photon background, supporting the idea that the latter is composed mostly of atomic <unk> C < /sub > 4 </sub> and < Si > nuclei.

We calculate the iron line profiles from a relativistic Kerr disc around a Schwarzschild black hole. We find that the line is strongly distorted in the inner parts of the disc by gravitational light-bending and becomes virtually line-less at high altitudes above the black hole, where it is fully dominated by reflected fluorescence iron lines. In contrast, we find that for a maximally rotating Kerr black hole, the disc emits strongly distorted lines all the way to the event horizon. At high altitudes above the black hole, the line is strongly distorted and suppressed at low inclination, while at low altitudes it is practically fully transversing the black hole and essentially indistinguishable from a delta line. We apply our results to the microquasar SS 433, finding that the expected profiles can be well fit by our Kerr model, but not by a Schwarzschild model and furthermore that, while our Kerr model can fit all current data, a Schwarzschild model cannot be conclusively ruled out. We calculate the observable spectra and light-curves for various combinations of Kerr and Schwarzschild models and find that we are likely observing SS 433 close to the transition from a Schwarzschild to a Kerr geometry.

Two of the most fundamental properties of early-type galaxies (ETGs) are their stellar mass and light-weighted mean stellar age. While stellar masses of ETGs are relatively insensitive to the precise mechanism by which they lose their mass (i.e., mergers or monolithic collapse), the mean stellar age of ETGs correlates strongly with their projected spatial distribution. Early-type galaxies located in dense environments (i.e., the cores of clusters or proximate to other ETGs) are typically older than their field counterparts, with many showing significant signs of rejuvenation following a major dry merger. Conversely, those ETGs in the field have relatively recent mean stellar ages, even in the densest regions of the Universe. Here, we present a model in which the cores of ETGs grow gradually over a Hubble time via minor dry mergers, secular processes, and environmentally driven gas exhaustion, leaving behind an old, red population at the center surrounded by a younger outer region. In this picture, the dichotomy of early- and late-type galaxy populations arises naturally as a consequence of environmental processes regulating the rate at which galaxies merge, with denser regions permitting only a small number of dry mergers which do not affect the outer regions of the remnant. The feedback -regulated dry merger model prevents ETGs from exhausting their cold gas , effectively terminating dry mergers and leaving a static, red population of stars at the core of the remnant. As gas is funneled toward the central regions of the remnant, the process of cooling and the conversion of cold gas to stars via feedback-driven blowout shocks generate s an old, blue central population with distinct optical and near-infrared photometric and kinematic signatures. We apply this model to recent dry mergers in the field (i.e., NGC 4621 and NGC 4874) and in dense regions (i.e., NGC 4889 and NGC 4874) and find a strong match to the mean stellar age gradients across these structures. We also present predictions for the surface brightness and radial velocity dispersion profiles of the model, and compare these to those of other ETGs in the nearby universe. This feedback-regulated dry merger model naturally explains several hitherto disparate aspects of early galaxy populations: the spatial distribution of mean stellar age, the formation of stellar disky isophotes and counter-rotating cores in conjunction with recent accretion events, the increased incidence of dust and active nuclei in dense environments, and the expected decrease in the number of dry mergers over time in dense regions. This model provides a unifying framework for interpreting the various relations between mean stellar age, color, structure, gas content, and star formation observed in early-type galaxies and their environments. While most theoretical models for the formation and evolution of ETGs have concentrated on the role of dissipational mergers in the origin and assembly of the galaxy population, our results highlight the fundamental importance of environmentally regulated processes in establishing the present-day structure and diversity of early-type systems. .... The VVDS and CFHTLS-Wide surveys are designed to study the evolution of the stellar mass assembly over the last 10 Gyears. These data reveal the presence of a major build up of the red sequence between z=2 and z=1.5. The stellar mass assembly up to z=2 is consistent with passive evolution of present day mass functions, while the significant growth of the red sequence at higher redshifts points to the major role of ongoing galaxy mass assembly, most likely via star formation. The build up of the red sequence is more rapid at higher stellar masses, and is fully established by z=1 only for galaxies with Mstar>10^{10.75} M_{\odot}. This results in a star formation rate density of today only for galaxies with Mstar>10^{10.25} M_{\odot at z=1.5. The observed evolution is in good agreement with expectations from theoretical models of hierarchical structure formation, and indicates that the most massive galaxies had the largest build up in stellar mass since z=2. This Letter is aimed at presenting the first results from the VVDS-Wide and the CFHTLS-Wide surveys, which were designed to study the evolution of the stellar mass assembly over the last 10 Gyears. The combined dataset covers an area of 0.5 deg2 and comprises Keck I/DEIMOS data and U,B,V,i,z imaging for more than 600 000 galaxies over the redshift range 0.5<z<2.5. The data allow us to measure the evolution of the stellar mass assembly rate in the most robust way to date, independently of any model assumptions, and at stellar masses well below present-day massive galaxies. This Letter is structured as follows. The observations and the data reduction are presented in §2. The analysis of the evolution of the stellar mass assembly rate with cosmic time is presented in §3, while a discussion of these results is given in §4.

The specific heat, mean square displacement and alpha relaxation scaling function are calculated and it is found that they are consistent with the predicted scaling forms of the random energy model. It is also found that the spatial scale of the low energy excitations is set by the microscopic lengthscale of the interfacial binding energy between the polymer segments and the solvent. In the investigation of quantum chiral perturbation theory (QCD), there are bound states of quarks and, in particular, the π0 is the lightest single-charm meson. Extensive experimental and theoretical evidence indicates that π0 is not a scalar but rather a vector particle with JPC=1+--. If this empirical observation is borne out by the realizations of low-energy effective theories for the strong interaction such as QCD, then the existence of a ninth fundamental force, assumed-universal in all sectors of the standard model, would be vindicated. Here we show, however, that the most general renormalizable couplings of the standard model Higgs to two pions imply that π0 is not a vector particle but rather a Goldstone boson and, thus, a pseudoscalar. We proceed to show that a more general renormalizable potential for the pions, generated by quantum fluctuations in a phenomenological theory of the strong interaction known as chiral perturbation theory, implies the existence of an additional scalar particle, which could explain the experimental evidence for a ninth force. We thus offer a new perspective on the classic Goldstone boson scenario and suggest that not only the pions but also the meson species could have both conventional and unconventional scalar numbers. We also consider the interaction of QCD with modern discretizations of the Dirac operator that exhibit multi-site superexchange at smaller values of the lattice spacing. The existence of a ninth fundamental force implies the existence of magnetic charges, both fundamental and emergent, in this theory, which suggests a fascinating connection between the proposed topological interpretation of nature's 'dark' or 'heavy' matter and the existence of exotic matter in nature.

A rotating sunspot hosted by the active region 1132 produced several ephemeral regions as observed by the EUV waves. The interaction of these two structures led to the formation of a continuous mass ejection (CME) on December 13, 2006 that presented a rotational-velocity larger than 900 km/s. The authors suggest that the rotation of the sunspot produced the ephemeral regions that propagated to the east with the EUV wave. These ephemeral regions generated an unstable magnetic configuration that led to the production of a fast CME with a rotational velocity larger than 900 km/s. The sunspot rotation could produce the ephemeral regions that propagated to the east with the EUV wave. These ephemeral regions generated an unstable magnetic configuration that led to the production of a fast CME with a rotational velocity larger than 900 km/s. Thus, the rotation of the sunspot hosted by active region 1132 was the main responsible for the generation of the EUV waves that occurred on December 13, 2006.

The quasar PHL 1811 was discovered on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) by Fan et al. (2000) and was selected for follow-up observation because of its unusually low ratio of X-ray to optical luminosity. Subsequent observations with the Chandra and XMM-Newton observatories revealed that the X-ray spectrum of PHL 1811 is in fact completely dominated by emission reflected from dust and gas along the line of sight, suggesting that the quasar is in fact a “mirror quasar”, similar to the quasars found by Mateos et al. (2005) and Fu et al. (2007). Subsequent analysis of the SDSS spectrum revealed that the optical emission is dominated by a power-law component, with no evidence for the presence of broad optical emission lines, typically found in quasars. Based on these results, PHL 1811 has been suggested to be an extremely dusty version of a quasar, where the power-law component observed in the optical spectrum is reflected from dust completely surrounding the emission line region. The combination of extreme obscuration and the presence of a power-law optical component has been proposed to explain the large magnitude difference between the X-ray and optical emissions from the quasar. The SDSS spectrum of PHL 1811 used for the original analysis was of relatively low quality, with only a few moderate-quality optical spectroscopic observations made with the Apache Point Observatory 3.5-meter telescope. More recently, Page et al. (2012) obtained an exposure time-weighted average of five exposures with the MOS spectrograph on the Isaac Newton Telescope (INT) located at the Observatorio del Estado de los Muchachos on La Palma, Spain, providing a much higher-quality optical spectrum for use in analysis of the nature of PHL 1811. In this new analysis, we show that the optical spectrum does in fact show the presence of prominent broad emission lines, but that the strength of the lines is nearly twice that observed in typical quasars. Fitting the optical spectrum with a typical quasar template we find that the quasar is highly reddened, with a hydrogen column density of N(H) = 5.8 ± 0.3 x 1022 cm-2, corresponding to a total visual absorption of A V = 14.4 ± 0.5 mag, nearly nine times greater than that observed in the more extreme mirror quasars IIICMUSS J134752.97+341958.1 and PDS 456. We present possible explanations for this extreme obscuration, including a torus of gas and dust significantly larger than that observed in typical quasars, or the presence of an additional strong obscuring medium along our line of sight. Based on the strength of the hydrogen emission lines, the SED is well described by both a typical quasar and the more extreme “hyper-luminous” mirror quaar (HLQ). Thus, we find no evidence to support the proposal that PHL 1811 is a particularly obscured

Adiabatic magnetization in the Ni50Mn34In16 magnetic shape memory alloy induces a strong tunability of both its structural and magnetic symmetries. This results in strong coupling between magnetism and elasticity, manifested by a rapid variation of the lattice parameter of the tetragonal crystal structure and simultaneous change of the magnetic structure from a collinear to a non-collinear helix.
