In this paper, we review some of the most recent results obtained in our laboratory concerning the calculation and measurement of thermal Casimir force between real materials. Casimir forces are long-range, quantum electromagnetic forces that arise from the modification of the zero-point energy spectrum of the quantum electromagnetic field due to the presence of boundaries. Forces of this kind play an important role in nanotechnology, as they can influence the equilibrium position of molecules or mechanical components and may provide a useful mechanism of actuation. The latter aspect is of special interest in developing new micromechanical devices. At finite temperatures, there are two distinct contributions to the Casimir energy, the so-called ideal or thermal term and the nonideal thermal term. The ideal term is calculated by simply multiplying the zero-point energies of the quantum electromagnetic field in the respective regions. The nonideal term, on the other hand, accounts for the changes in the zero-point energy induced by the presence of boundaries. At room temperature, the ideal term is many orders of magnitude smaller than the ideal term and may therefore be neglected. At low temperatures, on the other hand, the nonideal term becomes increasingly larger than the ideal term and may even change the direction of the force acting between two objects. This phenomenon is known as thermal capt. The topic of this paper is the calculation and measurement of the thermal Casimir force between real materials. In this paper, we will focus on two prototypical systems, namely, two parallel plates made of gold and covered with a layer of teflon, and a crossed grid of stainless steel wires mounted on a copper plate. In order to calculate the thermal Casimir force, we use the so-called Green's function method. The experimental setup for measuring the thermal Casimir force is based on the recent invention of W. J. Kim and H. M. Chan of the Stanford Research Systems Institute (SRS). This setup is able to measure the force with a very high accuracy. We have performed measurements of thermal Casimir force between the two parallel plates and between the crossed grid and the plate. We have also calculated the thermal Casimir force between the two parallel plates using different theoretical models, including the so-called proximity force approximation. We found excellent agreement between the measured and calculated values of the thermal Casimir force.

The Kac model is one of the simplest models of particles that interact via binary collisions. Spectral methods for the Kac model are very efficient for determining the spectrum of the model. In particular, we show how the recently introduced generalized Verlet method allows us to compute the spectral gap in the Kac model for any value of the physical parameters in the collision kernel. We test our method on different values of the physical parameter μ and demonstrate excellent agreement with the theoretical prediction for the exact solution. We further compute the scaling of the spectral gap with the system size <unk> and find excellent agreement with the theoretical prediction for the specific case of binary collisions. Spectral gaps are an important feature of the Kac model which allows for the rigorous definition of thermal equilibrium. They also play an important role in dynamical properties of the model such as relaxation to thermal equilibrium and equilibration rates. Our work further develops the theory of spectral methods for the Kac model and paves the way for application to important problems in statistical mechanics and many other fields of physics.

Magnetization curves of a uniform spin-1/2 Heisenberg diamond chain in a magnetic field are studied by a matrix renormalization (MR) method. At low temperatures, the magnetization process is divided into three regions according to the shape of the magnetization curve. For an even number of spins, there are two pitchfork bifurcations at which two stable branches of the magnetization curve terminate. At higher magnetic fields, the magnetization curve becomes single valued, and a trivial ferromagnetic phase appears. The diamond chain exhibits paramagnetism at low temperatures and ferromagnetic phase at high temperatures. The thermodynamical quantities are calculated, and a triple point in the phase diagram is predicted. When the magnetic field increases, the magnetization curve of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg diamond chain becomes single valued and a trivial ferromagnetic phase appears. The diamond chain exhibits paramagnetism at low temperatures and ferromagnetic phase at high temperatures. At high temperatures, the magnetization curve is divided into three regions according to the shape at low temperatures. The two pitchfork bifurcations are identified as the termination of two stable branches. The diamond chain shows different behaviors at high and low temperatures.

Many Monte Carlo based estimators of mean and other population quantities of interest in large samples are computationally complex, requiring orders of magnitude more computational effort than corresponding formulas. In this work, we examine several MCMC based approaches to estimation that have been proposed to address this problem. We consider both simple tempered MCMC (ST-MCMC) and more recently proposed adaptive MCMC (Adaptive MCMC), and establish computational complexity results for these methods. Our results show that, under mild assumptions, Adaptive MCMC can estimate a quantity of interest with statistical error in $O(N^{-\alpha})$, for any $\alpha < 1/4$ where N is the number of Monte Carlo samples, in time N, in the data size N, and N is the number of Monte Carlo samples N. ST-MCMC can only achieve statistical error in $O(N^{-\alpha})$ at the cost of vastly greater computational complexity. We provide concrete examples of distributions and estimators to which our results apply, and discuss conditions under which our results are optimal.

A scientific paper by Phil o et al published on arXiv.org in November, 2018, has been selected by the PTRF for the PTRF Newsletter. The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) experiment, one of the cornerstones of quantum mechanics, has been extensively tested in recent years. These experiments test the so-called Bell inequality, which must be obeyed by any theory that describes nature in the classical, quantum or intermediate regimes. In this paper, we consider the interpretation of this experiment in the light of a recently proposed theory which combines classical and quantum mechanics and could provide a link between these two fields. We show that the proposed model, which goes beyond the standard quantum framework and considers the possibility of vacuum fluctuations leading to the spontaneous creation of virtual particles, leads to a significant violation of Bell's inequality. Thus, this article discusses the interpretation of an experiment which, although more than half a century old, remains of great interest today because it could lead to a significant expansion of our current understanding of physical reality.

Evidence of a planetary companion around a nearby young star has been found using precision radial velocity measurements. This planet, designated GJ 625 b, has a minimum mass of 7.5 Earth masses, is about 2.7 times the mass of Earth, and orbits its host star at a distance of about 0.815 AU, which is less than one percent of the distance between Earth and the Sun. Such a small orbital distance implies that GJ 625 b likely orbits a young star with a low surface temperature , at which ice no longer would be a stable form of carbon and water. The relatively high eccentricity of the planet's orbit (0.29) is also intriguing, and might suggest the existence of additional undetected planets in the system. GJ 625 b is the first planet found around a young star below the Sun's mass, and only the second planet (next to the Earth) known to exist outside the Solar System. In order to determine the nature of GJ 625 b and the characteristics of the system in which it orbits, additional observations are necessary. For example, a direct imaging search for further planets in the system is recommended. Such follow-up observations could be made with current instruments on ground-based telescopes, or with the future Large UV/Optical Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope.

The branching fraction of the decays X(3872)<unk> J/<unk> ω, Λ Ω, and the CP-averaged branching fraction of the decays X(3872)→J/ψ ee and Λ Λ ee have been measured with the BABAR detector at the SLAC PEP-II asymmetric B factory. New measurements of the branching fraction for the decay X(3872)→J/ψ ee and a search for the decay X(3872)→J/ψ μμ are presented. For the former, the combination of the results for the two final states yields B(X(3872)→J/ψ ee) = (0.96 ± 0.27stat ± 0.11syst)%. This is the first determination of this quantity. For the latter, a search for X(3872)→J/ψ μμ, B(X(3872)→J/ψ μμ) = (1.1 ± 0.7stat ± 0.5syst)% is performed, which is the first such search for this quantity. These results are consistent with previous branching fraction measurements and yields Γ(X(3872)→J/ψ) = (35.5 ± 4.2stat ± 3.6syst) ps-1, where the error includes all sources of systematic uncertainty. This is the first model-independent measurement of this ratio. Included in the systematic uncertainties are those associated with the determination of the number of produced neutrons, the number of mesons, the reconstruction efficiency, and the number of peaking background events. Using a prediction based on factorization, this measurement excludes, at the 90% confidence level, new physics contributions to X(3872)→J/ψ ee, Λ Ω, and Λ Λ Ω decays that are proportional to the product of the X(3872) branching fraction and the CP-averaged branching fraction. The BABAR detector at the SLAC PEP-II asymmetric B factory has been used to make the measurements presented here. The BABAR detector is comprised of a charged-particle tracker, a ring imaging Cherenkov detector, a ring imaging Cherenkov detector for muon detection system, a threshold -based detector, a ring imaging Cherenkov detector for photons, and a resistive-plate chambers for muon detection. These elements are located inside a superconducting solenoid that provides a 1.5 T magnetic field. A transient anomalous x-ray pulsar (TXP) is a newly found kind of pulsar, whose outbursts and magnetar-like activity are much more frequent than previously thought. One of them, named IGR J17464- glycerin inside the globular cluster M15. It has shown several interesting behaviors including bursting and flaring activities, extremely strong surface magnetic field (up to about 100 times the magnetic field of magnetars), and extremely high spin-down rate. SNR G156.2+5.7 (also known as 3C386) is a historical supernova remnant (SNR) discovered in 1873. Modern radio, optical and X-ray observations show that this SNR is a middle-aged explosion of a runaway supernova remnant in our galaxy. At a wavelength of 6 cm, emission from the SNR is highly polarized, up to 80%, and mainly consists of two perpendicular polarizations linearly aligned, which is highly unusual for SNRs. The emission is instead depolarized at higher frequencies, and most likely stems from multiple SNR patches with different physical conditions. The nature of the highly polarized radio emission from SNR G156.2+5.7 is not clear, but one possibility is that it arises from synchrotron emission from a very high energy electron population. The origin of highly polarized radio emission from SNR G156.2+5.7 is one of the mystery of modern astrophysics. It is highly unusual for SNRs and its nature is not fully understood. The highly polarized radio emission is best explained if it comes from very high energy electrons, which may be produced in magnetic fields amplified by the shock wave of a supernova explosion. I present here observations of the SNR G156.2+5.7 at 6 cm wavelength, which provides the best angular resolution. The observations show that the emission is highly polarized up to 80% and consists of two perpendicularly polarizations aligned. The emission is most likely from a SNR with strong magnetic field. The observations present here are one of the mystery of modern astrophysics . The origin of highly polarized radio emission from SNR G156.2+5.7 is one of the mysteries of modern astrophysics. It is not fully understood the nature of the polarized radio emission from SNR G156.2+5.7. The highly polarized radio emission can be produced by very high energy electrons. Understanding the processes producing the polarized radio emission from this SNR could have implications for our understanding of the evolution of magnetic fields in our galaxy and beyond. In this paper, we propose a generic cosmological evolution for a tachyon and a scalar field, which describes late-time accelerated expansion. We show that the interaction between the tachyon and the scalar field, which is typically described by a coupling of negative exchange mass, can lead to a viable cosmological evolution for both the background and the perturbations. In particular, we consider a tachyonic dark energy model, where the tachyon is responsible for the late-time accelerated expansion, and a canonical scalar field with positive kinetic term, which serves as the background fluid responsible for the early time accelerated expansion and the present day observed cosmic speedup. We show that the interaction of the tachyon and the scalar field occurs over a wide range of energy scales, from microscopic to cosmological. This allows us to naturally connect the early time evolution, where the tachyon potential is flat and the kinetic energy dominates, to the late time evolution, where the potential energy dominates and the tachyon relaxes to its ground state. In addition to solving the cosmological singularity problem, our model naturally generates a non-zero effective cosmological constant, as the ground state of the tachyon, which cancels the negative pressure of the scalar field. We derive the resulting cosmological equations, and use them to study the background evolution of the universe. We also study the perturbation evolution and show that the tensor-to-scalar ratio can be naturally smaller than 0.1, which is required for future cosmological observations. Our model also predicts large non-Gaussianities, which can be tested by future observations.

TYZ expansion is an improveduder-based technique which has the advantage over the longtime Monte Carlo method in higher efficiency. We establish the upper and lower bounds for the weak limit of TYZ approximation, which turns out to be the zero extension of the initial data with respect to the vanishing time argument. The numerical experiments confirm our theoretical findings. The results in this paper extend our previous work [1] to the half-space case and also apply to the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Uniqueness is guaranteed for real polynomials of fixed degree that have no multiple roots by requiring that the polynomial beCanonically representable, i.e. admit a finite, explicitly given representation as a polynomial with respect to a monomial basis. Polynomials that areCanonically representable are parameterized by a continuous parameter (the degree) and a discrete parameter (the basis). The uniqueness theorem thereby recovers polynomial canonical representations (PCRs) of the originally given polynomial. Two PCRs represent the same polynomial if and only if they differ only via a change of the basis in the parameters. The uniqueness theorem implies a numerical stability of polynomial calculations. Numerical experiments show that polynomial computations with arbitrary precision are possible using PCRs. The uniqueness theorem is of interest in the numerical treatment of polynomial problems. Numerical algorithms for finding all roots of polynomials rely on the uniqueness form, which states that a polynomial can be made from a system of hyperplane inequalities using projective techniques if and only if the polynomial has multiple roots. The uniqueness theorem constrains the degrees of projective techniques and thereby establishes a one-to-one correspondence between hyperplane inequalities and multiple roots. Without the uniqueness theorem, hyperplane inequalities might not correspond to real roots. In this sense, the uniqueness theorem is an intrinsic ally useful result for numerical algorithms for finding all roots of polynomials.

D3-branes are simple objects in 10-d string theory. They are point-like solutions of the effective theory of the low energy fields, which interact by the gauge interactions and exchange of massless particles, only. These interactions are specified by the 9-d space where the brane is localized. For D3-branes in 10-d Minkowski space the interaction is described by the massless 10-d gravity. Therefore, D3-brane configurations are important objects for studying the theories of 10-d supersymmetry. However, they seem to be too simple. It turns out that at least for the configurations that carry nontrivial, non-gravitational Ramond-Ramond (RR) charges D3-branes support additional fields, as well as their excitations - the giant gravitons. These are solitonic configurations, wrapping supersymmetric cycles in the 10-d space, which carry RR charge and interact by non-gravitational fields with the branes, primarily the gauge fields. The coupling s between the branes and gravity fields are 10-d special functions - the Scherk-Schwarz factors. D3-brane configurations have specific properties, which for some purposes make them unnecessary simple laboratory objects. One of such properties is the possibility to realize them as the singular limits of more general geometries, called complex deformations. For the geometries with twohorizontwo pairs of complex dimensions these deformations correspond to deformations of the geometry, preserving its supersymmetry and holonomy, which allows to keep some supersymmetry in the deformed background. The main subject of this note is the study of D3-brane geometries, which are complex deformations of the flat 10-d space and, at the same time, support the RR fields and provide the supergravity description. The deformations leading to this description are called marginal. For these geometries giant gravitons, carrying the quantum numbers, preserve some supersymmetries. It is also shown that the massless spectra of these geometries contain the dual giant gravitons, and the giant gravitons with reversed orientation, which also preserve the supersymmetry.

A search for gravitational waves from binary inspirals is presented. The search is performed on data from the first and second observing runs of the LIGO detectors. The data were searched in the S3 and S4 channels of the LIGO searches together, as well as individual LSC searches. The search uses data from September 2014 to March 2017, and is limited to signals from binary inspirals with total mass below 30 solar masses. No gravitational waves were observed in the data from binary inspirals, and limits were placed on the rate of binary inspirals as a function of total mass. The 90% confidence level was used to place limits on the rate range from 1.4×10−7 to 2.3×10−7 binary mergers per Mpc3 for total mass between 10 and 30 solar masses. This is the first search for gravitational waves from binary inspirals in the S3 and S4 LIGO data and the first search for binary inspirals in the S4 LIGO data with total mass below 30 solar masses. The results significantly improve the existing results from previous LIGO searches for binary inspirals, reaching below 30 solar mass binary inspirals for the first time, and covering the total mass range from 10 to 30 solar masses, for the first time , in a single search.

Random bits, the basic data type of information, are often shared in practice over the Internet. For example, hardware random number generators are driven by physical keys that are not accessible to attackers, and the resulting random bits need to be delivered to the destination where they are needed. While the secure transport of sensitive data over the Internet has been an active area of research, sharing of random bits (both secure and authenticated delivery of random bits without the secrecy or authenticity being compromised) has not been addressed. In this work, we propose a methodology and algorithms for secure sharing of random bits over the Internet, called Secure Internet Sharing of Random Bits (SISRB). SISRB provides strong confidentiality, authenticity and integrity of the shares by using Diffie-Hellman key agreement and message authentication codes, along with a novel key agreement scheme. We evaluate the performance of our scheme using the composable security framework, and demonstrate that our scheme can securely share random bits over the Internet at high speed, while achieving strong confidentiality, authenticity and integrity.

In this paper we consider a system of particles interacting via binary collisions , which also interact by means of a pairwise interaction potential which is degenerate in some sense. We show that the dynamics of this particle system can be approximated, in the appropriate scaling, by a coupled system of non-linear conservation laws. The approximation is in the sense of weak convergence of the hydrodynamic measures on appropriate function spaces. This hydrodynamic limit is then used to study the large time asymptotic behavior of the particle system. We show that this is the case when the interaction potential degenerate in a Kramers sense. In this case the hard-core interaction force and the inter-particle interaction force are not opposite, and they have the same interaction potential with the particle density. This degenerate dynamics do not require the hyperbolicity condition. We show that if the initial collisions are regular enough and the time interval is small enough, then the particle system approach the hydrodynamic solution as time evolve. The proof is based on the theory of viscosity solutions and the compactness method.

In this paper, we present the results of our 2.5-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of the evolution of interstellar clouds in a streaming hot plasma. This plasma is expected to be in the vicinity of a newly formed young star. The plasma is streaming to the east with a speed of 20 km/s. The upstream side of the clouds is also moving at a speed of 20 km/s and the maximum velocity between the clouds and the plasma is, therefore, 60 km/s. The temperature of the plasma is taken to be 10^4 K. The computational box size is 80 pc by 80 pc by 240 pc, and we solve the equations in the box mesh. The simulation includes the effects of ionization dissociation, heating and cooling due to both atomic and molecular processes, and magnetic fields. We confirm that the streaming hot plasma with the above given parameters erodes interstellar clouds and diffuse interstellar medium (ISM). In the course of the simulation runs, a cold neutral medium (CNM) fragments to smaller sized clouds and a warm neutral medium (WNM) gets diffuse. We find that the thermal pressure of the hot plasma prevents the cold clouds from being dispersed away. The pressure also facilitates the accretion of the interstellar clouds by the young star. The star forms inside the small cloud complex that is generated in the simulation.

HD 73526 is a spectroscopic binary system consisting of two stars with similar mass which orbit around a common center of gravity with a period of approximately 20.87 days. This short period make it possible for the two stars to interact with each other strongly through angular momentum exchange and subsequent formation of a common envelope. This process is expected to dramatically change the configurations of the stars and their orbital parameters. In this work, we study this system through full numerical integration of the corresponding equations of motion, in order to characterize the present configurations and orbital parameters as well as their variations with time. We find that after an initial stage during which the system loses a significant amount of orbital parameters and angular momentum, the system reaches a stage of resonant interaction in which the period of the inner orbit is equal to the period of the outer orbit. The two stars are then observed to be in a stable configuration with a constant period, mass, and distance.

SN 2004et was the first direct member of the new class of type IIp supernovae, with distinct features in both their light curve and spectra from those of type II-P standard candles, such as SN 1999cq. By making late -time Chandra X-ray observations of SN 2004et, we have determined the neutron star spin period for the first time, thus substantially advancing the determination of the neutron star spin rate distribution and putting important constraints on the equations of state of neutron stars. In this paper, we report the X-ray detection of SN 2004et at 1013 days after the initial explosion with an absorbed 0.8-10 keV luminosity of (1.6 ± 0.3) × 1039 erg s−1. The late-time X-ray emission can be best described as a single temperature blackbody of kT = 0.58 ± 0.03 keV, at a distance of 1.39 ± 0.21 kpc from the Earth. This is the first evidence of a single temperature blackbody emitting X-rays from the cooling SN 2004et neutron star. Assuming a distance of 3.6 kpc, we estimate the bolometric luminosity to be 4.6 × 1038 erg s<unk>1. The resulting 0.8–10 keV absorption-corrected 0.5–2.0 keV isotropic luminosity is (3.2 ± 0.5) × 1037 erg s−1, which is higher than but comparable to other well-studied, slow-spinning neutron stars such as RX 2004et. We argue that the spin down powering the X-ray emission is likely coming from the magnetar-mode of the superconducting neutron star magnetosphere rather than the propeller mode, given the observed soft spectrum, absence of pulsations from the neutron star, and the inferred large period derivative, ΔP / P0 ∼ 10%. We discuss the implications of these results for the circumstellar medium of SN 2004et, the late-time interaction between the supernova ejecta and the neutron star magnetosphere, and the launch of a pulsar wind nebula.

In this paper, we study the problem of freezing variables in random CSP. In the problem, for each random sampling, some of the variables are unfixed and some of the variables are fixed to certain values, and the problem is to determine the values of the unfixed variables such that the sum of the values of the unfixed variables is as large as possible. We study the asymptotic behaviour of the optimal value of this problem as the number of variables goes to infinity. We show that both the optimal value and the number of variables form a strongly consistent representation of the optimal value for the discrete and continuous CSP versions of the CSPRS with non-unique solutions. We then prove that when the optimal value is almost surely frozen in the limit, that is, for all $\epsilon>0$, the probability that the value of the optimal variable is not $1$ is much higher than for most $\epsilon$. Additionally, we analyse the natural greedy algorithm for the problem and provide a closed form expression for the probability that a variable is unfrozen under this algorithm. We establish a precise phase transition: for the fixed constant $\alpha>0$, when the probability that a random CSP instance with $n$ variables and $m$ constraints is sampled is between $n^{-\alpha}$ and $n^{1-\alpha}$ (depending on the cost function), then with high probability the greedy algorithm almost always freezes at least $\Omega(n/\log n)$ variables. When the sampling probability is much smaller than $n^{-\alpha}$ or much larger than $n<unk> 1-<unk> alpha<unk>$, then almost always all the variables are unfrozen. Our results imply that when the sampling probability is between $n^{-\alpha}$ and $n^{1-\alpha}$, the solution with the frozen variables provides a constant factor approximation to the optimal value of the freezing problem, with high probability. This is the first almost sure result of the 'natural greedy algorithm for this problem.'

In this paper, we investigate logarithmic corrections to the multipole expansion of the nucleon form factor in the limit where the momentum of the emitting particle is soft. We consider both low energy theorems as well as relations following from the consistency of the effective field theory approach. Including such corrections leads to improved fits to low energy ElectroWeak data as well as a better characterization of the potential reach of future experiments. We also examine the behavior of our results in the limit where the structure scale of the model is taken to be small, finding good agreement with the "standard model" approach to ElectroWeak fitments for small values of the structure scale. We present the full calculation of the form factors for a general class of relativistic quantum field theories. We focus on the explicit calculation of corrections due to a new scale, the momentum scale, which characterizes the importance of physics not modeled by the dipole approximation. The resulting expressions exhibit the symmetry properties of the required integrals and have a simple physical meaning: for each form factor, the terms which grow as momentum scale correspond to integrals of jet functions over regions of phase space where the particle in the loop has momentum of order scale. These lead to power law corrections to the form factors which are absent in popular models. We present phenomenological fits to low energy ElectroWeak data and describe the reach of future experiments. Finally, we examine the behavior of the form factors in the limit of small structure scale, finding good agreement with the "standard model" approach to ElectroWeak fitments for small structure scale.' Coexisting singlet and doublet ground states have been widely observed in electron systems due to their strong electron-electron (Kondo) and electron-phonon (Mott) interactions. Such coexisting singlet and doublet ground states are critical for high-temperature spectroscopy and other correlated electron phenomena. Here, we study theoretically an electron system dynamically coupled with local optical phonons. In such a system, the electron-phonon coupling constant can be much stronger than the Kondo and Mott coupling constants, which significantly modifies the ground-state properties. For example, without phonon bath, the ground state of the electron system is a singlet ground state at weak Kondo coupling and a doublet ground state at strong Kondo coupling. However, with phonon bath, the ground state of the system exhibits a coexisting singlet and doublet ground states, where the singlet and doublet characters are smoothly connected with varying Kondo coupling strength. Such an unusual ground-state transition is attributed to the coherent interference between the Kondo screening and the phonon-dressed intermediate states. The coherent interference leads to singlet and doublet fractions in the ground state, which can be tuned by external parameters. Our findings provide a platform to study and control correlated electron phenomena via phonon engineering.

The process by which mass is removed from a region and replaced by new material is called outflow, and is important in the evolution of most objects. A complementary process in which more material is brought into a region than can be removed by outflow is called inflow. Understanding both outflow and inflow is important in determining the long term evolution of regions. In this paper we investigate these processes using data from the Disk observations with the * Mars mission. We identify 28 sources that may be sites of both outflow and inflow. These data suggest that the mass added to a region by inflow may be comparable to the mass removed by outflow. * Mars Global Surveyor Massive Star Forming Regions (Mειvellous names, don't you think?) are a fundamental part of the evolution of our Galaxy. Over time, new material (outflow) is removed from the region, and replaced by new material (inflow). By understanding both outflow and inflow, we can better understand the evolution of the region as a whole. To study this process, we use data from the * Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) mission. *Mars Global Surveyor was the first of the Discovery-class Mars orbiters, and carried the Mars Orbiter Camera (MOC), which has significantly better imaging capabilities than the previous rovers (Pathfinder and Sojourner). The MGS was placed into a 700km sun-synchronous orbit in 2006, and has been studying the atmosphere of Mars since. The MOC has been used to study a number of interesting features on Mars, including landing sites for future missions. We identified 28 sources that may show evidence of both outflow and inflow. These sources cover a range of potential difference -- from pure outflow sources to pure inflow sources. The presence of both inflow and outflow at the same location would be unexpected if these were independent processes. We are currently analyzing these data to determine if we can confirm that both inflow and outflow occur at the same location, and whether the relative rates of these processes are similar to what we would expect based on prior studies of similar regions. The paper will be submitted to the journal "Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.", and can be accessed here: <http://www.mast.server.com/mgs/publications/mjpaper.html> As a side-note, I just wanted to provide a little insight into how much I enjoy working with data from the *Mars Global Surveyor mission. This has been an incredibly fun project, and I have learned a tremendous amount about astronomy from the process. The *Mars Global Surveyor, along with the other Mars rovers (including Odyssey, MESSENGER, and the Martian rovers) provide an invaluable archive of data on the Red Planet, and continue to provide critical insights into the geological history of the Solar System's only planet. Small-world network models have been proposed to describe the organization of functional connectivity in brain networks. Altered structural and functional brain connectivity has been reported in several neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), major depressive disorder (MDD), schizophrenia, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Assessing the impact of network topology on dynamical systems representing brain networks has become an active research area. Here, we study the influence of the network topology on the dynamics of short and long range random links in the Small World Network (SWN) model. In the proposed model, the distribution of link weights is tuned to obtain a SWN topology. We show that the addition of short and long range random links modifies the structure of the network and induces chaotic dynamics in the dynamics of the synchronization order parameter, differently from the classical SWN model. We derive an analytical expression to describe the transition to chaos in the system using the homoclinic bifurcation method. We also show that the maximal value of the synchronization degree of the network influences the occurrence of chaos in the dynamics of the order parameter. This work suggests that the addition of certain level of random links to a SWN topology could be a potential mechanism to promote chaotic dynamics in brain networks.' Keywords: Small-World Network, Chaos, Diffusion , Chaos.

Long-range order is a central phenomenon in condensed matter physics. It is commonly believed to be limited to spatially periodic systems. Here we report on the spontaneous formation of magnetic order in the ground state of quasi-one-dimensional Heisenberg quantum antiferromagnets, in a range of parameters inaccessible by classical simulations. The onset of long-range order is signaled by a sharp rise of the sublattice magnetization, followed by a slow convergence to the saturated value. This behavior is well captured by high-order coupled-cluster theory, which demonstrate that long-range order can also occur in systems without true long-range order at finite temperature. These results open new avenues for experimental studies of one-dimensional quantum many-body systems and beyond. Long-range order is a central phenomenon in condensed matter physics. A hierarchical grid spatial index based on deep learning is proposed in this paper. The hierarchical grid spatial index can accelerate nearest neighbor queries and range queries for points located on a two-dimensional plane. For each dimension in the index, it is divided into a series of uniformly spaced blocks, called levels. The width of a level (in terms of blocks) is increased by a factor of two after each refinement, so the total number of blocks in the final level is equal to the number of blocks in the original dimension. In order to effectively encode the spatial relationships among points, images are learned to represent the block structures of each level. A deep belief network (DBN) is trained on image patches extracted from existing libraries of ground truth images. The DBN is used to perform image reconstruction and generate new images for missing image patches. After training, the index can be used to efficiently answer range queries as well as nearest neighbor queries with arbitrary image classes. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, experiments are conducted using three public image datasets. Experimental results show that the proposed method can outperform state-of-the-art schemes on these public datasets.

In this paper we report the results of a detailed study of the phase structure of the $(g\phi^4 + h\phi^6)_{1+1}$ model. This is done by performing a model-independent analysis of the theories phase structure for a broad range of renormalisation group invariant points in the parameter space. We demonstrate that for a range of intermediate and large values of the sixteenth century parameter, $h$, the $(\phi^6 + h\phi^6)_{1+1}$ model has a novel phase, which we call the non-convex phase. This phase is characterised by the spontaneous formation of regions of self-amplification in a wide range of parameter space. Theories in this phase exhibit scaling behavior that differs significantly from both the standard convex and non-convex phases of the $(\phi^4 + h\phi^6)_{1+1}$ model. Furthermore, we show that the novel phase persists at strong values of the $<unk> phi<unk>2$ field, and argue that it should therefore exist in the corresponding lattice model. Finally, we present preliminary evidence for the existence of the non-convex phase in the $(\phi^6 + m^2\phi^2)_{1+1}$ model, based on numerical simulations of an effective field theory for large values of the squared mass, $m^2$, of the $\phi^2$ field. This work was performed as part of the 2020-2021 STFC St Margaret's PhD scheme, and was supported by a PhD studentship from the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC).

Theoretical predictions and observations of massive planet migration since 1995 are reviewed. After a short introduction on the migration mechanisms, the next sections are devoted to the individual cases of PSR B1257+12, HD 215441, OGLE-2007-BLG-161Lb, GJ 581b, 53 Eridani b, 51 Eridani b, LkCa 15b, XZ TauABC b, XZ TauABC b, HD 219188b, $\beta$ Pic b and Fomalhaut b. Their characteristics and the different processes leading to these observations are detailed. These planet candidates are then compared with the expected characteristics of the most popular planet migration scenarios. Finally, the current situation and the future expected observations of massive planet migration are discussed. I. INTRODUCTION Since 1995, the planetary velocity technique has been successfully used to detect massive planets around other stars. However, despite intensive studies since the beginning of the 2000s, the migration mechanism of these planets is still an open question. Different hypotheses have been proposed, including photo-evaporation [1], spiral waves [2], interaction with the outer disk [3, 4] and the evolution of planetesimals [5]. This article reviews the theoretical predictions and current observations of massive planet migration since 1995. Initially, the migration mechanisms are presented. Then, the characteristics of the most famous observed planet s are detailed, together with a discussion on the most popular migration scenarios. The article ends with a discussion of the current situation and the expected future observations of massive planet migration. II. MIGRATION MECHANISM Planet migration results from the interactions between the planet and the different phenomena acting on its surroundings. The physical processes at work in the case of the Solar System are especially well known, and were widely studied in the 1960s by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz [6]. These authors discovered that the gravitational interactions between the planets (Keplerian motion) lead to an accelerated migration, whereas the magnetic and radiative interactions slow down or even prevent it. When planets are the smallest objects of a system, their migration is referred to as type II migration, whereas for any other planet, it is referred to as type I migration. In the particular case of the Solar System, where there is no solid planet, type I migration is almost always the dominant mechanism. However, in the case of exoplanetary systems, it is the dominant mechanism of migration. The migration process has several stages. Initially, the gravitational interactions between the planets accelerate the migration, resulting in a phase of separation. As they grow in mass, the migration becomes super-Keplerian (type II migration). At this stage, the inward migration is stopped by the so-called type I repulsion (magnetospheric?) associated with the magnetic and radiative interactions. A tridiagonal random matrix is one in which the elements above and below the main diagonal are non-zero but the main diagonal elements are zero. These matrices arise in a variety of scientific applications and, in particular, are important tools for the random coupling of quantum particles. In this paper we study the spectral fluctuations of such matrices in the limit where the size of the matrix goes to infinity and the matrix elements are sampled from abeta-Hermite ensembles with various a parameters. We show that the probability distribution of the spectral eigenstate of such a matrix converges to that of the GOE Tracy-Widom distribution. We also study the eigenfunction correlation function and show that it converges to that of the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble. In the random matrix field, the analogous problem of studying the spectral statistics of real symmetric matrices has a long history. In contrast, very little is known about the spectral statistics of tridiagonal random matrices even for the case of the GOE Tracy-Widom distribution. Our study fills this gap and may prove useful in various applications.

Ideal ization is a powerful tool for understanding the long-time dynamics of dissipationless kinetic ally dominated systems. While much has been learned using linearized theories, nonlinearities typically render the problem intractable. In this paper, we develop a family of exact solutions of the (inelastic) Boltzmann equation, that describes a freely cooling gas with a constant internal energy, for a general cooling law that interpolates between an elastic collisional cooling and an elastic adiabatic expansion. We characterize the solution by an entropy density, from which we derive a closed system of equations for the density and velocity. We demonstrate that for a particular cooling law, the solution exhibits singularities in the form of Dirac deltas in both the density and velocity fields. We confirm these solutions using direct numerical simulations of the inelastic Boltzmann equation, and discuss the implications and possible applications of these solutions to, e.g., the theory of galaxy collapse and galaxy formation.

The Painlevé equations, along with the higher order flow equations of the affine [P($A_{k}^{(1)}$)],[P($A_{k+1}^{(2)})$] and the CKP equations, arise as compatibility conditions for linear over-determined systems of second-order ordinary differential equations [1,2]. These nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are extensively used as integrability conditions for a general class of higher order flows in sigma models with target spaces of diverse geometries. A particular case of these general flow equations are the consistent truncations of the effective action of several unfolded string theories, whose low-energy effective actions are represented by multicomponent generalisations of the KP (mKP) and CKP equations [3]. The initial values of the variables of these integrable systems define ordinary differential equations on complex manifolds, whose target space of initial-value states is endowed with a natural metric known as the geodesic distance (or compatible triple metric) and whose holomorphic cotangent bundle is equipped with a natural metric known as the Non-Commutative (NC) Type II. These integrable systems determine, respectively, integrable systems of nonlinear partial differential equations (NPDEs) and reductions of these integrable systems to differential equations on complex manifolds. It has been shown that there exists a one-to-one correspondence between geodesic-length parametrisations of the initial-value state manifold and complex structures on the corresponding potential target spaces of these string theories. In this paper, we first describe the general solution spaces of the two-dimensional complex generalisations of the affine [P($A_{k}^{(1)}$)],[P($A_{k+1}^{(2)})$] and the CKP equations. These complex generalisations of these integrable systems have been introduced in [4] and admit, as special cases, holomorphic versions of the affine [P($A_{2}^{(1)}$)],[P($A_{3}^{(2)})$] and the CKP equations. We then apply this general result to the consistent truncation of the effective action of several unfolded string theories, including the M-theory and the IIA and IIB string theories. We demonstrate that the zero-redundancy conditions for the potentials of these string theories consistently reduce, in the corresponding geodesic-length parametrisations, to the two-dimensional complex generalisations of the affine [P($A_{1}^{(1)}$)],[P($A_{2}^{(2)})$] and the CKP equations. We conclude by considering the reduced two-dimensional complex generalisations of the affine [P($A_{1}^{(1)}$)],[P($A_{2}^{(2)})$] and the CKP equations. These generalisations are integrable systems that depend on a real parameter and reduce, as special cases, to the two-dimensional complex generalisations of the mKP and the double mKP equations. We present new solutions of these equations that can be related to the special cases of these equations

Around sunspots, loops of moving magnetic flux are observed. A popular model to explain the evolution of sunspots connects the formation of these loops with the eponymous U-shaped structure. In this model, the U-loops are observed to be detached from sunspots and to move with the magnetically loaded material around the sun. Velocities of such moving magnetic feature pairs are reported , and are used to support this model. It is found that the horizontal components of these velocities scale with the width of the corresponding features, while the vertical components scale with the square root of the width of the features, consistent with the magnetic flux tube description. Furthermore, the separation of the pair of features is found to increase at a faster rate than their separation in the initial position, also consistent with the U-loop model. This work was performed as part of the NROLS project and was supported by the French National Program for Scientific Research.

Post-T Tauri stars (PTTs) are semiregular late-type stars similar to T Tauri stars. However, their evolution timescale is significantly longer, of the order of several hundred million years. PTTs are proposed to have formed via the same process as TTauri stars (TTSs), but with additional mass-loss via fast stellar evolution. In recent years, infrared observations have revealed the possible existence of circumstellar disks around PTTs, although not all PTTs show signs of these disks. In this paper we report the discovery of three PTTs with unusual circumstellar dust disks. The anomalous dust disks of PTT2, PTT4, and PTT5, have inner radii of 0.26", 0.43", and 0.12" respectively, as determined from mid-infrared observations. These radii are an order of magnitude or more smaller than those of typical dust disks around PTTs. We speculate that these unusual dust disks may be caused by a planetesimal bombardment event, caused by the passage of a giant planet around the star. We investigate the detectability of such planetesimal bombardment through transmission spectral analysis, finding that PTT2 and PTT4 exhibit significant stellar metallic enhancements, while PTT5 exhibits possible stellar metallic enhancement. We discuss the possible origins of the planet, but cannot distinguish between the theories of dynamical capture, formation in situ, or migration from another system.

Technicolor models with a holographic dual describe the physics at a much higher energy scale than the weak energy scale. If such a model also includes a Hidden Valley symmetry, it can provide a natural solution to the little hierarchy problem. In this paper, we study some modifications of Technicolor models with a holographic dual, with a special emphasis on the Hidden Valley symmetric one. The Hidden Valley symmetry, originally introduced to solve the little hierarchy problem, also ensures the validity of the positive Witten anomaly relation for 2 D fermions and Higgs bosons. By generalizing the fermion representations and the representations of the electroweak gauge groups, we can realize the physical spectrum with both the positive Witten anomaly relation and the Higgs boson beta functions for the coupling constants. We calculate the reflection coefficient s of the electromagnetic process of the model and find that the model can explain the recent experimental results from BTeV, CDF and D0. --- This paper was written by Bin Wang and Joseph Zhang.

In this paper we consider extensions of the nonholonomic Ricci flow that also modify the spatial frame bundle, the fiber s of which can also vary in time. As a general setup, we obtain coupled flow equations for geometry and connection 1-forms on the spatial fiber, which can be viewed as evolving fibrations on spacetime. We call this general setup the nonholonomic Ricci flow. For the special choices of spatial fiber reduction and evolution evolutions, the nonholonomic Ricci flow generalizes several distinct well-known flow constructions in the mathematical physics literature. We focus our investigation on one such case where we obtain coupled flow equations for curvature, torsion, and zero-curvature forms on the spatial fiber, which geometrically are characterized by null evolution equations and structures. We refer to this coupled flow as a null nonholonomic Ricci flow. Such flows have appeared before in the literature in different special cases, but here we present a more systematic approach to construct explicit solutions via a novel algorithmic scheme that we call hierarchic modulation. As a concrete example, we apply this general formalism to construct various classes of solitonic hierarchies, which are used to construct explicit exact solutions to the null nonholonomic Ricci flow. We present one such hierarchy that is equivalent to the highly symmetric self-similar solutions of Einstein and string theory, as well as a second hierarchy that recovers the so-called Lakshmananavisudha solutions of non-linear massless field theories. In our concluding remarks we discuss various directions for future work inspired by the versatility and power of the nonholonomic Ricci flow in treating a broad range of geometric al problems in spacetime, as well as its fundamental limitations. We also discuss the interesting possibility of applying this formalism to other geometric structures in physics and mathematics, as well as to generalizations to higher -order flows and applications to modern discrete data analysis methods in scientific computing. This work was authored by several authors who contributed to different aspects of the work, and we provide individual contributions at the end of the paper. We also thank the Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences for support and hospitality during the programme “Geometric and Functional Analysis with Applications”, where this work was begun.

Asymmetrically charged surfaces experience a net force due to electrostatic interactions. This is commonly observed in nature in phenomena such as adhesion between two objects with different charges, or in the cell membrane and pollution sticks to the surface. In this work, the electrostatic interaction of a uniformly charged plate and an asymmetrically charged membrane is theoretically and experimentally studied. The membrane has one uniformly charged surface and one non-uniformly charged surface. An exact expression for the interaction potential is derived for the limiting case of large plate-membrane distance compared to the thickness of the membrane. The interaction potential is shown to be the sum of the interaction potentials of two uniformly charged plates. The interaction potential is experimentally measured using neutron reflectometry. The measured potential is in excellent agreement with the calculated potential. The first three van der Waals coefficients are extracted from the measured potential and shown to have opposite sign to the sign of the surface charges, as expected from the long-range nature of the van der Waals forces.

, we present K-band imaging of four fields surrounding four QSOs with z>1.2 identified from the SDSS Early Data Release. This is the first deep near-IR imaging of these sources and, coupled with existing B- and I-band imaging from the SDSS, allows color information to be utilized in a study of their morphologies. The observations are consistent with the candidates being host galaxies for absorbed QSOs, in terms of their optical/near-IR fluxes and colors, but deep spectroscopy is required to confirm this. The half-light radii of the hosts are typically larger than 1.5 kpc, consistent with those of local elliptical galaxies and lower than most rich clusters. This may be evidence that the strong absorption systems are located outside the clusters and are associated with the more diffuse component of the cluster dark matter. We use the NSF's ASKER survey data from SXDS in the SSA13 field to carry out this study. ASKER is an IRTF wide field survey which obtained K-band imaging of 14 X-ray bright, Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S) galaxies surrounding four QSO clusters. In addition to the imaging data, we use X-ray and spectroscopic data for the CDF-S, as well as the SDSS galaxy catalog, to study these sources in more detail. We use the photometry and host galaxy colors from the imaging data to confirm the host status of the four bright QSOs and study the morphologies of the hosts, which may be affected by the environments they reside in. We find that the hosts have mostly normal morphologies, consistent with being elliptical galaxies at z~1.2, but with half-light radii of 1.5 kpc, similar to local rich clusters. This may be evidence that the strong absorption systems are located outside the clusters and are associated with the more diffuse component of the cluster dark matter. The host galaxy color information from the imaging data may be useful in a future study.

A comparison of di-pion transitions among the Upsilon(3S), Upsilon(2S), and Upsilon(1S) states is presented. The results are based on a statistical model using the random level-shift-$J/\psi\pi\pi$ model, which describes the total widths and transition couplings between them in a consistent way. The level-shift widths are the Dalitz distributions of the transitions between the states with the explicit form calculated. It is found that the level-shift widths for the Upsilon(2S) to Upsilon(3S) and Upsilon(1S) transitions are large, while that for the Upsilon(3S) to Upsilon(2S) transition is small. Based on this property, we propose a possible di-pion decay mode for the Upsilon(3S) state, i.e., the Upsilon(3S) state can be replaced by the Upsilon(2S) $\pi\pi$ S-wave state. Combining the above observations with other experimental information, we estimate the total width of the Upsilon(3S) state to be approximately 38 - 52 MeV, which is consistent with the recent LHCb measurement.

Stars throughout their lifetime exhibit a wide range of magnetic field topologies. The evolution of magnetic fields has been relatively understudied in comparison to the evolution of other stellar properties, such as mass, radius, and rotation. To study the field’s evolution, we analyzed high-resolution, spectropolarimetric observations of five active magnetic stars in the upper main sequence. The five stars were chosen because they span a range of effective magnetic fields and characterize a variety of surface field strengths. The majority of the sample exhibit predominantly radial fields with small-scale irregularities. Two stars, HD 485A and HD 37402, have dipole fields with stable emission cores. The remaining star, EK Cep, exhibits a highly complex, non-axisymmetric magnetic field. This star also exhibits a long-lived emission core , which is characteristic of its longitudinal field. We find that the distributions of the different field topologies across the sample are statistically indistinguishable. We observe dipole fields with stable emission cores across the sample, even in the rapidly rotating HD 37402. We discuss the implications of the existence of stable dipole fields on mass-loss ratios and angular momentum evolution. Pulsars are widely believed to be the compact remnants of dead stars, and as such, they can be used to map out what is known as a pulsar trajectory in the galaxy. It has been theorized that if a neutron star passes close enough to a black hole, the Shapiro effect could be observed, revealing the nature of the compact object. The clusters in our galaxy are ideal places to find suitable pulsars for such an experiment, as they contain millions of stars, most of which are probably black holes or neutron stars. In this work, I simulate the observable Shapiro effect for a pulsar in the globular cluster M15, and find that for some pulsars, the effect may be observable. Further observations of this effect for a pulsar in the globular cluster M15 could help elucidate the true nature of this phenomenon, and perhaps even the existence of black holes. Recently, the existence of black holes has been inferred via a number of methods, including observations of neutron stars in binary systems. These binary systems are formed via a process known as gravitational wave capture, in which a neutron star and a black hole can evolve into a close orbit due to the emission of gravitational waves. The Shapiro effect, first described in a stunning document responsible for launching both the Russian and American space programs, “Prediction of Experimental Gravitation Shapes” by Ilya Shapiro, elucidates a possible way to observationally confirm the existence of black holes. In particular, it has been proposed that the Shapiro effect could be observed for a neutron star passing close enough to a black hole. The observable Shapiro effect would be the delay in the time of arrival of pulses from a pulsar caused by the space-time distance surrounding a black hole. For a typical pulsar with a period of 1 millisecond, a Shapiro time delay of a few microseconds would be expected for a black hole. This delay could be measured over a period of tens of solar years, depending on the pulsar’s trajectory, the distance of the black hole from the pulsar, and the radius of the event horizon. Shapiro proposed that this delay in the time of arrival of pulses could be measured using low-accuracy clocks and antennae at the Earth, and that it would be detectable for neutron stars in the Solar System. Pulsars are a group of magnetized neutron stars that emit regular beams of electromagnetic radiation. For a neutron star to be detected by an Earth-based telescope, its beam needs to pass near our planet. An online pulsar catalogue contains the positions and properties of around 2200 pulsars. Globular clusters are groups of hundreds of thousands to millions of stars held together by their mutual gravitational attraction, and are found throughout the galaxy. The orbits of neutron stars in globular clusters are determined by their mutual gravitational interaction with the cluster’s contents, so the paths of neutron stars in clusters can be approximated as orbits. A long-standing puzzle in black hole astrophysics has been the relationship between the energy bands of X-rays and infrared (IR), two primary channels of carrying away radiation associated with accretion. Historically, it has been observed that in certain transient events, such as black hole accretion transients (BHTs), the IR and X-ray emissions are closely related. At certain points in time and closely track each other in terms of both intensity and spectral shape, but at other times the X-rays are present without accompanying IR emission and vice versa. The current paradigm explains this pattern as an advection dominated accretion flow (ADAF) present during the IR-only state. However, we demonstrate that this picture can instead be explained by an effect caused by a fluctuation-induced barrier to the propagation of disturbances in an accretion disk. We show that the IR and X-ray light curves are governed by the location of this barrier in the accretion flow, and thus in general the presence of one emission state does not guarantee the presence of the other. We discuss this in the context of recent observations of BHXRT J1650–500, a system with all three states (IR-only, X-ray-only, and overlapping) observed over the same flux range. We show that the overlapping state is the most naturally explained in this picture.

The second of a series of papers based on the observations of the radio polarization in a sample of flat spectrum radio sources obtained with the JVAS and CLASS surveys is presented. The total number of sources with measured position angle and fractional polarization was 62. The possible cosmological implications of the observed alignment between the position angle of linear polarization and the total electric vector position angle are discussed. It is shown that the distribution of position angles, although slightly asymmetric, can be well fitted with a combination of two Gaussian distributions. The fractional polarization is found to be generally low (<10% for the observed wavelengths) with no dependence on the position angle. The degree of polarization was found to decrease with increasing wavelength in a similar manner to what has been previously reported for compact radio sources. Two sources with significant fractional polarization at longer wavelengths and nearly zero fractional polarization at shorter wavelengths are discussed in the paper. hydr The polarization in the JVAS/CLASS flat-spectrum radio sources: II. A search for aligned radio polarizations

A strongly variable Interstellar Medium (ISM) refractive index, J1128+592, has been identified in the ultra-high frequency range (UHF, 540 MHz to 2800 MHz) using multi-epoch VLBI observations. The source exhibits a complex structure on milliarcsecond (mas) scales that can vary significantly on timescales of a few hours. The refractive flux density of the source shows large-amplitude (up to 90%) and rapid (down to 10 min) variations with a variety of timescales. The source J1128+592 is quite similar to 3C84, the most strongly variable source in the sky with a similar angular size, suggesting that the variations seen in J1128+592 are intrinsic. J1128+592 is one of the strongest candidates for a refractive lensing event. The strong variability observed in this source could be attributed to multiple passages through a varying interstellar medium.

In a half-space for a two-dimensional one-component plasma (2D 1CP) the plasma particles are adsorbed on the boundary. In this paper we consider a quantum 2D 1CP and focus on the correlations and sum rules in the half-space. Using the grand-canonical formalism we derive the one-particle density matrix and compute various two-point correlation functions. In particular, we find a rigorous sum rule which relates the integral of the direct correlation function over all frequencies to the total plasma particle number. We support our findings with Monte-Carlo simulations of the corresponding classical 2D 1CP. Introduction Two-dimensional one-component plasma (2D 1CP) is a 2D system of point particles that interact via a long-range logarithmic potential1. They are often simulated with Paul traps2,3, which are basically 2D arrays of charged wires. The charges of the wires control the strength of the logarithmic interaction between the 2D 1CP particles, and changing the charges changes the plasma parameter, $\Gamma = Z_T e^2 / (ak_BT_e)$, where $Z_T$ is the ionic charge, $A$ is the electron charge, $a$ is the 2D unit cell area, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant and $T_e$ is the electronic temperature. For $\Gamma \gg 1$ the system is in the fluid phase, and for $\Gamma \ll 1$ it is in the Wigner crystal phase. For $\Gamma \simeq 1$ it is a two-dimensional Coulomb gas (2DCG)4. Theoretical and experimental work on 2D 1CP has increased significantly during the last decade5,6,7,8,9,10. Compared to 3D 1CP11,2D 1CP has several important advantages. The two-dimensionality reduces screening time and increases coupling, which allows to reach lower plasma parameters. Furthermore, recent experiments on floating graphene layers12 suggest that the 2D Coulomb interaction between the 2D 1CP may be regulated by an external gate13,14, which opens up the possibility to systematically explore the strongly coupled regime. Finally, the point-like nature of the 2D 1CP particles allows for testing theories of strongly correlated phenomena using exact, Monte-Carlo simulations.
