The paper entitled “Bright-Dark Soliton Complexes in Spinor Bose-Einstein Condensates” was published on December 23, 2019 by Jing Li, Ying Li, Hongxia Wang, Shou Zhang, Junpeng Hu, and Xiaoliang Jiang. The authors carried out a complete and thorough theoretical and numerical investigation of the coherent dynamics of bright-dark soliton complexes in spinor Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). Spinor BECs, whose atoms are Bose-Einstein condensate (BECs) of alkali atomic gases, have become a powerful and versatile tool to study and simulate various spinor dynamics. The theoretical and experimental studies of dark and bright soliton solutions in spinor BECs have been extended to the complex domain. In the present paper, the authors obtained the analytical bright-dark soliton complexes, and carried out a detailed analytical and numerical study of their dynamics. The obtained results may be significant for the study of quantum and classical dynamics of spinor BECs.

TbFe(BO3)3 is a material composed of Tb4+ ions with empty 6s shells. Such ions are referred to as rare earth elements (REE) for historical reasons. In contrast to other REE compounds, the magnetic order of TbFe(BO3)3 shows a magnetic order below the freezing temperature Tf = 38 K. The magnetic order is characterized by propagation vectors k = (0,0,1/2) below Tf and (1/2,1/2,0) above Tf. The magnetic structure of TbFe(BO3)3 below Tf can be well described by a simple G-type arrangement of Tb4+ moments which is modulated by the crystallographic ordering waves. The influence of the magnetic structure on temperature, specific heat and magnetization is analyzed in detail. The specific heat data shows two phase transitions at T1 = 14 K and T2 = 38 K. The magnetization vs. temperature data reveals a linear behavior below T1 and an anomalous behavior above T2. The specific heat anomaly is related to the freezing of the magnetic order at Tf = 38 K. The crystal lographic ordering theory is used to analyze the electronic structure and provides a simple explanation of the magnetic behavior of TbFe(BO3)3.

The halo formation model of galaxies argues that galaxies form within dark matter halos, and the clustering of galaxies is related to that of the dark matter. Thus, satellite galaxies in a same halo are expected to have the same properties. But at the same time, satellite galaxies can be contaminated by Interloper galaxies, galaxies that fall into the halo for the first time while the original satellite galaxies were falling into the halo for the second time. The contamination can lead to divergent properties between satellites and interloper galaxyes. We explore this divergence using galaxies in two different halo mass regimes, bright and faint groups, using data from Galaxy Zoo 2 and SDSS. We find that the fraction of interloper satellites increases with the maximum height from the plane of the satellite galaxy to the plane of the interloper orbit, as the orbital energy is lower for more bound orbits. We conclude that while the dark matter clustering traced within dark matter halos is able to reproduce the divergent properties between satellites and interloper galaxies, the processes that drive the interloper fraction dependent on halo orbital energy should also be included.

We present a phenomenological theory for nonlocal interactions in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, which is applicable for an anisotropic pressure distribution with a strong external magnetic field. The nonlocality is expressed in a nonlinear form using auxiliary variables, which naturally separate the filtering and nonlocality effects. In our model, these effects are connected via the Reynolds and Dorch amplification processes. We show that the model has a similar flexibility as the local anisotropic MHD model but with additional Dopplershift and cross helicity currents. The model is applied to the analysis of recent 2D MHD numerical experiments with an imposed kink instability, and we demonstrate that it is able to quantitatively reproduce the nonlinear saturation state of the instability. Introduction The main difficulty in developing a theory for the nonlinear stage of the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) instability, called the kink instability, is a rapid growth of the cross helicity. In particular, in a simple local model of MHD with an anisotropic pressure, the energy containing scales (in what is called the Kolmogorov cascades) are accompanied by an exponential growth of cross helicity at the same rate. This is due to the simple local model that does not distinguish between the filtering effect, i.e. the generation of small scale energy by a large scale shear, and the nonlocality, i.e. the nonlocal interaction between the large and small scales. The rapid growth of the cross helicity leads to an infinite amplifier of cross-helicity fluctuations and a strong modification of the nonlinear stage. In this paper we present a phenomenological model for the nonlinear stage of the kink instability which separates the filtering and nonlocality effects. We show that in some sense this separation is equivalent to taking into account additional large scale flows, which appeared as a result of the cross-helicity amplification. We show that these additional large scale flows destroy the isotropic state of the cross-helicity distribution. We formulate the model in the form of a system of conservation laws for the tensor of Reynolds and Dorch amplification factors. To be specific, we consider a two-dimensional dynamical system, but this approach can be easily generalized to other spatial dimensions. We perform a detailed numerical study of the model with the aid of recent high resolution 2D MHD numerical experiments. We find that the nonlocality effects in the model are able to reproduce the cross-helicity amplifier, the destruction of the isotropic state of the cross-helicity distribution, and the nonlinear saturation of the instability. Our main finding is that the model is able to quantitatively reproduce the evolution of turbulent magnetic and velocity fields in MHD numerical experiments. More specifically, the simulations show a growth of velocity and magnetic field increments with a given slope at the intermediate times, which corresponds to the nonlinear stage of the kink instability. The velocity and magnetic field increments are transferred to smaller scales, and the system tends to an equilibrium state with a constant energy flux

The decay $B_c^- \to X(3872)\pi^-$ was studied via the decay channel $X(3872)\to \pi^+\pi^- J/\psi$ in the Covariant Light-Front Approach. The strong interaction responsible for the $B_c^-$ decay and the decay $X(3872)\to \pi^+\pi^- J/\psi$ was modeled via a effective Lagrangian. The intermediate states containing $B \bar{D}^{(*)}$ and $D \bar{D}^*$ were replaced by rational functions. The energy dependence of the partial wave amplitudes was modeled via a non-linear LFWFs. The partial wave amplitudes were then numerically integrated over the five-body time space. The strong interaction coupling constants and LFWFs were then fitted to reproduce the experimental masses and widths of the $X(3872)$, $\pi^+\pi^- J/\psi$ , and $B_c<unk>-$ decays. The strong coupling constants and LFWFs were sensitive to the regularization parameter in the effective Lagrangian. The value of the strong coupling constants and LFWFs were found to increase and decrease, respectively, with increasing regularization parameter. The obtained values of the strong coupling constants and LFWFs were also dependent on the choice of form for the non-linear LFWFs. An alternative functional form for the non-linear LFWFs was therefore proposed. The alternative functional form also regularized the effective Lagrangian. The effect of the alternative functional form on the strong coupling constants and LFWFs was then studied. The obtained values of the strong coupling constants were sensitive to the choice of form for the non-linear LFWFs. An upper limit for the coupling constant corresponding to the D-D\^\* intermediate states was estimated.

This paper studies post-model-selection inference for multiple response models. We derive an approximation for the distribution of the post-model-selection Nelson-Aalen estimate, which can be used to assess the strength of association between the outcome of interest and a given set of predictors. We then derive an approximation for the distribution of the post-model-selection predicting function, a widely used summary predictor. We show that under regularity conditions, the two distributions only differ negligibly, allowing us to use the former approximation to develop a procedure for estimating the latter's distributional properties, given only a sample of the response variables. Through a number of simulation studies and an analysis of the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian (PLCO) screening trial, we illustrate the practical benefits of our procedures. We provide R code for our post-model-selection predicting function approximation, as well as the raw data and simulation code for the simulations, in the associated R repository (https://github.com/joerish/can-one-estimate).

Recent multi-wavelength observations of neutron star X-ray binaries (NSXBs) have provided new insights into the accretion processes of these compact objects and their circumstellar environments. At X-ray energies, the accretion process and/or the interaction between the compact object and its companion star are often clearly visible. However, at lower energies, a substantial fraction of NSXBs are dim and otherwise hard to detect. In particular, current theory cannot explain the properties of these “transient” neutron star X-ray binaries (tNSXBs), which may include some of the nearest and most massive stars in our galaxy. Here, we report Very Large Telescope infrared and Hubble Space Telescope ultraviolet spectroscopy of two dim tNSXBs in outburst that exhibit strong, variable emission at near-infrared wavelengths. We show that these emission lines can be well modeled with an accretion-disc profile, but with a significant contribution from a fast ($v_{\mathrm{ej}} \approx 0.3 c$) and symmetric wind. This high wind velocity is at odds with models that postulate a magnetospheric radius for the wind capture, but it is consistent with previous measurements of the optical/infrared jet associated with tNSXBs. We also discuss the emission line variability that we detect, which can be better explained if the wind and the companion star orbit around the common center of mass at different orbital velocities and different angles to the line of sight. We speculate that these results may provide a new way to constrain the orbital configurations of tNSXBs and their wind-compressed streamers.

Recent developments in bioinformatics and computational mechanics offer new opportunities to study the function and evolution of macromolecules such as proteins. These studies often require the knowledge of how proteins move and deform in response to external forces. Such knowledge is encoded in the protein normal modes, which can be viewed as quantized versions of protein atoms' motions in response to an externalstimulus. In this work, we develop a numerical framework for computing protein normal modes, where the low-dimensional protein normal modes are obtained by diagonalizing the normal mode mass-matrix, and the normal mode mass-matrix is constructed using input structures via the finite element method. The framework is validated on several systems, and results for the normal mode eigenvectors and energies are in good agreement with previous studies. Application of the framework to Staphylococcal nuclease, a 24-kDa protein that binds and cuts DNA specifically, shows that the predicted normal and twisting modes account for a significant portion of the protein's total fluctuations and thus play important roles in nuclease functions such as binding and catalysis. The software and input structures are available at http://www.bio.umass.edu/ CaptTrp.

The puncture of the renal access (PRA) is an important skill for interventional radiologists. The traditional “wire-pass” technique is highly dependent on the interventionalist's skill and can be technically challenging. We present a novel ultrasound-guided puncture approach that utilizes virtual projection of the ultrasound (US) puncture tract onto fluoroscopic images to aid in needle advancement. Six novice interventional radiologists underwent a right and left kidney percutaneous biopsy, with a contrast-enhanced fluoroscopic image displayed to the operator as feedback. Each participant attempted the PRA at least three times. The puncture path length and path length of the patients with ultrasound feedback were compared to those without ultrasound feedback. Data was analyzed to determine the correlation between the two groups in terms of the time to puncture (TTP), path length, number of twists and number of needle exchanges. The group without ultrasound feedback had a significantly longer TTP than the group with ultrasound feedback (p = 0.03). The puncture path length was also significantly longer without feedback (p < 0.01). The number of twists was also lower in the group with feedback (p < 0.01). There was no significant difference in number of needle exchanges or total procedure time between the two groups. Our ultrasound-assisted puncture technique reduces the total procedural time by reducing the number of twists and improves the success rate and accuracy by increasing the path length of the puncture.

Type-II superconductors undergo a transition to a resistive state above the critical temperature Tc, the Meissner effect. In conventional superconductors, the resistive state is understood as a lossless state, known as the Vinen-WFlagsal state, named after the investigators who discovered it. In a three-dimensional (3D) superconductor, twisted magnetic field configurations known as vortex lines move from regions of higher to lower temperature, thereby forming a Bose-Einstein condensate of bosons. This phenomenon of supercooling was first observed in strongly type-II superconductors in a thin foil configuration. Here we report the observation of a Bose-Einstein condensate of bosons in thin films of the strongly type-II superconductor niobium tin (Nb3Sn). Unlike thin foils, thin films are two-dimensional (2D), and so exhibit 2D supercooling at lower temperatures. We find that 2D supercooling is complete at approx. 20 mK in our thinnest films, corresponding to a critical current approximately 500 times that of the Meissner state. At lower temperatures we observe thermally activated behaviour, and fit the Arrhenius law to extract an activation energy of <unk>100 μeV. We show that this is consistent with the proposed energy gap of the strongly type-II superconductor niobium tin (Nb3Sn), and argue that the large observed critical current is consistent with 3D supercooling in our thin films.

We present new Keck/DEIMOS data for a large sample of MgII absorption-selected galaxies at 0.7<z<1.4. These data allow us to measure velocity widths for a large fraction of the MgII gas in these galaxies at intermediate redshift, and to characterize their evolution with cosmic time. The width of the MgII 2796 absorption lines in these galaxies increases by more than a factor of two from z=0.7 to z=1.4, in excellent agreement with predictions based on the evolution of galaxy velocity dispersions. The velocity width of the MgII lines is largely due to the gravitational motion of the galaxy, with increasing contributions to bulk motions within the MgII gas halo and broadening contributions to thermal and non-thermal motions. The increase in velocity dispersion with time is much more rapid than the increase at lower redshifts, indicating that the cold dark matter model of structure growth has underestimated the early growth of dark matter . We estimate that between 50% and 90% of the total width of the MgII 2796 absorption lines is produced by non-thermal processes. The increase in velocity dispersion is greater at higher mass, with absorption-selected galaxies at z=1 having an effective velocity dispersion of $\sigma=167\pm29$ km/s, only 9% higher than for similarly sized galaxies at z=0. --Jie Lu, Joseph F. Hennawi, Cristian Hopp, Simon P.Driver, Donald P. Schneider, David J. Wilman

In a previous paper1, we described the scaling relations between the properties of galaxies and the masses of central supermassive black holes (SMBHs), that have been found to hold at redshifts up to z=0.89. Here, we present a similar analysis of the local (z=0.36) population, and show that the scaling relations are still very much in force there as well. Specifically, the SMBH masses and the bulge parameters (e.g. velocity dispersion and luminosity) are found to correlate with the properties of the host galaxies, with an offset of roughly 0.75 dex between the SMBH and the bulge masses. In addition, the central supermassive black holes are found to be hosted in almost exclusively by early-type galaxies, as opposed to the situation at higher redshifts. This may have significant consequences for the growth and evolution of supermassive black holes in the Universe.

Flavour-dependent type II Leptogenesis provides a novel explanation for the observed neutrino masses and bi-large neutrino mixing. The seesaw process of type I implies the light neutrino masses are proportional to the smallness parameters in the Yukawa matrices, which can be understood from the perspective of flavoured Leptogenesis. In this theory, CP is violated in the see-saw process, producing a stochastic energy density perturbation in the effective potential for leptons, which is trans-Planckian and leads to a later problem of inadequate cosmological perturbation. However, the flavoured Leptogenesis has an additional weak symmetry , which can ensure that the flavoured CP asymmetry vanishes at the lower order, and a small but non-vanishing contribution to the net asymmetry can be achieved through higher order contribution. In this way, the trans-Planckian problem can be naturally avoided, and the necessary baryon asymmetry can be obtained. Type II Leptogenesis can thus explain the observed neutrino masses and bi-large neutrino mixing simultaneously.

The luminosity function (LF) is one of the most fundamental statistics in cosmology and cosmology. The VVDS type-1 AGN sample represents the largest and most complete spectroscopic sample of active galactic nuclei (AGN) to date. This paper presents the VVDS-deep and VVDS-wide LFs at 2.2, 3.0, 4.9, 7 and 7.7 μm, based on 97, 37, 26, 53 and 20 unique redshifts respectively. We find that the space density of optically luminous AGN (Mλ≥−23.5) is highly correlated with the local redshifts at M<unk>24 and z≤2. The evolution of the faint-end slope is much more pronounced, with the bright-end slope found to be much higher for Mλ<−24, while most models prefer a much shallower evolution of the faint-end slope, suggesting the presence of substantial cosmic variance in the AGN luminosity function, possibly associated with large-scale structure. The effective wavelengths of the different bands sample the rest-frame UV, optical and near-infrared regime at z≤2, the observed frame far-infrared regime at z=2-3 and the rest-frame far-infrared regime at z>3. At all redshift levels, the LFs are relatively similar, suggesting that the bolometric corrections are almost constant at these redshifts. We attempt to fit a simple phenomenological form to the faint-end slope, finding that the evolution is well-described by λ*∝(1+z)−3.0 for z<2, while at higher redshifts we find λ*∝(1+z)−4.9. We also rule out the possibility that the faint-end slope is constant at α=-0.5, finding α=−1.8⪘(Mλ/−23.5)½−0.7 at Mλ<−24. This extreme evolution of the faint-end slope of the AGN luminosity function is driven by the presence of a relatively small number of luminous quasars, with number densities (per unit volume) up to eight times larger at z<unk>2 than today. Such a steep evolution in the space density of optically faint AGN suggests that most actively accreting supermassive black holes are very hard to detect, with most of the growth must have occurred at very high redshifts. The authors are with the VIRGO and VVDS collaborations, based in France and Switzerland. This work was partially funded by the European Union 6th Framework Program n° RITA-CT-2004-505304 & n° 011604 grant to G.P.

Recent studies suggest the existence of a Galactic halo, but it is still not clear whether there is a Galactic central diffuse emission (GCDE) from the Galactic center (GC). To understand the physical nature of the GCDE, we conduct a differential absorption and emission analysis on the ACIS spectra of the region near the GC. We find that the spectra can be well reproduced using a two-temperature plasma model with a collisional ionization equilibrium (CIE) model as a good approximation for the cooler component. The column density of the cooler component is $(2.6\pm0.3) \times 10^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$, which is higher than that expected from the GC region based on the conventional plasma models with a CIE approximation. Such a high absorption column density is naturally explained if the GCDE is emitted by the emission from the bremsstrahlung and line processes scattered and emitted by a population of tenuous and hot plasma in the GC halo. The GC halo population, with a temperature of $\sim$1.7 keV and a density of $\sim$0.2 cm$^{-3}$, is consistent with the prediction of the radiative cooling model assuming a typical pressure in the GC halo. Our analysis suggests that the two-temperature plasma model with a CIE approximation is a useful tool for understanding the GCDE, but the true nature of the GCDE might be more complicated than the two-temperature plasma model with a CIE approximation.

A hierarchical, layered neural network is proposed, in which the connectivity and tuning of each layer are defined by the sparse and dense components of a non-negative latent variable. Sparse codes are encouraged to be localized in each layer by an external competitive layer, and the whole system is trained by maximizing a lower bound on the marginal likelihood. The learning is driven by the competition between two terms: one regularizes the weights with the $\ell_1$ norm to encourage sparsity, and the other enforces the consistency of the local codes through an objective that imposes nonnegative over-completeness on the representation of each pattern in the data. Experiments with two matrix factorization tasks and an experiment on handwritten digit recognition demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model and learning algorithm. Sparse and dense encodings are two powerful paradigms in machine learning, learning representations that efficiently capture key information in the data. In this work, we propose a hierarchical, spiking neural network that learns sparse and dense encoding jointly. In the proposed network, a non-negative latent variable is introduced to each layer, and the network is assumed to have two sparse and dense encodings, which are the sparse and dense parts of the latent variable respectively. The whole network is trained by maximizing a lower bound on the marginal likelihood with two terms: one regularizes the weights by the $\ell_1$ norm, to encourage sparsity, and the other enforces the consistency of the local codes through an objective that imposes nonnegative over-completeness on the representation of each pattern in the data. The proposed model and learning algorithm are applied to two matrix factorization tasks and a handwritten digit recognition task, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model. Matrix factorization (MF) is one of the most fundamental unsupervised learning techniques in machine learning, and it has many applications in computer vision, such as face recognition and land use prediction. To learn the sparse and dense encodings for the MF, a hierarchical, spiking neural network is proposed in this work. The whole network is trained by maximizing a lower bound on the marginal likelihood with two terms: one regularizes the weights by the $\ell_1$ norm, to encourage sparsity, and the other enforces the consistency of the local codes through an objective that imposes nonnegative over-completeness on the representation of each pattern in the data. The proposed model and learning algorithm are applied to two matrix factorization tasks and a handwritten digit recognition task, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model. Two recent deep learning based machine learning approaches, DenseNet and Factorization Machines (FM), are adapted into the spiking neural network by converting the dense neural layers to Poisson spike layers, and all the layers but the final classification layer into spiking layers. In the dense layers, weights are dynamically modeled using a Boolean process through time (BPTT). In the Poisson spike layers, the incoming spikes are processed in Poisson distributed time windows,

NGC 7679 is a luminous infrared (LIRG) composite Seyfert 2 nucleus. It has a broad line region (BLR) and a narrow line region (NLR) with a very large distance of 12.2 kpc from the Earth. It also has two nuclei with separation of less than 10 pc. The distance between the nuclei and the physical size of the two nuclei are all really small compared with the distance between the two regions. We name this galaxy a very close Double Nucleus Galaxy (DDNG). NGC 7679 has been observed in many infrared surveys. The 12, 25, 60 and 100 μm luminosity are about 10.2, 5.8, 4.3 and 3.4×1038 [W] respectively. They are all at the level of LIRGs. The 12, 25 and 60 μm luminosity are not exactly equal and there is a big jump between 25 μm and 60 μm. This is usually interpreted as dust heated by young stars. There is also an active galactic nucleus (AGN) with a bolometric luminosity of 9.1×1039 [W]. The central AGN has two different types of spectrum, a typical Type 1 Seyfert 1 nucleus with a [O III] 5007 emission line and a heavily obscured Type 2 nucleus with no [O III]. A large scale outflow from the Type 2 nucleus with radius of 14.5 kpc was observed by CALIFA. The outflow has super-wind dynamics with an energy of 7.8×1053 [J]. This outflow may provide an alternative explanation for the two different types of spectrum. Based on this argument, the infrared spectrum is best described as an AGN heated by young stars in the center and a superwind in the outer region.

One-way permutations, first proposed by Bjorn Pomeranz in 2012, are functions that, given an input, return a permutation of that input but not vice-versa. For example, the function f(x) = x + 1 is one-way, as 1 is a permutation of x but x is not a permutation of 1. Despite the apparent randomness of permutations, they can be efficiently encoded as integers, and hence the computation of one-way permutations can be thought of as a challenge problem of compression given randomness. In this paper, I develop two protocols for generating one-way permutations, one based on randomness amplified via multitape logic and one based on hypercomputation. The first protocol, which I name the Reverse Tape Algorithm (RTA), allows one to efficiently sample random permutations by building a transducer that compresses a source of randomness (the Reverse Tape) onto a single tape with a precision determined by an algorithm. I demonstrate that, for a broad class of algorithms, this method leads to the generation of one-way permutations in the limit. I name this class of algorithms Reverse Tape Computers (RTC). The second protocol, which I name the Hypercomputation Algorithm (HA), creates one-way permutations by encoding the solution to the halting problem in a sufficiently powerful oracle. I demonstrate that this method leads to the generation of one-way permutations efficiently given access to a sufficiently powerful oracle. I call this class of algorithms Hypercomputation Computers (HCC). I apply these protocols to the generation of randomly generated permutations and to the generation of perfectly random permutations, respectively. I evaluate the randomness and asymmetry of these protocols by comparing them to current best-practice techniques in statistical randomness . My results demonstrate that, while the RTA and HCC are provably related by an information-theoretic reduction, their resulting permutations display quantitative and qualitative differences. I analyse these differences by considering both algorithmic and implementation-related sources of asymmetry. In particular, I demonstrate that the limits of computational randomness, Reverse Tape Randomness and Hypercomputation Randomness produce one-way permutations with surprisingly low algorithmic randomness and high implementation randomness, reverse tape randomness, reverse tape randomness and hypercomputation randomness, respectively. In contrast to algorithmic randomness, however, the Reverse Tape and Hypercomputation have quantifiable degrees of randomness. I conclude by considering applications and open problems for each of the three types of randomness. This paper develops the theory of Reverse Tape Computers (RTC), one model of computation that generates random permutations efficiently, and the Reverse Tape Algorithm (RTA), a method for sampling random permutations via the construction of a transducer that compresses a source of randomness onto a tape. The RTA is an efficient method for sampling from a distribution with a single global source of randomness. I call this class of algorithms the Reverse Tape Algorithm (RTA), which I call the Reverse Tape Randomness. I demonstrate

Reaction systems whose dynamics cannot be described by macroscopic equations, because they are driven into a macroscopically nonexistent state (for instance, a dynamic phase with positive specific entropy), have recently been the subject of intense research activity. An important paradigm in this context is provided by kinetically constrained models, in which a small group of possibly interacting particles performs random walks in order to explore the configuration space. Such models are analytically tractable in one dimension and have been shown to exhibit a very wide range of phenomena, including non-equilibrium phase transitions, dynamical exponents spanning several orders of magnitude, and the absence of Griffiths singularities (insulating clusters of rare secession modes). Despite these successes, important questions remain open, including the critical behaviour of such models near the phase transitions. Here, we show that, near such a transition, the system behaviour is governed by an effective lattice gas model, which exhibits a wide sequence of phase transitions, including both ordinary and extraordinary transitions, and is in a definite sense aimed at criticality. This approach, which is valid for a wide class of kinetically constrained models, is confirmed by an appropriate renormalisation group analysis and numerical simulations, and suggests the existence of a novel universality class.

The standard model of fundamental physics suggests that the universe we see around us is composed of matter and radiation, which interact through four fundamental force - the strong and weak nuclear forces, the electromagnetic force, and the gravity. On cosmological scales, these forces appear to be very well aligned - the gravitational pull of the entire universe is strong sufficient to cause visible galaxies and clusters of galaxies to be attracted towards each other, and the mutual electromagnetic forces between electrons and their negatively charged counterparts, protons, are strong enough to cause atoms to form. Despite this apparent uniformity, we now know that these fundamental constants in the standard model - the strong and weak nuclear coupling constants, the electromagnetic coupling constant, and the gravitational constant - vary in space and time. Through a range of experiments, astrophysics and cosmology, we now understand that these variations are small - the values of these constants have been very similar throughout the history of the universe, with the notable exceptions of the electromagnetic coupling constant and the gravitational constant, whose values have been within 2.2 standard deviations of each other for approximately 12% of the universe's history. This uniformity over time has been referred to as the cosmological uniformity, and forms the backbone of our current theory of cosmology. But in recent years, we have begun to suspect that these constants may not be constant at all, but may instead vary from place to place in the universe. A compelling explanation has been the putative "dark energy", believed to account for approximately 73% of the universe's energy density, which is known to vary in strength throughout the universe, causing its gravitational pull to vary. This pull, in turn, would cause the various fundamental constants in the universe to change in order to keep track of how much energy is available. While the search for dark energy has continued, new er and more precise cosmological data has suggested that the values of these constants may not only vary across space, but may even vary within the same place. For example, in 2013 the PLANCK spacecraft, launched by the European Space Agency, observed the presence of anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background radiation, suggesting that the value of the gravitational constant may have changed by 6.5 parts per million , in addition to small variations in the electromagnetic coupling constant. This is a significant difference between the time of recombination, when the universe was smaller than 1 1% of its present size, and the present time, caused by the variations in the pull of dark energy. In 2015, the DESI experiment, also launched by the European Space Agency, suggested that the fine structure constant - the value of the electromagnetic coupling constant - may have changed by 6.5 parts per million as well, in addition to small variations in the strong and weak nuclear coupling constants. These observations, if confirmed, could overturn the standard model of modern physics. A possible explanation for these observations is the "Standard Model Extension", which extends the standard model of fundamental physics with new fields and parameters that describe possible violations of the standard model's local symmetry - specifically, the symmetry of space itself. MWC 560 is a semi-detached system comprised of a M type giants and an unseen companion star. The MWC 560 system is unique in its ability to exhibit two very different types of highly collimated outflows. A molecular disk wind is observed in optical, near-IR and UV wavelengths. This wind is generated by the decretion disk which is believed to be formed due to the gravitational interaction between the two stars. The observed spectral characteristics of the emitted radiation are consistent with radiation driven outflows. An ion jet and a molecular red jet were first discovered by Corcoran et al. in 1988 and later confirmed by Muzerolle et al. in 1992. Both jets were originally observed in the X-rays. The origin of the X-ray jet is still unclear. In this work, we perform hydrodynamical simulations of the jet in order to study the effect of different parameters on the formation and morphology of the jet. We found that the most important parameter which can influence the morphology of the jet is the acceleration mechanism of the jet particles. In our simulations, we follow the acceleration of the jet particles via two different mechanisms, namely thermal acceleration and magnetic acceleration. We find that although both mechanisms can contribute to acceleration of jet particles, the jet produced by thermal acceleration is unstable and it breaks into knots, while the jet generated by magnetic acceleration is stable and no knots are observed. In addition, we study the influence of the different parameters on the formation and stability of the jet.

In a recent paper [1], a new gravitational theory was proposed, called tetrad theory, which improves the General Relativity (GR) by making the spin of particles an explicit entity, rather than a theoretical abstraction. In particular, in this theory the gravitational field is caused by the gravitational spin of the particles, and not by their mass. This implies that light is always described by the Minkowski metric, regardless of its motion. Here we apply this formalism to the case of the Reissner-Nordstr\"om spacetime, a solution to Einstein's field equations for spherical symmetry which describe an empty spacetime with a metrically singular ball of particles. Einstein coined the event horizon. By introducing the tetrad formalism, the Reissner-Nordstr\"om metric is turned into a NUT metric, which describes an empty spacetime with a metrically singular, singular ring. The singularity of this ring is only evident at the center of the ring, the location of the NUT object, which corresponds to the collapsed mass in the original spacetime. The spin of the particles causing the gravitational field in this case is shown to be the electromagnetic field, and not the Weyl tensor.

Lyman alpha emitters (LAEs) are galaxies with high luminosity at 1216 angstroms due to the emission of Lyman alpha photons. They are extremely important in the epoch of reionization due to their high efficiency in producing ionizing photons. However their low number density makes it challenging to understand their full nature and to characterize the epoch of reionization. Hierarchical models of structure formation, where small scale structures merge to form larger ones, can reproduce the observed galaxy population while inconsistent with current constraints from LAEs. In this work , we explore a new model for LAE formation that utilizes the merger hierarchies from previous works, but modifies the properties of the resultant galaxies. We find that this model is able to reproduce the observed luminosity function and spatial distributions of LAEs, and is inconsistent with current constraints from the epoch of reionization. For more information, please refer to the paper, “Lyman Alpha Emitters in the Hierarchically Clustering Galaxy Formation,” by Houdd al.

is a remarkable non-linear phenomenon in periodic dynamics. This paper rigorously establishes the period oscillation of an adiabatic piston in an infinite rectangular cuboid container with a phase change induced by thermal radiation. For an adiabatic piston, it is well known that the amplitude of oscillation of the top surface area is in direct proportion to the frequency of the applied periodic force. Surprisingly, we show that the period of oscillation is also in direct proportion to the frequency, even when the amplitude is arbitrarily small. The result is a remarkable non-linear phenomenon in periodic dynamics. This surprising discovery is confirmed by three different theoretical models. The physical system under consideration is a rectangular cuboid container filled with an ideal gas and with a adiabatic piston placed on top of it. The container and the piston are both in static and thermal equilibrium at the beginning of the process. The piston is connected to a piston rod, and is free to move up and down along the axial direction of the container, which is fixed in the lateral directions. Periodic oscillations are then applied in the axial direction, with the form of a cosine waveform. The amplitude of this force is constant but the frequency varies from 0 to the maximum value fmax. At this maximum frequency, the piston undergoes simple harmonic motion and the amplitude of the motion is independent of frequency. At lower frequencies, the amplitude of the motion decreases as the frequency decreases but the relationship between these two parameters remains unknown. An analysis of quantum error correction in holographic codes suggests that the error correcting properties of holographic codes rely on the causal structure of spacetime, which may be obscured by environmental influences and forgetable upon observation. By considering the effects of environmental interactions on black hole horizon states, we introduce a model of holographic noise which demonstrates that even in the error free case, the readout of local boundary data is statistically inevitable from an irreducible quantum uncertainty in the description of the horizon. Thus, environmental interactions render precise calculation of local boundary data uncertain, and any expectation of local boundary data is illusionary. While the precise form of the noise model presented here is unlikely to correspond to an accurate model of actual experimental conditions, we demonstrate that this noise model imposes a fundamental limitation on the ability to precisely calculate local boundary data and yields a very natural explanation for many experimental results which have previously been difficult to rationalize. Using data from the KVN and VERA arrays, we present the pre-Keplerian orbital, parallax , and post-Keplerian orbital parameters of the millisecond pulsar (MSP) J1852+0040 in the globular cluster M15. Combined with archival X-ray observations with the Chandra X-ray observatory and theoretical modeling of the magnetospheres of strongly-magnetized neutron stars (NSs), we show that J1852+0040 has a magnetic field of <3.8(4) × 10^8 G at birth, lower than the typical field of ∼10(5) G for radio pulsars. This result is consistent with a scenario in which J1852+0040 is the first example of a “core-collapse” MSP, formed from the direct collapse of a massive star. Magnetars, previously thought to be the only population of recycled NSs with inferred birth magnetic fields <10(5) G, are now known to include a significant number of low-field NSs like J1852+0040.

In this paper, we propose distributed algorithms for spectrum allocation, power control, routing, and congestion control in wireless networks. We consider the case where the wireless links are noisy and bandwidth is a scarce resource, and the goal is to efficiently share the spectrum and utilize the available bandwidth to serve the wireless traffic. We model the wireless network as a connected graph and assign each node a processor from a collection of nodes. The processors are connected via a network topology to the rest of the network. The node processes are able to exchange messages with their neighbors and are able to communicate according to the network topology. We propose efficient spectrum allocation and power control algorithms that guarantee a certain network utility while maximizing the bandwidth available among the nodes. We also propose distributed link-state routing and congestion control algorithms that guarantee a certain network utility while maximizing the bandwidth available among the nodes and utilize the available bandwidth fairly. Our spectrum allocation algorithm, which is based on the market clearing approach, has a convergence time of $O(\log \log N)$, where $N$ is the number of nodes. The corresponding time average allocation is set to within a constant factor. We also propose a fair power control algorithm based on randomized power distribution. The convergence time of the algorithm is $O(\log \log N)$ and the corresponding time average power is within a $O(1/K^2)$ factor of the optimal solution. Finally, we propose a distributed link-state routing algorithm that utilizes the available bandwidth fairly. We analyze the performance of the proposed algorithms and demonstrate the efficacy through simulations.

The interaction between electrons and phonons in graphene is severely restricted by the very light mass of carbon atoms, leading to an extremely weak electron-phonon coupling (EPC) of <unk>0.25 W·K−1. While carrier doping can provide a moderately large Fermi surface, the strong carrier interaction generally weakens the EPC and largely fragments the Fermi surface into pockets. Here, we demonstrate that a doping-induced electronic singularity can substantially enhance the EPC by promoting the effective coupling between electrons and phonons. For both n- and p-type doping, the EPC is greatly enhanced to Γ≈0.25 W·K−1 at the charge-neutral point, with the singular Fermi surface driving an unprecedented logarithmic divergence of the EPC at the Γ=const critical temperature. Notably, the singular EPC is robust even in the presence of moderate carrier interactions, preserving the metallic ground state while opening up a sizable temperature window of dominantly phononic thermal transport. Our findings offer an effective and versatile route to achieve strongly coupled electron-phonon coupling in graphene and graphene systems, which are critical for engineering novel quantum and hybrid devices.

In this paper, we investigate the performance of wireless networks that operate in highly unlicensed spectrum and use packet-forwarding for data transmission. In such networks, nodes can fully or partially observe the transmissions of other nodes, and act as malicious nodes that simply forward the packets for profit. This could cause significant interference to other nodes in the network and degrade the overall performance. To mitigate this issue, we study the coalition formation game, in which multiple nodes decide whether or not to form a coalition and share the cost of forwarders. We characterize the structure of the coalitions, and develop efficient algorithms to find the coalitions with arbitrary accuracy requirements. We apply the developed framework to a simple example and show that our approach yields substantial performance gains over other baseline schemes. Next, we apply our framework to a more complex example and show how it can be used to achieve fully-utilizing clustering in a heterogeneous network. We also study the general scenario with arbitrary network densities and show how the proposed framework can be leveraged to achieve efficient load balancing. Our analysis and simulations show that the developed coalition games can yield substantial gains in terms of throughput and energy efficiency.

In this paper, we consider a generalization of the BBGKY hierarchy to describe the dynamics of systems with long-range interactions. We first derive a multicomponent Brownian equation from the hierarchy and show that the correlation functions of the solutions can be expressed in terms of a few generating functions, which can be solved recursively. In particular, if the interaction is isotropic, the solutions become diagonal and the multicomponent Brownian equation reduces to a system of scalar Brownian equations. We then introduce a Hamiltonian structure to the system and show that the resulting equation is a Hamiltonian system with Poisson equations as components. We also discuss how to obtain conservation laws for the system. We finally apply the results to two physical models of physical interest, such as the FPU and Thomson-elaide models, and present some numerical simulations to support our results. Long-range interactions (LRI) have been observed and studied in many different fields of physics, such as plasmas, plasmas, turbulence, dislocation systems, and biomolecular systems (long-range Coulomb, electrostatic, and van der Waals forces). While much work has been done on short-range systems, there has been very little work on systems with LRI. In this paper, we begin to fill this gap by studying Hamiltonian and Brownian systems with LRI. We start with a short-range system and derive a multicomponent Brownian equation from the BBGKY hierarchy. We then introduce a Hamiltonian structure to the system and show that the resulting equation is a Hamiltonian system with Poisson equations as components. We also discuss how to obtain conservation laws for the system. We apply the results to two physical models, the FPU model and the Thomson-elaide model, and show that the resulting equations have the same form as those in the short-range case, but the parameters in the long-range models are different. Some of the long-range effects, such as non-additivity, become important in the long-range models. Thus, our results can be viewed as a unifying framework for understanding the dynamics of short- and long-range systems and can also be used to study the long-range effects in short-range systems. Recent experiments with dilute quantum gases have demonstrated the control over interactions that is possible with the cooling and the Feshbach resonance. Theoretical descriptions of these systems are often based on a pairwise, or s-wave, approximation to the interparticle potential. While the s-wave is widely accepted to be a good approximation for the scattering length, a constant, $|a_{s-wave}|\gg r_e$, where $r_e$ is the effective range, higher partial waves might be important for determining the equation of state of the system. Here, I use the lowest order constrained variational method to determine the equation of state of quantum systems beyond the s-wave approximation. I present calculations of the equation of state for spin-1/2 fermions using a contact interaction that has a range of $r_e$. The equation of state is compared to the equation of state of an ideal gas and a pairwise, paramagnetic spin-1/2 sigma model. I then present calculations for spin-1 systems using the Hertog correction to perturbation theory to determine an interparticle interaction with a range of $r_e$. The equation of state is again compared to that of an ideal gas and a pairwise, ferromagnetic sigma model. In both cases I use the lowest order constrained variational method to determine the ground state for a range of values of the scattering length from $|a_{s-wave}|\gg r_e$ to $|a_{s-wave}|=0$.

The Blazhko behaviour of RR Geminorum (RRG) is investigated for the first time for a long period of time (7.5 years). The new light curves show the typical characteristics of the Blazhko effect: regular spacings between the dominant and the first and second subdominant modulation, as well as smaller spacings corresponding to the structure of the so-called $F$ mode and the $O$ mode. The light curve analysis shows a linear decrease of the Blazhko amplitude with the decreasing of the star’s pulsation period. This is the first time when the evidence for the linear decrease of the Blazhko amplitude with the decreasing of the star’s pulsation period is found for the first and second subdominant modulations. The nonlinearity parameter and the trial quotient parameters describing the light curves give additional confirmation of the decreasing of the pulsation period with the decreasing of the Blazhko amplitude. RR Geminorum belongs to the class of double-mode pulsators. The light curve analysis shows the dominant frequency $f_1$ = 0.696831 cd$^{-1}$ and the first subdominant frequency $f_2$ = 0.696831 cd$^{-1}$. The frequency $f_2$ is close to the so-called “Blazhko frequency” $f_B$ = 0.673966 cd$^{-1}$. It is the first time when the evidence for the close relations between the frequency $f_2$ and the Blazhko frequency $f_B$ is found for a star with the Blazhko behaviour.

Modern society is evolving towards a distributed intelligence paradigm where individuals and groups of any size and nature can generate, obtain, process and share information in an inexpensive and fast manner. This evolution is fostered by the growth of new communication technologies and the decreasing costs of computing resources, and enables novel interaction patterns that give birth to communities of interacting individuals called crowds. Crowds significantly increase the volume and velocity of information generation and distribution, augmenting the collective knowledge and improve decision-making abilities of groups of individuals. However, at the same time they also introduce unprecedented challenges for managing and securing information flow, including information overload, misinformation, and cyber-attacks. In this paper, we study information diffusion processes in social networks with bias towards the dynamics of information overload and misinformation. We propose a mathematical model of an information dissemination process in a social network, which accounts for dynamical aspects such as re-shares, information bottlenecks, media attention, and other social networks effects. We analyze the impact of exogenous parameters such as knowledge sharing, social reinforcement, and network homophily on the model dynamics. We also analyze the impact of endogenous parameters such as social networks on the model dynamics to identify self-stabilization effects. We validate the model with empirical data from several information overload/misinformation events.

The cosmological constant, also known as the vacuum energy, represents the contribution to the density of energy of the universe from the zero-point energies of the quantum fields, and has been assumed to be positive since the discovery that the universe is flat. However, we show that it can in fact be positive or negative, in accordance to the assumptions of many theories of cosmology and particle physics. If the cosmological constant is positive, then many possible theories that give a natural explanation for its small positive value are excluded. If the cosmological constant is negative, then some of these theories are reinstated. These conclusions are reached by using a combination of observational constraints, coupled with detailed theoretical calculations in specific models. We demonstrate that within the standard model of particle physics, the QCD sum rule gives a naturally small and positive value for the cosmological constant. This reinvestigation of the cosmological constant has the potential for the anthropic solution of the problems of the initial conditions of the universe, and for the explanation of the nature of dark energy.

The simplest model of dark energy with constant equation of state (EoS) constant equal to -1 is the cosmological constant (CC). However, according to experimental data it suffers from the fine-tuning problem and the coincidence problem. Many modifications of CC have been proposed in order to solve these problems. One of them are the so called transient acceleration models. In this model the EoS constant is time dependent and CC only describes the early stage of the universe evolution. The simplest model of this kind is the so called T model. In this paper we consider the T-models with a vacuum component in the dark fluid. This new model describes the universe evolution in the same way as the T-model but, in addition, it explains the observed accelerated expansion of the universe. The article contains a solution of the corresponding modified Friedmann equations and a description of the characteristics of the model evolution. Additionally, we present constraints on the model parameters coming from latest observational data.

In this work, we consider the cosmology in the context of a TeV scale quantum gravity model called universal extra dimension (UED) [1, 2], in which the Standard Model particles are hidden from view by a hidden thick wall with finite extendibility in the extra dimension. In UED, the physical size of the wall is inversely proportional to the scale of the physics, cosmologically this corresponds to a null tension brane which is a sub-Planckian energy density solution. In this scenario, the stable particle in the bulk can act as dark matter. In this work, we focus on a class of models with a U(1) darkphoton and two singlet neutrinos, with the latter acting as hot dark matter. We compute the dark matter relic density considering thermal freeze-out, via a Boltzmann equation approach. We consider both a Left-Handed and a Right-Handed neutrino scenarios, and investigate the effect of the active-sterile mixing angle on the relic density. In the Right-Handed neutrino case, we find that there is a region of the parameter space that gives the right dark matter density whilst remaining consistent with the collider and cosmological observations.

Optical pulse propagation in natural materials usually gives rise to pulse self-steepening and nonsoliton pulse compression is often observed. The existing theories based on either Kramers-Kronig relations or group-velocity dispersion fail to explain the existence of different scaling laws in different frequency regions for the pulse self-steepening and pulse compression. Here we show that the nonsoliton pulse compression can be explained by the existence of cascaded quadratic nonlinearities, which exhibit different scaling laws in different frequency regions. The scaling law in the region that the pulse width is much larger than the pulse center-of-mass wavelength coincides with the scaling law of the usual pulse self-steepening and pulse compression. However, in the region that the pulse center-of-mass wavelength is much larger than the pulse width, we show that the initial pulse width can be compressed to a self-similar nonsoliton form with a factor of two difference from the initial pulse width. The existence of a scaling law for nonsoliton pulse compression is consistent with the observed pulse compression in many materials and may provide an avenue to generate nonsoliton pulses with a similar scaling law for potential use in pulse metrology, time-stamp and micro-manipulation.

Maximum weighted edge biclique is a fundamental problem in combinatorial optimization. It has numerous applications in wireless networks, financial markets, system reliability, and scheduling. Despite its importance and the long history of studying it, the problem remains wide open and extremely challenging. In this paper, we present several new inapproximability results for it. Specifically, we prove that even approximating the maximum weight edge biclique to within a factor of 2 is strongly NP-hard, and within a factor of 1.2858 is fixed-parameter intractable under the truthful parameter reduction. We also show that it is unlikely to be fixed-parameter tractable, even if the algorithm has access to an additional parameter that reflects the edge weight distribution of the input graph. In addition, we apply our techniques to obtain inapproximability results for several related problems, such as computing a maximum weight disjoint cycle cover and a maximum weight maximal matching containing a given graph factor.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) provides the most detailed information about the history of the universe to date. It encodes a nearly complete blackbody spectrum imprinted with initial conditions at the moment of last scattering, some 0.5 billion years ago. The statistics of this initial conditions preserve a close imprint of the Gaussian fluctuations present at the time of last scattering. However, the evolution of these fluctuations proceeds somewhat differently in different regions of the universe, due to intrinsic inhomogeneities in the initial conditions, cosmological distances, and cosmological processes intervening between the epoch of last scattering and the current epoch. These intrinsic differences lead to a degradation of the tensor-to-scalar ratio for measurements of the microwave sky and hence a loss of information about the full initial conditions tensor perturbation field. The best current analysis suggests a limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio of r < 0.07 at 95% confidence level, corresponding to a limit on the intrinsic inhomogeneities of the initial conditions on size of the microwave sky of a few hundred thousand million light-years.

We present a set of catalogues of simulated galaxies with which galaxy shape measurements in cosmological simulations can be compared. Galaxies are placed at a range of distances with a range of properties (e.g. axis ratios, triaxialities, inclinations, merger histories, colors). The catalogues have been built to make it straightforward to produce a set of realizations that span a range of parameters. We present a method for fitting these galaxies to models that have different parameters, with a minimization method that efficiently explores the parameter space. We apply this method to a sample of galaxies from a S0 galaxy at the heart of a groupfinder Hicksachs group, finding that ϕ=20° and Q=0.8 provide an acceptable fit to the data. We make these catalogs and the code to fit galaxies to the sample available to the scientific community. Formed from mock galaxy samples, the GEMS catalogs enable galaxy shape measurements and fit to cosmological simulations. The catalogs are available for free download from https://gemsgalaxies.wordpress.com/gems/. The GemSim galaxy shape measurement code, along with examples of how to apply it to observations and simulations, is described at https://github.com/michael-virani/GemSim. The catalogs and code are expandable to enable measurements of higher order galaxy shapes, as well as fit to other galaxy properties (e.g. stellar populations). Lithium is destroyed at high temperatures. This makes the presence of lithium useful for determining the ages of stars. The turn off stars in a globular cluster have reached the end of their life and no longer produce lithium. By looking at how much lithium is present in these turn off stars we can determine how old the cluster is. We obtained high dispersion spectra of the lithium abundances of the turn off stars in the globular cluster 47 Tuc using the Apache Point Observatory 3.5 m telescope. These spectra cover the region of the Li doublet at 6708 Å and are sufficient resolution and quality to determine the lithium abundances of the stars. We found wide variations in lithium abundance between stars. The lowest lithium abundances are present in stars that are metal rich or significantly metal poor. The highest lithium abundances are found in stars with moderate to high metallicity. These results are in line with predictions from current model of Galactic chemical evolution. We propose a new model that includes a variable depletion rate for lithium.

The star OO Serpentis is a young star of the class of Be stars. It has an orbiting dust decretion disk and an eruptive counterpart which is visible from the ejection radiation. In this paper, I describe the outburst of this star between 1995 and 2006, which was followed from 2005 by a period of low activity and since 2012 by a new outburst. Using infrared observation from Spitzer and mm observation from ALMA, I study the properties of the ejecta and its environment, which allow me to put forward a model of the outburst and the evolution. Indeed, we see since 2005 that OO Serpentis entered in a new phase of low activity, which did not stop the formation of new ejecta. During this time, the dust decretion disk moves away, then reaches a quiescence distance at 2.5 A.U. from the central star. In 2012, the outburst again becomes visible. From the infrared observation, I show that the brightening of the star led to the ejection of new ejecta and an enhanced rate of ejection for the whole period of outburst. Using the mm observation, I characterize the ejecta and the density of the medium around the outburst. I put forward a model of the ejection of the ejecta, based on the variation of the dust decretion disk of the star, which explains the sequence and the temporal correlation between the dust and the ejecta.

Next-to-leading-order corrections to exclusive processes in $k_T$ factorization are presented. The corrections are obtained by computing the associated NNLO corrections to the associated three-body process, i.e., the parton shower, taken at next-to-leading order. The corrections are applied to the inclusive Wjj, Z+jets, and top-pair production processes at the LHC. The corrections reduce the theoretical uncertainties of the associated production processes and hence enhance the experimental sensitivity of these processes. Here, “exclusive processes" refer to processes with one hadron in the initial state and at least two hadrons in the final state. Wjj production is characterized by the presence of a hadronic W-boson and two tagging jets, while a Z+jets process is characterized by the presence of a hadronic Z-boson and at least two jets, and a top-pair production process is characterized by the presence of a top-quark and at least two jets.

In this paper, we present a quantum-like representation of extensive form games. This representation allows us to solve two classical problems: (i) computing the optimal strategy, i.e, the value of the game; and (ii) computing the core, i.e., the set of Nash equilibria. Our representation of a game with a density matrix allows us to solve these two classical problems using linear algebra techniques, without any iterative method. The effectiveness of this representation is illustrated on a wine tasting game, where several humans have to taste wines using a 10 point scale. We also show that in some cases, our method allows us to compute a Nash equilibrium point, even if this equilibrium point is not computed by most classical methods. Useful link to find wine tasting game: https://web.archive.org/web/20180827090151/https://konekt.kapsi.com/web/game/wine-tasting-game

The hot white dwarf companion to Sirius B recently announced to have a planetary orbit may have actually been a brown dwarf rather than a planet after all. When imaging the sky with the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher (HARPS) spectrograph at the European Southern Observatory's La Silla observatory in Chile, a 2.2 Jupiter -sized companion was detected in a 24 hour period, extremely close to the edge of a 4.7 day revolution of its host white dwarf. This planetary system, although within the limit for ejection by the Sirius B white dwarf through the General Relativistic Paczyński-Wiita effect, seems to have survived ejection with minimal perturbation. The dynamics of the system imply that the original orbit of the planet had a highe eccentricity of 0.93 and an initial semi-major axis of 1.76 au, far too close to the white dwarf for stability. The planetary evolution is believed to have followed a dynamical instability leading to a chaotic reorganization of its orbit, leaving the system with the present stable configuration. The common envelope evolution of Sirius B has thus been initiated by this recent announcement.

A kinetic and kinetic study of the ring conformers of cycloalkanes byCBS-QB3 calculations is presented. The activation barriers for the chair, boat, and half-chair conformers of cyclohexane are predicted to be 22.4, 22.7, and 35.5 kcal mol-1, respectively. The corresponding barriers for cycloheptane and cyclooctane are predicted to be 31.8 and 43.2 kcal mol-1. These results are in good agreement with experiment and other CBS-QB3 calculations. The intrinsic barriers obtained for the chair conformer of norbornane and half-chair conformers of cyclohexane are predicted to be 25.0 and 33.6 kcal mol-1, respectively, in good agreement with experiment. The large difference between the intrinsic barriers of the chair and half-chair conformers of cycloalkanes is discussed. The zero-point energy and thermal corrections are found to have a significant effect on the ring conformer heights. The rates for cyclohexane and norbornane at 200 degrees C are predicted to be 1.05 x 10-12 and 3.39 x 10-13 cm3 molecule-1 s-1, respectively, by using the modified Kamal equation. These results are in good agreement with experiment and other CBS-QB3 calculations. The intrinsic barriers of cyclohexane and norbornane are predicted to be 36.0 and 39.1 kcal mol-1, respectively. The former is consistent with the difference between the barriers of the chair and half-chair conformers, and the latter is consistent with the experimental intrinsic barrier of cyclohexane of 39.7 kcal mol-1.

The mass of a planet is one of the most fundamental characteristics of a planet. Planets are classified as either'super-Earths' or 'gas giant planets' based on their sizes and compositions. Gas giant planets are made of hydrogen and helium, in addition to other light chemical elements. The standard model used to explain their compositions postulates that the planets attained their gaseous state after developing cores of rock and metal through the process of core accretion. This standard model, however, has significant problems in explaining the masses of a large number of exoplanets whose host stars have very similar characteristics to the Sun. In particular, the distribution of exoplanets with initial orbits near their host stars and those with initial orbits farther out, do not show the expected division between super-Earths and gas giant planets. This discrepancy, termed the inward migration problem, has led to the proposal of different solutions. In one proposed solution, planets in the early stages of evolution are pulled towards their host stars by the angular forces of forming gas disks. If a forming planet's initial orbit is sufficiently near its host star, the planet's gravity is able to clear its initial gas disk. However, this early phase of migration, dubbed 'Type II migration', leaves an imprint on the planet's final mass. Planet migration and structure are intimately related. Therefore, understanding the early phases of migration is important for understanding planet structures as they evolve. In this study, I present the results of a large number of Type II migration simulations designed to examine how the early phases of migration affect a planet's final mass at the end of the migration process. The formation locations of the planets span the range from those that are close to their host stars to those that are far from their host stars. The mass ratios of the planets span a wide range from 0.1 to 0.5. By comparing the migration rates and structures, I found that the formation positions of planets do have an effect on the mass of the planets. Planets that started close to their host stars, but migrated farther out, end up as low mass super-Earths, while planets that started further away from their host stars ended up as gas giant planets. I propose that this dichotomy in final masses is a result of the dynamical effects of multiple interacting planets, known as Lindblad resonances, that form during the early phases of migration. The extent to which a planet stirs up particles in a disk is proportional to its Hill radius, which is also the distance at which a planet's gravitational force penetrates into the disk. Lindblad resonances, the locations where a planet's Hill radius is equal to the radial separation of adjacent disk particles, occur at separations of almost two-thirds and one-half of the planet's Hill radius. In most cases, Lindblad resonances form first between the planets and the particles in the disk residing at the same locations. These interactions stir up additional particles in the disk, increasing the scale height of the disk at those locations. Because the planets' gravitational force

The Dicke model is an exactly solvable model of quantum many-body physics, which describes a collection of N two-level systems, or qubits, all of which are in the same quantum state, interact with each other through dipole-dipole coupling, and are subject to an external driving field. The model exhibits a quantum phase transition from a normal phase to a cooperative phase as the dipole-dipole coupling strength exceeds a critical value. As an exactly solvable model, the Dicke model has been extensively studied and is well understood, but its extension to an N-qubit model with general multipolar interactions is significantly limited. In particular, such general multipolar interactions are found to lead to rich quantum phases beyond the simple cooperative phase of the Dicke model, including a subradiant phase with non- vanishing expectation values of the excitation number operator and a Luttinger liquid phase with continuously varying correlation functions. Here, we present a method to characterize these phases, with an emphasis on the identification of the Luttinger liquid phase, based on the parafermionic quantum field theory developed by Abanov and Wiegmann. We apply this method to a specific family of Dicke models with multi-dipole interactions and general dipole-dipole coupling. We find that the Luttinger liquid phase can be accurately captured by a low-level truncation of the parafermionic field theory, but the subradiant phase is not described correctly. This example illustrates the utility of the parafermionic quantum field theory as a method to characterize phases beyond the cooperative phase of the Dicke model, and further investigation may reveal its broader applicability.

Explanations for the alignment of the major axes of galaxies with their spin axes, such as observational biases, imply that galaxy discs are not randomly oriented in space. However, previous measurements of the orientations of galaxies have been averaged over large volumes of space, and are therefore not suitable for detecting coherent alignment on small scales. We calculate the orientations of galaxies within their large-scale cosmic environments using a sample of 50,000 bright galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7. We use the positions of satellite galaxies around these galaxies as a probe of their local cosmic environment, and find that the distribution of satellite galaxy locations is strongly anisotropic. This is consistent with previous observations that galaxies tend to be aligned with the large-scale structure in which they are embedded. We find that the major axes of satellite galaxies are preferentially aligned with the direction of the large-scale structure to which their central galaxy is most closely bound, but that the distribution of orientations is only consistent with isotropy at the 98% confidence level. This anisotropy is most likely caused by interactions between galaxies and their dark matter hosts, as the inverse of the alignment with the large-scale structure persists even when controlling for galaxy shape and other properties.

The current status of the analysis of systematic uncertainties in hadron parameters obtained by the QCD sum rules is presented. We consider the dependence of the results on the Borel window and on the quark condensate parameter. We discuss the treatment of the perturbative contribution in the analyses and estimate its effect on the quality of the results. We show how the method of QCD sum rules enables us to reduce the impact of some of the sources of uncertainty by using additional information on the spectral density. We illustrate the method of QCD sum rules based on the example of the determination of the strangeness magnetic moment of the proton. M. A. Shifman, A. I. Vainshtein and V. I.
