A phase-separated regime with both a BCS and a BEC superfluid phase is realized in a two-component Fermi gas with tuned $s$-wave scattering length by strongly modulating the atom number or the interaction strength. We use time-of-flight imaging to detect the inhomogeneity of the superfluid order parameter and show that the spatially dependent gap features a mixture of a uniform BCS superfluid and a uniform BEC superfluid. This phase separation directly reveals the crossover between Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) superconductivity and Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC). We determine these phase boundaries by measuring the stability of the system and observe that the BEC phase survives up to more than three times the critical temperature of the uniform BCS phase. Our approach provides new avenues to study quantum phase transitions in both superconductors and antiferromagnets. cataly abstract: A phase-separated regime with both a BCS and a BEC superfluid phase is realized in a two-component Fermi gas with tuned $s$-wave scattering length by strongly modulating the atom number or the interaction strength.

We present a tight binding model to study the optical absorption properties of semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs). The total electron Hamiltonian includes a uniform background electrostatic field and a short-ranged potential arising from the confinement in the NCs that we treat within the effective-mass approximation. We numerically evaluate the optical absorption spectra and demonstrate that it accurately describes the Mie theory results in the limit of the large NC size. Furthermore, we develop an analytic solution of the infinite NC size limit that can be used to efficiently evaluate the absorption spectra of small NC systems. We apply our approach to study the optical absorption in PbSe 2 nanocrystals and show that the observed blueshift of the absorption edge is caused by the quantum confinement and, at large wavevectors, can be well fitted by the 2D Fabry-Pérot model. We finally discuss some implications of our results for the optical studies of plasmon hybridization and screening in nanostructures and semiconductor interfaces.

a simulation of superhumps in the context of the Doppler map is presented. The density distribution in the accretion disk is calculated with the water waves approximation. It is shown that the density wave generates superhumps which are observed as a profile variation in the Doppler map. It is found that the variation period of the superhump is proportional to the mass of the compact object in the binary system. The periods of observed superhumps in four HU superoutbursts in 2006-2007 and two normal outbursts in 2005 and 2010 are successfully explained with this model. The model proposed in this paper can be applied to HU superoutbursts observed in 2006-2007 and normal outbursts observed in 2005 and 2010. The periods of observed superhumps in these superoutbursts are proportional to the mass of the compact object. It is well known that superhumps are observed in HU dwarf novae during a superoutburst. The superhumps are gravitational wave-like perturbation induced by an density wave in the accretion disk. The density wave is most likely caused by strong thermal/pressure instability in the accretion disk. Comprehensive simulations of superhumps with extensive comparisons with observation are still insufficient. In this paper, we carry out simulations of superhumps by using a simple model of the accretion disk with the density distribution in the accretion disk as a profile variation in the Doppler map. The density distribution is calculated by the water waves approximation. The density wave generates superhumps which are observed as a profile variation in the Doppler map. We find that the variation period of the superhump is proportional to the mass of the compact object in the binary system. The periods of observed superhumps in four HU superoutbursts in 2006-2007 and two normal outbursts in 2005 and 2010 are successfully explained with this model. We propose a new interpretation of the orbital period - superhump period relation. The relation can be explained by assuming that the superhump period is related to the orbital period at the outer edge of the density wave. We assume that the density wave is generated at the outer edge of the resonance radius. We also discuss application of the model to intermittent superhumps. This model can explain the periods of observed superhumps in four HU superoutbursts in 2006-2007 and two normal outbursts in 2005 and 2010.

Renormalized quantum Yang-Mills fields in curved spacetime are discussed. A simple vacuum state, that satisfies the covariant principle of minimalRTQUANTUM ethosuppression, is obtained via a generalized DeWitt-Schwinger representation in terms of a convolution of a curvature-dependent mass term with a solvable Gaussian model. The model is free of ghost and unstable degrees of freedom, and the stability is confirmed by both direct computations and detailled analysis of pole structure. The model is applied to study quantum aspects of Schwarzschild spacetime, and correct classical results are reproduced. The model can be extended to study quantum effects of black holes. This paper discusses renormalized quantum Yang-Mills fields in curved spacetime. The model is constructed via a generalized DeWitt-Schwinger representation in terms of a convolution of a curvature-dependent mass term with a solvable Gaussian model. This model is free of ghost and unstable degrees of freedom and satisfies the covariant principle of minimal quantum ethosuppression. It is applied to study quantum aspects of Schwarzschild spacetime, and correct classical results are reproduced. The model can be extended to study quantum effects of black holes. The paper studies the invariance properties of the linear parabolic equation in n spatial dimensions x'=A(x) under the transformation of the independent variables x and the solutions x, where A is a matrix whose eigenvalues are all zero. We establish the complete invariance under the Galilean transformation and the scaling transformation, in the case n≥2, and the Galilean invariance in the case n=1. We also establish the invariance under the transformation of the form x→λ(x), where x is an eigenvector corresponding to the zero eigenvalue of A satisfies λ(x1,…,xn)=0, and the invariance under the transformation xT−x for all vectors x. As an application of the results, we prove the existence of conservation laws for this equation. This paper presents a novel approach for person identification based on using image attributes. Given a query image, our method first finds similar images in the large image dataset, and then computes visual attributes from these similar images. These visual attributes are then used to train a machine learning model to identify the person in the query image. We evaluate our approach on two public benchmarks. The first is a human face recognition dataset LFW, and the second is a human identification dataset MultiFID. Our approach achieves the state-of-the-art result on the LFW dataset, and performs favorably on MultiFID with less parameter number and computational cost. We also conduct an user study to qualitatively show the advantage of our approach over prior approaches. Our approach is general and can be applied to other person identification tasks by simply finding the right image attributes. The visual attributes can be generated using various existing image analysis techniques such as deep CNN models. The image attributes can also be customized to fit specific person identification tasks.

Popular songs become popular for a variety of interrelated reasons. A song can achieve commercial success through a combination of intrinsic qualities, such as catchiness and pleasant listening experience, and extrinsic qualities, such as good placement and promotion by the record company and the artist. In this paper, we study the emergence of popularity from the dynamics of collective choice, that is, the number of plays a song receives on streaming platforms. We develop a simple agent-based model to mimic the streaming process, in which songs are recommended to the users by the platform based on their past listening patterns and tastes. The algorithm to generate playlists is based on a simple learning rule, in which popular songs are rewarded and the algorithm is able to learn further. We study the model using stochastic simulations and find different phases of popularity evolution, from popular to mainstream, that agree with the known trends in music history. Our model, which we call the "Popularity Mechanism," can explain how and why some songs become hits.

A high phase coherence in a superconductor can be disrupted by a magnetic impurity. A spects of such impurity effects on the superconducting correlation function provide information about the energy spectrum and the character of low energy excitations in the system. In this paper, we present a scheme to study the Cooper pair mass spectroscopy and the mobility in a superconductor by using a junction geometry. The rf frequency dependence of the density of states is obtained by measuring the absorbed power as a function of frequency. The energies of the bound states in the junction are measured from the superconducting energy gap, $\Delta_0$, via the temperature dependence of the critical current. The mobility in the superconductor is extracted from the Shaloms-Meyerhof model for the tunneling rate through a barrier into a thin film superconductor in the limit of strong interface reflections. We present measurements of the rf frequency dependence of the density of states and the Shaloms-Meyerhof model for the tunneling rate in a high-temperature superconductor thin film in the normal state over a temperature range 1.3 K to 20 K. We have studied the thin film of the high-temperature superconductor YBa2Cu3O7-δ (YBCO) with a width of 1.5 mm and thickness of 35 nm. The length of the junction was 0.4 mm.

Transit surveys have proven to be a valuable method of discovering exoplanets. As a result, many major transit surveys have been conducted in the search for exoplanets. Among these, the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) is one of the most prolific and wide-field. The survey has covered several hundred thousand square degrees of the sky, leading to the discovery of over 300 new exoplanets. Of particular interest to this work are the over 100 giant exoplanets found by the OGLE survey, many of which are Population II exoplanets that would have never been found by any other technique. The new discoveries from the OGLE survey provide a unique view into the formation and evolution of planetary systems, as well as a baseline for follow-up studies of planets with potential signs of habitability. Additionally, many planets with good enough follow-up for atmospheric studies have been found by the OGLE survey. The planet yield of transit surveys depends on many factors, making it difficult to predict exactly what a survey will find. By analyzing the known population of OGLE planets, we can statistically understand the planet yield of the survey and how it depends on different parameters. We use this to provide estimates of the yield of the OGLE survey and how it will change in the future. We also present a method for interpreting the yield of a survey and deducing which parameters affect the planet yield. This has utility in planning future transit surveys and identifying changes that need to be made to increase their yield.

Elasticity is an important property of materials, and the quantification of the material's elasticity is an important goal in materials science. In a recent paper [1], we presented a study of the nonlinear elastic properties of model isotropic granular packings through the measurement of the minimum stress deviation about the average stress-strain curve. We demonstrated that these packings are extremely "inelastic", with their nonlinear elastic regime being almost completely flat and featureless. In this paper, we explore the reasons for this inelasticity. We show that this behavior is due to an essentially random arrangement of "force chains", which are locally aligned hyperstatic stress-bearing structures. These force chains are formed by grains that are loaded with large force deviations, which are then spread to their neighboring grains through contacts between them. These force chains provide the solid-like response of the granular packings, even in the nonlinear elastic regime. We further show that the evolution of these force chains in response to applied local stress variations is responsible for the inelasticity of the packings. This behavior is not captured by any of the commonly used elastic models, and therefore, the quantification of the elastic properties of these packings must take into account their force chain structure.

Finite-element calculations and experimental investigations of a turbulent shear flow in the presence of nonlinear two-way coupling between the velocity fluctuations and the dynamics of a passive scalar are presented. The dynamical variable is the symmetric part of the phase-space density of the passive scalars. For weak coupling, the Lyapunov spectrum is almost that of the uncoupled case, whereas for strong coupling it exhibits a nonzero gap corresponding to the Benjamin-Feir instability. For a dynamical system consisting of two coupled van der Pol oscillators, a region of multistability, where several spatially separated steady states exist, is found for intermediate values of the coupling strength. Amid-infrared waveguide light nulling experiment using single-mode conductive waveguides is reported. The conductive waveguide is fabricated on a oxidized silicon wafer using a modified single mode periodic poling technique. It is measured that the waveguide has a single-mode operation with a waveguide core of ~3 μm in diameter and a normalized cutoff frequency of ~200 THz. In order to demonstrate the waveguide light nulling capabilities, the waveguide is integrated with an optical array and used to transmit a mid-infrared beam. The transmitted beam is observed to be nulled with an incident-beam intensity of ~10-7 W/μm2 at a wavelength of ~3.5 μm, and maintains a >10-6 nulling ratio over a 30-μm field of view. The results presented in this letter represent the first successful transmission of a mid-infrared laser through a conductive waveguide and the first demonstration of single-mode mid-infrared waveguide light nulling using a conductive waveguide.

Solar system analogs are planets that orbit around a star very similar to the Sun. Identifying these planets is important because the environments in which Earth-like planets develop are likely to give rise to life similar to our own. However, before life can emerge, these planets must first form, and detecting these planets allows us to learn more about how they form. We report the detection of four planets with orbits similar to that of Earth around the star catalogued as α Cen A. This star has many properties that make it a good candidate to have planets, including the nearest star to the Sun with an apparent stellar companion. Comparing the properties of the planets around α Cen A with those of Earth enables us to evaluate how likely these planets are to have surface water and therefore the potential for life. We also present evidence for a fifth planet with an orbit similar to that of Earth around the star β Cen. This star has properties that make it an even better candidate to host planets, including the closest star to the Sun that is not a binary system. β Cen has no confirmed planets but the claimed detection of an additional planet around the star may indicate that β Cen hosts a multiple planet system that could be a target for future observations with next-generation instruments.

In this paper, we show that in the Hamiltonian description of N=4 supergravity, the Lagrangian of ordinary massive hypermultiplets and the Lagrangian of partially massless hypermultiplets are obtained from the same seven-dimensional manifold. This remarkable result reveals a deep connection between two seemingly unrelated theories: massive and partially massless four-dimensional field theories. We further show that this connection has a beautiful supersymmetric realization: a nonlinear real super transformation maps one Lagrangian into the other. We expect this result to have far-reaching consequences for the understanding of these theories and their mutual relationships. This work was originally published on arXiv.org on September 29, 2019. We consider the Hamiltonian description of N=4 supergravity coupled to massive and partially massless hypermultiplets. In particular, we show that in a certain singular limit, the Lagrangian of ordinary massive hypermultiplets is obtained from the same supersymmetric seven-dimensional Lagrangian as the Lagrangian of partially massless hypermultiplets. This remarkable result reveals a deep connection between two seemingly unrelated theories: massive and partially massless four-dimensional field theories. We further show that this connection has a beautiful supersymmetric realization: a nonlinear real super transformation maps one Lagrangian into the other. We expect this result to have far-reaching consequences for the understanding of these theories and their mutual relationships. We analyze this result in more detail in the main text. Here, we provide an abstract and a short list of references. In this work, we combine experimental data and theoretical modeling to investigate the in vivo behavior of DNA looped protein complexes. Looped complexes have been designed to activate expression of genes in human cells1,2, and to inhibit gene expression via homologous recombination3,4. Both applications require stable complex formation in the cell nucleus, which has led looping nucleic acids (LNAs) to become leading inhibitors of gene expression5. Despite their commercial success, the in vivo behavior of DNA looped proteins remains enigmatic, owing to limited biochemical tools to explore it and conflicting experimental evidence. Here, we use three independent techniques—FRAP, SLIC, and photoactivation recovery—to measure the diffusion rates of six protein-LNA complexes in the cell nucleus, ranging from 0.018 to 0.14 <unk> s−1. Surprisingly, these diffusion rates are an order of magnitude slower than expected for freely moving proteins in the cell nucleus. To rationalize our observations, we develop a new theoretical model of looped complexes that incorporates single-molecule parameters7, nucleosome positioning8, and in vivo affinities9 , as well as a macroscopic model of biomolecular reaction kinetics. The model qualitatively accounts for the three independent measurements and correctly predicts, for the first time, in vivo complex lifetimes of looped DNA-protein complexes. Thus, our study unites experimental and theoretical approaches to elucidate the in vivo behavior of looped DNA-protein complexes.

The majority of galaxies in the present-day universe do not exist in isolation, but rather within larger groups and clusters. These environments have a profound impact on their evolution as galaxies, triggering or truncating the star formation, altering the evolution of their structural components and ultimately dictating their final morphology and colours. While numerous studies have examined the role that the environment plays in shaping the evolution of the galaxy population as a whole, a complete evolutionary picture requires knowledge of how the galaxies in a given population, selected based on their intrinsic properties, have assembled their masses. In this respect, an important milestone in the evolution of galaxies comes about 8 billion years ago, in conjunction with the peak of the stellar mass assembly history (AMuseum). As demonstrated in recent studies, this critical epoch was characterised by a surge in both the rate and amplitude of mass growth, with a rapid rise in the specific growth rate of the global stellar mass density, seemingly driven by the abundance of newly formed stars observed in the ultraviolet-optical-infrared universe. How did the galaxies achieved this enhanced mass growth? What were the physical processes that led to this peak in the stellar mass assembly history? The VIMOS VLT Deep Space Survey (VVDS) aims to provide the answers to these and other related questions, by tracing the galaxy stellar mass assembly history over the last 8Gyr. With an unprecedented volume and depth, and together with the full spectral coverage and high precision of the stellar mass estimates, the VVDS shall be the next critical step in our understanding of how galaxies have evolved and will continue to do so in the epoch in which the majority of them are located.

Cosmological simulations of structure in the universe contain many elements that can be explored via computational analysis, and gravitational instability is the main organizing principle behind the hierarchical formation of large-scale structure. The development of non-linear structures, such as galaxies and galaxy clusters, requires an additional level of dynamics, called galaxy growth, that relates the cosmological environment and the large-scale distribution of galaxies. In this work, we investigate the growth of structure in a simulation of cosmological evolution, with the inclusion of massive neutrinos. The simulation uses flat Massive Gravity, a variant of general relativity that includes a disformal metric term that suppresses the dispersive growth of simulated structures below the scales relevant for cosmological observations. The resulting late-time growth of massive neutrinos is in quantitative agreement with $\Lambda$CDM, allowing for accurate predictions of large-scale structure on all observable scales. This provides strong evidence for the existence of light, non-interacting neutrinos as favoured by current cosmological experiments, and allows for the exploration of other modified gravity models that share similar late-time dynamics.

Wireless networks are widely used to provide broadband internet access to devices such as smartphones and laptops. These wireless networks are composed of multiple access points that communicate with each other to form a distributed access infrastructure. Multimedia content such as videos, songs, and pictures are frequently distributed to users through these wireless networks. The access points can be composed of either cellular base stations or WiFi access points. The growth of multimedia content has increased the traffic loads on these wireless networks. In this paper, we present a weighted clustering technique to optimize the distribution of multimedia content across the access points of a wireless network. The technique uses a weight to each access point that represents its content and assigns content to the access points based on these weights. Simulation results show that the clustering technique reduces the traffic loads on the network and increases the network resource efficiency. "}](#sec1){width="1\columnwidth"} The proliferation of multimedia content has increased the traffic loads on today's wireless networks. These wireless networks are composed of multiple access points that communicate with each other to form a distributed access infrastructure. Devices such as smartphones and laptops rely on these networks to provide broadband internet access. The growth of multimedia content, including videos, songs, and pictures, has further increased traffic loads. Currently, wireless networks use an unweighted, or binary, clustering technique to distribute multimedia content across access points. This technique simply categorizes the access points into two categories, "on" or "off", with no regard for their efficiency. The access points categorized as "on" are assumed to be fully occupied, while the access points categorized as "off" are assumed to be idle. These assumptions lead to suboptimal use of network resources and increased traffic loads on the wireless network.

Two years of high-precision LBT exposures have produced an angular resolution map of scattered light in the night sky. This map is more than 10 times darker than the host galaxy cluster Cl 0024+17 and traces the potential structure of the interstellar medium from which most of the light of the galaxy originates. The central region of the galaxy appears as a smooth, almost round ring, measuring 21 kpc in diameter and composed ofmaterial more than 10 times more massive than the Sun. The existence of this structure, if confirmed, would have major implications for our understanding of galaxy formation. Aims: The Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) is a pair of 8.4 m telescopes designed to be precisely co-mounted and used together for a wide range of astronomical investigations. This unique combination offers both the high resolution and the large collecting area required to study the inner regions of galaxies. In this paper, we present the first High-Angular Resolution Imaging of a Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) map of scattered light in the night sky obtained with the laser guide star (LGS) laser, which reaches an angular resolution as fine as 14.3 milliarcseconds (mas) at a wavelength of 0.82 µm. After careful quality control, a total of 358 science exposures in 5 filters were processed into a map of the interstellar medium. The central region of the galaxy appears as a smooth, almost round ring, measuring 21 kpc in diameter and composed ofmaterial more than 10 times more massive than the Sun. The existence of this structure, if confirmed, would have major implications for our understanding of galaxy formation. This research was presented in a paper entitled “Discovery of a Ringlike Dark Matter Structure in the Core of the Galaxy Cluster Cl 0024+17”, by Raffaella Averick-Browne et al.

The paper proposed a finite element model updating using response surface method. First, it presented the general principle of the response surface method. Then, according to the material parameter of the model to be updated, a response surface is established by experimental design. The updated model is obtained by solving the surface model with the weighted least squares method. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated by several examples and applied to two case studies. Although the general principle of the response surface method has been presented in many literatures, the application in the field of model updating has some difficulties. First, it needs to establish a response surface for the model to be updated by the experimental design, and then the updated model needs to be solved according to the general principle of the response surface method. This two-step process will increase the cost and decrease the efficiency. Moreover, the material properties of the response surface model needs to be validated by the new material parameters, which is difficult for some complex models. These drawbacks limits the application of the response surface method in the field of model updating. In this paper, the establishment of the response surface is established by the experimental design. And the updated model is solved by the surface model with the weighted least squares method, which improve the efficiency and avoid the validation of the material parameters. The proposed method is validated by several examples and applied to two case studies, and the results demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of the proposed method.

In this paper, we study arborescence structures in directed graphs with both weighted and directed edges. An arborescence is a tree in which the root is designated as the root node, and in which each non-leaf node is assigned either an ordered pair of in-degree and out-degree or an unique in-degree. We assign each edge a weight, and a digraph is said to contain an arborescence of a given root node and a given weight if the digraph can be made into an arborescence by assigning the root node the given weight. We define WDM (Weighted Directed Mass) and DSA (Directed Star Arboricity), the weighted and directed versions of arborescence mass, respectively. We give approximate algorithms for WDMA and DSA. We study WDMA and DSA. We give approximate algorithms for WDMA and DSA. Both WDMA and DSA are [1-approximation] for any digraph. For DSA, we present a linear time (in the size of the input) and 0-1 integer (in the size of the input) based $0.25$-approximation algorithm, which in turn implies a linear time and 1/4-approximation algorithm for WDMA. We show that WDMA is NP-hard by reducing minimum vertex cover to WDMA. Finally, we present approximation algorithms for WDMA and DSA on certain well-structured digraph classes.

This component is composed of Olivet refractory silicates with a median size of 0.1 μm and a power-law size distribution. Its peak wavelength(s) are approximately 10 μm, indicating the presence of very small grains. This dust component is not associated with any observed stars, planetary systems, or molecular clouds. This component is composed of Olivet refractory silicates with a median size of 0.1 μm and a power-law size distribution. Its peak wavelength(s) are approximately 10 μm, indicating the presence of very small grains. This dust component is not associated with any observed stars, planetary systems, or molecular clouds. Its origin remains a mystery. This component was also discovered in NGC 3628, an edge-on spiral galaxy approximately 2.5 Mpc away. Since this dust component is similar to dust in our own galaxy, it would take a minimum of 5000 years for this dust to travel from NGC 891 to NGC 3628. This discovery poses significant questions regarding its origin and the implications for the Sombrero Galaxy's evolution.

We present new ALMA data of the luminous far-infrared molecular hydrogenCN (HC3N) v=0-1 infrared line emission in the Antennae galaxies,NGC4038 and NGC4039. The analysis of these data provides us with the first view of the central 10pc of this system and provides us with a clear view of the nature of its luminous infrared nuclear starburst (even in the presence of an active galactic nucleus,AGN) and its possible link with similar galaxies and their nuclear activity. The bright infrared nuclear starburst in NGC4418, shining as a dominant contributor of infrared luminosity in the Antennae system, has been known for many years (Braine et al. 1993, Downes & Solomon 1998). However, the origin of this starburst and its relation to the presence of an AGN was a long-standing mystery. New ALMA data of the luminous far-infrared molecular hydrogenCN (HC3N) v=0-1 infrared line emission has now provided us with a clear view of the dynamics and energy source in the central 10pc of this system. We detect high velocity outflowing motions in this region, of up to 400 km/s. This is in sharp contrast to the expected speed for purely neutron star collapse at the distance of this source, estimated to be only 50-100 km/s. It is likely that these high-velocity motions are due to the interaction between a buried molecular gas and a yet-to-be-detected counter-rotating molecular gas component, as previously proposed for the situation in the Milky Way based on other lines (Bronfman et al. 2016; Zhao et al. 2017). Our data is in perfect agreement with the recent findings of Fu et al. (2019), who detect a radio-loud active galactic Seyfert-1 nucleus with star formation in NGC4418. This suggests that the growth of supermassive black holes and their activity are intimately connected with the growth of host galaxies and the onset of nuclear starbursts, just like in the case of the Milky Way. In summary, our new ALMA data of the nuclear starburst in the Antennae galaxies has provided us with a clear view of its nature and dynamics. It is likely powered by a combination of both the gravitational forces driving a yet-to-be-detected counter-rotating molecular gas component as well as a buried active galactic nucleus. We detect molecular gas driven high-velocity outflowing motions in the central 10pc of this system, in agreement with the recent findings of Fu et al. (2019) who detect a radio-loud active galactic nucleus in this source. This suggests that the growth of supermassive black holes and their activity are intimately connected with the growth of host galaxies and the onset of nuclear starbursts. In summary, these ALMA data of the nuclear starburst in the Antennae galaxies provides us with a clear view of its nature and dynamics.

The merging cluster system ESO137-001 is composed of two subgroups in the process of merging, the larger one Abell 3627 with a redshift of 0.1 and the smaller one ESO137-001 at a redshift of 0.0174. The former is indicated by an X-ray luminosity non-detection, while the latter is visible in the X-ray band as a galaxy cluster. The ESO137-001 subgroup is located in the middle of the plane of the sky between the two main clusters. The ESO137-001 galaxy subgroup contains two H-II regions with sizes of 10 and 15 kpc which are ionised by an evolved, low-mass star cluster. They are also associated with extended H-alpha emission and excess blue light. The star-formation rate in the H-II regions is 2-3 × 10−2 M☉ yr−1. It is likely that the H-II regions have been recently ionised by a series of star clusters with typical ages of 1-3 Myr, too small to detect individually in current observations. The total star-formation rate in the ESO137-001 galaxy subgroup is 1-2 M☉. The estimated contribution of this to the hot gas mass in the cluster is 20-30%. The X-ray luminosity of the cluster is thus mostly created by non-ionising stellar emission. The subgroup is located at the projected crossing point of the two infall regions of the main clusters, so the fraction of recent merging activity might be higher than in the average cluster.

V773 Tau A is a spectroscopic binary system in the Taurus star formation region located approximately 16.5 light years from the Earth. The primary component of the system has a mass of 1.2 M⊕ and an age of 1.6 Myr. The secondary component has a mass of 0.5 M⊕ and is approximately 0.4 arcseconds distant from the primary. The components are in a circular orbit with a period of approximately 7.2 days and a low eccentricity. When combined with the previously determined distance to the system, the components of V773 Tau A have previously determined dynamical masses which can be compared to spectroscopically determined masses. The primary component has a mass of 0.71 M⊕ determined from mass and radius viaevolutionary models. The spectroscopic mass of the primary is within 2.2% of the dynamical mass. The secondary component has a mass of 0.72 M⊕ determined from its spectral linewidths and an estimated radius. The dynamical mass for the secondary is within 1.4% of the spectroscopic mass. The agreement between the dynamical and spectroscopic masses for the primary component of V773 Tau A demonstrates that evolutionary models can be used to determine the physical properties of pre-main sequence stars.

Infrared (IR) power law-selected galaxies and X-ray sources have similar physical properties and likely reside in the same obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) host galaxies, but X-ray selection is more efficient in uncovering heavily obscured and heavily spun-up AGN. To further investigate this selection effect, we study optical variability of a matched X-ray sample and a matched IR power law-selected sample in the GOODS-South field. We find that the IR power law-selected sources are more variable on monthly timescales and in particular have more variability on $\sim$weekly timescales, which may be related to accretion-disk size variability, changes in the dominance of the narrow-line region over the narrow-line region obscuration, or changes in the strength of the torus molecular absorption. We also find that variability may be obscured in the X-ray selected sources because they have much lower observed-frame -length luminosities. These results may suggest that X-ray selection misses heavily obscured and rapidly varying accretion-disk states in infrared power law-selected sources.

We present a novel approach to probing the space-time geometry using the statistical properties of the observed structures in the universe. Using the redshift-temperature relation of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and the distortion s from the Integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect, we investigate the so-called "entropy-temperature" plane. We show that the cosmological constant, which is believed to drive the current expansion of the universe, affects the theoretical predictions in this plane in a distinct manner from various dark energy candidates. As an example, we apply our method to the latest observed Sloan Digital Sky Survey (BOSS) data and put a tight constraint on the space-time curvature tensor in the universe. Using the full galaxy sample, our analysis improves the constraint on the non-flat universe from the previous result by Anderson et al. (2013) by more than a factor of two. We forecast that the new results from the completed Sloan BOSS survey will further improve the constraint on the curvature parameters.

XMM-Newton observed the massive binary system WR 147 for 38 ks on June 30, 2005. An unprecedented increase in the flux of the stellar wind absorption of the primary star was detected in the X-ray band 0.3-10.0 keV, at a rate of 2.8(6) x 10-8 erg cm-2 s-1. Analysis of the spectrum indicates significant circumstellar absorption along the line of sight, with a hydrogen column density of 2.3(2) x 1022 cm-2 and an ionization parameter of approximately 7 x 10-4 cm-3 s-1. We also detect a strong absorption line from 0.76 keV, likely associated with, a low-ionization spectra of, with an equivalent ionization of 160 eV. The data are consistent with a significant increase in the absorption, with a time-scale of approximately 3.3 days. We do not detect the companion star, a highly probable red hypergiant, but place an absolute limit on its luminosity of less than 4.3 x 1030 cm-2 s-1. These X-ray observations, of a massive star undergoing dense stellar wind absorption, demonstrate the ability of XMM-Newton to detect wind variations over small time-scales.

We present numerical results for scalar field perturbations from a particle in circular orbit orbiting a rotating black hole. We evolve the perturbation equations using numerical methods presented in previous work. We evolve the perturbation equations in 2+1 dimensions in Misner-sharp variables, using an elliptical foliation in place of a tortoise-like radial coordinate. We obtain radiated quantum modes (QNMs) of various discrete values of angular momentum, $l$, and charge, $q$, for Schwarzschild black holes and for Kerr black holes with different spin parameters. The frequencies and damping times of QNMs are tabulated. We also discuss the computation of energy and angular momentum radiated in gravitational waves, using a new integral definition of radiated quantities for perturbations of any spin. Finally, we apply our results for scalar field perturbations to an estimate of energy and angular momentum radiated in scalar waves from a particle in circular orbit around a Kerr black hole. We find that the emitted energy and angular momentum are both negligible compared with the mass and spin of the hole, respectively.

Villamayor's algorithm is an algorithm for solving systems of polynomial equations. It was introduced by Antonio Villamayor in 1989 and has found several applications in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra. The algorithm works by substituting the polynomials by their values until a monomial is found that does not evaluate to zero. The algorithm is implemented in the software Macaulay2. The computation of the complexity of Villamayor's algorithm in the general case is open, and only a few special cases have been studied. In this paper, we study the complexity of Villamayor's algorithm in the non exceptional monomial case. We give a precise complexity analysis for this case and we provide some generalizations of this analysis. In particular, we prove that in most cases the algorithm has doubly exponential complexity. We also study the complexity of Villamayor's algorithm in a special case in which the polynomials are all quadratic. In this case, the algorithm has linear complexity.

In this paper we show that the recently introduced DGP brane model can provide a unified description of dark energy and dark matter in the universe. The observed accelerated expansion of the universe on the DGP brane is explained by the 5D cosmological constant $\Lambda_5$, while on the 3-brane the usual 4D energy densities for dark energy and dark matter are produced. In the context of DGP, the usual assumption of fine-tuning of 5D density to 4D density in quintessence models is naturally avoided. The evolution of the scalar field on the DGP brane is consistent with the current universe being of near-de Sitter nature, with small perturbations on either the scalar field potential or the cosmological constant. Furthermore, the observed galaxy clustering on large scales is explained as a bulk effect on the brane. The work presented here is a follow-up on the first paper introducing the DGP brane model, [1]. In the earlier paper , the 5D cosmological constant was invoked to explain the acceleration of the universe on the DGP brane. Here we show that the 5D cosmological constant can also account for dark matter on the brane. This has the advantage that the theory no longer requires a dark matter component on the brane. In addition, the evolution of the scalar field is consistent with the current universe being of near-de Sitter nature, with small perturbations on either the scalar field potential or the cosmological constant. Finally, the observed galaxy clustering on large scales is explained as a bulk effect on the brane, without the need to invoke modified gravity or new forms of dark matter on large scales. The equation of state of dark energy (DE) can be modeled using modifications of the general relativity (GR). To distinguish the DE models from the standard cosmology, the parameter $w$ in the equation of state is often assumed to have a value close to -1, as predicted by the theory of GR with a cosmological constant. Such a model can be in conflict with the result of modern observations. The data from such experiments as WMAP, BOOMERanG, or PLANCK, together with the results of standard cosmology tests, such as the Large-Scale Structure (LSS) analysis or the analysis of the of the Integrated Ferrometric Macroclimate Report (IFM), can be used to restrict the parameter space of DE models. In addition, one can introduce a new parameter that changes the gravitational constant in the equation of state, which leads to the fact that the DE models with a constant $w$ can not explain the anomalies observed in the LSS analysis or the results of the IFM experiment. Thus, the models with a variable $w$ are more preferable. In this case the density perturbations in the model can be generated, and the parameter $w$ can evolve from -1 at late time to a value less than -1 during the structure formation, thus can be in agreement with the mentioned observations. In this work we consider one such model. We consider the extension of the $R+f(R)$ gravity, which leads to a divergence free modified gravity with a constant $w$. We model the dynamics of matter and analyze the influence of the introduced constant $w$ on the structure formation. We also describe a way to reconstruct the MGG from the results of the future experiments.

In this note we show that quantisation commutes with reduction for the dual pair of discrete series representations of semisimple groups. More precisely, for each element w in the Weyl group of a universal covering group of the Lie group G, there is an automorphism 'w' of the ring of the quantumObserve operators such that 'w' acting on G infinitesimally equals the action of w on the Lie algebra via the Lie algebra representation obtained as the unique central extension corresponding to the relative discrete series representation of G considered as a dual pair with a fixed admissible representation of the Langlands –Weil group. As an example, if W is the Weyl group of the universal covering group of the Lie group G and if ρ is an irreducible representation of W, we deduce that the corresponding infinitesimal representation of the Lie algebra is isomorphic to the Brauer–Weil representation. Our result recovers and generalizes a similar result of Tirao [1] for the dual pair corresponding to a principal series representation, as well as a remarkable coincidence for the pairs corresponding to a principal series representation and a singleton representation [2, 3]. We also discuss the analogue for quantum groups at a root of unity and mention some of the conjectures by Vogan and Zuckerman [4] concerning the infinitesimal action of the Weyl group on the Lie algebra of a real reductive group.

The generator coordinate method (GCM) is an approach to computing eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of operators, such as the time-dependent Kohn-Sham equation, in many-body quantum systems. The GCM solves the Schr[ö]dinger equation in a symmetry-breaking manner, using a unitary transformation to cast the problem in a fully symmetry-preserving form. This allows for the separation of low-lying states of the Hamiltonian into separately optimized approximations, by optimizing each state in a different, yet internally consistent, approximate form of the ground state. The GCM has been widely used to study quantum mechanics in electronic structure, particularly with the development of linear-response time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). In this work, we show that in the case of the TDDFT Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian, the same separation of low-lying states into separately optimized approximations can be achieved without symmetry-breaking, by instead optimizing the generator coordinate itself in a self-consistent manner. We call this method the generator coordinate method in TDDFT . We illustrate this approach for the polaron, the Shcrödinger equation with aScreening Coulomb potential, and an iron pnictide.

In this paper we examine cosmological perturbations in Palatini modified gravity. We derive the field equations and consider the linear regime. We find two separate modes: a tensor mode and a scalar mode. For the tensor mode, the propagation is constant, but the evolution is modified due to the non-geodesic nature of the wave-frame. For the scalar mode, we find that the perturbations are highly conserved, similar to a dissipative system. We perform an stability analysis and conclude that the model exhibits an unstable branch of solutions. As a second step, we study the evolution of the perturbations at the superhorizon scales. We find that the perturbations depend on the Lagrangian of the theory, which could in principle allow for a detection. We finish by discussing some potential problems with the theory and its relation to observations. This paper studies cosmological perturbations in Palatini modified gravity. Mass-loss rates of hot stars are inferred from the analysis of the He<--H secondary eclipse in the UV resonance lines. Assuming a spherically symmetric, thin-shell outflow, the so-called CompTT-model is widely used to derive the density profile of the outflow from the absorption line profiles. In contrast to this simple model, recent studies suggest that hot-star winds are structured due to a high porosity. Depending on the chosen macroscopic geometry, the derived mass-loss rates can be up to two orders of magnitude higher than the actual rates. Here, I present the first application of the CompTT effect to O-star winds. With a radiative-hydrodynamic simulation, I self-consistently account for the small-scale structure of the hot-star wind and calculate the equivalent average properties of the wind, i.e. the mean opacity, mean wind velocity, and the drag force acting on dust grains. I demonstrate that a porosity of 50% leads to an effective wind filling factor of more than 90%, thus significantly increasing the mass-loss rate. Furthermore, the temperature in the upper wind regions increases by more than 2000 K, leading to significantly larger ionisation fractions and smaller ionisation fractions of molecular species. In contrast to the spherically symmetric, thin-shell outflow, these asymmetric flows significantly influence the dynamics of outflowing material and thus also have to be taken into account in the analysis of UV resonance line profiles.

The pre-main-sequence (PMS) system UZ Tau E consists of a spectroscopic binary with an orbital period of approximately 7.5 days and an age of 1-3 Myr [e.g., @tout+95; @pravdo+01; @tout+02]. Its disk has been resolved in many transitions of CO, including the v=0-0 S(1) line at 2.3218 $\mu$m [e.g., @whit+01; @quanz+07; @keny+12], the v=0-1 S(1) line at 2.2467 $\mu$m [e.g., @pott+06; @krau+12], the Br-$\gamma$ line [e.g., @tori+98; @simo+12], the H$_2$ and $\mu$m feature [e.g., @akes+01; @ake+04; @dutr+12; @maci+12; @tori+12], and the Br-$<unk>gamma$ feature [e.g., @meye+97; @tori+98; @simo+12]. The disk has an inner radius of $\sim$20 AU and a mass of $\sim$0.25 M$_{\odot}$ [e.g., @akes+01; @tori+98; @simo+12]. The recent discovery of a companion near the edge of the orbit of the binary system UZ Tau E [@quanz+13] provides new insights into the architecture and evolution of this pre-main-sequence binary system. This companion, UZ Tau W, is a low-mass young star of spectral type M4.5 and has a projected separation of $\sim$15 AU from UZ Tau E, placing it close to the frost line, where icy material may be trapped into the atmosphere around the stars. The presence of close-in material has the potential to affect the evolution of both UZ Tau E and UZ Tau W. It may stabilize the orbit of UZ Tau W with respect to the orbit of UZ Tau E through dynamical processes such as the Kozai mechanism [e.g., @fabr+01; @fabr+03]. UZ Tau W may also accrete close-in material from the circumbinary disk of UZ Tau E, affecting its evolutionary status.

Noncolliding Brownian motion (NCBM) is a probabilistic system that describes the positions of non-intersecting Brownian paths in space. In this system, Brownian particles perform independent continuous time random walks, with each step having an equal probability of being negative or positive, as well as being shifted by an independent Gaussian random variable of zero mean and variance proportional to the number of steps. Given a particular initial configuration, the paths particles take settle into a steady state that can be modeled by a determinantal process. The determinantal process provides a probability law in which points are simultaneously determine and encode the positions of the non-colliding Brownian paths. The steady state behavior of the NCBM system can be characterized through the stochastic process known as linear exponents. These exponents determine the rate of separation of initially nearby paths and can be used to classify the steady state behavior of the system as either strong or weak chaos. Determinantal processes also arise as the steady state distribution of a system of particles interacting through a two-parameter family of delta function potentials. In this system, the positions of the particles interact through a pairwise interaction determined by a non-negative Hermitian operator, known as the Rider model . The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of this operator determine the types of interactions between the particles. For particular choices of this operator, the eigenvector correlation functions can be computed in a closed form, and in the limit of infinite interaction strength these reduce to the appropriate correlation functions of the determinantal process.

Radio waves traveling through the atmosphere are reflected in the sky, revealing the shape of the celestial sphere. Because stars are warmer than their surroundings, they preferentially emit into these cooler regions, creating the well-known temperature inversion in their atmospheres. For the most part, AGB stars emit most strongly at shorter wavelengths, so this provides a way to detect them. We collected photometric data from the U.K.’s White Mountain Array and analyzed it with a machine learning algorithm trained on data from the IRAS satellite. We also developed a new approach to interpolate K-band photometry from WMA and 2MASS data, which makes it possible to detect temperatures as low as 2000 K. Using these two techniques, we compiled a catalog of nearly 100,000 AGB stars in the Milky Way. We then used this catalog to measure their radiative mass loss rates. We found a strong correlation between these rates and spatial extinction, which can be used to trace mass loss in three dimensions.

In this paper, we investigate certain purely transmitting defect configurations in affine Toda field theory. These defects are located at the intersection of two (or more) branches of the affine Weyl group element, and carry non-zero affine Kac labels but vanishing scaling weights. By analyzing the scattering properties of the one-strings of such defects, we show that these defects correspond to unstable particles in the corresponding sigma model. We further show that such purely transmitting defects are in one-to-one correspondence to certain magnetic excitations of the underlying SU(2) spin chain. We then present various examples of such purely transmitting defect configurations, and demonstrate how they combine to form a set of general defect configurations which can also undergo scattering . We then conclude by discussing a number of interesting open questions arising from our analysis. This work develops a new cyclic voltammetry (CV) based technique for characterizing electrochemical phase transitions and predicting equilibrium composition. CV, the measurement of current as a function of voltage, is the main method used to investigate electrochemical phenomena. The traditional approach to CV measurements is to slowly increase the voltage from an initial value of 0 until an asymptotic value is reached where the electrochemical system has progressed through one full reaction. This standard approach, known as linear CV, has several shortcomings when characterizing electrochemical phase transitions. In some cases a phase change occurs but not complete reduction or oxidation of the system. This incomplete reduction or oxidation means that the system has not reached an equilibrium composition. The traditional linear CV approach does not report whether the system has reached equilibrium composition. Another shortcoming of the linear approach is that only one voltage value is reported even though multiple phases may be present at different voltage. This work develops a new approach to CV measurement, called E-C FORC, that tracks the voltage path the system takes as it progresses through multiple phases and reaches equilibrium. Using a genetic algorithm E-C FORC is able to determine both the path the system takes as it transitions between phases and the voltage corresponding to equilibrium composition. The technique is demonstrated using ferricyanide as an electrochemical system. E-C FORC is able to determine the equilibrium composition in both highly polyphasic systems and those with very sharp phase transitions. Additionally, E-C FORC can track multiple phase transitions and accurately determine the voltage corresponding to each phase transition. This work describes a promising approach to characterizing electrochemical phase transitions and predicting equilibrium composition.

We study the problem of quantile estimation, which aims to estimate the occurrence rate of failures of a random variable given a random sample from that variable. A sample is drawn from the target distribution, and the quantile is estimated based on the rate of failures below the estimated quantile value. The estimation is performed using a causal algorithm which can observe the feedback only causally. In the classical communication-free setting, such a problem can be solved efficiently using the weight decay algorithm, where the feedback consists of the sign of the weight of the variable furthest away from zero. We consider the situation in which feedback is restricted to a single bit per sample, and give an $O(1/\log n)$ algorithm which uses $O(n)$ bits of communication. This is near-optimal, as we prove a lower bound of $\Omega(n/\log n)$ bits of communication. We also consider the more general setting of bandit weight decay, where the algorithm can observe the quantile in a time interval instead of single bit. In this more general setting, we give a fully parallel weight decay algorithm which uses $O(1)$ bits of communication per sample. Finally, we show that the weight decay algorithm with causal feedback and bandwidth of one bit per sample does not work in the classical communication-free setting, and we prove a lower and upper bounds of $\Theta(n)$ and $O(n^2)$, respectively, on the number of bits of communication required by any algorithm for solving this problem.

Using an AdS/CFT inspired holographic QCD model, we investigate the confinement/deconfinement phase transitions of mesons in an AdS space with a varying radius and found that the QCD phase transition is a second order phase transition with a lambda-like critical exponent. We also found that the number of degrees of freedom of the dual strongly coupled conformal field theory increases rapidly near the phase transition, which is characteristic of a 2nd order phase transition. Furthermore, we study the properties of mesons in the deconfined phase transition and observe masses that are consistent with previous studies on heavy-light mesons. We hope this work can shed some new lights on holographic QCD. In this note we generalize and apply the geometric Langlands duality for partial flag manifolds between two consecutive levels to certain quiver gauge theories. We describe the resulting duality between the quantum cohomology of the partial flag manifold and the quantum cohomology of certain quiver representations. This duality can be used to calculate the basic BPS indices, and we illustrate this by computing these indices for certain groups and by providing some examples. We also explain how this paper fits into the recent extension of geometric Langlands duality to three quiver gauge theories, and describe some of the open questions. This work was done while the author was an undergraduate student at Harvard University. More information about this work, and the author's perspective on the open questions discussed can be found on his personal webpage. Riemann zeros are the set of points where the Riemann zeta function, ζ(s), has zeroes. Fractal dimension, a method of fitting a curve to data to represent its complexity, has been shown to fit the zeros well. In this work we fit functions of the form f(x) = a[1 - α(x - b)^c] to the Riemann zeros, where a, b, and c are the fractal dimension parameters, and α, β, and γ are the function parameters. We find that the parameter β corresponds to the fractal dimension of the curve fit, and we find that γ has a minimum value of approximately -0.2 at the real axis. Additionally, we compute the error on these fits and find that the error is consistent with being normally distributed. We compute the Hurst exponent h using the following equation: H = −γ / (a log(2) sqrt(ln2) β) where β is the fractal dimension, computed above. We find that Hurst values tend to fall in the range of 0.5 < 0.5 <unk>0.5 < 1, indicating non-random fractal behavior. We compute the q entropy using the following equation: q = a log(2) / (ln2) and find that it behaves similarly to the Hurst exponent, H, and thus is also a reliable metric for non-random fractal behavior. Finally, we show the results of these fractal fits on a Riemann surface, with particular focus on the vertical (X) axis. We observe that f(x) = a[1 - α(x - b)^c] fits the Riemann zeros very well, with errors consistent with a normally distributed random variable. We conclude that Riemann zeros fit the assumptions of fractals, and that fractal functions provide good fits to the Riemann zeros.

Aerosol optical depth (AOD), SO2, NO2, PM2.5, PM10, temperature, and relative humidity were measured at a urban site in Greater Tokyo, Japan (36.5N 137.5E) from January 2014 to December 2017. High-pollution episodes (HPE) were defined as days with PM2.5 concentrations of over 50%. HPEs accounted for 42% of the total days and were dominant during the warm seasons. HPEs were characterized by high AOD, high SO2, high NO2, and low wind speeds. Diagnostics of the dominated aerosol processes revealed that 61% of HPEs were related to secondary aerosol formation. 24% of HPEs were related to re-suspension, 11% to regional transport, and 5% to gas-phase chemical reactions. These processes were more active in winter, indicating the importance of wintertime transport in greater Tokyo. Analysis of the emission inventories showed that fossil fuel combustion and industrial processes were the primary sources of SO2, NO2, and PM2.5. Estimated secondary aerosol formation contributed 44% of SO2, 61% of NO2, and 5% of PM2.5. These processes, along with the high temperature and low wind speeds during HPEs, were major contributors to the high AOD. The dominant aerosol processes were different from what was observed in previous studies, which were mainly related to regional transport. This may be because of the different emission patterns and climate conditions in Japan, compared to North America or Europe.

Strain localization in a shear transformation zone (STZ) model for amorphous solids is examined. In this model, the amorphous solid is composed of particles interacting via a short-range, attractive core and a long-range, attractive tail in a potential that is sheared, below the glass transition temperature, Tg, in the amorphous solid. In quasistatic deformation, regions of high shear stress,τ(shear), form from localized regions of high strain, e(loc), which propagate as wave fronts described by a strain localization theory. Specifically, a transition from spatially extended to localized strain is observed as the ratio of the localization length, λ, to the initial system length, L0, increases. An analytical theory describing the spatial, temporal, and frequency dependent shear modulus, G(τ,ω), and its relation to the shear stress and strain waveforms is developed, which allows for analysis of the spatial and temporal dependence of localized shear stress and strain, τ(loc)(ω) and e(loc)(ω). τ(loc) is observed to have three distinct regions with decay characteristic of critical exponents in scale-free space, increasing with frequency as 1/τ(loc)∼ω^{νz}, where ν=0.5 is the divergence of the correlation length, and α and β, which depend on details of the decay of the potential, describe the frequency dependence of the critical strain amplitude required to induce strain localization. e(loc) exhibits similar decay of critical exponents to τ(loc) except with different critical amplitude exponents α=νz=1/2 and β=1/2. Furthermore, the critical exponents and scaling laws are compared to those of supercooled liquids (in which this model was originally proposed to explain) and those of amorphous solids with a different potential, demonstrating consistency between the predictions of the STZ model and these observations. These results show that the strain localization theory for amorphous solids, derived from a theory for supercooled liquids, can provide a framework for understanding the mechanical response of amorphous solids across various different model systems.

In machine learning, one of the most powerful learning paradigm is ensemble learning . In ensemble learning, multiple base learning algorithm(s) are combined to produce better generalization performance than any of the constituent learning algorithms. Evolutionary algorithms (EAs), especially evolutionary computation (EC) based EAs like Genetic Algorithm (GA), have been successfully applied to many machine learning problems. In this paper, we explore the use of EC based EAs like genetic algorithm (GA) to solve the machine learning problem of hyper parameter optimization for ensemble learning. We design a single GA process to automatically search for multiple hyper parameters (such as number of base learning algorithms, K, and the weight factor for a given base learning algorithm, w, in a weighted sum of the base algorithms) of a given base machine learning algorithm for achieving best generalization performance on the training data. We test this GA based GA (GABGAS) algorithm on five benchmark machine learning problems where GA has not been previously tried. The results show that GABGAS can automatically find good values for K (between 1 and 20) and w (between 0.1 and 0.9) achieving significantly better generalization performance than the best known hand-tuned values for K and w for each of the benchmark problems. We also show that GABGAS has significantly lower computational complexity than existing approaches.

In this paper we study random antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin chains in a transverse field using the iDMRG algorithm. We compute the correlation function amplitude and the entanglement entropy using CFT techniques, and compare the results with iDMRG numerical simulations. We find that the CFT predictions match the numerical simulations very well for system sizes accessible with iDMRG. Moreover, we argue that the numerical results are consistent with a conformal field theory in the vicinity of the vicinity of the large spin limit, where the spin chain can be thought as a large number of decoupled one-dimensional segments. In particular, our CFT analysis allows us to compute the conformal blocks decomposition of the correlation function amplitude, that in turn permits to explicitly calculate the entanglement entropy. We find that the leading term in the entanglement entropy is linear in the subsystem size, in contrast to the logarithmic law expected from conformal field theory in one dimension. Finally, we demonstrate a finite size scaling of the entanglement entropy, finding that the leading coefficient is independent on the subsystem size, in agreement with the CFT prediction.

For hierarchical multiplanet systems, tides raised on distant planets can shrink their orbital semi-major axes and even drive type II catastrophic mergers. In systems with more modest outerplanet orbits, tides raised on distant worlds can likewise shrink their orbital semi-major axes, but the tides raised on the outermost planet can damp the orbits. Here we show that if the innermost planet has a strong non-zero eccentricity, tides raised on the planet can cause apsidal motionward oscillations that drive eccentricities above the dynamically defined upper limit and shrink the orbits. We carry out N-body simulations to validate this analytic theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of this mechanism for shrinking the orbits of non-resonant planets in multipleplanet systems. We show that this process is efficient enough to explain the proximity of the Earth and Mars to the Sun, and could have contributed to the capture of planetesimals into Earth and Venus. The long-term behavior of hierarchical multiplanet systems is largely determined by the planets’ orbit and spin orientations. If the planets’ spins are misaligned with their orbital planes, the system can enter a Cassini state where the forced eccentricities of the planets damp out but their orbital angular momenta remain coupled. If, on the other hand, the planets’ spin axes are initially coplanar with their orbital planes, they can enter a Kozai state, in which the planets’ eccentricities oscillate with a period equal to a full cycle of eccentricity-raisingnode precession. During this time, the planets’ semi-major axes can shrink enough to cause a type II or type I migration depending on the characteristics of the adjacent planets. We demonstrate that the inclusion of even a single testparticle in apsidal motionward precession significantly increases the fraction of Kozai cycles completed before apsides align. Planetary systems that enter the Kozai state and subsequently undergo type II or type I migration may exhibit changes in their orbital axes that are larger than observed in the Solar System. Here we demonstrate that, if one or more planets in such a system have sufficiently non-zero eccentricities, the Kozai cycles can drive eccentricities above the dynamically defined upper limit and drive the systems into collision. We carry out N-body simulations to validate this analytic theory and demonstrate that this process is efficient enough to explain the proximity of the Earth and Mars to the Sun in the Solar System. We also show that the capture of planetesimals into Earth and Venus is facilitated if the planets are brought into very large orbits , and that this mechanism could have contributed to the observed mass of Earth and Venus. This work was done in the context of the NExT (Numerical Experiment for Terrestrial planet Formation) project, which is an experiment in Planet formation and Dynamics supported by the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Studies, the University of Western Australia, the University of Tokyo, and the RIKEN Institute in Japan, and is funded by the Australian Research Council’

Massive black holes exist in all massive galaxies. They grow over time due to accretion of matter. Their masses can be estimated using the fundamental plane of black hole activity. The plane is based on three parameters, namely the velocity dispersion of the host galaxy, the stellar velocity dispersion and the radius of the sphere of influence of the black hole. The first two are measured for the galaxy, while the third one can be estimated using the black hole's mass. The latter two are strongly correlated and can be used to estimate the mass of the black hole. Such estimation has been done for a large sample of galaxies and it was found that more massive galaxies have on average more massive black holes. This correlation can be expressed as a linear relation of the black hole mass - spheroid luminosity = A x M_{spheroid} + B where M_{BH} is the mass of the black hole, M_{spheroid} is the mass of the spheroid, A is a coefficient close to 7 and B is a constant. This relation was found to be true for galaxies of all Hubble types, but especially for early-types. The correlations with the host galaxy's properties were stronger for the spheroid than for the black hole mass, which can be explained by the merger driven growth of black holes. The scatter of the black hole can be reduced by using another observable, namely the luminosity of the spheroid. The latter can be estimated using the velocity dispersion and the radius of the sphere of influence, which are required for the former. The latter can be estimated from the B-band luminosity of the galaxy. It was found that the scatter of the black hole mass - spheroid luminosity relation is significantly lower than for the other relations, and the best-fit coefficient is closer to 10, which can be explained by more accurate measurements and less stellar scatter in the spheroid . It is suggested that the black hole mass - spheroid luminosity relation can be used as a new standard for estimating the black hole mass. Neutrinos are the most abundant fermions in the universe, and their properties are expected to extend beyond the standard model of particle physics. Recently, neutrino parameters have been limited by studying a period of cosmological dark matter domination. These cosmological constraints, in combination with non-detections from current and previous experiments, lead to an extremely complex framework for neutrino properties. Here we point out that the relic neutrino abundance can be modified by decaying or annihilating into a photon and neutrino, or into two photons. Using existing cosmological data, we show that these processes can relax the neutrino lifetime bound by many orders of magnitude, opening up new avenues for experimental verification. In particular, we show that a future CMB stage EDGES-like experiment has the potential to probe lifetimes as small as 10^{-8} s, corresponding to a new cosmological horizon at $z \sim 0.87$ that could be explored.

The elongated structure of the Hercules dSph was discovered using deep images from the Large Binocular Telescope. The dSph was found to have an intrinsic size of at least 12 kiloparsecs, with a high ellipticity and an orientation pointing to us. The observed structure may be the result of a recent merger with a smaller dSph or a primordial shape transformed by tidal forces. The elongated structure of the Hercules dSph was discovered using deep images from the Large Binocular Telescope. The dSph was found to have an intrinsic size of at least 12 kiloparsecs, with a high ellipticity and an orientation pointing to us. The observed structure may be the result of a recent merger with a smaller dSph or a primordial shape transformed by tidal forces. Many dSphs have been observed before, but most are round. The discovery of an elongated structure near the Milky Way has several implications for the formation of our galaxy as well as for dSphs in general. The elongated structure of the Hercules dSph may be the result of a recent merger with a smaller dSph or a transformation of its original shape through tidal forces.

In this paper, we present a practical Seedless Infrared-Safe Cone (SSISC) jet algorithm for hadron collider physics processing. This Cone algorithm extends the conventional Seedless SISC algorithm [1] by introducing the cone size parameter sR, which allows the algorithm to be IR-safe and to achieve good performance in hadron collider physics processing. We carry out detailed studies of the SSISC algorithm in terms of its asymptotic relative error (ARE) and its numerical stability. Comparative studies show that the SSISC algorithm has better performance than both the Seedless SISC algorithm and the conventional Cone algorithm. We apply the SSISC algorithm to Higgs candidate reconstruction in VBF Higgs boson production and to W + jets and Z + jets production processes at the LHC, and discuss the corresponding physics implications. The SSISC algorithm improves on the Seedless SISC algorithm in the following aspects: (1) It is IR-safe and numerically stable. (2) It does not require any tuning of parameters. (3) It has the same asymptotic behavior as the Seedless SISC algorithm. We apply the SSISC algorithm to Higgs candidate reconstruction in VBF Higgs boson production and to W + jets and Z + jets production processes at the LHC, and discuss the corresponding physics implications. We encourage readers to consult the accompanying technical report , in which the SSISC algorithm is introduced in greater detail and several appendices are included.

Generic black holes in de Sitter spaces are characterized by three parameters: horizon radius, de Sitter horizon radius and de Sitter temperature. It has been shown that these black holes can be realized as physical black holes in anti-de Sitter spaces via analytic continuation, and they always contain a de Sitter anomaly. It has also been shown that these black holes thermally radiate de Sitter energy with the black hole entropy. This de Sitter radiation is not pure thermal radiation but it contains de Sitter anomalies. These black holes also have some similarities with Fyinyorev-Lorentz shock waves, and their de Sitter radiation is similar to Melnikov radiation. In this paper, we show that these de Sitter anomalies are different aspects of Hawking radiation and they have the same emission characteristics. We also show that these black holes thermally radiate not only de Sitter energy, but also mass, and the corresponding radiation resembles Kerr-AdS black hole radiation.

The L-functions ratios conjecture states that certain Dirichlet L-functions may be interpreted as interpolators for certain families of quadratic twists of the general linear group. This is expressed by a classical Siegel-Weil formula where, for, the -function is the usual, and for, the functionals satisfy for all primitive -th roots of unity. The integral is over the nontrivial -power torsion elements of the fundamental domain for the arithmetic quasi- auto-mo-Graphic mod. This article proves this conjecture for a certain family of twists, which are represented by for non-square, symplectic representations of Galois over the rational number field. The method of proof is a new and simple test for the L-functions ratios conjecture, based on the classical geometry. Using this test, the L-functions ratios conjecture is verified for all. The method of proof relies on an initial application of the global functorial representability of Galois representations associated to Hida families of toroidal cusp forms, to obtain associated continuous automorphic representations of GL(2, ℂ), for which a global treatment will follow by the subsequent work of W. Luo. A crucial input here is the precise determination of the behavior of a certain period integral on the Shimura variety Ψ(n) after descent to the automorphic side. This is possible via the recent work of X. Yuan on the arithmetic quantum product, as modified by M. Saito, and under the assumption of the generalized Riemann hypothesis of the Eisenstein series. The precise results achieved are the following: for each, there is a primitive -th root of unity such that the representation defined by the Dirichlet series has special value after mod, and for every choice of sign, the value is a symmetric2 × 2 matrix with coefficients given by an automorphic integral of the Shimura variety <unk>(n) and some Hida family of cuspidal automorphic forms on GL(2, ℂ) over the totally real field. The value depends on the choice of sign only through the symplectic trace, which is a classical Hasse invariant. The proof of the L-functions ratios conjecture for a certain family of twists then follows by observing that there is a fourth moment correction factor which is given over all odd square roots of unity. The arguments of the two classical test functions for the L-functions ratios conjecture, namely the highly concentrated Gaussian and the divisor function, do not satisfy this multiplicative property. On the other hand, the value for any odd square is given by the classical Siegel-Weil formula. Since the representation is symplectic, and the symplectic trace is constant, the result follows.
