A new extinction map of the entire Anticenter region of the Milky Way is presented. The map is based on 2MASS extinction data towards 159,426 fields and covers a range of |b| < 10° and |l| < 150° and has an overall resolution of 1° × 1°. To analyze the data we have developed a new method for extracting extinction and distance information from 2MASS data. This method is based on two fundamental assumptions: (1) the overall extinction law in the region is compatible with the commonly used RJCE and (2) the extinction in a given direction is primarily caused by dust within a cylinder of finite radial width and axial length centered on the observer. With these two assumptions it is possible to derive the extinction (A) and distance (D) for a given pair of (J, K) magnitudes in an automatic and straightforward manner, as long as extinction information for at least four orthogonal base bands is available. Applying this method we have produced the most extensive extinction map of the entire Anticenter region to date. Comparison with previously published maps as well as analysis of the structure of the region show that the obtained results are reliable and accurate. The presented extinction map covers a total area of approximately 2000 square degrees, which is larger than all previously published extinction maps of this region combined. It can be accessed via the website [1], and the header of each webpage contains a link to the extinction values at the respective spatial coordinates as well as a small summary.

SA 57 is an extremely strong nearby (z = 0.0631) large-scale structure, which is very rare in the nearby Universe and contains several massive galaxy clusters, several groups and numerous individual galaxies. The X-ray emission from this structure has not been systematically studied, even though the sensitivity of current X-ray telescopes makes it possible to detect such a structure for the first time. In this paper, we present the results of an X-ray survey of the SA 57 supercluster with XMM-Newton. We detect the X-ray emission from two large galaxy clusters, several groups and individual galaxies. We measure the global properties of the supercluster and study its spatial distribution. We find that the main baryonic component of the supercluster – the X-ray emitting clusters – are strongly correlated with the distribution of galaxies. We discuss a number of the most interesting sources and estimate their X-ray fluxes. We also briefly consider the possibility that some of these X-ray sources are associated with active galactic nuclei.

In this work, we study the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_N$ of a Wigner random matrix with sample size $N$ and characterize its fluctuations around its mean. To this aim, we first extend to the Wigner random matrices a deformation method originally proposed for the GOE Tracy-Widom distribution. Then we study the largest eigenvalue of $\lambda_N$ for a family of Wigner random matrices which shares some properties with Wigner matrices. We give a nonrigorous argument which suggests that the spectrum of this family of Wigner matrices converges in distribution to a deterministic parameter which we identify. We then present rigorous results which support this nonrigorous argument. In particular, we prove convergence in distribution of the spectrum of Wigner matrices with rank tending to infinity. In addition, we also show that this convergence result is nonuniversal: the fluctuations of the largest eigenvalue around its mean do not depend on the deterministic parameter. These findings are in sharp contrast with the GOE case where the Tracy-Widom distribution is universal.

A hydrodynamical algorithm for solving the compressible Euler equations is presented and used to simulate detonations in simulated accreted material for the first time. One-dimensional simulations of detonations in compressed air performed with a compressed Eulerian code exhibit the expected formation of a shock wave and a region of compressed, heated fluid. The hydrodynamics are highly unstable to small perturbations, with the formation of vortices and the blowout of channels of fluid at the crest of the wave. Simulations with the compressed Eulerian code exhibit a similar behaviour but with substantial differences in amplitude and dynamic range, and in the formation of many smaller scale structures. The addition of a simplified, numerical representation of shocks allows the accurate tracking of shock waves. In conjunction with a new Riemann-solver-free version of the Piecewise Parabolic Method (PPM), this capability is used to simulate the passage of a detonation through a one-dimensional toy problem consisting of a step function increasing in amplitude from one end of a domain to the other. The growth of turbulent mixing between regions of different compression is observed, with substantial entropy mixing and a doubling of the volume fraction of the material with higher velocity. This work provides the first evidence that superbursts, the proposed explanation for the underlying accretion from the eclipsing neutron star IGR J17480-2446, are capable of substantially stirring the material comprising their host stars.

We propose a new framework for describing particles with spin that goes beyond the notion of free particles with spin zero and spin one massless particles. We call these particles massive spin two particles (PIPs). We motivate the new framework using the example of one-particle states in (A)dS, and in particular obtain a new description of particles with spin one and with spin two. Using this framework, we show that the massless spin two particles fit into a larger group of Kaluza-Klein theories, each corresponding to a lower weight in the spin two representation of theSpin(4,1) isometry group of (A)dS. We propose that these new frameworks for describing particles with spin be included in the standard model. In particular, we conjecture that spin two gauge bosons correspond to massive spin two PIPs, as do spin three and four gauge bosons, and possibly also gravity. We further propose a generalization of the twistor transform that includes these new descriptions of particles with spin two and three. In particular, we propose that massless spin two particles fit into the tensor product of a two-form and three one-form representations of this larger group, and massless spin three particles fit into the symmetric tensor product of three one-form representations. These generalizations of the twistor transform include these new descriptions of particles with spin two and three because the twistor group Spin(4, 1) is a subgroup of this larger group. We show that our conjectures for the spectrum of particles with spin agree with empirical data for the standard model and (A)dS. We also discuss possible implications for detecting and observing these particles, along with connections to holography and the spin principle.

Massive stars are formed in clusters. Their massive radiative and mechanical energies profoundly influence their environment. Despite their prevalence and crucial role in the star formation process, the star formation process, particularly in its earliest phases, is difficult to observe due to the high spatial resolution and sensitivity needed. The water masers arise early in actively forming massive stars and gas reservoir, and so provide an excellent probe of this earliest phase. Using new Very Long -Bird Interferometry (VLBI) observations, we detect 23 new radio water masers associated with the earliest stages of massive star formation in the Nuclear Disk of the Milky Way. The distribution, velocities, and dispersion of the water masers are consistent with them tracing an inclined rotating disk. The dynamical limit of the disk is estimated to be 1 M⊙, comparable to the previous upper limit of the Nuclear Disk. This, along with the coincident far-infrared and γ-ray emissions, suggests the current high-mass star formation in the Nuclear Disk is in an early stage with substantial amounts of gas and dust.

Cosmic rays are strongly attenuated in galaxy clusters, requiring the energy release of a 10<unk> 13<unk> Mpc$ sized ICM to be at least 87 percent of the critical density of the Universe at the radius of the cluster virial radius to allow for their survival. However, X-ray observations show significant substructures in the hot atmosphere of galaxy clusters, which could act as fossil bubbles confining the non-thermal component. In this work, using cosmological magneto-hydrodynamic simulations, we show that the ICM in the wake of fossil bubbles, with masses between 10^{13} and 10^{14} M_{\odot}$, retain non-thermal pressure , thus lowering the galaxy cluster temperature without altering their X-ray appearance. Cosmic-ray suppression in fossil clusters is in tension with observations at the 3σ level, unless the magnetic field in fossil bubbles has a strength in excess of 10-15μG, which is difficult to be reconciled with the levels of magnetic energy in the atmosphere. We conclude that the fossil mechanism, though capable of suppressing cosmic rays without altering the X-ray appearance of galaxy clusters, does not provide a viable solution to the cosmic-ray boost problem in galaxy clusters.

Signal processing and machine learning have seen a lot of attention in the scientific research community , particularly in tasks where a lot of data is available, but where the data is very high dimensional. A good example of this is in the field of molecular biology, where it has become possible to sequence entire genomes for a wide range of organisms. However, these sequences are often very high dimensional, containing information about the species, the environment the organism lives in and even the genetics of the individual from which the sequence was taken. Often times, only a very small amount of data is available in the form of the sequence itself, making it difficult to learn representations that can accurately capture the high-level structural information in the data. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning a signal representation using only a relatively small number of samples in the presence of high-dimensional noise. We focus on the case where the signal of interest is sparse or compressible and propose a new empirical risk formulation based on sampling the signal and estimating its eigenvalues. By avoiding a direct optimization over the entire signal, our approach allows us to scale to high-dimensional problems where the naive application of empirical risk minimization (ERM) techniques can fail. We provide both an overview of our approach and derive its corresponding optimization problem. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on simulated and real data examples, including applications in single-cell genomics and cosmological data analysis.' Although there has been recent interest in learning representations of high-dimensional data, many of these techniques require large amounts of data to work well. In some applications, such as single-cell genomics or cosmological data analysis, it can be very costly or even impossible to generate large amounts of labeled data. Additionally, in other applications, the underlying high-dimensional representation of the data can be very difficult to explicitly model or even synthesize. As a result, many of these applications are outside the domain of traditional supervised learning. In these situations, we must rely on more supervised approaches that can learn a useful representation using only a relatively small number of labeled examples. In this paper, we propose a method for representation learning that can work well in these very difficult settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on simulated and real data examples, including applications in single-cell genomics and cosmological data analysis.

Short-period comets are unique and potentially dangerous objects for spacecraft in orbit around the Sun. We present a survey of recent results relating to the dynamical evolution of short-period comets and their nascent dust trails, with a specific emphasis on the behavior of candidate interstellar objects. We describe the history of short-period comets as a class of Solar System objects, including unique samples obtained by recent spacecraft flybys. We then summarize the complex interplay between short-period comets and their dust trails and how this has been improved with new analysis techniques. Finally, we discuss the implications for short-period comets as potential interstellaire objects and how future surveys may characterize this population. Comets are icy bodies located in the outer solar system that repeatedly come into the inner system. Over time, their orbital parameters can vary significantly, from stable long-term Neptune or Saturn orbits to highly hyperbolic orbits crossing the Sun-planets region in less than a year. Comets entering the inner Solar System are of particular interest because they may release dust and other volatiles, generating gas and smoke comets. As such, comets have long been implicated in shaping the geological and biological evolution of Earth. Although most comets orbit the Sun outbound, there is a long-period population with eccentric orbits that return to the inner Solar System. These long-period comets (LPCs) are of particular interest to astronomers and astrobiologists, as their activity may expose them to the impact of interstellar objects or dust clouds. The Centaurs were the first to establish a population of LPCs. However, there may be more massive LPC populations whose activity is subject to observational selection effects. We therefore describe a search for short-period comets (SPCs) that cross the orbits of planets, whether through direct observation or gravitational effects. We describe the dynamical evolution of short-period comets, their dust trails, and how this has been improved with new analysis techniques. Finally, we discuss the implications for short-period comets as potential interstellaire objects. We find a diverse population of short-period comets, including stable remnants of the Trojan asteroid system, hyperbolic comets with one comet fly-by of Earth in the last 50 years, highly eccentric Comet C/2017 O4 (Johnson) that flew by Mars in the first half of 2018, and hyperbolic Comet 2I/Borisov, whose closest fly-by to the Sun came in 2023. We describe the dynamical evolution of comets and their dust trails, as well as a search for the population of SPCs as a function of the Sun’s semimajor axis, including a search for the J2 period distribution for long-period comets. We then describe a series of proposed surveys with a large number of young main-belt asteroids that could be followed-up as LPCs or SPCs. These surveys include the Nightlinger and Haulani projects, and the proposed Large Synoptic Survey Telescope and Mars sample return

It is a widely accepted idea that diversity is good for a society, workplace or any community. It has been shown that a diverse community is more resilient, has better problem solving capabilities and has higher overall satisfaction. Based on these observations, many organizations strive to build an inclusive and diverse environment. However, diversity can also lead to divergence in opinions, and within a group with diverse opinions, people tend to like some ideas but not others. A diverse group is more susceptible to polarization which could lead to inefficient problem solving and worse overall satisfaction. Diverse groups are more likely to use excessive criticism, accusation and blaming, which can erode trust and understanding. This could also reduce the efficiency of the problem solving. Therefore, it is necessary to analyze if diversity is indeed beneficial or if we should avoid such diversity. In this article, I will discuss the tradeoff between diversity and polarization. I will argue that diversity can lead to divergence of opinions and increase in uncertainty about the true state of the world. This can lead to undermining of people's trust in each other and ideas. This can increase the amount of blaming and accusation which can reduce understanding and lead to further divergence. Therefore, diversity can reduce overall satisfaction and problem solving capabilities. I will provide empirical evidence to support these assertions using a series of experiments. I will first describe the hypothetical situation in which people think they are participating in a debate. Then I will describe the actual debates that participants were misled into believing that they believe were a debate between a few individuals but were in fact a debate among a larger group of people. In the first experiment, I asked the participants about their opinions at the beginning and end of the discussion. I found that the participants felt that their opinions were unchanged but in fact they had diverged a lot. In the second experiment, I asked the participants to rate their disagreement scores with other participants after the discussions. I found that their disagreement scores were significantly higher after the discussions than before the discussions, which means that they polarized more during the discussions. In the third experiment, I asked the participants to rate their satisfaction after the discussions. I found that the participants' satisfaction scores were significantly lower after the discussions than before the discussions. In the fourth experiment, I asked the participants to rate how much they blamed each other after the discussions. I found that the amount of blaming was significantly higher after the discussions. These experiments show that diversity can lead to divergence of opinions and polarization which reduce overall satisfaction and problem solving capabilities. On the other hand, enabling diverse opinions can lead to more inclusive, broader perspective and increased understanding of other viewpoints. By working in diverse groups, people can learn to tolerate diversity and embrace different viewpoints as different points of view. They can learn to focus on the core idea rather than the minor differences and find common ground. Therefore, enabling diverse opinions can increase overall satisfaction and problem solving capabilities. I believe that instead of focusing on diversity , we should focus on what we have in common. In order to achieve a better understanding of the world, we should focus on what we have in common. By working

Cosmomass & Cosmologist Smas (COSMOSOMAS) is an Italian space mission selected by the European Space Agency (ESA) in 2021 and planned for launch in 2023. The primary goal of the COSMOSOMAS is the study of the dark matter distribution in the Universe through the observation of the weak gravitational lensing . For this purpose, the satellite will carry out several observations of large, well-defined galaxy clusters. In addition, COSMOSOMAS will carry out spectral surveys of the whole sky in several frequency domains, with particular emphasis on the CMB spectral region (below 100 GHz). In this contribution we present results of the first observations of the CMB and the Galactic foreground performed with the COSMOSOMAS core observatory at 11 GHz. We observe negative levels of around -30 dBm in both the Stellarlite and Tenerife point scans, with rms fluctuations of around 10 dBm across the full observed area. We investigate possible causes for these features and conclude that the negative levels are consistent with thermal emission from the atmosphere at this frequency. However, we see significant deviations from this simple model in both the time and frequency domain. We therefore investigate the possibility that these observations may be pointing to an unidentified dark matter component in the W Hz-1/2 () region. Further observations at lower Galactic latitude are needed to confirm the robustness of these results and to investigate the possibility of spatial fluctuations in the emission.

pions are considered as the basic degrees of chiral symmetry near the nuclear saturation density. They play an important role in different fields of science such as in nuclear and particle physics, astrophysics and chemistry. In Quantum Field Theory, pions are the Goldstone bosons resulting from the spontaneous breaking of the global chiral symmetry in the limit of vanishing up and down quark s. The mass of the pi meson is generated through the interaction of pions with the QCD vacuum. In Quantum Chromodynamics, this interaction is described by the ΔS = 1 chiral effective Lagrangian, where S is the quark condensate (the classical order parameter of spontaneously broken chiral symmetry). The nuclear matter based on the up, down andenergetic quarks, can be thought of as a Fermi sea of pionic atoms. The interactions between the pions and the nuclear medium are described by the strong interaction, the same that binds the pions themselves into mesons, nucleons and hyperons. In asymmetric nuclear matter, the Fermi sea of pionic atoms is not symmetric with respect to the pion momentum. Due to the chiral anomaly, the interaction between pions and such an asymmetric Fermi sea of pionic atoms is also not symmetric. It is shown that such asymmetry can generate a difference in the speeds of pions traveling in the up and down directions. Such a result, although expected theoretically, is of interest, since its detection could be an indicator of the existence of the axial U(1) anomaly in asymmetric nuclear matter.

A rapidly rotating black hole has distinctive astrophysical signatures, such as a rotational Doppler-shifted spectral line and a magnetic feature. To detect these signatures, one must measure the black hole’s dimensionless spin parameter, Ω = τ / M cl, where τ is the black hole’s relativistic spin torque and M cl is the spin velocity of the black hole. The measurement of τ requires an estimate of the black hole’s spin torque, <unk>/ M cl, which can be obtained from models of the accretion flow. A common model of a thin, rotating accretion disk invokes a balance between the accretion torque and an approximate variant of the Poynting-Robertson (PR) effect, such that the total accretion torque and radiated PR flux are comparable. In contrast, recent works have shown that in the inner regions of thin accretion disks, the dominant torque mechanism is a transition from the classical, inwardly radial accretion torque to a viscous torque, such that the total accretion torque and viscous torque differ by a large factor. In this Letter, I show that viscous torques, unlike accretion torques, are not form dependent. As a result, viscous torques dominate in the inner regions of thin accretion disks. The outer regions of the disk correspond to the classical regime in which viscous and accretion torques are comparable. Consequently, viscous torques produce larger estimates of the black hole spin. Viscous torques have been studied previously using phenomenological arguments and/or numerical simulations. In contrast, I present a fundamental equation of motion for thin accretion disks and demonstrate that viscous torques are the solution to this equation of motion. The viscous torque is a form-invariant under scaling of the angular frequency and length, such that it cannot be distinguished from other forms of the accretion torque using traditional thin accretion disk models. In addition, viscous torques can be positive or negative, which is a fundamental asymmetry not present in the other torques. This Letter presents a physical model for viscous torques in thin accretion disks and highlights the importance of including viscous torques in models of the inner regions of accretion flows in order to accurately calculate black hole spin.

In this paper we present a measurement of the sensitivity of searches for anomalous Wtb couplings in the Wtb quark decay channel at the LHC. We focus on 13 TeV data and update our previous measurements, presented at the Moriond EW session in 2018, with the full dataset collected so far in 2015. The results are presented in the case of simplified models involving non-standard Wtb couplings, with the goal of testing the fundamental symmetries of the Wtb vertex, namely its hermiticity and gauge s. We find consistent limits with those obtained at the Moriond conference, and we update our results in the case of non-zero scalar and pseudoscalar couplings. The results presented in this paper are the most constraining to date for the vector and scalar couplings, and we exhibit the first limits on the Tensor couplings. We also present first limits on anomalous Wtb couplings involving the pseudovector interaction, which can arise in models beyond the standard model (BSM). We expect our results to be directly applicable to new phenomena characterized by these anomalous couplings, and we illustrate this point by considering the case of Minimal Flavour Violation (MFV).

The Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS) is an infrared camera with capabilities similar to those of the Infrared Space Observatory (ISO) operating on the Spitzer Space Telescope. This camera was used to make observations of several stellarforming galaxies at 70 μm. Absolute calibration and characterization of the camera at 70 μm are presented. The accuracy of the 70 μm transfer function is quantified by observing a set of optical standards, and uncertainties are found to be 5.3% at 30 μm brightness, 6.1% at 45 μm, 7.7% at 60 μm, and 9.3% at 90 μm. Stellar color and temperature estimates are compared to those derived from Infrared Array Camera data, and the two datasets are shown to be in excellent agreement given the expected errors from both instruments. Next, the 70 μm PSF is characterized, with the measurements indicating that the half-power resolution is 14.3 μm, the peak brightness at half-maximum is 23.2 μm, and the average background surface brightness within the PSF is 1013.2 MJ/sr^2. Absolute calibration is performed by observing Uranus at 70 μm and yields a flux of 357.8225 μJykpc2. Additionally, observations of the outer regions of five galaxies at 70 μm confirm that the 70 μm emission spectrum is clearly extended, with surface brightnesses of 23.2 μm−2 less than that of the background at the 50% level. Further analysis of these data indicates that the observed intensity is in good agreement with that of an exponential disk at 70 μm with scale lengths of ~4.2 kpc, smaller than but still in good agreement with other wavelengths of stellarforming galaxies at 70 <unk> m.

We present new Spitzer MIPS 24 and Herschel PACS 70, 160, and 250 observations of the Far-Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Telescope (FUSE) selected galaxy cluster CIZA J2242.8+5301 at z = 0.55. Spitzer data consist of new 23.88' x 11.20' coverage of the cluster core, plus 7.5' SDSS coverage of two wide-field telescopes covering 61% and 42% of the MIPS field of view. Spitzer data are used to measure the integrated 24 Ɠ, or rest-frame 13.39 μm, flux from the galaxies in the cluster field. Combined with existing FUSE data and HST/WFC3 data over the fields of view covered by PACS, we use these data to measure the mean, spread, and statistical significance of the far-infrared emission from galaxies in the cluster core. The mean redshifted 24 Ɠ emission is 13.39 μm = 0.1687±0.0064 Jy sr−1. The far-infrared luminosity distribution is similar to that of local galaxies, but the dispersion in the 70-160 μm far-infrared luminosity for galaxies at this redshift is a factor of 2.2 larger. This may be an indication that the buildup of stellar mass in cluster galaxies requires a minimum dynamical time, and thus that either pre-heating or feedback processes are required. The high dispersion in the 70-160 μm far-infrared luminosity is not seen in lower-redshift clusters, which have much less dispersion at fixed cluster-centric radius. This may imply that the source of the 70-160 μm far-infrared luminosity dispersion at high redshift is distinct from that of galaxies at lower redshift.

Recently, the Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) with Cyclic Prefix (CP) has been considered as one of the promising candidates for the next generation wireless standards such as Wireless Personal Area Networks (WPAN) and Wireless Local Area Networks (WLAN) with UWB pulse-shape modulation. However, one of the major challenges with OFDM is the high cost of filters needed in the receiver to filter out the broadband symbols and the presence of channel aliasings. One of the possible solutions to this problem is to combine OFDM with CDMA. In this regard, we propose a CP-free UWB OFDM with CDMA (CP-free UWB-OFDM with CDMA) system. In this system, the frequency domain CDMA interleaver is used to spread the spectrum of the multicarrier symbol while the cyclic prefix in time domain is used to overlapping CDMA remapping function of the OFDM demodulation filter. Using extensive computer simulations, we have demonstrated the improvement in the BER of up to 3.26 dB compared to CP-free UWB-OFDM without CDMA for a BER of $2\times 10^{-3}$. As an example, we present the frequency and time domain graphs for the proposed system.

Recent discovery of high-frequency quasi-periodic objects (HFQPOs) in a few X-ray binary systems and X-ray binaries has opened a new window to study the inner region of these strongly gravity regions. A possible mechanism to generate the observed HFQPOs has been suggested in terms of orbiting hot-spot(s) in a curved accretion disc, with the associated continuum becoming depleted at the orbital frequencies of the hot-spot(s). In this paper, we study, for the first time, the orbital behaviour of a hot-spot in a Keplerian disc orbiting near-extreme Kerr black hole (i.e, extreme Kerr black hole with dimensionless spin parameter |a|=0.98), and demonstrate the possibility of developing a HFQPO mechanism in such systems. The model presented in this paper, for the first time, successfully explains the recently observed HFQPOs in the X-ray binary system GRS 1915+105, which are usually in the frequency range of 102 - 128 Hz, by assuming a Keplerian disc orbiting near-extreme Kerr black hole.

We present X-ray observations of a sample of 23 normal galaxies from the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey field (GOODS). These X-ray observations are obtained from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and span an approximately 12-year time period from 2003 to 2014. We perform X-ray spectral fitting on the resulting data set and compute X-ray luminosity functions (XLFs) in different soft (0.5–2 keV) and hard (2–10 keV) X-ray bands. While the XLFs in the soft and hard X-ray bands show significant variability on time scales of years, there is no strong variability on time scales of years nor any clear correlation between the soft and hard XLFs. We compare our XLF results to those from other surveys and discuss implications for the diffuse hot gas in normal galaxies.

Cooling flow clusters of galaxies have extraordinarily high rates of galaxy cluster-scale cooling: up to 30 million degrees Celsius per square degree. This intracluster medium, while of low entropy, is nevertheless observed to be cooling via the X-ray s. Z3146 is one of the most dramatic cooling flow clusters, owing its name to its extreme X-ray temperature of Z=3146 keV, the highest of any cluster known. Observations from the Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray observatories , along with the Keck-II telescope and the Very Large Telescope have been used to study the morphology, physical state, and dynamics of the cooling flow gas. We find that the gas is distributed in two massive and morphologically distinct flows: a western cooling flow that extends across much of the cooling radius and a smaller eastern flow that is offset from the cool core and much more concentrated. Both flows are smooth, free of bubbles or irregularities, and have well-behaved temperature, pressure, and entropy . The total mass of the gas in the cooling flow is estimated to be 2.8 x 0.5 (massiveyon $h_0 = 0.704$ - see figure 5.1) and approximately 3.3 x 0.5 x 0.5. Most of this is likely to be in the form of galaxies, making Z3146 one of the most massive galaxy clusters known.

Neural networks have been successfully used to solve complex supervised learning problems. However, training a neural network that outputs an encoding of an image or a shape, that can be later decoded to reconstruct the original shape or image, is a challenging problem. Such a network is called a sequence to shape map, or renderer, and has a number of potential applications, such as rendering, animation, and game development. However, existing renderers are trained on large datasets of random images, which can be expensive or difficult to obtain. Recently, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used to train renderers from random vectors. However, GANs suffer from mode collapse and require cumbersome hyperparameter tuning. In this paper, we present Neutral Networks of Sequence to Shape Maps (NNS), a new approach to renderer training. NNS uses a “geared” style of learning that speeds up training and eliminates the need for hyperparameter tuning. NNS uses a simple feed-forward network to learn a mapping from a random vector to a distribution of renderers. NNS does not try to generate a random vector, but simply outputs a distribution over different styles of renderings. We apply NNS to two challenging problems: (1) encoding of virtual objects, that can be later used for video animation; and (2) frame-by-frame rendering of complex 3D scenes, that can be used for visualization and virtual reality. Our results show that NNS can achieve results comparable to the state of the art on traditional image benchmarks, and outperform GAN-based renderer training approaches.

I present an analysis of Spitzer spectra of four planets exposed to different levels of irradiation. Water vapor is found in the atmosphere of Earth, which is partially explained by the effect of water vapor in increasing the radius of the planet and reducing the amount of energy from the Sun hitting the surface. This suggests that if a planet’s atmosphere has a significantly higher water vapor abundance than Earth’s, then the energy hitting the surface would be reduced enough that the planet could have a smaller radius and be classified as a “super-earth.” One of the objects in my sample has a higher water abundance than Earth’s, but still has a larger radius than many planets listed in the Guinness Book of World Records. I also examine atmospheric abundances of other volatile species. For one object I find evidence for hydrogen cyanide, which could be produced by a potentially extinct plant life form. The four planets I study are Erakis ($P = 5.3$ days, 1.1 $M_{earth}$ radius), Ganeko ($P = 9.2$ hours, 0.82 $M_{earth}$ radius), Gliese 832 b ($P = 5.7$ days, 1.2 $M_{earth}$ radius), and Kepler-13Ab ($P = 6.5$ days, 1.8 $M_{earth}$ radius). The dataset used was collected by the Spitzer Space Telescope in the framework of the mission’s GALEX project.

The first galaxies were very massive, with virial temperatures of tens of thousands of K. Their intense ultraviolet radiation ionised most of the gas in minihalos, suppressing the formation of subsequent galaxies. We report the detection of lower metal enrichments in the gas in the virialized minihalos than in the intergalactic medium (IGM), which likely originated from primordial star formation in minihalos. The detection of the metals in the minihalos supports the predictions of hierarchical structure , in which small dark matter halos first formed near the regions where the intergalactic gas was later incorporated. It also supports a scenario in which the stars in these earliest galaxies had masses of 1010–1022 M⊕. Such stellar masses imply the primordial stars could have produced the necessary metals only with contributions from non-thermal processes, likely from primordial star formation in very massive stars.

A long, abstract-heavy version of this article can be found on arXiv.org. Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are highly luminous cosmological explosions that are used as distance indicators and probes of the universe's accelerated expansion. Their high brightness permits many tests of cosmology by observation of distant SN Ia. However, the observed homogeneity of SNe Ia is left to the nature of the progenitors and the exact nature of the explosion. One popular hypothesis is that SN Ia result from the detonation of a white dwarf (WD) star in a close binary system. Detonation-based models of SN Ia require the WD to achieve a critical density in carbon and oxygen to trigger a detonation. While most WDs have a sufficient amount of this species near the core, the burning stops before significant amounts of silicon are reached, leaving an under-processed WD star. In this paper, the burning rate of carbon and oxygen to form Si in a WD near the critical density for a detonation is modeled. It is found that the ignition densities and flame speeds are sufficiently high to permit a deflagration phase to occur instead of a detonation. The net effect is that the WD is successful in achieving a thermonuclear explosion, but the nature of the explosion differs from that of a typical SN Ia. Instead of reducing the expected result of a deflagration phase to a full detonation, a gravitationally confined detonation (GCD) occurs. This is analogous to the gravitational deflagration of a fluid, where the deflagration speed is sufficient for detonation formation but not large enough to overcome gravitational suppression. The GCD model for Type Ia supernovae has successfully reproduced many properties of SNe Ia, including peak brightness, light curve width, and late-time color, without the need for unobserved features such as unprocessed silicon. Overall, the results presented in this paper show that a GCD model is a promising framework for Type Ia supernovae without the need for unobserved features such as unprocessed silicon. Reconstruction of the deflagration phase in the GCD model of Type Ia supernovae enables successful reproduction of many observed properties of these events.

The characterization of instrumental phase stability is necessary for several applications in astronomy such as the detection of meteors, the study of the atmosphere or for the detection of artificial satellites. In the field of radio astronomy, phase stability is necessary to achieve the coherence needed to conduct precision astronomical observations. The coherence is obtained by referencing the signal to an external source . This phase stability is known with great precision (a hydrogen maser for example). The stability of the astronomical instrument itself is the amount of jitters that does not degrade the coherence of the signal. To characterize the phase stability of the IRAM 30-meter telescope, we implemented a phase referenced signal at 10.5 cm in the form of a dual -channel Bracewell . By doing this, we could measure the phase stability between two channels every 20 minutes with a 1.1 millas m jitter. We have also shown how to compute the equivalent closed loop transfer function of the system. This is relevant for the control community because this kind of measurements are often used as a probe for the stability of an aircraft such as an A300 airplane or a satellite. This stability is very important for their reliability.

Floating balls that are not satellites, but co-orbit around a star are a common sight in the night sky. These co-orbitals have been observed around both normal planets and moon-like objects. However, the existence of co-orbital oligarchies has only recently been confirmed by numerical simulations, with no analogous explanation in planet-disk models. This raises the question of how co-orbitals can be sustained, particularly in the face of strong radial diffusion. I present an analytic model of the dynamical environment around stars, in which I identify three conditions necessary for the long-term stability of co-orbitals. First, the Laplace pressure from the central star must be large enough to overwhelm disk torques, allowing co-orbital oligarchies to form and survive over time. Second, the co-orbital region must be isolated from the co-orbital region of other stars, in order to prevent stochastic ejection. Finally, the stellar density profile must be steeply decreasing with distance from the star, so that close encounters are rare and impact angles are small, allowing the satellites to remain intact. These three conditions are met in most stars, and can account for the observed co-orbital populations.

In the standard brane world scenario our universe is viewed as a domain wall consisting of two domains separated by a thin flat brane in a higher dimensional space-time. For simplicity we will assume that the bulk has five dimensional AdS spacetime. The Randall-Sundrum fine-tuning relation, between the five dimensional AdS curvature and the four dimensional effective gravitational constant, implies a relation between the energy exchange parameter in our brane and the energy density parameter in the bulk . This implies that the currently observed acceleration of the universe cannot be explained in the standard brane world scenario but could be a result of this energy exchange. We use recent observational data from the SDSS main Galaxy sample and BOSS LOWZ and CMASS samples to constrain the different cosmological parameters. We find that the new parameters which have to be introduced are a bulk cosmological constant, a dark energy component with dynamical equations similar to those of Modified Chaplygin Gas and a bulk equation of state governing the energy exchange between dark energy and the dark matter fields in the bulk. This latter parameter is physically reasonable and ranges between -1 and 0.5. For this range of the bulk energy exchange parameter, the Newtonian acceleration of the universe can be explained without the need for a fine tuning between the brane and the bulk parameters. Our model predicts a transition from matter domination to acceleration in the evolution of the universe similar to that of the $\Lambda$CDM model. This transition also depends on the bulk energy exchange parameter. Finally we consider the modification of gravity on the brane caused by the exchange of energy between dark energy and the dark matter fields in the bulk. This leads to an additional correction to the Newtonian acceleration which could be tested in the near future with planned tests of gravity using Extrasolar Planets (ESPRESSO) and Space based Gravitational Lensing (libration point observatory).

Modules over operads and their relationship to functors have been the subject of much recent work. The most precise of these results, a strong form of the Yoneda lemma, equates modules over an operad with functors from that operad to the category of abelian groups. This result relies on work of Smith and others in the derivation of a module over a PROP from a functor into the category of chain complexes. The method of proof relies on the structure of PROPs as universal algebras. We show that a version of the Yoneda lemma holds for small, skeletal operads, including those corresponding to stable, homology theories. A method of proof of the skeletal Yoneda lemma applies to any operad in well-generated monoids in spaces. This generalizes the general theorem of Smith and Eisenbud that coherent rings correspond to associative, unital monoids in spaces. The skeletal version of the Yoneda lemma implies the more precise form. We give a number of examples of skeletal operads arising in homology theories, including K-theory, connective K-theory, extended K-theory, complex bordism, and motivic homology theories.

In this paper we present a study of the metal-insulator transition in the TMTSF organic conductor (TMTSF)2FSO3 by means of infrared microspectroscopy. The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in (TMTSF)2FSO3 was first observed in 1981, and has been the subject of extensive studies since. The MIT occurs at Tc = 38 K and is associated with the two-dimensionalization of Fermi-surface sections caused by interlayer s. The compound exhibits Shubnikov-de Haas-oscillation-based evidence for 1D optical conductivity behavior below 10 K. The optical conductivity spectrum undergoes a drastic change across Tc, which we attribute to the opening of a Mott-Hubbard gap in the metallicity below Tc. We observe characteristic features of a strongly correlated Mott insulator over a wide frequency range, which is consistent with reported transport, thermodynamic and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements.

Massive black holes (MBHs) are common at the centres of galaxies, and it has been predicted that they can grow significantly through a process known as stellar capture, in which incoming stars are torn apart by the strong gravitational field of the MBH, and their material is accreted. However, it has not been predicted how rapidly MBHs could grow by this process, or whether a self-gravitating disc of accreted material around the MBH could enhance the capture process. Here we show that a self-gravitating disc around an MBH can significantly increase the cross-section for stellar capture, compared to the case without a disc. We find that this can greatly enhance the rate of growth of MBHs by a factor of millions relative to the stellar-capture-only case. We show that the growth of MBHs by this capture assisted by a disc is both very rapid (on a dynamical time) and smooth (without dynamically-important fluctuations), and we provide simple analytic expressions that describe the growth. We perform a series of numerical simulations to test our theory and show that our predictions agree with the results of the simulations. This work suggests a novel mechanism for the fast growth of MBHs at the centres of galaxies.

The Serpens survey is an identifier of several large, bright interstellar clouds. Serpens is one of these clouds. It was observed with the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS). New detections of eight continuum sources and a list of eighteen further potential protostars are reported. A * denotes new detections, and T indicates that the source was previously detected but was not observed to be variable in the MIPS observations. Serpens IMM VLA 1, BIMA 2, and Serpens SMM 1, are the sources detected in the MIPS images. All of the detected sources are found to be variable. Four sources in the cloud are detected in both the MIPS 24 and 70 μm bands, with brightnesses of between 0.09 and 14.0 mJy/bm. The luminosities of these sources range from 0.004 to 1.2 Lsun. A subset of these sources is also detected at 8.0 μm, and in general the 24 μm emission is found to be brighter than the 8.0 μm emission. One particularly bright source (Serpens SMM 4) is observed to brighten by a factor of 10.6 between the 70 and 8.0 <unk>m bands. The observations presented here are based on data acquired with the Spitzer Space Telescope, which is operated by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology under a contract with NASA.

The first stars and galaxies were probably very massive, more massive than $100M_{\odot}$. It is thus natural to expect the existence of very massive stars (VMSs), with initial masses $M_{\rm i}\geq8M_{\odot}$, in the high-redshift galaxies that might have been their hosts. We present an epoch of VMS formation and evolution that indicates that the predicted lifetimes of these stars, and thus their possible contribution to the high-redshift galaxy populations, depend critically on the assumptions made regarding both mass-loss and binary interactions. Based on the inferred properties of the most massive stars in the Universe today, we suggest that high-redshift galaxies could have produced up to $30\%$ of their present-day metal masses via supernovas and supernova explosions from a unique population of very massive, binary stars. Our results have profound implications for the formation of low-mass stars and galaxies, and suggest that the epoch of high-redshift star formation may have been more energetic and complex than anticipated.

Recently Kirillov and Reshetikhin conjecture became one of the central problems in the representation theory of quantum groups. It states that the character of an irreducible representation of a quantum affine group in certain specialization coincided with a combination of special value of the quantum group and special value of the quantum invariant. This conjecture was proved for some cases, in particular, for classical and negative level. The proof uses the idea of truncation. In the present paper we prove the conjecture in the general case. The proof is based on the Sklyanin's quantum elliptic approach to the method of separation of variables. We would like to thank S. Sergeev for valuable discussions. Kirillov-Reshetikhin conjecture. The general case. Kirillov I. A., Reshetikhin N. Yu. (1996). J. Math. Sci. (New York) : pp. 97-108. ( transformed in 2002 into an article with collaboration of Yangian double). Email address: uriskevich.lists.io. For a long time the conjecture was regarded as one of the central problems in the representation theory of quantum groups. Recently, the conjecture was proved for some cases. In particular, the conjecture was proved for the classical and negative level cases. In this paper we prove the conjecture in the general case. The proof is based on the Sklyanin's quantum elliptic approach to the method of separation of variables.

On February 24, 1987, the star was very smalland the Sun were close to coincide in the sky. Consequently, SN 1987A was easily visible to the optical telescopes and appeared as one of the most intensively studied supernova since. observations from the Chandra X-ray Observatory confirm the explosion center location as inferred from optical observations and provide the first reliable measurement of the physical extent of the supernova shockwave. The explosion angular size is 0.5 milli-arc-seconds and the blast wave is radiating at approximately 1053 erg/sec. These measurements provide important constraints on the properties of the supernova shockwave and the material between the star and the shockwave at the time of the explosion. Supernova SN 1987A was a typical Type II supernova. Early spectra showed strong lines from the H and He nuclei. As the ejecta expanded, the lines evolved into features from stripped nucleons. (In Type II, the star did not become a neutron star.) Finally, the spectrum became featureless at late times, revealing the nature of the exploding star. Supernova SN 1987A was extraordinary because it was within 50 parsecs of the Sun and was one of the closest Supernovae to Earth in nearly two decades. Consequently, details of the shockwave propagation and the early emission could be studied in great detail. The blast wave reached the center of the star in under 20,000 years (the time it took the light to reach Earth). The derived explosion energy is 1053 ergs. The first X-ray emission was observed two days after the explosion. It was a faint point source, much dimmer than the stellar optical emission. As the shockwave propagated, the radio, optical and X-ray emission increased in intensity. By day 800, the X-ray flux was 5.5 x 10^-17 W m-2. As the optical emission peaked, the X-ray emission was 5.5 x 10^-17 W m-2. The light curves show a slower rise for X-ray than for optical and radio. The peak optical and radio fluxes were reached around day 400, whereas the peak X-ray emission was reached around day 800.

Nano-triboelectrification is the phenomenon where nanoparticles of one material acquire electrons from another material. This induced electron cloud can attract other similar charged nanoparticles or surfaces, thereby forming non-contact adhesive forces. The attraction between two spherical nanoparticles can be accurately described by the Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek (DLVO) theory of electrostatics, except that the induced charges are situated on the nanoparticles, not on the surfaces. We report experiments measuring the adhesion forces between two silicon wafers, two Au-coated glass slides, and two graphite slides. These test surfaces were parallel and charged by rubbing them with various materials and surfaces. Our apparatus allowed us to continuously rotate one surface while the other was fixed, probing different directions to determine the induced charges and hence the adhesion forces. We found that the adhesion forces were largest between like silicon and silicon, lowest between like gold and gold, and nearly non-existent between unlike materials. The maximum observed adhesion force was 62.5 μN. These findings agree with DLVO theory, and indicate that nano-triboelectrification may be used to facilitate non-contact bonding or coating of materials that are difficult to bond or bind otherwise.

How mergers may affect the scaling relations between black holes, galaxies, and other gravitationally bound systems is an open question. Here we use high-resolution N-body simulations to show that, after a merger, the host DM halos have a decreased spin and a smallertotal mass scaled to their normally defined total mass. The decreased spin is a result of angular energy transfer to the DM particles and residual gas. The decreased total mass is attributed to the dissipation of orbital energy through gravitational drag. We show that these two effects are correlated to an effective reduced Mach number for the merger. Using the decrease in the effective Mach number, we are able to extend the Virial mass definition to the DM halos and derive a new scaling relation that is consistent with the behavior of bound systems after mergers. We also show that this new scaling relation can explain the observed mass-activity relation of galaxies without requiring DM self-interactions. Finally, we propose an extension of the fundamental plane of ellipticals, which shows that early-type galaxies lie on a track that is different from that of non-merged galaxis, in terms of galaxy sizes, dark matter densities, and velocity dispersions, after mergers. The new plane shows that early-type galaxies, after a merger, lie on a track that is different from that of non-merged early-type galaxies, and that is well-explained by our new scaling relation.

The development of rotational support in low-mass stars is complex, as evidenced by the presence of multiple distinct rotational populations in many regions of the main sequence. Within the range 1.2 < M/M⊙ <unk> 2.0, lower-mass main-sequence stars undergo so-called core-hydrogen burning, during which they expand to significantly cooler temperatures, becoming fully radiative at M/M⊙ ≳ 1.8. Core-hydrogen-burning stars of this mass range are generally poorly-aligned rotators, with v<unk>reaching i~5-10% of their breakup velocity. However, as their cores hydrogen-deplete, they begin to contract, eventually culminating in the formation of degenerate cores. This evolution is accompanied by a pronounced increase in equatorial velocity, driven both by hydrostatic and radiative pressure, with v⃗⃗ reaching 70% - 80% of the initial velocity. This intense rotation is preserved on the main-sequence, with v⃗⃗~ 110 km/s at M/M⊙ = 2.0. A small number of these stars, in particular those with initial periods P < 10 days, undergo second-birth phases, during which strong equatorial magnetic fields are generated through a combination of internal and external dynamical mechanisms. These magnetic fields dramatically inhibit the operation of rotational braking, leading to break-up speeds in excess of 200 km/s. These rapid rotators are responsible for several astrophysical phenomena, including the population of fast-moving stars within our galaxy, and the high-energy gamma-ray bursts observed throughout the observable Universe. We present the discovery of a population of rapidly-rotating, degenerate stars at M/M⊙ < 2.0. Contrary to previous expectations, we find that their rotation is not limited to the initial stages of main-sequence life, but can survive the post-degeneracy phase, long after the cessation of hydrogen fusion. Using mixed-Rossby number calculations, we show that these stars retain appreciable amounts of differential rotation to the final stages of their evolution. These results provide a unique and exciting perspective on the spin evolution of low-mass stars, and may have important implications for gamma-ray burst progenitors and the structure of their degenerate cores.

In this work, we study the Tayler instability of a spherical layer with z-dependent differential rotation in the shearing sheet approximation. Using both analytical and numerical methods, we show that this instability generates helicity in the layer and is manifested through the generation of a large-scale zonal flow. The resulting zonal flow exhibits Hall-stable differential rotation when the magnetic Prandtl number Pm is sufficiently high, but becomes unstable when the magnetic Prandtl number Pm decreases. We find that for decreasing values of Pm, the generated zonal flow becomes more unstable and ultimately decays into a chaotic state. When decreasing Pm towards the instability threshold, the growth rates and the wave numbers of the most unstable modes depend linearly on the mean magnetic helicity of the initial conditions. We discuss the implications of these results for the dynamics of the solar spherical layer, which is characterized by z-dependent differential rotation and a low Pm. We also note that, according to the results of previous numerical simulations, the Hall-effect-driven alpha-effect does not generate significant shear in the tachocline. As a result of this work, we believe that it is now possible to self-consistently model the generation of large-scale zonal flows and the alpha-effect in the same framework.

Emulsion stability is essential for many applications, such as cosmetics, paints, agriculture, and medicine. It depends on various physical and chemical parameters including the particle size, particle charge, oil/water ratio, and polymer/co-polymer composition. One widely used approach to emulsion stabilization is by means of surfactants that stabilize the emulsion at the oil/water interface and reduce the surface tension. However, surfactants are toxic, cost intensive, and can negatively affect the emulsion properties. A more versatile approach is to use a polymer that forms a network at the oil/water interface. The characteristic length of the network should be comparable to or larger than the average oil droplet size. This allows the network to span the interface and stabilize the emulsion. A very attractive candidate for the polymer is a co-polymer, which is a linear combination of different monomer types. This paper presents a mathematical model for a copolymer in an emulsion, which is derived by means of the multi-scale method. The method is used to link molecular dynamics simulations with coarse-grained particle simulations. The resulting mathematical model can be used to perform virtual screening of co-polymers for a specific application. For example, virtual screening can predict the necessary composition and structure of the co-polymer that should stabilize a specific emulsion with specific physical and chemical properties.

The Comoros Effect, named after the formerly independent country of Comoros in the Indian Ocean, is the belief that brushing your teeth regularly reduces the number of cavities you acquire. This has been scientifically disproven, yet many people maintain the belief to this day. To further examine the psychology of the Comoros Effect, I present the first quantifiable measurement of the free energy of activation for the abrasive action of toothbrushing. Using a detailed biophysical model of a tooth in motion, I demonstrate that the energy cost of toothbrushing is tolerable and is therefore easily allowed for in the total free energy of activation of diet, leading to the erroneous belief that brushing regularly would reduce cavities. This is the first known scientific measurement of the free energy of activation for the abrasive action of toothbrushing, and serves to educate the public on the actual energy costs of various common practices.

Coherence and phase synchronization are a pair of multivariate extensions to the computation of cross-correlation used in time series analysis. In its most basic form, coherence measures the proportion of the two signals' in-phase behavior, while related phase synchronization quantifies the consistency of the signal phase. These metrics have been used to characterize the phase-locking behavior exhibited by systems as diverse as nuclear reactors, heart cells, and Josephson junctions. The most widely-applied multivariate extension to coherence and phase synchronization is the computation of delay-embedded correlation. This metric not only quantifies in-phase behavior, but can also be used to estimate the influence that one signal has on another, coupled system. The delay-embedded correlation approach has been successfully applied to spatially-coupled electrochemical systems, coupled financial markets, and coupled network models of quantum oscillators. While the delay-embedding approach is conceptually simple, its computations are frequently unstable, especially when applied to non-stationary data. To address this, the pair-wise multivariate extension has been introduced. This metric generalizes the computation of delay-embedding correlation to account for cross-correlation between two signals at non-zero time lags. In this manner, it is able to estimate the influence that one signal has on the other, even in the presence of non-stationarity and zero-lag influence. It is important to emphasize that the pair-wise approach can only estimate the influence that one signal has on the other. It is unable to separate the two signals. In contrast, multivariate approaches such as transfer entropy and information dynamics measure the influence that one signal has on both itself and the other. This paper will describe both the pair-wise and multivariate formulations of coherence and phase synchronization, and will provide illustrative examples of their application to synthetic data as well as to real-world systems.

In this paper we describe the action of the absolute Galois group on the set of connected components of the Hurwitz scheme of models of X over finite fields in the moduli space of surfaces of general type. We show that this action is faithful and topological, i.e. does not preserve the underlying schemes. Let X be a smooth projective variety over a field k. The absolute Galois group of k, written Gal(k), acts on the set of connected components of the Hurwitz scheme of models of X over finite fields. We show that this action is faithful if and only if the Picard number of X is not rational. We then show that the action of Gal(k) on the set of connected components of the Hurwitz scheme is topological if and only if the Picard number of X is at most 1, if and only if the canonical bundle of X is trivial. We apply this result to describe the action of Gal(k) on the set of connected components of the moduli space of surfaces of general type.

A substantial fraction of bright AGNs are largely unrecognized in X-ray surveys, even with the aid of deep wide-field surveys. One possibility is that these AGNs are "hidden" in the so-called normal, star-forming galaxies. In this work, we investigate the hidden active galactic nuclei (HAGNs) in a luminously-red quasar host galaxy at z = 6.4 selected from the Chandra Deep Field-North (CDF-N). The total X-ray luminosity of the quasar host galaxy is 1.7 × 1046 erg/s, higher than 1043 erg/s in ultraviolet/optical/NIR, which is largely dominated by the emission from a buried active galactic nucleus (otherwise being classified as a QSO2). The X-ray to optical luminosity ratio (X/O) and near-infrared flux density are used to distinguish between the HAGN and the QSO2 nature. By combining the HST/WFC3 grism survey and the 3D-HST survey, we identify an extremely strong Lyα emitter (EELG), hinting at a bright, hidden active galactic nucleus (HAGN) with an extremely high luminosity of 1.7 × 1042 erg/s (estimated from the observed Lyα luminosity and the relation between AGN luminosity and host galaxy bolometric luminosity). The absolute magnitude of the EELG is M{sub g} ≈ -22.8, which is extremely luminous even for the red galaxies with high redshifts. The spatial scale of the EELG is ~6 kpc, indicating an on-going starburst rather than a pure galaxy assembly process, although the merging process cannot be fully ruled out. Our results suggest that the combination of extremely high AGN luminosity and an extremely strong star formation activity may help to drive the exceptionally large outflows observed in this system (equivalent width of H{alpha} line is as high as 270 Å). We find two other candidates (one is an ultra-luminous infrared starburst, the other one may have a low-level AGN) from the HST/WFC3 grism survey, and re-analyze the EELG from the 3D-HST data, which support this finding. These three candidates are interesting in terms of the interplay between AGNs and host galaxies and the feedback from them. In the future, high spatial resolution X-ray observations with the Athena X-ray observatory and the next generation optical/NIR telescopes like JWST and Euclid may help us better understand the demographics of AGNs, and whether H{sub e}-mode feedback is a common phenomenon in the high-redshift Universe.

A robust developmental program is essential for multicellular organisms to carry out their functions, such as formation of body plans and limbs, and to adapt to environmental change. Here we develop a theoretical and experimental framework to investigate multicellular developmental robustness, based on an evolutionary model for gene regulation. The model encompasses, for the first time, the role of cell division in developmental robustness, and our theory and experiments reveal that developmental robustness can arise from a compromise between developmental tempo and program, and between robustness to variability in cell type composition. Using this framework, we propose non-mutually exclusive avenues to improve developmental robustness. For example, increases in developmental tempo can enhance robustness; and alternative strategies to increase robustness may be to (i) reduce the influence of noise in gene expression, or (ii) reduce heterogeneity in cell type composition. These results establish a theoretical foundation for multicellular developmental robustness, and we propose that our theory should enable the identification and implementation of strategies to improve robustness in synthetic systems and in regenerative medicine.

A recent development in homology theory is the introduction of a new layer of structure - the covering homology - that enables one to perform many of the same calculations as singular homology, but with improved behavior in several key situations. In this short note, we describe covering homology, as well as two situations in which it is particularly well-behaved: when a space is sequentially weakly contractible, and when it is shellable. A new layer of structure has recently been developed to enable one to perform many of the same calculations as singular homology, but with improved behavior in several key situations. We give a brief overview of covering homology, and two situations in which it is particularly well-behaved: when a space is sequentially weakly contractible, and when it is shellable. DRect uses the term "covering homology" rather than "singular homology." The phrase "covering homology" is already in wide use in topology, in part because it has some advantage over singular homology in certain situations. For example, it is known that covering homology is invariant under topological invariance operations such as suspension and passage to the loop space. In contrast, singular homology is not invariant under passage to the loop space. Since the 1980s, a popular approach to the problem of computing homology groups has been to construct a chain or cochain complex and then apply a homology functor to this complex. The resulting Betti numbers, which count the number of generators of each homology group, can be hard to compute. However, the complex of covering groups, with the appropriate functors applied, has more structure and can produce more manageable Betti numbers. This approach was developed in the 1980s and 90s by Marius Dadarlat and Harry Wu, and more recently it has been put on a rigorous foundation by Georges Habdsky, Jerzy Madysiewicz, and the University of Michigan, among others.

A new technique for the detection of gamma-ray bursts with the Swift Burst Alert Telescope is presented. It is based on searching for a strong optical and/or radio afterglow from very high redshift bursts, and it is fully independent of any pre-existing catalog of gamma-ray bursts. It has already resulted in the discovery of one very high redshift burst, at a redshift of 12. The implications of this discovery for the nature of gamma-ray bursts are discussed. ory: A new technique for the detection of gamma-ray bursts with the Swift Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) is presented. It is based on searching for a strong optical and/or radio afterglow from very high redshift bursts, and it is fully independent of any pre-existing catalog of gamma-ray bursts. It has already resulted in the discovery of one very high redshift burst, at a redshift of 12. The implications of this discovery for the nature of gamma-ray bursts are discussed.

A generic discrete-event random simulation model, VOODB, is introduced to evaluate the performances of OODBs. OODBs refer to online analytical processing (OLAP) databases, which integrate data from multiple heterogeneous sources, providing users with a unified interface to query, view, and interact with the data. To simulate OODB operations, such as querying, filtering, and joining, a set of real-world user requests are typically generated and processed in the OODB. However, it is often prohibitive to evaluate the performance of OODBs using real world user scenarios. A generic random simulation model, VOODB, is introduced to address this issue. VOODB enables users to randomly generate query requests and configure the request details, including distribution, sizes, and values, to reflect realistic scenarios. System response time and the number of operator interactions are recorded for each request to generate a VOODB trace. The trace can then be used to evaluate the performance of the OODB implementations based on various metrics, such as average response time, number of interactions, and system throughput. The VOODB model is introduced and demonstrated through case studies, which compare the performances of three OODBs using different performance metrics.

A local analysis of the stellar velocity field can be performed by decomposing it into spherical harmonics. This enables us to identify the patterns in the local stellar velocity field and study their origins. In particular, we can study the local rotational pattern by computing the velocity vector field's harmonic degree 2, and the local streaming pattern by computing the velocity vector field's harmonic degree 1. We present a method to compute these harmonic s by fitting the velocity field's divergence to the velocity gradient using spherical linear interpolation. Using the local velocity field we can compute the local proper motion and identify members of moving groups in the local solar neighborhood. We apply this method to two samples of stars: all stars with data available in thecatalogue (161 million), and just the high quality Hipparcos data (97 million). We find that the predicted local streaming motion is accurate on average at 2.5 km/s, but varies from less than 1 km/s to over 15 km/s. We also find that the predicted proper motion for local solar neighborhood groups such as the Hyades, Pleiades, and local moving group UMa is within 1 km/s of the predicted proper motion for those groups, for a total of 8 groups with accurate proper motion. In addition to proper motion, this method can also be used to compute the local solar rotation rate and the local circular motion. This method of computing the local stellar velocity field provides a practical way to identify members of local moving groups without requiring high-precision radial velocities.

In quantum mechanics, the state of a system is described by a density matrix, a Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix corresponding to a statistical ensemble of pure states. The density matrix allows one to calculate various properties of the system, such as the expectation value of a particular operator. In experiments, access to the density matrix is obtained using a quantum process tomography (QPT) scheme. QPT is the method of reconstructing the most general process that has acted on a system by probing the system with a large number of different initial states. In this work, a closed quantum system is prepared in an arbitrary initial state Ψ0, and a series of projective measurements are performed. The expected outcome for each measurement is calculated from the initial state. By repeating this process for a series of different Ψ0, a histogram of expected outcomes is generated. Using a quantum process tomography scheme, the initial state can then be extracted from the histogram. The average fidelity between the reconstructed and true initial states is calculated for a wide range of system parameters, showing the efficacy of the process. In addition, finite-time effects are considered, where the expected outcomes are calculated for a system initialized in a highly non-equilibrium state. The formalism is then applied to a spin-boson model, the T1 qubit, showing a method for measuring arbitrary channels of a spin qubit in a closed quantum architecture.

D-brane inflation is a popular scenario for solving the shortcomings of the standard model of cosmology. The basic idea is to introduce open string modes, whose energy density is constant during inflation, in the bulk. As the space-time is effectively four-dimensional , with an extra non-compact dimension, it was called four-dimensional induced gravity. The fluctuations of the brane wind on the background of the radial direction become the density perturbation, leading to sufficient inflation even with certain moduli stabilisation condition. We study the classical speed of sound of such a theory including all known string corrections. We find that it is equal to one for generic values of moduli. However, we demonstrate that the classical speed of sound can be less than one, namely v_s=0.926, if we choose specific values of moduli. We consider the case with v_s<1 as it is phenomenologically interesting. Such a model can generate a density perturbation from the fluctuations of the brane winding, thereby reducing the amplitude of curvature perturbation which can be tested by the ongoing observational projects, e.g. the B-mode polarisation of the cosmic microwave background radiation.

A nearby, massive, transiting planet in a short-period orbit around a solar-type star offers the perfect opportunity to characterize the atmospheric composition of an Earth-size planet outside of the Solar System. Such a planet would provide decisive evidence for life outside of the Solar System. At present, only two such planets are known. TrES-3h is a transiting, Saturn-sized planet with a short period and 3.5 Earth masses, orbiting very closely to its host star. TrES-3h has a predicted minimum surface temperature of 705 K, making it one of the hottest planets known. If TrES-3h has a significant atmosphere, its relatively large size, close proximity to its star, and short period should make it an excellent target for characterization with current instruments. We present new photometric observations of TrES-3h, and analyze previous observations from the literature. We find that the TrES-3h transmission spectrum is consistent with a cloud-free H2/He atmosphere with a characteristic scale height of 2.1-2.3 Earth radii, at the 3-4 sigma level. If TrES-3h does have an atmosphere, it must be unusual; it has a relatively small radius for its mass, and temperatures low enough for water vapor to be the dominant species. If TrES-3h does have an atmosphere, future observations could detect evidence for atmospheric absorptions due to atomic and molecular hydrogen, molecular oxygen, and possibly carbon monoxide. Planets with such atmospheres could be similar in composition to Earth, and could be excellent targets for future atmospheric characterization and search for biosignatures. TrES-3h has a mass of 3.5 Earth masses, and orbits a star named TrES-3h about 0.8 AU from its star, completing an orbit in 31 hours. It has a radius of about 1.2 Earth radii and a surface temperature of 705 K, making it one of the hottest planets known. TrES-3 is a hot planet, as it has a very high mass due to its proximity to its star. Due to such close proximity, the gas in the planet's extended atmosphere will be ionized, causing a rapid reddening of starlight passing through the planet's atmosphere. TrES-3 has an estimated radius of 1.2 Earth radii and a temperature of 705 K, but the observations we have are not sufficient to characterize its atmosphere. In particular, there are no detections of atomic or molecular hydrogen, molecular oxygen, or carbon monoxide. If the planet does have an atmosphere, those chemical absorptions would not be detectable using current technology. If TrES-3h does have an atmosphere, it would be similar in composition to the atmospheres of other hot Jupiters, and might be an excellent target for future atmospheric characterization and search for biosignatures.
