The epoch of reionization (EoR) was one of the most critical periods in the early history of the universe, and its outcome influenced the formation and evolution of the first galaxies and their environment. While the EoR was mostly completed by $z \sim 6$ revealed by the late-time brightening of the Gunn-Peterson trough in the spectra of high-redshift quasars, the small fraction of neutral hydrogen left at $z\gtrsim 7$ potentially allowed for the discovery of the first clusters of galaxies and their intergalactic environment via the detection of the redshifted Lyman-alpha (Ly-alpha) radiation from the same. Significant progress has recently been made in the pursuit of this goal via the completion of two Ly-alpha surveys: one at $5.7<z<6.5$ using the 10-meter * Subaru Telescope and another at $7<z<8.8$ using theLas Cumbres Observatory equipped with the * Subaru Integral Field Spectrograph. This work presents the mass-to-light ratio of Ly-alpha emitters (M_* / L_{Ly\alpha}$) derived from these two surveys, spanning a total comoving volume of $1.5\times 10^5 h^{-3} \text{Mpc}^3$ and spanning a range of $0.43 < \log_{10} (M_*/h^{-1}M_\odot)< 8.3$ for luminosity ranges of $3.2 < \log_{10} (\lambda L_{\lambda} / (\text{erg <unk>$). This M/L ratio is found to be approximately constant with luminosity, which can be used to test models for the formation and evolution of early galaxies. The rate of decline in the M/L ratio with increasing luminosity is also found to be consistent with theoretical predictions for star-forming galaxies at high-redshift. The lack of observed trend with luminosity, however, suggests that most of the Ly-alpha radiation originates from the most massive galaxies, while the strong dependence of observed M/L on halo mass suggests that the M/L of Ly-alpha emitters depends strongly on halo mass, with higher-mass halos hosting more luminous Ly-alpha emitters.

An autonomous distributed admission control scheme for IEEE 802.11 DCF is proposed, which can intelligently allocate the channel capacity for improving the utilization efficiency of the wireless medium and fully utilizing the capacity of the available bandwidth. The admission control scheme consists of a controlling mechanism and a controlled algorithm. The controlling mechanism divides the overall network into a number of virtual channels with a fixed size through assigning a range of channel access priorities. All stations in the network sense the wireless medium and calculate the corresponding transmission data rates. The controlled algorithm selects the stations for establishing connections in the controlling mechanism according to their network requirements and moves the whole network among different virtual channels according to the scheduling results. Simulation results show that the channel utilization efficiency can be enhanced effectively. In the standard model (SM), the mean lifetime of a charmless B meson decay involving a scalar boson (π, K, <unk>) or a vector boson (ω, K*)) is expected to be dominated by tree level processes involving a W boson, and is expected to be significantly shorter than the mean life expectancy of a neutral meson. In the past, this distinction has been difficult to quantify, since the large datasets available for such decays from the B factories and LHCb have enabled the contribution from competing tree level amplitudes to be a small correction. In addition, the impact of these amplitudes on the global fit to the SM parameters has not been well quantified. In this paper, we study these charmless B decays using a data set of ~400 million decays recorded by the LHCb experiment, and precise results from αs(mμ) and αs(mJ/ψ) amplitude wave forms. We find that the difference in the mean lifetimes of these two samples of charmless B mesons is significant at the 4.1σ level. The significance of this difference is well explained by the predictions of the SM, which can therefore be tested to high accuracy. We measure branching fractions of the form Br(B hadron -> σ(π, K, φ) or ω(K*)) × 10 -6, and set 90% confidence level upper limits of Br(B hadron -> σ(π, K, φ) or ω(K*)) × 10 -5. We also search for direct CP violation in these decays and set an upper limit on the CP asymmetry.

. The afterglow of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are detectable by electromagnetic telescopes for up to several thousand years following the GRB event. This long duration light curve is surprising, because GRB radiation is thought to be beamed into a small solid angle (in order to produce the observed gamma-ray energy output in the form of a narrow beam). If the gamma-rays are beamed into a narrow solid angle, this implies that the afterglow light is beamed into a much larger solid angle, and therefore it should rapidly decay following the burst. A number of GRB afterglow light curves do indeed decay according to a single power law, but approximately 1/4 of afterglows decay as two power laws - an early fast decay, followed by a much slower decay. The origin of this second decay is not understood, and has been called the "chromatic break" problem.

Neutrino flavor evolution and interactions with matter are described using four mass eigenstates , referred to as, in order of increasing mass, 
u_1, 
u_2, 
u_3, and 
u_4. These four states each interact with matter via a charged current interaction and a neutral current interaction. The former has been well measured in solar neutrino experiments whereas the latter has been well constrained in the KamLAND experiment, resulting in a model with three mixing angles and one CP violating phase. New physics could contribute to this phase in addition to the standard model CP violating phase. We present results of a global comparison of the standard model to current neutrino data, including new data from the NOvA and T2K long baseline experiments. We find the standard model is consistent with new physics contribution to the CP violating phase greater than 2.2 standard deviations. This could indicate that new physics is causing a distortion of the neutrino evolution that is not parameterized in the standard three-angle, one CP violating phase model.

In this paper we generalise the decomposition number introduced by James and Kerber for the case of the symmetric group. We do so by defining the decomposition number for finite Coxeter groups and prove some basic properties. We apply these decomposition numbers to give a bijection between semipartition partitions and compositions with at most $n$ parts. We also show how to use these decomposition numbers to give a combinatorial interpretation of the generating function for the number of generalised non-crossing partitions of type $A_{n-1}$.

Environmental effects on galaxies are known to have profound impacts on their evolution. Indeed, the large-scale environment in which a galaxy resides dictates where it can efficiently capture dark matter and new star mass, affecting both the rate at which baryons can collapse into the potential wells of dark matter halos and the transport of gas to the galaxy. Additionally, the nature and spatial distribution of neighboring galaxies can also affect the evolution of a galaxy through both internal processes, such as mergers and galactic harassment, and external processes, such as mergers and accretions. These processes can induce, trigger, or enhance signatures of active galactic reionization and AGN activity, which in turn can fuel new star formation as well as heat and eject gas from galaxy reservoirs. Thus, the large-scale environment in which a galaxy resides acts as a catalyst for its evolution, driving both internal processes, such as reionization and AGN feedback, and external processes, such as mergers and accretions.

We present new ultraviolet to submillimeter photometry and spectroscopy of the quasar APM 08279+5255, which is gravitationally lensed into a multiple system with two distinct components at an angular separation of ~ 2.6 arcsec (Fan & Hewett 2010). One component is an $z = 1 quasar with a bright far-infrared luminosity of ~ 2 × 10$^{13}$ L$_{\odot}$ that is sufficiently luminous to maintain ionization of the IGM at z ~ 6–8 (Fan et al. 2006). The fainter, neighboring component has a near-infrared spectral energy distribution consistent with a star-forming galaxy and a 1.2 mm flux consistent with a star formation rate of ~ 50–100 M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. We find that the brighter quasar is correlated with a rapid increase in the visibility of the 21cm absorption against the radio background from the epoch of reionization at z ~ 6–8, and that the infrared-luminous companion to APM 08279+5255 is in a neutral region of the IGM with no detected absorption. We interpret this correlation as strong evidence of quasar-induced reionization, and a possible constraint on the quasar duty cycle.

Galaxy clusters have provided key astrophysical constraints over wide wavelength ranges from the radio to the X-ray. Yet despite this success, the process by which clusters assemble their mass remains a central question in modern astrophysics. Analytic theories of cluster assembly (e.g., @rs82) have long been superseded by hydrodynamical cosmological simulations (e.g., @nm04 [@ds08]), which have successfully reproduced key observables such as the cluster luminosity function and temperature function. However, the most massive clusters predicted by these simulations are somewhat under-abundant in comparison to the number of clusters in the real Universe (@k07 [@l06]; see also @s07 for a detailed description of this problem). This “mass discordance problem” has inspired numerous explanations, including environmental filtering (@w84 [@k84]), cannibalism (@gm02), and massive cluster progenitors (@mm01). However, while these astrophysical theories have been successful in predicting the total amount of mass in clusters, they have not addressed the question of how individual clusters assemble their mass. Recently, we have found that the mass function of globular clusters in nearby galaxies may be directly correlated with the amount of galaxy light in the cluster vicinity. In contrast to previous explanations that cluster mass is gradually acquired over time through mergers or environmental processes, we have shown that if most massive clusters formed instead by early dissolution of lower-mass systems, then there should be a negative correlation between the cluster mass and cluster light. Indeed, we have found that the cluster mass-light correlations are consistent with the dissolution scenario, such that massive clusters are less common in the Universe and more readily dissolve. However, our results were based on small statistical samples. Here we report on a larger compilation of 22 clusters, for which we have homogeneously derived kinematics and presented a strong evidence for stellar evaporation in 10 of them. We estimate that stellar evaporation is a robust explanation for the dissolution of these clusters, and it also explains the mass-light correlation without any further dynamical processes. Thus, we suggest that the stellar evaporation may represent a novel mechanism for regulating cluster mass, which has the potential to significantly influence the total amount of mass in clusters in cosmological simulations.

H2CO is an important prebiotic molecule, involved in the production of more complex biomolecules such as nucleotides and amino acids. L1204 and S140 are two adjacent clouds in the solar neighborhood. Observations of H2CO in these two clouds suggest that H2CO exists in two different states. In one case it appears as discrete cores with cometary shapes of about 0.2 pc in length, temperature of about 20 K, and linewidth of about 0.2 km/s. In the other case it appears as a ring-like structure around dense cores with temperature of about 10 K and linewidth of about 0.15 km/s. The difference in the H2CO structure between these two structures has not been explained. We suggest that the difference in the H2CO structure may be related to the formation of a surrounding core of warm molecular hydrogen. The formation of this molecular hydrogen may be due to the photodissociation of H2CO at 6 cm wavelength. In this case, the existence of warm molecular hydrogen would prevent the formation of cometary H2CO cores.

The influence of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) on the mean fitness of unicellular populations in static environments has been previously analyzed by Claveria and Sokal (1977). However, this previous study only considered fixed environmental conditions and no mutations were allowed. Here, we consider both fixed environmental conditions and mutations and show that in static environments without random genetic drift, the mean fitness of a population is strictly increased by HGT. We also show that without HGT, the mean fitness of a population decreases with increasing environmental variation, even if mutations are also taken into account. We discuss the significance of these results for unicellular gene- and organismal fitness in various environments. +-------+----------------------+ | row | title | +=======+======================+ | 1 | The influence of HGT | +-------+----------------------+ | 2 | on the mean fitness | +-------+----------------------+ | 3 | of unicellular | | | populations in | | | static environments | +-------+----------------------+ | 4 | No HGT: mean fitness | | | decreases with | | | increasing | | | environmental | | | variation. | | | Populations in static environments | | | | With HGT: mean | | | fitness strictly | | | increases | | | regardless of | | | environmental | | | variation. | +-------+----------------------+

We present a proof for the quantum relative entropy and its application in quantum information. The quantum relative entropy is an extension of the classical relative entropy for quantum systems. We prove a general theorem that bounds the quantum relative entropy of the quantum states in order to determine the fidelity of these states. As an application, we give a proof for the data security of quantum key distribution with a helper quantum key, which was recently shown to be possible under the most general conditions using only pure state communication. Our proof is valid even when the two communicating parties share a quantum channel with a nonspurious maximal length of the quantum state. Soft gamma-rays (E<10 {}^} {31}) provide a unique probe of the extreme conditions present in neutron star interiors due to their accessibility across a wide range of processes governing these environments. Polarization observations in this energy range could, in turn, be used to discriminate between competing models of these environments. The PoGOLite mission, comprised of two identical satellites in low Earth orbit, provides the first opportunity to measure energy dependent polarization in this energy range. As the Compton scattered angle is equal to the angle between the incident photon and the incoming direction of the scattered photon, measurements of energy dependent polarization could provide a new method of identifying chemical constituents in the neutron star crust. Polarization levels of up to ~3% are observed between 2 and 10 {}^} {31} for incident photon s between ~100 and 1000 keV. This level of polarization is inconsistent with polarization levels measured in other astrophysical objects and is instead consistent with the polarization levels predicted from models of transition layers in neutron stars consisting of non-equilibrium ensembles of nuclei.

The MiniBooNE experiment at Fermilab announced new data in March 2017 constraining the possiblenum of sterile neutrinos mixing with ordinary neutrinos. These results were based on data taken between 2008 and 2011. The new data supported the hypothesis that there are at least two sterile neutrinos with square-mass difference of (0.15 - 2.29) eV2 and at least one with a non-zero mass. Several neutrino mass schemes were tested with no evidence of flavon fields driving mass to a large value, as might be expected in an underlying theories such as the See-Saw mechanism. The oscillation parameters determined in this analysis are also consistent with recent results from the Daya Bay and RENO experiments. This paper provides a critical evaluation of recent results from the MiniBooNE and other experiments in light of possible sterile neutrino mass schemes. We summarize three common hypotheses for the allowed sterile neutrino masses and mixing, including the minimal, mixed, and two-zero schemes. We present the formalism for each hypothesis and show the associated range of oscillation parameters for three representative sets of light neutrino mass splittings. We discuss potential models for sterile neutrino generation that could explain distinct behaviors in light neutrinos. We also discuss some of the possible sterile neutrino mass schemes. We conclude by summarizing the implications of recent sterile neutrino results in light of the possible neutrino mass schemes. Authors: M.Maltoni et al. In this paper, we propose generalized asymmetric diffusion (GIDA), an approach to accelerate the convergence of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by exploiting the disparity in diffusivity between interacting particles and non-interacting particles. The underlying physical basis is that the interacting particles tend to move along the direction of high gradient of the pair potential, while the non-interacting particles exhibit normal Brownian motion. To reduce the computational cost, GIDA is applied only to the non-interacting particles, and the interacting particles are evolved according to the classical Newton’s equations of motion. We apply GIDA to both bond-switching MD (BS-MD) and event-driven molecular dynamics (ED-MD), and demonstrate the effectiveness of GIDA through extensive tests on multiple systems. In particular, we find that with the same number of MD steps, GIDA allows BS-MD to sample significantly more phase space and allows ED-MD to reach a given numerical temperature with fewer event records. Finally, we apply GIDA to enhance the efficiency of replica exchange MD simulations, and show that GIDA can help speed up the convergence of replica exchange MD simulations.

Galaxy clustering is a powerful tool with which to study the relationship between galaxies and the underlying dark matter distribution. Much of the focus has been on the parameterization of bias as a function of scale, denoted b(k); the RMS fluctuation in a sphere of radius k scaled by the RMS fluctuation in all space. Current work in this area has largely focused on the development of a scale-independent bias model, in which bias is a constant with scale. While work has been done to extend the range of scales considered, this work has largely been performed using simulations, and in many cases these extensions have been obtained by fitting to data. We propose an approach in which bias is modeled as dependent on scale, with bias diverging at small scales and saturating at large scales. By comparing to large scale structure (LSS) data, we demonstrate that this model can accurately describe bias and can provide a much improved fit to the power spectrum. Furthermore, we find that the implementation of scale dependence can lead to a robust determination of the non-linear mass scale, <unk>(M). We apply our model to a suite of cosmologies and show that the derived Ω(M) can be a powerful discriminator of cosmology. Our method can be applied to LSS data from any scale, and can be easily incorporated into existing cosmological analyses.

In this letter, we propose a novel structure of a black hole (BH) : a plasma puddle, in which plasma is accreted into the black hole and behaves as an envelope surrounding a black hole. In contrast to a normal envirnment such as a event horizon and an accretion disk, the plasma puddle has a surface, through which the black hole emits no news. The plasma puddle becomes a perturbative BH as the plasma density is sufficiently large, i.e., the Schwarchild radius is less than the radius of the puddle. For pulsars, the inner region of the accretion disk can be considered as the plasma puddle. The existence of the perturbative BH can explain the fast fluctuation of the emission direction of pulsars without invoking a small scale BH embedded in the pulsar. We conclude that the plasma puddle provides a new perspective for BH physics and pulsar emission mechanism.

A pulsar with aconal structure, similar to a cylinder, as a result of removal of the inner most region of the neutron star, is known as a peeled pulsar. In this paper, we consider the electromagnetic induction equations for the presence of an external constant uniform magnetic field parallel to the axis of the cylindrical pulsar, and show that the pulsar plasma consisting of electrons and positrons is stabilised against the diocotron instability, with a growth rate comparable to the analytical approximation of the kelvin-parity mode. We then apply our results to the case of a recently discovered peeled pulsar, PSR J1648-6050, and show that the charge imbalance due to the presence of a cloud of unbound electrons and positrons is sufficient to stabilise the cylindrical electrosphere against the diocotron instability and sustain the observed relativistic jets. The present work deals with the study of a recently discovered peeled pulsar PSR J1648-6050 in some detail. In particular, we show that the charge imbalance due to a cloud of unbound electrons and positrons is sufficient to stabilise the cylindrical electrosphere against the diocotron instability and sustain the observed relativistic jets.

The Amati relation is the correlation between the width of the optical afterglow of a gamma-ray burst (GRB) and its fluence. The afterglow is produced by the forward shock ionizing the circumburst medium (CM). The fluence is the total energy emitted by the GRB in the gamma-ray band. It is a very useful tool to study the high-energy emissions of GRBs. The Amati relation is linear in the ordinary cosmological evolution scenario. The slope of the Amati relation is related to the circumburst density, which is an indicator of the the type of the progenitor of the GRB. If the Amati relation slopes at high redshifts, this would imply that the circumburst density increases with redshift, i.e. that the progenitors of high-redshift GRBs are significantly different from the low-redshift ones. This is contrary to the expected cosmological evolution. The hypothesis of the selection effect, i.e. that high-redshift GRBs with larger energies are also more peculiar (i.e. have different progenitors), can explain the Amati relation 's slope at high redshifts.

The strong interaction between quarks and gluons, which occurs during the hadron collision, is modeled by quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Calculating the cross sections of these interactions at high transverse momentum is necessary to understand the multiple features that emerge from experimental data. One such feature, which is receiving significant attention, is the scaling of particle production with respect to the number of partons in the hadron, known as multishin scaling. In particular, the logarithmic scaling of particle production with respect to the mean transverse momentum of the number of particles, or hard processes, has been observed in a large range of center of mass energies and has been used to motivate the 327sevenseven scheme, in which partons are organized into a finite number of hard processes. Gluon initiated processes are known to produce more particles on average than quark initiated processes. To elucidate the relationship between partonic subprocesses and the difference in particle production, studies have been performed at center of mass energies near 10 GeV. The data indicates that although the total particle yields for both quark and gluon initiated processes scale with center of mass energy, the differential scaling is not logarithmic. In particular, the quark fragmentation functions exhibit a power law scaling at high transverse momentum, whereas the gluon fragmentation function scales as a simple exponential. Furthermore, the multishin scaling functions, which quantify the average number of particles as a function of the scaling variable, exhibit exponents that are dependent on the degree of scaling. The difference in particle production as a function of partonic subprocesses is therefore dependent on the scaling variable used, and the 327sevense scheme cannot be used to organize partons into a finite number of hard processes.

An map of the day-night contrast of the extrasolar planet HD 189733b is presented. The contrast is derived by multiplying a Kurucz model of HD 189733b's infrared spectrum by a corresponding ALMA satellite image. The planet is revealed to be a poor occupant, with a nightside comprised of mostly empty space, with a temperature upper limit of ∼230 K, about as cold as the far side of the Moon. The most striking aspect of this map is the clear detection of a latitudinal variation in temperature, with the substellar point hottest at σ = +15.2 K. This equator-to-pole temperature contrast is a factor of 2.2 greater than the amplitude of the equator-to-pole temperature contrast measured via infrared observations, suggesting that radiative processes limit the day-night temperature variation on HD 189733b. If the longitudinal variation in temperature is real, then it might be explained by weaker atmospheric zonal winds, with the substellar point coinciding with the region of greatest wind speed.

Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. Its receptors, which are positive ionotropic glutamate receptors, are essential for normal brain development and function. Most glutamate receptors are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum and then distributed to the cell surface via the Golgi complex. This cycling between the cell surface and the Golgi complex is critical for their normal function, because the cell surface is the primary interface between the neuron and its environment, and glutamate receptors at the cell surface are readily poised to transmit a signal following stimulation by glutamate. Here we demonstrate that cell surface glutamate receptors are continuously shuttled to and from the plasma membrane in a ligand-dependent manner using at least two pathways. The first involves diffusion from a reservoir in the Golgi complex to the plasma membrane. The second involves recycling to the Golgi complex, followed by re- recycling to the plasma membrane. Both pathways are critically dependent on the GluA2 subunit of the AMPA receptor, which may provide a mechanism to regulate the number of glutamate receptors at the cell surface. We also observed a similar cooperation between the two pathways in a mouse model of fragile X syndrome, and found that the drug 4-aminopyridine can activate both pathways, leading to increased levels of cell surface glutamate receptors and improved behavioral responses in the mouse model. Our results suggest that increasing the number of plasma membrane receptors in the brain could enhance cognition and has potential as a therapeutic approach for neurological disorders caused by low levels of glutamate receptors.

Hot Jupiters are gas giants that closely orbit their parent stars, completing each orbit in only days. These short period orbits make hot Jupiters extremely sensitive to their host stars’ tide, and previous research has shown that many of them are unable to retain their gaseous envelope. Up until now, all exoplanets discovered outside of our solar system were in single -star systems. However, recent analysis of the Kepler space telescope dataset indicates that approximately 20% of hot Jupiters exist in systems with a second, companion star. These planets, dubbed “hot Jupiter” twins, maintain significant quantities of gas around them due to the tides from both stars in the system. The existence of these systems, which contain a hot Jupiter binary star and a hot Jupiter binary star, poses several interesting questions. Are hot Jupiter twins more common than previously thought? Are they able to maintain their gaseous envelope? What factors contribute to the longevity of their hot Jupiters? And what environmental factors determine the existence of these dual systems? Addressing these questions will require further analysis of the Kepler data, as well as new modeling and simulation of hot Jupiter evolution.

On 14 February 2017, the first direct detection of gravitational waves (GWs) announced by the LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration. The detected GW was emitted by two black holes (BHs) merging, in the final stages of their merger driven by a loss of potential energy due to the GW emission. Since then, a large number of papers studying the detectability of GWs emitted by other astrophysical scenarios has been posted to the arXiv pre-print server. In this paper, we analyse in detail one of these scenarios: the collapse of rotating stellar cores. We carry out fully general relativistic (GR), three dimensional (3D), pseudospectral numerical simulations of the collapse of rotating stars, using the BSSN system and the moving-punctures formalism, to characterize the GW emissions. We focus on two scenarios: initially differentially rotating neutron stars (NSs) and supramassive neutron stars. For the latter, we explore a sequence of models with a fixed rest mass but with different couplings between the crust and the rest of the NS, representing a schematic representation of possible NS-to-BH hyperaccretion flow conversion. We characterize the GW emission from the moment at which the BH-formation threshold is first overcome up to BH formation, defined as the time at which the maximum density in the grid center reaches a value of $10^{10}$ g/cm3. Our main results can be summarized as follows: (i) Regardless of the EOS, all models collapse to BHs (except for one model in the non-spinning NS , for which the maximum density never reaches $10^{10}$ g/cm3), in agreement with previous studies. (ii) When differential rotation is present at the beginning of the evolution, the rotational energy of the fluid is partially radiated as GWs during the collapse, with $10^{50} - 10^{51}$ erg emitted for typical NSs. This signal is most prominent when the initial differential rotation is strong and has a short timescale, i.e., a large initial jump in the initial specific angular momentum across an equator-near pole axis. (iii) When BH formation is successful and the fluid remains above the BH-formation threshold, a sharp gravitational tone is emitted during the BH formation process, whose peak frequency is between $0.7 - 2.5$ kHz (for uniformly rotating NSs) or $2 - 4$ kHz (for non-spinning rotating NSs), and which, depending on the mass, spins and EOS, has a 10<unk> - 10^{-21}$ esu strain amplitude. (iv) When hyperaccretion flow is not halted by the centrifugal barrier and the collapse produces a successful BH with low enough spin (as indicated by the amplitude of the emitted gravitational tones), the model may bypass the centrifugal barrier and form an accretion disk. (v) We find no significant difference in the GW emission produced by NSs

The AnITA generic tutoring system is developed to help students improve their academic performance. In this work, we present an empirical study on its development process and experiments from multiple perspectives. We first analyze the system through its design documents and reference architecture, which consist of requirements, use cases, design documents, and tests. Then, we study the system implementation from architecture, development, and testing perspectives. Additionally, we present several system-level experiments to study their impacts on tutoring sessions. The findings indicate that the system achieves an average rating of 4.3 stars out of 5 on system usability, 4.8 stars out of 5 on system content quality, and 4.7 stars out of 5 on system performance. Furthermore, we find that when using multiple experiments, the tutor’s fluency and engagement could be increased by 5.2% and 6.8%, respectively. Overall, this work provides a detailed case study on the development of a generic tutoring system and presents several practical optimization s and lessons learned that are potentially useful to others.

Neel order parameter in the square and triangular lattice Heisenberg models was examined using the longitudinal spin wave method. We find that in the isotropic case, the Neel order parameter has a cusp-like divergence at the ferromagnetic Heisenberg critical point in both cases. However, a subtle difference is observed in the dispersion of spin wave excitations near the ferromagnetic quantum critical point. In particular, the longitudinal spin wave excitation in the square lattice model shows a non-analyticity at the critical point, in agreement with the ferromagnetic mean field result, while the corresponding result in the triangular lattice model is analytic. This behavior is discussed in the framework of the recently proposed theory of quantum renormalization group, and a comparison with experimental observations on Ca$_{2-x}$Na$_{x}$V$_2$O$_5$ is also made. Information theoretic measures have been widely used in Statistics and Information Theory to quantify the amount of information contained in a given distribution. In this work we show that the Kullback-Leibler divergence can be used to measure the amount of information filtered from multivariate data by a given statistical model. This provides a link between two widely used families of Information Theory measures, namely those derived from the approximation theory and those derived from the Fisher discrimination theory. We illustrate the usefulness of this approach by applying it to describe how the amount of information of a multivariate Gaussian distribution is affected by model parameters, such as its mean and covariance matrix. We show that the Kullback-Leibler divergence can be used to characterize how much information is observed in multivariate data that have been deviated from Gaussianity. Such deviation is quantified in terms of the mean error rate of the maximum likelihood estimator, the divergence always being non-negative. We also discuss the relations with the Cramer-Rao and Rissanou inequalities. We provide some explicit examples for the Gaussian case, as well as a comparison with the mean error rate and the mean error of the maximum likelihood estimator. We illustrate the usefulness of this framework to characterize the information contained in macroeconomic time series, such as inflation and GDP.

NodeTrix preserves the expressiveness and flexibility of NetworkX graphs while aggregating and presenting a compact network summary in an emotionally-inspired, compact, and easily consumable format. Insulin-degrading enzyme (IDE) is a zinc metalloprotease shown to be responsible for the progression of many types of cancer through the degradation of insulin, insulin-like growth factors and other growth factors. In the current study, several human tissue types were evaluated for the expression of IDE, and many previously reported findings were confirmed. The strongest IDE staining was seen in breast, prostate, liver and pancreas tissue. Surprisingly, some previously reported IDE-positive normal human tissue types (including: brain, eye, kidney and small intestine) were demonstrated to be negative for IDE, and in a few instances, the opposite was true (i.e. some IDE-negative normal human tissue types were shown to be positive for IDE). These findings raise doubts about the validity of many previous studies examining the expression of IDE in normal and neoplastic human tissue. *Citation: Jaggo N, Jalkanmaa M, Mannisto P, Saloheimo J (2018) . Potential pitfalls in the demonstration of insulin-degrading enzyme in normal and neoplastic human tissues. The onset of the compact nebula phase of low-mass star formation is conventionally dated to when the progenitor molecular cloud’s angular momentum is largely consumed by the newly-formed star (or stars), which leave behind a circumstellar disk. Subsequent evolution is thought to be relatively simple; gas slowly leaves the disk on viscous timescales, while infalling gas is diverted to the young star(s) via the disk’s spiraling shockwaves. This classic view is supported by recent results from continuum and molecular line ar simulations of such systems, which find a high incidence of strong, eccentric disks and low levels of infall (e.g., Gao et al. 2017). A competing paradigm postulates that the early evolution of protoplanetary systems is significantly more complex, and that a phase of runaway accretion preceded the onset of the classic disk phase. This early phase of evolution is rarely observed, as it has yet to leave a permanent mark on the Solar System’s architecture; runaway growth is thought to be halted by the buildup of a large gas envelope that sweeps away the forming star(s) through sub-Keplerian disk s (e.g., Kokubo & Gommer 2013). The authors present new simulations exploring this putative early-accretion phase, which predict a high occurrence of eccentric disks that survive on viscous timescales, and thus continue to funnel gas toward the forming star(s) over the course of a protoplanetary system’s evolution. The long-term impact of these early stages of evolution on the final architecture of planetary systems remains an open question. However, it is clear that future observations of the architecture of protoplanetary systems will bear important clues about this critical and potentially chaotic period of their evolution.

This paper analyzes a binary world trade web, whose structure is derived from a normalised mutual trade dependence (NMTD) measure. The pattern of flows are shown to follow a modular structure, where a handful of dominant flows rule a large portion of world trade. The analysis is conducted for three timeframes - 1975-1985, 1986-2000, and 2001-2013, revealing persistence of these dominant patterns even in the face of globalisation. A small set of industries dominate global trade across all the time periods, while the patterns of dominant flows exhibit greater mutability. These insights into patterns of dominant flows can provide new lens into the structure and evolution of international economic networks. The world trade web (WTW) has been the subject of much research in the recent past. A major shortcoming of most of this research has been the assumption of a fully connected network, with each trade link between any two countries being significant and non-zero in magnitude. This has led to several misleading conclusions, such as the non-existence of large sections of the trade web, or a fully connected network describing the WTW as "not strongly coupled"." To address this shortcoming, this study obtains the WTW through non-normalized mutual trade dependence (NMTD) measure, a method capable of identifying significant and non-zero trade flows between countries, accounting for both the magnitude and directionality of trade, and normalizing the results to ensure a fully connected network. The NMNTD approach is applied to an aggregate normalised matrix of international trade for 1975-2013, representing $5,000 \times 5,000$ dimensional trade web. The analysis is conducted for three timeframes - 1975-1985, 1986-2000, and 2001-2013, revealing persistence of patterns in world trade even over short periods. The world trade web is comprised of 147 countries, and within each of these countries - 37 industry sectors. The analysis is conducted on a sectoral level, which reveals a handful of industries dominate world trade - across all the timeframes. The dominance of these industries in the global trade web also persists, even though these industries may change over time. The pattern of flows follow a modular structure, where a handful of dominant flows rule a large portion of world trade. This is revealed by first generating a binary world trade network, by thresholding the normalised matrix at 0.5. The pattern of trade links are then used to cluster the binary matrix into communities or clusters. Finally, a Louvain optimization is performed on the modularity matrix, assigning each trade flow to the community to which it is most strongly associated. The dominant flows are then shown to constitute six dominant clusters or patterns of trade flows. The first pattern is of dominant length four, and is comprised of import substitution industrialization (ISM) driven countries, or countries with well developed manufacturing sector. They are primarily located in the Americas, Europe and EMEA regions. The second pattern is comprised of three flows of dominant length five, and is comprised of the B2

Stimulus and noise distributions for optimal information transmission via suprathreshold stochastic resonance (SR) are derived and exemplified for the archetypal nonlinear SR system, the diffusiely coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo model. Optimal information transmission is achieved for the full range of coupling constants . In contrast to previous studies, the information-carrying signal is a white noise, that is, it has zero mean. The optimal noise, in contrast, has a non-zero mean, and its variance vanishes as the signal amplitude increases past a critical value. The derived results provide clear design guidelines for maximizing the communication capacity of nonlinear dynamical systems through appropriate signal modulation. Introduction One of the longstanding paradigms of information transmission in nonlinear dynamical systems is stochastic resonance (SR), where a weak, random signal amplifies itself and noise-induced signal fluctuations are enhanced above the level of the signal's mean amplitude.1-3 For over three decades, this counterintuitive phenomenon has been demonstrated experimentally and corroborated with theory for various nonlinear systems, both experimental and theoretical.4-7 More recent studies have focused on information transmission via suprathreshold SR, where the signal is above a certain threshold level.8, 9, 10 The optimal signal structure for suprathreshold SR was shown to be a white noise, i.e., it has zero mean.11, 12 Here, we derive the optimal stimulus and noise distributions for information transmission via suprathreshold SR. We focus on the archetypal diffusiely coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) model, where the signal represents the spiking activity of the neuronal membrane, and the noise represents the synaptic and neuronal noise.13, 14 In contrast to previous studies, the optimal information-carrying signal is not a white noise, but has a non-zero mean. Moreover, the optimal noise has a vanishing variance as the signal amplitude increases past a critical value, and the optimal information transmission performance is achieved for the full range of coupling constants. The derived results provide clear design guidelines for maximizing the communication capacity of nonlinear dynamical systems through appropriate signal modulation. In 2010, the radial velocity method was introduced to search for exoplanets by measuring the radial velocity of the host star and detecting the wobble caused by the planet’s gravity. In order to confirm that the detected wobble is indeed caused by the planet and not other causes such as noise, a confirmation method was developed by measuring the Doppler Shift of the emitted spectrum and thus detecting the wobble of the planet around the central star. The method worked so well that for the next two decades, thousands of exoplanets were confirmed. However, in recent years a strange trend was noticed where the number of confirmed exoplanets was declining. Although the reason for this decline is not clear, scientists have several theories including the possibility of false positives. In this paper, I will explain false positives, explain why they are a problem, and present a new mathematical confirmation method that can reduce the number of false positives. I will also discuss how more observations are needed to confirm whether this decline in confirmed exoplanets is real or not.

A cold interstellar cloud core rich in ice-mantles material is investigated with a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to gas-grain chemistry. The model includes rate equations for the most important surface reactions between grain surface radicals and gas-phase radicals and molecule, and direct collisions between molecules. The gas and grain temperatures are kept fixed at 10 K and 20 K, respectively. The gas density is of the order of 10-11 cm-3, the position in the interstellar cloud core where the observed NH3 (1-0) line is emitted (Green et al. 1993). The model results show that NH3 mainly forms on dust grains through the N-methylation of NH3 molecules, such as N-methylformamide (CH3NCHO) and N, N-dimethylamine (NH2CHCH3). In turn, N-methylformamide is formed through a hydrogen abstraction reaction between CH3NH and CH3. N-Methylformamide is also destroyed through its hydrogen abstraction reaction with H2. Nitrogen and carbon chains are also formed on dust grains. Their formation depends on the onvil hydrogen atom concentration. When this concentration is low (as it is expected in the interstellar medium where the cloud core is localized), N-methylformamide is the main carbon chain precursor. These results highlight the key chemistry of dust grains in the interstellar cloud core rich in ice mantles, and demonstrate that a microscopic Monte Carlo approach can be a powerful tool to study the complex gas-grain chemistry.

Water molecules in Earth's atmosphere naturally emit radiation in the infrared part of the spectrum due to internal vibrations of the hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The radiation has a spectral distribution characteristic to its wavelength and it is strongly dependent on the temperature of the water molecules and their environment. In the past, water masers were the most precise thermometers for clouds and molecular layers in Earth's atmosphere, providing temperatures as low as a few hundred Kelvin. In the present work, we report the first detection of the 658 GHz water line with the Submillimeter Array. Contrary to expectations, we did not find strong spectral variations in this line. We suggest that this may be due to the rapid dynamics of the emitting region, likely related to the fact that the observed water masers are associated with a cluster of young stars. The study of water line emissions is of interest to the astronomy community as it may allow us to better understand how our planet and other water-rich planets in the solar system were formed. In the future, the study of emission and absorption patterns of other water lines may allow for better mapping of the water cycle in our planet's atmosphere and for improved characterization of water-rich planets outside of our solar system. The presented work utilized data from the Submillimeter Array, an array of twelve telescope located in the United States of America. The observations were conducted in the 2013 and 2014 periods in the range of 658-750 GHz. For further details on the methodology and data analysis, please refer the reader to the paper attached to this record on arXiv.

We study global polarization of QGP ( Quark-Gluon Plasma ) in non-central heavy ion collisions at high energies in perturbative quantum chromodynamics . Gluon distribution functions in a longitudinally polarized QGP are computed to one-loop order in the infinite top-quark mass limit using Witten'swarf invariant method. The induced gluon polarization is shown to be uniform in the longitudinally polarized QGP and is shown to survive even after quark spin anti-parallel scattering of the gluon distribution functions. The induced polarization is long-range and is shown to lead to a global polarization of QGP in non-central heavy ion collisions at high energies. In the Standard Model (SM) with additional $n$ extra spatial dimensions, the Higgs boson is a zero-mode of the sixth dimensional gauge field. If the Higgs boson is a zero-mode of the sixth dimensional gauge field with a degree of freedom of the extra -dimensional vacuum energy, then it is natural for the electroweak symmetry breaking (EWSB) to take place due to the gap between the zero-mode profile and extra-dimensional vacuum energy. We present a concrete model with the Higgs in the bulk and identify the breaking patterns of the global Higgs symmetries. We show that the usual quartic Higgs coupling is generated at one loop by quantum corrections from the SM fields and from the fermions in the bulk, whereas the Higgs-portal couplings are generated only by fermions in the bulk. This is a two-stage breaking, with the corresponding light Higgs boson predominantly generated by the top loop in the first stage and then acquiring mass via a small but essential fermion contribution in the second stage. The light Higgs boson will necessarily have some small but non-negligible couplings to SM fermions. If the number of spatial extra -dimensional dimensions is as low as one micron, the Higgs mass is predicted in the range 126 GeV <m_h < 128 GeV at the 99% confidence level. If the Higgs boson is discovered at the LHC with a mass of 126 GeV, this would be direct evidence for EWSB taking place due to the gap between the zero-mode profile and the extra-dimensional vacuum energy.

In 2017, Marcus, Abreu, and Yamashita proposed a new concept of constant coefficients differential operators which generalizes the constant coefficients Riemannian metrics and differential operators. A key question follows: can one characterize these operators with zero operators? The main goal of this work is to present a conjecture on this topic and a method to solve it for the two-dimensional case. Furthermore, using this characterization, we present a proof for the three-dimensional case and a proof of the full two-dimensional case by providing a proof of the vanishing hypothesis. As a side product, this characterization also provides a new way of viewing the operator Hilbert polynomial and a proof of it for the two-dimensional case. Moreover, we show that the vanishing conjecture is true for this two-dimensional case by providing a proof of a new theorem for constant coefficients differential operators using this characterization. The vanishing conjecture and this characterization may have further applications in geometry, differential geometry, algebraic geometry, singularities , algebraic geometry, and algebraic geometry theory. Finally, this work was published in Compositio Mathematica, although the characterization is relatively short and the full proofs were posted on arXiv.

In this work we present a method to model the three-point correlation function of cosmological large scale structure. By the three-point correlation function we mean the number of objects as a function of their separation, and the scale over which the separation is measured. Our method is based on the coupling of a N-body simulation to a peak-bagging algorithm, and is able to capture the signal on both large and small scales. We illustrate our method with real data from the WiggleZ Dark Energy Survey, and show that we are able to reproduce both the one- and two-halo terms of the correlation function. We further apply our method to mock WiggleZ survey data, and show that we can place competitive constraints on the bias parameter of dark energy survey data, especially on small scales, compared to other methods. Finally, we discuss potential extensions to this method that may allow us to reduce the sampling error and increase the range of scales over which we can probe the three-point function, ultimately allowing us to map out the full non-linear three-point correlation function.

The quantum vacuum is a magical place where particles pop in and out of the vacuum in a probabilistic fashion. The behavior of such quantum fields underlie all known phenomena. In particular, their exchange leads to the stability of the Standard Model (SM) electric charge, the spin of the particles, and the form of the interactions. If we extrapolate the particle spectrum of the SM to the lowest possible energies, we expect the particle exchanges to involve gravitons, which could explain the observed gravity, and, possibly, also photons and fermions. In this work, we discuss the first option. Gravitons are the expected carrier of the gravitational interaction, which otherwise feels indirect through intermediate messengers. Photons and fermions are the two most abundant particles in the SM. Therefore, it seems plausible that they could be the corresponding force carriers. However, the fact that they are spin-1/2 fermions rather than spin-2 bosons has so far prevented them from being observed. In this work, we propose a way for photons and fermions to interact directly, through a new Lorentz- and CPT-violating term , the Standard Model Lagrangian. We present a way to test this proposal in current and future colliders. Gravitons carry both the gravitational and Lorentz-violation interactions, leading to a unique signature of the missing particles, with two corresponding jets emerging at high invariant mass. Photons and fermions only carry the gravitational interaction. Therefore, their phenomenological implications are not clear. Photons and fermions can decay to gravitons, and the signature would be two jets plus missing energy. If the graviton is the lightest of the new particles, the signature would instead be four jets. An excess of any of these signatures would be a hint of the underlying theory, which could also give an explanation for dark matter and the strong and weak forces.

The Crab pulsar is the first discovered rotating neutron star. It is an ideal source to test models of pulsars, since it is extremely stable and has very high density. Giant pulses are a type of pulses emitted by the Crab pulsar, with amplitudes much larger than the rest of the pulses. It has been observed that the giant pulse rate increases with the frequency of the observing system. However, all previous observations were done over a short time period, with only a few hours of data coverage at a time. In this work, we study giant pulse properties over a long time period, about a month. We observed that the giant pulse rate decreased with time and no single giant pulse was seen for a long time. Furthermore, the average giant pulse duration decreased with time, and the intensity modulation of the giant pulses became smaller with time. The dataset used in this study was collected using the DeUSTer (Deutsches SchweröLiteraturterminal) and the High-Hybrid Imaging (HHI) radio telescope in Bad Berleburg, Germany. The observations were made with the 13-Bit, 2.16 ms time resolution, and 2048 pt FFT size channel. The dataset spans from 2014-12-18 15:04:16 to 2014-12-18 10:22:33, corresponding to a time span of 21 days. The Giant Pulses Digital Filter was used to extract the pulse sequences. The observed Giant Pulses properties are quite different from those reported in previous studies. The complete set of data and analysis tools are available at https://doi.org/10.25919/5d78cc16d84ce. It is reported in previous studies that the giant pulse rate increases with the observing frequency. However, we found that the giant pulse rate decreased with the time. We also observed that no single giant pulse was seen for a long time, which means the giant pulse duration decreased with time. Furthermore, the intensity modulation of the giant pulses became smaller with time. The complete set of data and analysis tools are available at https://doi.org/10.25919/5d78cc16d84ce. The maintaingabilty of the Crab pulsar is one of the unsolved mysteries in astrophysics. The giant pulses we observed from the Crab pulsar may provide new insights into the nature of pulsars.

Shock waves are a common phenomenon in the atmosphere, where they occur as brief periods of instability in the atmospheric pressure and density. They are characterized by a sharp change in atmospheric variables, and are often observed as sudden changes in hue and cloud patterns. At the speeds at which shock waves occur in the atmosphere (sonic velocities), hypersonic shock waves also affect the airframe of aircraft. These are typically caused by a combination of friction and compressibility effects, and are characterized by a sharp gradient in temperature and pressure as well as a transition in the chemical composition of the air. When used in high-speed flight, such airframe deformations can result in severe mechanical damage, an increase in fuel consumption, and can lead to structural failure of the aircraft. In hypersonic flight, airframe deformation occurs on a much smaller scale than atmospheric variability. In response to these rapid changes, thermal effects become significant, as the airframe is capable of responding on shorter timescales than the thermal inertia of the fuel and passengers. In this sense, hypersonic flight differs from subsonic flight, which is characterized by low mass transport and slow thermal dynamics. Recent advances in computational fluid dynamics have enabled the accurate modeling of hypersonic shock waves, including thermal and aerodynamic effects. We implement this approach in the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, to model the shock wave in a nonlinear manner. In particular, we investigate the effect of the Grashof and Sack Rosenbloom-Kempen tensor terms on the shock dynamics. These terms are normally negligible in the low Mach numbers of atmospheric flight, but they become dominant in hypersonic flows. In particular, we find that Grashof and Sack Rosenbloom-Kempen diffusion s can influence the strength of the shock and modify its aerodynamic properties compared to the classical shock. Our results demonstrate that the strength of hypersonic shock waves can be affected by Grashof and Sack Rosenbloom-Kempen diffusion. In turn, this suggests that aerodynamic and structural characteristics of the shock wave can also be affected. We conclude that the methods proposed in this work can be applied to other fields in aerodynamics, such as Laminar flow control and boundary layer control.

Nested Sampling, first proposed by Skilling (2006), is a novel algorithm for sampling from a complicated posterior distribution. The method builds on a similar idea to Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, namely using a sequence of distributions that approximate the true posterior, with the final distribution yielding a sample that efficiently approximates the ideal sample. Nested Sampling differs from MCMC methods in two key aspects: firstly, it uses analytic conjugates to determine the parameters of the distribution; and secondly, the sample sizes needed are independent of the number of parameters in the model. Multimodal nested sampling , first proposed in Howard & Pypbell (2013), is a nested sampling algorithm that can be used to identify the local maxima in the posterior, and determine the number of modes in the chain. This is done by fitting a multimodal nested sampling model to the MAXIMA-1 likelihood and prior, and using this model to compute a probability distribution over the number of modes in the posterior. This method can also be used to determine the optimum number of samples in the chain, with longer chains performing better at mode-finding. This paper presents an extension to multimodal nested sampling, which we call multimodal nested sampling with functions (MNSMF). This method further develops the idea of using the density estimates produced by multimodal nested sampling to find the optimum number of samples in the chain, and then extends this to use the number of samples and parameter vector to determine the optimum length of the chains. As a result, multimodal nested sampling with functions finds the mode, number of modes, optimum chain length and parameter vector for each mode in a single chain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of multimodal nested sampling with functions through implementation and testing on both simple test cases, as well as more complex ones taken from astrophysics. We show that multimodal nested sampling with functions returns accurate estimates of the parameter vector, as well as the number of modes and their parameter vectors, in a small amount of time when compared to other algorithms. Additionally, we show that multimodal nested sampling with functions can be used on complex models where other algorithms fail. Finally, we apply multimodal nested sampling with functions to the MAXIMA-1 prior likelihood to show that the resulting chains find the global and local maxima in the posterior space, and return accurate estimates of the Bayesian evidence.

The SSS phase of RS Ophiuchi was observed with Chandra and XMM-Newton. Using the data obtained from the analysis of these observations, we report on the first detection of hard X-rays from the system and on the analysis of the temporal and spectral characteristics of the source. We also discuss the properties of the supersoft source and the dynamical status of the system based on our modeling of these data. We report on the first detection of hard X-rays from the supersoft X-ray binary (SSS) system RS Ophiuchi. The observations were performed with the Chandra and XMM-Newton satellites. Using the data obtained from the analysis of these observations, we also discuss the properties of the supersoft source and the dynamical status of the system. Our analysis of the available X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton reveals hard X-ray emission from RS Oph. The observed spectrum can be fitted with a multicolor disk blackbody (diskbb) model with a hard component. The estimated coronal temperature of the source is in the range 0.3-0.8 keV. Assuming that the hard component originates from the accretion disk, we can estimate the inner radius of this disk using the corona temperature and the emitting area obtained from the hard component. We also discuss the properties of the supersoft source based on the modeling of these data. The analysis of the available X-ray data suggests that RS Oph is a dynamically stable system. We present the best-fitting parameters of the published eclipse model based on the observed spectroscopic and photometric variability of the source. Using these best-fitting parameters, we compare the light curves assuming different scenarios for the system and determine the amount of parameter space that can be excluded based on our analysis of the available X-ray data. This paper describes the analysis of the available X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton satellites of the supersoft X-ray binary system RS Ophiuchi. Using the data obtained from the analysis of these observations, we report on the first detection of hard x-rays from the system and on the analysis of the temporal and spectral characteristics of the source. The results of our analysis suggest that RS Oph is a dynamically stable system and contains a hot corona located in the outer region of the accretion disk. We also discuss the properties of the supersoft source and the dynamical status of the system. RS Ophiuchi is a low-mass binary system containing a white dwarf and an optical star of late type . The latter is transferring material onto the former via an accretion disk. The spectral class of the optical star is K5Ve, which corresponds to a late type star of spectral class K5Ve.

Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP), the first form of matter conjectured by particle physicists several decades ago, is the densest form of matter known to humans. It exhibits many remarkable properties, including color charge and net-baryon number fluctuations, that can in principle be measured in the LHC. While most of the properties of the QGP were confirmed in the LHC Run 1, the observation of the novel phenomenon of photon emission from the QGP, reported by the ALICE collaboration, remains a great mystery. In this work, using the kinetic theory of heat and angular momentum transfer, we show that the QGP can emit virtual photons with an intensity that depends only on the temperature and the properties of the plasma, obviating the need for a dynamical calculation within the standard model of particle physics. The virtuality of the emitted photons, defined as the square of the momentum scale at which the induced photon vanishes, is determined by the temperature, and hence, the emitted photons may possess the energy and virtuality required to explain the ALICE anomaly. The proposed mechanism is not constrained by Lorentz invariance, and therefore it can operate in any QGP-like system that exhibits large momentum scales and non-trivial thermodynamics. In order to explore this mechanism, we make use of the uniqueness and robustness of the QGP thermodynamics to perform predictions for photon emission from strongly coupled plasma, which we confront against available data from lattice QCD. We find that the predicted photon rates are sufficient to resolve the ALICE anomaly, should it persist upon the completion of the Run 2 of the LHC. The ALICE collaboration has recently reported photon emission from the QGP in Pb-Pb collisions at the CERN LHC [1]. This observation has remained a mystery to the scientific community for over three decades, as most of the expected QGP signatures were observed in the first run of the LHC. However, the observation of photon emission, with an energy of approximately 9 GeV, and at an average rate of 1010 GeV-1 s-1, has remained a mystery. The emission of real photons is a Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) process, whereas the emission of virtual photons is not constrained by the symmetries of the standard model of particle physics, and may occur via a myriad of different processes. In this work we show that QGP can emit virtual photons with an intensity that depends only on the temperature and the properties of the plasma, obviating the need for a dynamical calculation within the standard model of particle physics. Three-dimensional space is filled with a thicket of 3-dimensional curves. All of these can be classified by their topological type, their algebraical type, or a combination of these. The most interesting 3-dimensional curves are singular ones: they are generically n-dimensional and transversal to n-dimensional space. Singular curves are also classified by their genera, i.e. by their codimensions in the parameter space. A comprehensive theory of singular curves was developed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, see in particular the works of Harris and points of view of Coppo and Garrone. These works prove a deformation theoretic framework for understanding the birational classification of such curves, i.e. their ability to be infinitesimally deformed into another one. This framework implies also that, for a generic choice of a curve, there is a plane in the nine-dimensional projective space of quadric hypersurfaces where the curve doesn’t intersect, and such a plane is called an exceptional plane. Curves with exceptional planes are called decomposable. This paper studies the case when the generic curve is not decomposable: it has a unique (up to projective equivalence) exceptional plane. Such curves are called non-decomposable. The most common case is when the exceptional plane is a plane of linear dependency for the general curve: such a plane is called an exceptional secant plane. The present paper develops a comprehensive theory of non-decomposable curves, and among other results, gives a birational classification (the so-called Wahl map) and describes how the variety of non-decomposable curves with a given exceptional plane (which is open of infinite type) fibers over the space of curves with a given exceptional secant plane (which is of finite type).

GRB 050724 was one of the first short/hard gamma-ray bursts (SHB) detected by the Swift satellite. It also had the highest redshifts and gamma-ray fluence of any SHB, possibly due to its high luminosity and circumburst density. The optical/X-ray afterglow of GRB 050724 was monitored with a number of telescopes for several days after the burst. These observations span a wide wavelength range, from the X-ray through the ultraviolet (UV) and into the optical. The afterglow of GRB 050724 was remarkably stable in color, fading steadily in all bands by approximately a factor of 10 over 100 days after the burst. GRB 050724 was remarkable in many other respects. Its bright X-ray afterglow was quickly discovered by BeppoSAX and achaived to within 12 hours of the burst, while the optical afterglow was detected on the first night by the few remaining ground-based telescopes. The ratio of the rest-frame extinction-corrected gamma-ray fluence to the rest-frame observed X-ray flux is the highest of any gamma-ray burst (which may explain the fact that it had the highest initial spin-down rate), while its optical/X-ray spectrum is the hardest of any gamma-ray burst, and it exhibited a super-burst (a second emission peak in the X-ray). Its host galaxy (with a diameter of z = 0.1685) is the most distant such galaxy to be known. The wavelengths of the afterglow of GRB 050724 span a wavelength range of more than 4 orders of magnitude, from X-rays to the UV/optical. These observations allow both its temporal and spectral behavior to be determined in considerable detail. The fading optical/X-ray light curve implies a standard afterglow fireball model, in which the debris blastwave decelerates as it sweeps up material from the circumburst medium. The broad band spectrum is well fit by a simple non-relativistic fireball model, with a low-energy electron energy distribution consistent with a single power law of index -p = 2.0 $\pm$ 0.2.

The CNGS neutrino beam produced by the Centro Nazionale Granulosatire (CNGS) laboratory in Italy is dedicated to the NOvA and GNO experiments. The detector installed at the LNGS, in the true neutrino mass scheme, consists of a 150 kilotonnes active detector target, made of a wide cylindrical tank containing 250 tons of liquid argon, inside a 2.67 kilotonnes phase overburden. The collaboration MODULAr, composed of researchers from Italy, United States, and Slovenia, proposes to build a new, very massive Liquid Argon Imaging Chamber, with the main goal to search for very low energy neutrinos, in a region not covered before by the CNGS beam. The detector will consist of a 2 level chamber with an internal diameter of 4 meters, and a height of 3 meters. The inner volume will be divided into 18 Verticale slices (VLSI), each hosting 30.48 Kg of liquid argon. The expected sensitivity is in a region of interest between 1 and 10 eV, where the expected number of signal events depends on the adopted simulated neutrino fluxes, and on the position of the detector in the phase volume. The unprecedented very large and compact design of the detector, together with its high sensitivity to very low energy neutrino interactions, make it an ideal candidate to search for spectral distortions, therefore exploring new physics phenomena in the neutrino sector.

Long-distance properties of strongly-coupled $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills (SYM) theory can be studied using classical strings in AdS space. Using this string picture, we compute four-point functions of operators with large R-charge, both at strong coupling and at finite ’t Hooft coupling. At strong coupling, these operators form a small-$\mathcal{N}$ WZW model, and we reproduce the exact scattering amplitude in the planar limit. At finite ’t Hooft coupling, the string description becomes reliable for shorter distances compared to the strong-coupling calculation, and we reproduce the known exponentiation of intermediate quantum effects in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM. We will describe some recent progress in understanding long-distance properties of $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills using classical strings in AdS space. We compute four-point functions of operators with large R-charge , both strong coupling and finite ’t Hooft coupling. At strong coupling, the string computation correctly reproduces the exact amplitudes in the limit of large $\mathcal{N}$. At finite ’t Hooft coupling, the string description becomes reliable for shorter distances compared to the strong-coupling calculation, and we reproduce the known exponentiation of quantum effects in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM. This research was partly performed at the Aspen Center for Physics, which is supported by National Science Foundation grant PHY-1607611. The results of this work were published in the journal Nature Communications. 2018

Quantum spin liquid (QSL) states have been the subject of active research in recent years due to their possible relationship to the high-temperature superconductivity and the central spin model. Despite intensive studies, however, QSL states remain elusive in many materials. Here, we report a deuterated inorganic kagome lattice material, Zn0.9Cu0.14-OD6Cl2, which does not exhibit zero magnetic entropy at low temperatures without long-range order, and instead, exhibits fractionalized excitations in a novel QSL state. Our results provide new evidence for QSL states in two-dimensional quantum magnets and open the way to studies of their fundamental physics and potential applications. INTRODUCTION Quantum computing exploits quantum mechanical phenomena to achieve very fast computation. This is achieved by using at least two quantum bits (qubits), which can be mapped to small energy zones in the space. When these zones are in resonance, the qubits can exchange energy very fast, effectively increasing the computing speed. The qubits can also be designed to never go out of resonance. This energy exchange is called quantum entanglement. Quantum entanglement can also occur between multiple spaces. Two spaces are called semi-coupled when the energy transfer between them is fast but not infinite. If more than one space is added, the energy transfer will decrease but will never stop completely. This chain of spaces is called coupled Energy Transfer (CET). CET was first discovered in a 10 dimensional space which is known as Graffiti Calabi-Yau. II. THEORETICAL APPLICATIONS The 10 dimensional Graffiti Calabi-Yau space was discovered by theoretical physicists in a simulation known as Curved Sec 14. This simulation was done on a computer with 10^14 particles. The CET zone starts at the 6th space from the smallest, called B1. The CET zone ends at the 11th space from B1, called B2. The energy transfer between these spaces is very fast and can be analysed with quantum field theory. The theoretical calculations show that the B2 space will have some portion of energy transferred to B1, which is a direct energy transfer. This portion is called direct coupling. The rest will remain in B2, and a small portion (around 10^-15) will be transferred to B1 ACK-ack because B1 was the destination of the energy. This is called ack-ack. III. SIMULATIONS The calculations showed that for the B1 to B2 coupling, the direct coupling is around 7.3 x 10^-5, and the ack-ack is around 9.2 x 10^-6. The difference is almost 10 times larger than the direct coupling, which means that the energy ends up in B2 almost completely without ever passing to B1. This difference is called transmissivity. This theoretical simulation is used to check if it is possible to find CET zones in the other 10 dimensional Graffiti Calabi-Yau spaces. The result is that in 43 of them, there is at least one CET zone, and in 31 of them, there is at least one CET zone with transmissivity over 5%. IV.
