HW2 (J2000) is a massive star-forming region located in the constellation of Aquila at a distance of 235 pc, as determined from the Gaia DR2 parallax. It contains at least 30 IRAS sources with bolometric luminosities in the range 8 - 13 x 10^4 L⊙, making it one of the most densely populated and massive star-forming regions in the entire Galaxy. The region is excited by the infrared source IRS 7, the driving source of a cometary radio telescope powered by a bipolar molecular outflow. We have performed high-resolution $^{13}$CO, 3 mm, and 7 mm observations of this region to better understand the processes of star formation and initial mass function (IMF) construction. We find that the cluster containing IRS 7 has a mass of 2,200 M⊙ and is in an extremely advanced evolutionary state, with many of its members in the process of becoming massive stars. We observe 35 high-mass OB stars with initial mass above 8 M⊙, 15 of which have initial masses greater than 10 M⊙. We detect two extremely massive stars with initial masses of 19 and 21 M<unk>. We also observe 28 more low-mass stars with masses below 8 M⊙, and 63 likely brown dwarfs. We identify 922 low-mass candidate members with masses between 0.5 and 8 M⊙. The cluster is also unusual in that it contains two stellar groups with distinct systemic velocities, each of which is accelerated by more than 4 km/s, and an indication of differential rotation. Despite the massive nature of the cluster, we do not see any clear evidence of an upper mass cutoff in the IMF, and instead see a slow rise in the number of stars per unit initial mass with decreasing mass. This is the second time such a deficit has been observed in the same region, suggesting that this is a signature of the IMF in the earliest stages of star formation. We also find an anti-correlation between the presence of high-mass stars and of low-mass stars, possibly because high-mass stars tend to form in regions where accretion is low. This evidence of extremely rapid and efficient star formation, with a strong potential for future exoplanet habitability, makes HW2 the most likely location for future searches for extraterrestrial life.

Young massive stars are surrounded by regions of heavy cloud collisonal and magnetohydrodynamic effects, also known as outflows and winds. These processes accelerate dust and gases out of the regions, radically changing their appearance in the process. We have performed a multiwavelength study of three young massive star forming regions, W33A, W33ABC, and NGC 7538, using data from the Infrared Astronomical Satellite, the Spitzer Space Telescope, the IRAS and MSX databases, and ground-based telescopes including the 100-m Green Bank Telescope, the National Radio Observatory 45-m Telescope, andNOEMA. In this work we present an analysis of the dust environment of these regions, and we examine the implications of the dust outflows on the young massive stars in the regions. We discuss our results in the context of current theories of young massive star formation, and we suggest new ways to investigate the influence of young massive stars on their natal clump.

In this paper, we formulate the Hamiltonian cosmological dynamics in Friedmann universe using ADM decomposition. Since the total time evolution is a constraint, we use the Abandoned Dirac procedure to introduce the time evolution for the phase space variables. The complete dynamics contains two secondary constraints, which can be used to eliminate two pairs of the canonical variables. After this process, the resulting system is described by one pair of the canonical variables and the symplectic two-form is completely defined. The quantization of the system is straightforward by using the correspondence between the classical and quantum variables. The physical inner product can be defined by two methods: one is using the conventional Schrödinger representation, and another is using the Berezin integral. In the former case, the Wheeler DeWitt equation is a Schrödinger-like equation. In the later case, the Wheeler DeWitt equation can be obtained by taking the normalization factor of the Berezin integral.

Solar radio spectrograph observation of the off-limb active region on 22 June 2014 at 04:30 UT is presented. Spectral analysis shows that the observed radio emission is mostly composed of two thermal components: one is the spectrally broad and kinetically cool accelerated component, which is usually interpreted as electrons and heat deposited by the precipitating beams; the other is the spectrum with little variance across the line profile, which may be contributed by the Maxwellian electrons accelerated by the magnetic field. Compared with the off-limb observation on 21 May 2014 at 14:00 UT, we found that the beam-related emissions have a higher spectral strength, whereas the mean electron density and the temperature of Maxwellian electrons decreased by 20% and 10%, respectively. This paper analyzes the spectral lines and their spatial derivatives to reveal how the density and velocity distribution of the thermal electrons change along the solar atmosphere. The results show that the density stratifies downward from the corona to the transition region, and the velocity distribution becomes more anisotropic with decreasing temperature. The density stratification indicates the beam-generated hot plasma is rooted in the lower solar atmosphere, and the velocity distribution anisotropy suggests that the beam particles propagate along the magnetic field. These results imply that both the beam formation and the propagation processes occur simultaneously in the lower solar atmosphere.

Reed-element oscillators (also known as the van der Pol s phase-lead oscillator) are used in a wide range of engineering applications due to their simplicity, robustness and ability to support a range of oscillatory states. Of particular relevance to this work are their use as low-power sensor nodes for "Internet of Things" applications and more recently, for "outside of me" applications using 802.15.4 low-power wireless networks. In both of these latter applications, the performance requirements for such nodes (including power consumption, number of supported sensors and accuracy of sensor readings) mean that reducing the energy consumption of the sensor node is a key design goal. In this paper, we demonstrate that when using a specifically tuned primary resonance of the mechanical structure in which the node is embedded, the overall energy consumption of the sensor node can be reduced substantially. More particularly, we study the energy required to sustain a particular oscillatory state, and show that this can be significantly reduced by judicious tuning of the primary resonance of the structure. A representative device is shown to consume 6.2μJ to sustain a resonant state, as compared to a minimum of 290μJ for the sensor node in "run-away" oscillatory mode.

This work investigates the second-order optimality of electrical impedance tomography (EIT). For the standard elliptic EIT inverse problem, a state that has minimal energy relative to the specified electrical boundary conditions does not necessarily have a corresponding physical shape. This phenomenon is often referred to as impedance artifacts. It has been shown that this problem can be cast as a constrained second-order minimization, subject to the incompressibility constraint and a globalization condition. In this work, we present a unified first- and second-order approach to shape optimization for EIT. We show that the associated shape functional is of the second order in the deviation of the current state from an optimizer. We apply a convex relaxation to the second-order shape derivative in order to characterize the second-order shape derivative by means of the Dirichlet energy, and thereby reduce the analysis to the level of convex analysis. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the theory.

Ca$_3$CoRhO$_6$ is a new class of ordered insulators, with the interesting feature of a metallic ground state despite fully compensated, nonmagnetic electron count. We characterize the electronic structure of this material using a combination of density functional theory and many-body insulator theory, showing the coexistence of nearly localized t 2g states with significant, partially broken symmetry spin-orbital character with mostly itinerant states of cener 3z 2-1. We demonstrate that the orbital entropy is reduced by the on-site coulomb interactions and demonstrate that the balance between the localization of the t 2g states and the itinerancy of the cener 3z 2-1 states results in a robust insulative state, with strong evidence of the Mott insulator behavior. We further show that the anisotropy in the spin-orbit coupling, which is of the order of 100 meV, is a major factor in determining the electronic properties of this material.

The light-cone power spectrum (LCP) has been proposed as a novel statistics to measure the large-scale structure (LSS) in the universe1. In the standard rulers and clocks (SCR) approximation, the LSS forms a light cone due to the recession rate of the galaxy or the sound speed of the baryon field2. Using the LSS as a natural ruler and clock, we can measure the geodesic distance and the expansion rate of the light cone respectively. In this way, the LSS provides a unique test bed to study gravity in an highly anisotropic universe3. Recent observations of the LSS show that the universe is dominanted by dark energy with 73.8% of the total energy density4, while the density of matter is only 26.2%. This result is known as the cosmic acceleration. The nature of dark energy is one of the most important open questions in fundamental physics and astronomy. Since the equation of state (EOS) of dark energy strongly correlates with the expansion history of the universe, a precise measurement of the dark energy EOS can be achieved by using the LSS as a natural ruler. In this work, we build a model-independent LSS statistic by measuring the anisotropic multipoles of the LSS. By using a cubic-mapping formula to interpolate the LSS from the SCR simulations, we measure the ratio of the first two multipoles up to the order of 10 in the anisotropic case. To test the efficacy of this statistic, we apply it to the most recent simulation produced by the IllustrisTNG project. We find that the measurement of the first two anisotropic multipoles can break the degeneracy between the EOS and the parameterized post-Newtonian (PPN). Furthermore, the ratio of the first two multipoles is independent of the bias between the LSS and the dark matter. Therefore, this LSS statistic provides a promising method to study gravity and shed light on the nature of dark energy.

A large number of stars have undergone at least one episode of deep mixing, since heavy elements are not preferentially sequestered into radiative zones. In advanced stages of this process, photospheric abundances of most elements are nearly constant, with the notable exception of Be. Be is destroyed at temperatures below its freezing point, so it is not abundant in fully radiative interiors. In contrast, Be is readily burnt in the deep mixing region, soBe signatures may be obliterated in radiative interiors. Fortunately, Be sinking below the surface may be regenerated in the cool radiative zones of evolved stars, allowing it to be used as a probe of past episodes of deep mixing. We present new measurements of beryllium depletion factors <unk>in three open clusters: NGC 2516, the Hyades, and M67. The clusters span a range of age (2.2 - 2.2 million years), distance (3.3 - 17.1 kpc), and metallicities (--0.7 to +0.4 in logarithmic scale), covering a broad parameter range likely to include stars of many different internal structures. Lower Be is detected in 18 cluster members; upper Be values are calculated for an additional 18. We perform a Fourier Chain Monte Carlo analysis of 13, 15, and 17 Be combinations for the three clusters, respectively, and characterize the resulting distributions of Be depletion factors α. All three clusters exhibit clear evidence for deep mixing, with median depletion factors of α = 0.58, 0.61, and 0.60 for NGC 2516, the Hyades, and M67, respectively.

We study QCD with N flavors in the presence of a singlet on with the gauge group SU(N) x SU(N). We show that the N = 1 SQCD theory has a dual description in terms of N flavors of hypermultiplets in the vector-like gauge group SU(N) x U(1) with an arbitrary number of fundamental and anti-fundamental hypers. We show that under certain conditions on the bare gauge and z bias couplings, theories with this dual description are dynamically equivalent to those obtained by confining the N = 1 SQCD theory in a 1+1d z bias interval. This generalizes Seiberg's duality between N=1 SQCD with one active quark and N=1 SQCD with one active quark to the case of arbitrary number of fundamental hypers, and implies that all N=1 SQCD theories with the same global symmetry symmetry are equivalent. We support this claim with explicit examples, including the large N limit and the entire duality web of N=1 SQCD theories with different number of fundamental hypers. We also explain how to construct explicit supergravity duals and explicit supergravity duals for some of the dual theories, and describe how to obtain the theories with N=2 and N=4 supercharges from them by the same method.

In this paper, we present our results regarding the occurrence of disordering transitions and peak effect in polydisperse systems. Disordering transitions occur when a solid mixture transitions from a solid-like state to a density-like state, and peak effect is a phenomenon which occurs when the volume fraction of a solid mixture at the peaks of the density -like state is greater than the average volume fraction of the mixture. These phenomena have both been observed in a wide range of material systems, including glass forming liquids, granular materials, and heterogeneous mixtures. In this paper, we demonstrate that the frequency of disordering transitions and peak effect can be manipulated by altering the variance of the particle size distribution. We perform event-driven molecular dynamics simulations to model a binary mixture composed of particles with the same size but with different levels of variance. Through the use of radial distribution functions, we are able to demonstrate that disordering transitions and peak effect occur at lower volume fractions for systems with higher variances. Additionally, we observe an increased frequency of disordering transitions and peak effect as the variance of the particle size distribution increases, and we identify an approximate scaling relationship between these two quantities. We provide a physical argument for this scaling relationship based on the average interparticle force, and compare our results with prior works which have explored similar relationships. We also discuss the broader implications of these results in the context of recent theories on the origins of disorder in solid matter systems.

A Bianchi model, which describes a homogeneous but anisotropic spacetime, has been used to describe the early evolution of the universe. This model includes three scale factors, which correspond to the overall size, the directional size, and the patterning of the universe. The Bianchi model has three characteristical scale factors: the anisotrophy parameter Ω and the trace of the energy momentum tensor normalized to the speed of light weighed multiplied by the speed of light , the current values of <unk>and ΩT, and the total energy E. The current values of Ω and ΩT, and the total energy E, as measured by modern cosmological observations, are roughly equivalent to the values of Ω and ΩT, and the total energy E, assumed by Bianchi models in the early universe. Given the current values of Ω and ΩT, and the total energy E, the anisotropic stress caused by a residual entropy bias in the early universe, which occurs in the plasma after it decoupled from the radiation, can approximately satisfy ΩT and lead to the observed pattern of large-scale structure. A residual entropy bias leads to an increase in the average energy of the particles in a region of space, which causes a corresponding increase in the average scale factor of the universe. If the temperature of the particles, relative to the scale factor of the universe, decreases with the average scale factor, then the residual entropy bias can lead to the current value of ΩT. Alternatively, if the particles have an effective spin which decreases with the scale factor, then the residual entropy bias can lead to the current value of Ω. While current cosmological observations are consistent with the Ω and ΩT values predicted by the model of the early universe with a residual entropy bias, the predicted amplitude of temperature fluctuations at large scales is larger than current observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) imply. This apparent discrepancy is called the "CMB anomalies". The Bianchi model with a residual entropy bias can also simultaneously explain the lack of large-scale tidal alignment in the observed large-scale structure, as well as the CMB anomalies. The residual entropy bias generates a preferred direction in the model, and if the matter in the early universe also had a preferred direction, then when the residual entropy bias led to an increase in the average scale factor of the universe, it would generate a corresponding increase in the average direction of the matter's preferred direction. This increased average direction of the matter's preferred direction would cause a suppression of large-scale structure along that direction. The CMB, on the other hand, is not able to distinguish between directions on scales of the suppression. Thus, the residual entropy bias can explain the lack of large-scale tidal alignment as well as the CMB anomalies. In summary, a Bianchi model with a residual entropy bias can explain current observations of the early universe, the lack of large-scale tidal alignment in the large-scale structure, and the CMB anomalies. Recent observations of the Sun’s convection zone by GOLF and of the surface layers of the Sun by BiSON suggest that convective overturning may be accompanied by torsional oscillations, with typical horizontal wavenumber k = 2-4 m−1 and near-inertial frequencies f approximately 2-5 mHz. The observed amplitude of the p-mode spectra in the Sun and Procyon A indicates that the fluid in the interior is relatively unconvective, with significantly less than about 10% of the star’s mass in convective regions at any given time. Torsional oscillations may thus be driven in most or all solar-type stars by the buoyant, non-convective regions that generate the pulsations in the same frequency range. The current view of the generation and driving of torsional oscillations in the Sun is summarized, and the ability of proposed driving mechanisms to operate in solar-type stars is evaluated. The possibilities for future detection of torsional oscillations in these stars, and their observational constraints are discussed. Finally, the implications of these findings for our understanding of the interiors of solar-type stars and the process of stellar evolution are considered. Third dredge-up and hot-bottom burning ( HBB ) are important processes during the AGB evolution. The surface abundances of the material processed by these two processes are expected to be different from the initial abundances of AGB stars. Thus, the study of the surface abundances can give us information about these nucleosynthesis processes. Recently, a new kind of AGB star, namely intermediate-mass AGB stars, have been identified and, because of the favorable temperature and density conditions for HBB in their interiors, these stars are believed to be the most likely site of SMS fabrication. In this work, we present the surface abundances of seven intermediate-mass AGB stars that undergo third dredge-up and HBB. The observed surface abundances agree with the predictions of third dredge-up nucleosynthesis. However, we detect a number of elements in the surfaces of three stars that do not exhibit [hs]: two of these stars are also hosts of (sub)millimeter sized SMS discs and are therefore very likely descendents of SMSs. The study of surface abundances could therefore be a good method to identify the SMS descendants.

Atomistic simulations based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations are presented for the dissociation of oxygen molecules on the Al(111) surface. Calculations were performed using the method of rapid adiabaticfollowing, which permits the first description of non-adiabatic dynamics by solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation on a mixed normal-Wigner representation Hamiltonian. The simulation method is first validated against experimental reaction coordinates for both the associative and dissociative pathways. The results are then presented in the first series of non-adiabatic dynamics simulations of the oxygen molecule dissociation on Al(111). It is found that the non-adiabatic effects can play an important role in the associative, as well as in the dissociative, pathway, notably by affecting the transition state ensemble. The influence of the substrate in the dissociation process is finally investigated. In particular, these simulations permit the first description of the non-adiabatic dissociation process of O2 molecules on the Al(111) surface. The simulations show that the dissociative pathway is adiabatic, whereas the associative one is adiabatic up to the transition state. In the dissociative path, the coupling is very strong at the entrance of the transition state, whereas it is negligible in the associative path. Finally, the simulations evidence that the substrate plays a significant role in the dissociation process. The Al(111) surface hosts two stable configurations for the O2 molecule: 1x2 and 2x2. The 1x2 structure corresponds to the linear geometry with the oxygen atom in the top position and the two hydrogen atoms in the bridge position, whereas the 2x2 structure corresponds to the bent geometry with the oxygen atom in the second position. These two structures differ by the orientation of the molecular axis. In the present work, we will refer to the 2x2 O2 structure as “bent” and to the 1x2 O2 structure as “linear”. Initially, the O2 molecule is located on the top of the surface in the linear geometry, either in the top or bridge position. A sufficiently high energy excitation could then lead to the rearrangement of the molecular axis with a 1x2 O2 structure, in which the molecular axis points towards the substrate. The nuclear wavepacket corresponding to this excitation has a large amplitude on the top position of the linear structure, and essentially vanishes on the bridge position. These simulations show that the molecular axis is located above the bridge position of the Al surface, as observed in experiments. This excitation could also lead to the dissociation of the O2 molecule into two atomic oxygen atoms. However, only a small portion of the wavepacket localised on top of the linear structure is initially involved in the dissociation process, in good agreement with the available experimental data. This means that the associative pathway is adiabatic. In this work, we go one step further and consider the non-adiabatic dynamics of both pathways. We use the DFT method for that purpose

Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) is the governing equations for the motion of electrically conducting fluids. These equations describe the dynamics of magnetic fields together with their mass, momentum , and energy transport. For geometrically thin, hydrostatic disks around black holes, these equations are reduced to the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) approximation, in which the dynamical stress of the magnetic field is frozen into the gas. In the thin disk approximation, the magnetic field is frozen into the gas, and is described by a single integral relation between the rotational and magnetic stresses. Here we compare the time-dependent coupled equations for MHD disk accretion with the vertical structure computed from the conformal wedge thin disk equation, where radiative cooling is calculated self-consistently. We find that the maximum efficiency of the gas to convert gravitational energy to radiation is achieved for MHD turbulent viscosity parameter, α=10−3. The MHD solution shows the predicted thermal equilibrium in which the radial, azimuthal , and vertical components of the stress are related through a single temperature, and the expected gas pressure and energy densities together with accretion rates in agreement with observations of AGN.

The paper explores the effect of exchange frustration on the magnetic caloric effect (MCE) in the J1-J2 model on the square lattice. The J1-J2 model describes coupled layers of spin-1/2 moments, where ferromagnetic (FM) intra-layer and antiferromagnetic (AFM) inter-layer exchange constants are assumed. The MCE in the J1-J2 system was shown to result from both a latent heat and a magnetic field effect. The former arises from the modification of the magnetic order upon cooling through the Néel temperature T_N, whereas the latter results from an induced uniform magnetization in the non-magnetic background of thermally excited domain walls. The latter effect becomes particularly pronounced in the presence of strong magnetic fields, as it allows the MCE to remain large even at very low temperatures. Using state-of-the-art large-scale cluster Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate this issue in the J1-J2 model on a square lattice, varying the coupling temperature of J2/J1 from 0 to 1. We demonstrate that the presence of frustration has only a minor effect on the Néel temperature, T_N ∝ (J2/J1)−1, but it has a profound effect on the magnetic field effect. Although the induced uniform magnetization grows continuously from zero for T>T_{NL}, where T_{NL} is the Néel-like temperature defined by T_{NL} <unk> (J2+J1)/2, it becomes systematically non-zero below a critical frustration value of 0.67 J1. We determine the scaling behavior of the MCE across the full range of J2/J1 and find that it is largely determined by the induced uniform magnetization, although a residual field-dependent latent heat remains and contributes to the MCE heat capacity across the entire ordered range. We extract the field- and magnetic field-dependent isothermal entropy change ∆S(T,H) and show that it diverges as the magnetic field approaches the saturation value B_{sat}, whereas its isothermal derivative ∂∆S(T,H)/∂T decreases monotonically with increasing temperature. These findings are consistent with recent theories for the field-dependent behavior of ∆S in frustrated magnets, which predict ∆S(B)∝B−B_{sat} for fields close to B_{sat}. Our MC simulations also demonstrate the presence of thermally induced domain walls, which become more numerous with decreasing temperature and give rise to an exponential increase in the corresponding domain wall tension with decreasing temperature. As the wall tension increases with system size, ∆S(T,H) is expected to increase exponentially with system size at low temperatures. These findings are consistent with

In quantum gravity, the AdS/CFT correspondence is a conjectured duality between a certain type of quantum gravity theory in a certain asymptotic region of AdS space and a certain type of quantum field theory in one higher dimension. Quantum gravity in this context is hypothesized to be described by string theory in a specific type of asymptotical region of AdS space known as an anti-de Sitter space, or AdS space for short. One of the major open problems in quantum gravity is the quest to describe the process by which classical gravitational fields emerge from the quantum gravitational regime. One approach to this problem is the imposition of unitarity constraints on the description of gravitational scattering processes. These constraints imply the so-called gravitational light-cone, or "beables" principle, which states that the past and future light-cones of a given point in space-time completely determine the state of the gravitational fields located in that point. This in turn implies that the entropy carried by a gravitational wave must be entirely encoded in the symmetric portion of the two-point function of the corresponding CFT operator. This implies that the entropy, or information, carried by a gravitational wave must be fully contained in the degrees of freedom of the CFT on the spatial boundary of the AdS space in which the gravitational wave resides. Conversely, one can think of the CFT as encoding the information about the gravitational fields of its spacetime horizon. It was shown in earlier work by the present author and his colleagues that for a wide class of gravitational theories, the renormalized stress-tensor two-point function satisfies a semi-group property. This in turn implies that the entropy of the gravitational wave must be conserved in time. These results suggest that gravitational entropy must be non-local and distributed throughout the entire CFT. In this work, we present explicit calculations of the corresponding non-local gravitational entropy current for a large class of gravitational theories. We demonstrate that the entropy current has a well-defined algebraic structure and obeys a local conservation law. This allows us to derive a general expression for the metric's contribution to the energy-momentum tensor. We then specialize to four dimensions, and show that the resulting equations of motion imply general covariance and the Einstein equations up to the infinite set of higher-order equations for the metric and its derivatives. These latter equations can be thought of as encoding the gravitational influence on the dynamics of the CFT. Our main result is a formula for the gravitational anomaly, or obstruction, to the equation of motion induced on the spacetime boundary by the infinite set of higher-order equations for the metric and its derivatives. We show that this anomaly takes the form of a gravitational Chern-Simons anomaly. We conclude by outlining a program to compute the full entropy current and anomaly in higher -order equations. Resistances in distance-regular networks can be calculated recursively, based on Bose-Mesner algebra and Christoffel-Darboux identity. For complete networks, the recursive calculation reduces to solving a linear system. For incomplete networks, the recursive calculation becomes a Fixed-Point Iteration, which converges to the effective resistances very fast. The effectiveness of the algorithm is demonstrated by numerical examples. In this paper we present the detection of X-ray and gamma-ray emission from the distant blazar 1ES 1101-232 with H.E.S.S. and broadband characterisation. 1ES 1101-232 is one of the most distant and strongly detected TeV emitter. The H.E.S.S. observations cover a baseline of more than 5 years and provide the first spectral measurements of this distant TeV blazar with two different methods: a broadband spectral analysis and a correlation analysis of the different epochs. We find a positive correlation of the gamma-ray flux with the X-ray flux and a positive spectral slope between 1 and 10 TeV. The gamma-ray energy flux between 1 and 10 TeV is (2.1 ± 0.2) × 10-13 ph cm-2 s-1. The comparison of the spectral data with various epochs allows to put constrains on the intergalactic magnetic field and on the source redshift.

In this paper, we present a scheme for laser-assisted pairing-based cooling of Fermi gases. We start with a simple theoretical model describing two-body collisions in the low energy limit, i.e., for non-zero range (scattering volume) and zero effective range. We describe the two-body collisions in a simple analytic form using an effective separable potential, allowing us to easily perform numerical calculations. We apply this model to describe laser-assisted cooling of Fermi gases, where the Feshbach resonance is used to reduce the effective range of the collisions. Our theoretical model is in good agreement with numerical calculations of the full dynamics. We discuss how our scheme can be implemented in current laboratories, and present numerical estimates for achievable temperatures. We note that the separable potential used in this work has also been applied in other works on laser-assisted dynamics, e.g., in generation of multiple condensates. We present detailed comparisons of our scheme with other schemes for laser-assisted dynamics.

This paper presents a continuum study of the millimeter dust cores found in the VMR cloud D using data from the Spectral and Photometric Imaging System (SPIRE) on the European Space Agency's (ESA's) * * * Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (* * *). Dust emits heat in the form of IR radiation. As one or more molecules acquire enough energy to overcome their vibrational degrees of freedom, they emit visible and Near Infrared radiation. The cores are resolved into filaments, interpreted as being due to the growth of coalballs under the influence of the pressure from the surrounding molecular material, which at a temperature of 7 K, produces a uniform distribution of ice crystals. The filaments are also revealed to be bendier, with a changing orientation to the magnetic field, possibly caused by the interference from different polarisation modes within the dust particles. The cores are located in both the near and far IR, with the majority of the radiation associated with the cores occurring in the far-infrared. In the * * * map the long axis of the filaments is mostly parallel to the long axis of the core, in contrast to what would be expected from the models of gravity dominated collapses. In addition, the IR intensity profile of the cores, as shown by the orange lines in the * * * figures, can be well fitted by the profile of a Bonnor-Ebert sphere, which suggests that the cores are not in the final stages of collapse. The authors suggest that, due to the filamentary nature of the cores, it is likely that the cores are subject to a combination of collapse and external pressure from the surrounding molecular cloud.

In this paper, we investigate the evolution of the superconducting phase in the cuprates from a microscopic model of pairing based on an extended Hubbard Hamiltonian which includes nearest-neighbor pairing, forward-scattering, and a truncated version of higher-order pairing terms. Starting from an uncorrelated normal state, we find that the inclusion of pair-hopping (off-diagonal interaction) causes pairs of opposite sign to form away from half-filling and for weak pairing. Inclusion of the particle-particle channel in the truncated model yields Cooper-pairs with $\mathrm{d}$-wave symmetry. We establish the phase diagram of this system at zero temperature and focus on the region near the antiferromagnet/superconductor (A/S) gap. We show that the sign structure of the gap changes at the tetracritical point, from subdominant to leading component, indicating the underlying pairing symmetry changes from $\mathrm{d}$- to $s$-wave. Further, we demonstrate the existence of an exotic co-existing phase comprising $d$-wave Cooper-pairs and a Fermi-surface Griffiths phase of $s$-wave symmetry. The co-existence of these two types of superconducting order over a contiguous region of the phase diagram is shown to yield a nodal $d$-wave superconductor with nodal $s$-wave states along the Griffiths Fermi-surface. The results are discussed with reference to observations of the phase diagram, like pair correlations, and coexisting $s$-wave and $d$-wave behaviour in the cuprates.

Using the three-dimensional (3D) galaxy correlation function from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7, I investigate the anisotropic magnification distortion on the tangential and radial wavelengths. The conventional longitudinal magnification distortion is prominent on the very large scales, while the transverse distortion emerges on the relatively small scales. The anisotropic magnification distortion is found to be proportional to the cosmic matter density parameter Ωm. I fit the model of distorted power spectra to the galaxy correlation functions and estimate the Ωm from the best-fitted values of the amplitude ratios. For the fiducial Ωm, I measure Ωm=0.27_{-0.07}^{+0.09 (stat.)}_{-0.06 <unk>$ (Planck const.+assumptions)}, which indicates that the cosmic average matter density is relatively high at the 2σ level. Assuming a Ωm=0.3, I estimate the bias between the observed distribution of galaxies and the projected matter distribution to be b=1.07_{-0.25 (stat.)}^{+0.22 (sys.)}, 1.09_{-0.21 (stat.)}^{+0.19 (sys.)}, 1.17_{-0.20 (stat.)<unk>+0.17 (sys.)}, and 1.27_{-0.19 (stat.)}^{+0.17 (sys.)}$ for radial and tangential angles of Δ=20°−60°, Δ=20°−20°, Δ=20°+20°, and Δ=20°+60° at the 2<unk>and 2σ confidence level, respectively. These values indicate that our Universe is elongated in the direction of ∼30°−50° from the line of sight.

One of the most prominent features in the UV spectrum of galaxies with star-formation is the Lyman break. The Lyman break is caused by absorption of ionizing photons from young, massive stars by intervening systems of neutral hydrogen clouds. Studying the appearance of the Lyman break at different redshifts provides us with a powerful tool to trace the evolution of the intergalactic medium, as the ionizing photons from young stars are only able to reach the surrounding medium after traversing several absorption systems. Several recent studies at z = 2-3 have shown an increase in the rest-frame UV (observed optical) Lyman break opacity, which is interpreted as an increase in the average dust content of star-forming galaxies over the last 9 billion years. However, new studies of individual Lyman break galaxies at higher redshifts (z = 1-3) show that the average dust content has actually been decreasing over this same epoch, which is more in line with expectations from a Λ Cold Dark Matter cosmology. Alternative explanations such as changes in the Initial Mass Function, dust geometry, and the escape of ionizing photons are all ruled out as the cause of this evolution. We instead suggest that a more plausible interpretation is a decrease in the average dust content of star-forming galaxies over this same epoch. At high redshifts, bright, young star-forming regions are enshrouded in dust cocoons generated by the first generation of stars, reducing the average dust content of galaxies. By analyzing the decline in dust attenuation with increasing radius at different redshifts, we estimate that the average dust content of galaxies to have decreased by a factor of 9 from z = 1-3 to the present day. This decrease in dust content may be due to the increasingly efficient radiation - driven escape of dust grains, which has been demonstrated in simulations. Furthermore, possible interactions between galaxies and the Hubble flow could have blown away most of the dust surrounding high-redshift galaxies. If this interpretation is correct, then the Universe has not been entirely covered in dust at all times, but only at certain times due to local enhancements in the amount of dust in the intergalactic medium.

Galaxy clusters are the most virialized structures in the Universe, and have played a critical role in our understanding of galaxy structure formation and the evolution of the Universe. Measuring their properties, including their temperature, mass, and metal abundance, is key to these studies. Thanks to X-ray observations with the Chandra and X-ray observatories, we now have precise measures of cluster properties out to high redshifts. Here, we present a Chandra study of the temperature and metal abundance profiles in the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) clusters at 0.1 < z < 0.3. Our sample size of five clusters with a total of 14 observations is the largest to date at these redshifts. We measure strong evidence for temperature declines with radius in our five clusters. Using hydrostatic equilibrium to relate the temperature and density, we find that the cores of our clusters are much hotter than their outskirts, with the temperature differences increasing with radius. The radial temperature differences are significant at the 4.3 - 12.5 sigma level for the five clusters combined. We also find significant excesses of heavy elements in the cores of our clusters. These are the first measurements of the temperature and metal abundance profile in a sample of galaxy clusters at intermediate redshifts, and they demonstrate the power of Chandra and large surveys in furthering our understanding of the evolution of clusters.

Recent works on string dualities and beyond have substantially deepened our understanding of gauge theory and string theory. In particular, in the context of flux compactifications, it was proposed that non-Abelian strings could be a dual description to certain fluxvacua of nonsupersymmetric higher dimensional gauge theories. Here we build upon this framework by proposing a highly nontrivial system of non-Abelian strings with a velocity-dependent tension, whose low energy dynamics is expected to provide a ultraviolet completion of Lifshitz gravity. This construction includes a class of general solutions parameterized by an arbitrary number of dimensions , and a class of Abelian or non-Abelian string systems with a scalar field and gauge groups. We also examine the cases with critical and noncritical inverse corrections to the worldsheet beta functions. The former admits an effective field theory solution, and reduces to a simpler example of a logarithmic electrodynamics recently found in the context of five-dimensional gauge theories. The latter admits an effective field theory description in terms of a modified gravity theory with a Gauss-Bonnet term plus a scalar field, and includes the general non-Abelian string systems with constant string coupling found by other authors. Additionally, we show that for a large class of configurations, the tension of the strings may have a velocity-dependent expectation value, dynamically solving the equation of motion for the scalar field, leading to a deconfined tension of the strings with asymptotic freedom. Finally, we study the supersymmetric generalizations of this system, where we find that when the strings are nonsupersymmetric they necessarily contain local excitations of the scalar field, and thus their strings loop s are not vanishingly small.

We present the first three-dimensional X-ray cluster correlation function based on a flux-limited sample of X-ray selected galaxy clusters from the ROSAT North Ecliptic Pole (NEP) survey. The cluster sample is drawn from the compilation of Gregor et al. (2007) and covers a volume-limited, flux-limited range of 2-5×10^-15 W m−2 in the 0.5-2.0 keV band. The resulting 3D cluster correlation function, measured in the plane of the sky, shows no indication of the usually observed decrement towards small separation, for separations up to 20 arcmin. The 3D clustering amplitude is determined to be A = 0.436 ∓ 0.058 = 0.3064 ∓ 0.0852, where the 95 % error interval is determined from 22 bootstrap resamples. This is in excellent agreement with the previous results from 2D analyses of this cluster sample. The corresponding projected correlation length is z0 = 8.25 ∓ 0.61 h Mpc, where the 95 % confidence interval is determined from 20 bootstrap resamples. This is larger than the expected strength of the cluster correlation function for a random distribution, suggesting that the X-ray selected galaxy clusters are biased with respect to the underlying mass distribution. The 3D redshift-space cluster correlation function, r(s), is determined up to separations of 40 arcmin, yielding z0 = 0.3064 ∓ 0.046, where the 95 % error interval is determined from 22 bootstrap resamples.

Single molecule methods were used to observe the process by which RNA polymerase (RNAP) produces RNA in real time. Previous single molecule studies on this process have observed the initial landing of RNAP at a specific site on DNA, termed the promoter, followed by progressive formation of a stable initiation complex. During this process, RNAP can frequently be observed pausing and rapidly switching between forward and backward motion. These pauses are often due to transient occlusion of the RNA exit pathway by the enzyme’s bound core. We demonstrate that the addition of the four nucleotide triphosphate CTP increases the rate of RNA synthesis by RNAP without increasing the frequency of pauses or switching between forward and backward motion. Using a computational traffic flow model, we show that the observed increase in the rate of RNA synthesis is robust with respect to variations in the input parameters, and that the observed increase is only observed when the system is mildly congested. Our data and modeling suggest that RNAP can transcribe at increased rates when the spacing between RNAP molecules is reduced due to transient congestion on the DNA.

Two-dimensional square tiling was discovered long ago, and three-dimensional cubic tiling was discovered in the 1980s. Recently, a new type of three-dimensional periodic tiling has been discovered, which we call brane tiling. It is a tiling of 4-dimensional space. Two different kinds of walls exist in brane tiling: electrical walls, which are periodically arranged, andGuideline walls, which are continuously arranged in one direction. Several biological applications of these unique properties of brane tiling are suggested. About a decade ago, a novel type of three-dimensional periodic tiling, called brane tiling, was discovered. It is a tiling of 4-dimensional space. Similar to the well-known Tübingen tiling, it can be described with square and cubic tiles. But the third dimension gives new features. Two different kinds of walls exist in brane tiling: electrical walls, which are periodically arranged, and Guideline walls, which are continuously arranged in one direction. Several biological applications of these unique properties of brane tiling are suggested. For example, the well-known brane tiling can be used to orientate molecules on the walls. The unique physical properties of the Tübingen tiling can be used for orientating molecules on the walls. In the last section, it is shown that this technique can provide the basis for a new technology for producing electricity. Since its discovery, the brane tiling has been applied to the topics of physical chemistry, catalysis, and electric power generation. The article presents two physical applications of the brane tiling. First, it can be used to orientate molecules on the walls. Second, it can provide a new technology for producing electricity. The unique physical properties of the brane tiling are described. The physical applications of this tiling are also presented. The article presents a short overview of the discovered properties and the potential applications of the brane tiling. It presents the discovered properties and potential applications of the Tübingen tiling and the brane tiling. The Tübingen tiling has been applied to physical chemistry, catalysis, and electric power generation. However, it is now known that the Tübingen tiling was only one of the possible 3D tilings. However, the unique physical properties of the Brane tiling are presented and suggest these applications. On 15 November 2014, an extremely rare and remarkable galaxy cluster merger was witnessed by the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). The collision product exhibited an extraordinary distribution of diffuse matter (DM) of some 2 Mpc (84 million light-years) along the projected collision axis, strongly suggestive of a recent merger between two larger systems. While dynamical evidence supports the hypothesis of a recent collision between two large galaxy clusters, a conclusive identification of the diffuse matter (DM) component of the collision remains challenging. Here we report the discovery of a bullet-shaped DM clump that passed through the northwestern subcluster, as evidenced by its deep, prominent tangential arc feature and symmetric X-ray morphology. The projected DM bullet’s path indicates that it was strongly bound to the subcluster, with an orbital energy of at least −3.8 <unk> 1054 J, or −7.6 × 1052 ergs. A radial DM trail was also observed connecting the bullet to the main cluster core. We estimate that a DM mass of at least 4.4×108 M⊙ is needed to explain the observed features, of which the bullet is a responsible fraction of at least 4.4×1011 M⊙. While the DM bullet only accounts for a minor fraction of the total collision mass, our result demonstrates the feasibility of discovering and studying such minor components with forthcoming DM halo observations from large x-ray telescopes, such as the Future x-ray astrophysics telescope (FXRT), the LOFAR telescope, and the proposed Chinese-FrenchDark Matter Telescope (CFDT).

The ocean covers approximately 71% of the surface of our planet, and absorbs half of the carbon dioxide emitted by human activity. As we are increasingly aware of the influence of this important habitat for life, it becomes increasingly important to understand the dynamics of ocean and climate systems. In this work we present a modeling framework for the ocean that couples the Boussinesq system for ocean mass and heat transfer with the three-dimensional General Circulation Model of the atmosphere. The ocean model is based on a primitive equations solver, and the dynamical core is informed by the Princeton Ocean Model. The thermodynamic and carbon cycle extensions are based on the World Ocean Model, which has been updated to include a stochastic predictor to better represent small-scale processes. We employ this framework to model the response of the Indian Ocean to changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide. We show that, while the expected surface cooling associated with increased carbon dioxide emissions will not be detectable in observations of tropical Indian Ocean temperatures, the expected subsurface warming could have profound implications for the overturning structure and meridional momentum of the Indian Ocean Circulation Cell.

GRB051022 was an unusually long gamma-ray burst (γ-ray burst, GRB), lasting for at least 27sec. It was detected by the Burst and Transient Source Experiment on board the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope on October 22, 2005, at 04:56:48.6 UT, at a nominal distance of 220 million light-years from Earth. While GRB durations fall into several distinct categories, this long-duration, or long burst, exceeds most commonly accepted classification definitions by several orders of magnitude. In particular, it is more than 10 times as long as the second longest GRB, and many times longer than any other observed short/medium GRB. This extremely long duration could not be readily explained by standard models of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), which associate these events with the core collapse of massive stars or the coalescence of compact objects. However, current GRB models do not fully explain the very long, as well as shorter, bursts. Alternatively, the extremely long duration of this event could be explained by a highly beamed emission, with the consequent higher chance of being observed by a space-based observer at large distance. In this case, the burst would have produced significantly lower levels of prompt high-energy emission, as observed. However, the early-time optical and X-ray afterglow that would be expected in this case were not observed. GRB051022 emitted more than 10 times more energy than the typical long burst. The most likely explanation for this higher luminosity is beaming: the gamma-rays were beamed into our direction from a highly misaligned beam. We can place limits on the beam-opening angle of the gamma-ray beam using these limits on the optical and X-ray afterglow. Fermi's observations of GRB01022 provided the first broadband spectrum of a gamma-ray burst, from more than 10% of the total gamma-ray energy detected by the Burst Alert Telescope on board the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope down to the Stefan–Boltzmann limit of infrared observation with the GEMS. The detection of prompt optical and infrared emission in this case, despite the gamma-rays being beamed away from the observer, implies that the energy emitted in gamma-rays was less than 1% of the total. Thus the highest energy observed gamma-rays were not as narrowly beamed as previously thought, allowing for a wider range of possible sources. The prompt emission of GRB051022 lasted 27 seconds, which is the longest of any gamma-ray burst ever recorded. This event was notable not only for its extreme duration, but also for its proximity to Earth. It was the nearest GRB ever recorded, and the faintest optical and X-ray afterglow ever recorded. A scenario machine was used to calculate the luminosity function of binary X-ray sources in the galaxy. Using a large cosmological volume, the binary source population was modeled using an N-body tree, coupled with a population synthesis routine. Inputting reasonable binary system parameters, the scenario machine was able to simulate the spectrum and the variability of the sources, as well as the distribution of the X-ray flares. A galactic survey was then simulated, observing all sources above a luminosity threshold. By comparing the number of sources seen in the simulated galactic survey to the number of sources seen in actual surveys, the most likely binary system parameters were determined. The luminosity function of the binary source population was then calculated. The scenario machine was able to determine the most likely binary system parameters by comparing the number of sources seen in the simulated galactic survey to the number of sources seen in actual surveys. By counting the number of sources above a luminosity threshold, and by varying the binary system parameters, a best fit was determined for the distribution of sources by luminosity. The luminosity function of the binary source population was calculated, and found to be consistent with previous estimates from X-ray observations and population synthesis modeling. The results of this work are important for understanding the binary source population, and for calculating the binary system parameters that best fit the observed background. * The scenario machine was used to simulate binary source evolution, including binary formation, evolution through mass exchange , magnetic braking, and separation through the emission of gravitational waves * An N-body tree was used to follow the motion of individual binary sources through time, and a population synthesis routine was used to model the properties of the population as a whole * A galactic survey was simulated, observing all sources above a luminosity threshold. The comparison of the number of sources seen in the survey to the number seen in actual surveys determined the binary system parameters that best fit the observed population. * The luminosity function of the binary source population was calculated, and found to be consistent with previous estimates This work was done by researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics in Heidelberg, Germany, in collaboration with the Universities of Heidelberg and Potsdam, and the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the USA.

A theoretical study of the decoherence of a driven multilevel quantum system interacting with a multi-bath reservoir is presented. A general description of a qubit-bath model is presented where a reduced density matrix for the qubit is obtained using a hierarchical quantum master equation approach. Our result shows that, under the secular and rotating wave approximation, the reduced density matrix of the qubit converges to a product state for a weak system-bath coupling, which indicates that the qubit state becomes insensitive to its environment. However, for a strong system-bath coupling, we show that the off-diagonal elements of the reduced density matrix decay to zero much slower than the off-diagonal elements, which indicates that the qubit state becomes entangled with its environment. Our result also shows that the purity of the qubit state decays to one half in a short time for any coupling strength, which indicates the fast depletion of the qubit's quantum information. We illustrate our theoretical findings using a representative model of a three-level system interacting with a one-dimensional bosonic reservoir, and show that the entanglement between the system and environment becomes stronger as the system-bath coupling increases.

In this paper we introduce the mathematical theory of two-dimensional reversible and irreversible quadratic Lagrangian mechanical systems with an additional symmetry: they are conservative with a quadratic integral of arbitrary degree. The classification of these systems is performed in terms of their integrals and their singular points. As an application, an atlas of such systems, with a detailed description of their qualitative behavior, is provided. The theory of such systems, also known as Swallow Systems, was introduced in [1]. The case of quadratic first integral was considered in [2]. The case of a second integral of higher degree (hereafter called a quadratic integral) was considered in [3]. The case of three additional symmetries (reversibility or Lagrangian mechanics) was studied in [4] and [5], while the combination of these three additional symmetries (conservativity with a quadratic integral of arbitrary degree) was studied in this paper. In order to present the theory in a concise way, we introduce the abstract differential equations of such systems and we obtain an atlas, dividing the presentation into six sections, each one corresponding to a different kind of qualitative behavior of the solutions: - conservative singular point; - elliptic point; - hyperbolic point; - butterfly; - strange point; - generic point.

A spectropolarimetric analysis of the magnetic field strengths of the Ca II 8498 A and 8542 A lines in the quiet Sun is presented. The data were obtained using the Dutch Meteor Telescope with the new Waveslicer on the Meteor satellite. The spectropolarimetric data cubes cover a field of view of 30 by 30 solar radii and a resolution of 0.33 by 0.33 arcseconds. The observed area was close to the solar disc centre and included a granule of size 4 by 4 Mm in resolution. Polarization signals of both line profiles and the continuum were detected, but no circular polarization signals above the detection limit of 0.1 percent were observed. The line-of-sight component of the magnetic field strengths was measured using the forward polarimetric technique and was found to be around 100 G. The average values of the magnetic field strength in the centre of the granules were found to be in the range 50-200 G.

Computer networks are essential components of modern computer systems and contribute to increasing user productivity and efficiency. As network ed applications have become more central to people's work and lifestyles, network application protocol implementations (NAPI) have become an increasingly important aspect of computer networks, facilitating communications between networked applications and terminals. Unfortunately, NAPI implementations are often subject to various constraints that make them vulnerable to errors and failures. Consequently, effective NAPI implementation is essential to the proper functioning of computer networks. Recent research has shown that a programmer's choice of programming language can have a significant impact on the robustness of NAPI implementations. Specifically, programming in a high-level language can lead to more robust NAPI implementations compared to programming in a low-level language. However, existing high-level programming languages, such as Java and C++, often fail to adequately address various real-world hardware and software constraints that may adversely affect NAPI implementations. Consequently, today's high-level programming languages may fail to provide adequate robustness for NAPI implementations, especially in the presence of real-world hardware and software constraints. In this paper, we present a language-based approach for improving the robustness of NAPI implementations. We begin by presenting an overview of the language-based approach and identifying key components. Then, we present a case study of how this approach has been applied to a particular high-level programming language, Java, for improving its NAPI-implementation robustness. In particular, we show that by applying one particular key component of our approach, which is static checking, the robustness of NAPI implementations in Java can be significantly improved. We also discuss how these improvements can be further improved by using more advanced static checking techniques. We then describe other key components of our approach and how they could be integrated with our static checking technique. Finally, we present a case study of our approach as applied to the popular Jakarta NAPI Java implementation, showing that it can improve Jakarta NAPI's robustness by about 3.6x in the presence of common real-world constraints.

A pump-probe scheme is employed to measure the phase of stimulated emission as a function of optical path difference between the pump and probe pulses. The amplitude and phase are retrieved using a modified Abel inversion. A coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering method is used to provide a single phase coherent, intense, laser -pumped source of coherent light at a wavelength of 1064 nm. The stimulated emission is measured from a fiber laser pumped by a 1064 nm laser with a 1 kHz linewidth. The phase is retrieved with a 3.2 nrad precision and a 12.5 μs resolution at 10 kHz repetition rate. These measurements are performed using a 100 nm high resolution electro-optical phase modulator. These results provide a benchmark for stimulated emission phase measurements. Stimulated emission is an inelastic process resulting from a high energy electromagnetic field interacting with a system of two or more electrons, in which one of the electrons emits a photon and changes energy state, while the remaining electrons transition to a lower energy state. This results in a delay period where the energy of the electromagnetic field is transferred to the systems, and a resulting coherent optical field is emitted. The phase of the stimulated emission is dependent on the energy state of the interacting electrons, and provides a mechanism to control the coherent optical field for use in photon sources such as frequency combs or coherent light diodes. Measuring and controlling the phase of stimulated emission provides a mechanism to characterize the dynamics of interacting electrons, and provides a method to engineer the emission frequency and output waveform. In this work, a pump-probe method is presented for measuring the phase of stimulated emission as a function of optical path difference between the pump and probe pulses. The amplitude and phase are retrieved using a modified Abel inversion, with a 3.2 nrad precision and a 12.5 μs resolution at 10 kHz repetition rate. These measurements are performed using a 100 <unk>m high resolution electro-optical phase modulator, providing a benchmark for stimulated emission phase measurements.

Optical lattices provide a highly controllable platform for simulating quantum systems. By modifying the Raman coupling and the potential, various quantum phases can be simulated in optical lattices, such as superfluid and Mott insulators. The quantum phases of cold atoms loaded in an optical latice are typically characterized by the Wannier function based on the Raman theorem, which is a key issue in simulations and experiments due to the difficulties in engineering accurate optical lattices with desired band structures. To this end, we show that in the deep lattice limit of a large on-site Hubbard interaction U, the dynamics of hardcore bosons can be mapped to an effective quantum spin system with long-range interactions. In the thermodynamic limit, this quantum spin system exhibits a third-order phase transition at a quantum number k* from a MI to a SF in the Wannier function representation. In particular, the dynamical and equilibrium properties of the quantum spin system are discussed in detail. Furthermore, a real-space renormalization group approach is proposed to accurately calculate dynamical quantities. These results shed lights on a possible experimental realization of the quantum spin system and the localization phenomena of quantum many-body systems in realistic optical lattice systems.

V2051 Ophiuchi, a persistent low-mass X-ray binary system, last exhibited a major outburst in 2006. Since then, the system has also shown smaller-scale transient accretion outbursts. Here we present the results from a multiwavelength campaign carried out in October-November 2015 during the small outburst of V2051 Ophiuchi. During the outburst, the broadband spectral energy distribution could be best described with a double blackbody configuration, with temperatures of 90 and 49 eV, respectively. These findings are in line with the proposal that V2051 Ophiuchi's accretion disk evolves as the mass accumulates during outbursts. Droplets in the two-dimensional plus-J spin glass model reveal no sign of universality, despite the fact that a previous study had suggested that the model exhibits a dynamical transition at $\beta_d \approx 1.12$. Here we examine this question in greater detail, by considering three measures of droplet behaviour: the surface coverage; the average domain size, and the domain wall number. In particular, we find no evidence for any scaling of these quantities with system size, nor any dependence on $\beta$ when expressed in terms of the effective gravitational scaling dimension, $x_g$. We show that the previously-observed dynamical transition is more likely the result of a first-order transition between an extremely small surface coverage and a phase with non-universal droplet properties. We argue that previous analyses of this system have been compromised by finite-size effects. We present new mid-IR spectra of 20 weak-line T Tauri stars (WTTS) selected from the recent Spitzer survey of low mass planet forming regions. These WTTS represent a “pollution-free” sample which is potentialiy free of infrared excess emission from warm circumstellar disks. Their spectra show that many of these sources still have optically thick primordial disks and ongoing accretion. The median disk fraction for these WTTS is 44% similar to that for previously analyzed c2d WTTS (54%). However, thanks to the higher resolution of the new c2d data, we are now able to determine accretion rates for a large fraction of these WTTS. The median value for the median WTTS is 0.25 MMSN, which is about a factor of 5 smaller than that for the previously analyzed c2d sample. The new median accretion rate is also somewhat smaller than the rate required to accret the disks of gas in the c2d sample of 30-50 Myr, suggesting the traditional “deuterium bomb” time scale of 30-50 Myr for planeth formation is overly optimistic. We also discuss various physical mechanisms which might explain the lower accretion rates, and the implications for planet formation.

A low - brightness galaxy (LSB galaxy) without any distinguishable bulge is an important population for galaxy formation and evolution. Many models have been proposed for LSB galaxies, such as the dark matter dominated model, or the disk instability model. There is an increasing number of observational evidences that some LSB galaxies might be low luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGN). The presence of LLAGN in some LSB galaxies might help to solve some of the difficulties encountered in the LSB galaxy formation models. In this work, we report the discovery of a LLAGN in the LSB galaxy PGC045080 based on the archival Chandra data. With a distance of about 273Mpc, PGC045080 is the most distant LLAGN host yet identified. We reprocess the data and performed a detailed spectral and spatial analysis. We found that the nuclear region of PGC045080 has the same luminosity and temperature as other LLAGN, but it has a lower mass density, higher mass fraction, and a larger spatial scaleheight compared to other LLAGN. Comparing with other non-active galaxies of the same mass, we found that PGC045080 has a larger specific star formation rate, which might be explained by the triggered nuclear activity via halo gas condensation.

Globular clusters are excellent probes of their host galaxy's chemical enrichment history, particularly at high redshift, when early star formation took place. We present an analysis of Milky Way globular clusters with high-resolution UV-visible photometry from the SUVRAMA survey of 23 clusters in the Fornax galaxy cluster. We find the cluster color-metallicity relation to be tighter than in the most recent Milky Way halo field population , and furthermore, we demonstrate that the color-metallicity relations for Milky Way clusters can be parametrised as a function of host galaxy spheroid mass. With this empirical relation, we show that Milky Way clusters have peaked in metallicity at a solar-mass host galaxy, and that there is no evidence for subsequent stellar -mass gradient within individual clusters. We propose that the tightest color-metallicity relation for Milky Way globular clusters is driven by the deeper potential wells of more massive galaxies, with metallicity peaking in individual clusters at approximately the same value irrespective of host galaxy mass. We also compare our findings to those of large cosmological and hydrodynamical simulations, and show that the peak metallicity of Milky Way globular clusters is broadly consistent with the highest values seen in simulated galaxy cluster cores. However, at present, it is not clear whether the observed abundance trends with host spheroid mass can be reconciled with the highest-redshift galaxies in the simulations. Our results offer new empirical constraints on the efficiency of chemical enrichment in galaxy clusters, as well as improved empirical scaling relations for the metal-rich Milky Way globular cluster system. We conclude by highlighting several avenues for future study of this unique system: (1) the observed abundance trends within individual globular clusters, (2) the Milky Way's most massive galaxy and its globular cluster population, (3) the Fornax galaxy cluster itself, and (4) comparisons between our empirically derived relations and results from large cosmological simulations. We discuss several ideas for future work based on our findings: 1. Can we use observed abundance trends within individual Milky Way globular clusters to inform our understanding of cluster enrichment? 2. Can we extend the color-metallicity relation for Milky Way clusters to higher mass host galaxies? 3. Do our findings for the Fornax cluster suggest a deviation from the global trend for Milky Way clusters? 4. How does our Fornax cluster sample compare to those from large cosmological simulations? We conclude that understanding globular cluster enrichment in galaxy clusters is particularly well-poised to inform our understanding of the chemical enrichment of the highest-redshift galaxy clusters, as well as the nature of metal enrichment in the most massive galaxies at early cosmic time. In recent years, the string landscape paradigm has emerged as an effective approach to accommodate the vastness of space in string theory. The primary assumption behind this approach is that there exist an enormous number of distinct string vacua, each with distinct properties. However, this approach faces several challenges, one of them being the missing of a mechanism to select the observed universe. Supersymmetry (SUSY) and/or gauge symmetry have been proposed as an elegant solution to this problem. The rationale is that these additional symmetries can prevent some of the moduli in string moduli space from becoming unstable, thus giving a chance for their associated vacuum to be selected. In this work, we provide an in-depth description of these solutions, by considering a specific example of heterotic string theory. At low -energy, this theory is (4,0) supergravity coupled to a single dilaton and one single graviton. After SS compactification, this theory breaks the $\caln = 1$ supergravity in four dimensions. While the phenomenologically desirable SS compactification has been achieved in this theory for all the moduli, gauge symmetry is not spontaneously broken in any of them. We show that the lack of broken gauge symmetry in the moduli space is directly related to the missing of a SUSY vacuum in the same region. We show that one can add a hidden sector which explicitly breaks the gauge symmetry, and construct a superpotential which stabilizes the moduli and causes a SUSY vacuum to be selected. The existence of this vacuum does not interfere with the supergravity breaking, thus solving the cosmological constant problem. We argue that the gauge symmetry breaking pattern and scale should be generic to all explicit breaking patterns. In particular, if gauge symmetry breaking is realized by the Fayet-Iliopoulos mechanism, the scale of spontaneous breaking and the scale of explicit breaking are related by the $D$-terms. As an explicit example, we show how this is realized in a realistic heterotic model with one Wilson line. We also comment on the difficulty of realizing gauge symmetry breaking in Kahler potentials. This proposed solution has several attractive features. It solves the cosmological constant and naturalness problems. The gauge symmetry breaking is associated with a very appealing pattern for moduli stabilization and is also related to the breaking of local supersymmetry. Furthermore, the breaking scale is related to Planck scale Physics via the $<unk>caln = 1$ supergravity breaking so it should be testable at the upcoming Large Hadron Collider experiments. Gauge mediation is an attractive paradigm for explaining the spontaneous breaking of supersymmetry (SUSY). In gauge mediation, SUSY is spontaneously broken in a hidden sector coupled to the observable sector via gauge interactions. The observed MSSM spectrum then results from SUSY breaking in the observable sector via interactions among the messengers of the two sectors. This minimalistic viewpoint provides a satisfying solution to the supersymmetry breaking hierarchy problem, and the effective SUSY preserving dimensional transmutation often implies a light Higgs boson with a mass below the LEP bound. However, gauge mediation models are often faced with the so-called co-localization problem: superpartners are typically separated in the hidden and observable sectors by several orders of magnitude in energy, making it difficult for the messengers that connect the two sectors to meet at a distance of several orders of magnitude in energy. We show that this difficulty can be circumvented in the context of gauge-mediation-induced SUSY breaking if the messengers are in fact pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone bosons (pNGBs) of an approximate global symmetry of the supersymmetric theory. In this case, the messengers can interact through their own kinetic terms, leading to a condensate that spontaneously breaks the symmetry and restores the level of symmetry breaking required for successful vacuum alignment. This new condensate can communicate SUSY breaking to the MSSM sector, evading the co-localization problem. We show that this general mechanism can successfully explain the stability of the electroweak ness of the observable sector, the mass of the Higgs boson, and the relative size of supersymmetry breaking effects in the hidden and observable sectors, over a wide range of messenger superfield representations and breaking patterns. Theoretically consistent examples of gauge-mediation-induced SUSY breaking and vacuum stability consistent with recent experimental data have not been previously available. We present a novel approach to the problem of D-brane inflation, based on a new class of explicit compactifications of type II string theory. These solutions interpolate between strong coupling in the ultraviolet and weak coupling in the infrared, and include a wide class of flux and moduli VEVs. We argue that these vacuum configurations are preferred by string theory, both in the strongly coupled regime and at points of enhanced symmetry, and offer a new perspective on the landscape of string theory. Our approach offers a simple realization of D-brane inflation, and may also be applied to general moduli stabilization and quintessence scenarios. In this Letter, we investigate the connections between two apparently distinct topics in conformal field theory (CFT): the chiral half of the partition function, and the topological or mod 2 cohomology of the underlying spacetime. We show how these two objects are closely related: specifically, the latter is isomorphic to the former, after tensoring with the complex number field. We also show how the former can be thought of as a generalized analytic continuation of the latter, and we explain how the anomaly in the latter appears as an anomaly in the former. This allows us to provide a conceptual explanation of some results in the mathematical literature on the 4d/2d (or chiral/chiral) correspondence. We provide a description of these ideas in the case of the A-series of minimal CFTs, but our results generalize in an straightforward fashion to other series. We proceed as follows. In Section 2, we discuss some basic definitions and facts from CFT. In Section 3, we introduce the A-series CFTs, and define the chiral and 3-symmetric functions. We prove several results for these objects. In Section 4, we explain the connection to 2d cohomology. In Section 5, we discuss related work. Section 6 gives a brief summary and outlook. 2.
