The physical laws that govern the evolution of stars are very similar to those that govern the evolution of galaxies. Since the 1970s, many studies have attempted to simulate the evolution of individual stars using a large number of individual atoms, i.e., using the method of N-body simulation. In recent years, some authors have begun to simulate both the evolution of individual stars and the evolution of a population of stars within a single simulation. This approach, which combines the N-body method with the method of stellar populations, is known as the hybrid hierarchical-N-body/SPH (HYDE-PARC) simulation. In this paper, we will describe the HYDE-PARC Project, which was a long-term project funded by the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AA Research Group), with the aim of developing the technology for a hybrid hierarchical-N-body/SPH simulation of galaxy evolution. The HYDE-PARC Project started in January 2014 and ended in March 2019. During this time, we carried out numerical simulations of the formation of galaxies in three dimensions (3D). These simulations included the physical processes of star formation, feedback, chemical enrichment, hydrodynamical forces, and galaxy mergers. We also developed an open-source, parallel, high-performance stellar evolution and stellar population synthesis code, known as STARSPAZ. Our code combines the N-body method with the method of stellar populations, and it has been used to simulate both the evolution of individual stars and the evolution of a population of stars within a single simulation. Our project, which combined the N-body method with the method of stellar populations, was the first hybrid hierarchical-N-body/SPH simulation of galaxy evolution.

Galactic nebulae around core-collapse supernovae provide new insights into the death throes of evolved supernovae. Observations of the spectrum of light emitted by the central supernova offer a unique means of uncovering the nature of the progenitor, with direct evidence for the presence of a stellar wind (from the progenitor's rapidly-evolving main sequence phase) or a core-collapse explosion. Despite several decades of studies, the nature of the most common core-collapse supernova progenitor is still disputed, with massive (~8-25M⊙) main-sequence stars having been implicated for some supernova subtypes. One particular supernova subtype, type Ia, has been used to significant cosmological depth and has an established connection to one (presently debated) progenitor class: white dwarfs accreting material from a companion. These descendants of ~8-25M⊙ stars, more commonly known as luminous blue variables (LBV), have been proposed as a second, less well-understood class of core-collapse supernova progenitors. LBV outbursts (and the cessation of further evolution into a compact object) are generally interpreted as the result of either a sustained increase in mass-transfer from a binary companion, or as the onset of a thermonuclear explosion on the surface of the star. The region surrounding the supernova 1987A (Tycho) contains a contemporaneous LBV and a SN 1987A supernova ( Tycho). This is a remarkable coincidence, and may hint at the viability of LBV outbursts as a mechanism for at least some supernova subtypes. The ages of the LBV and supernova are comparable, and recent data suggest that the progenitor of the supernova may have been a luminous blue variable - recent simulations suggest that a rare LBV eruption, ~200 years before the supernova, was likely the starting point of rapid evolution towards a compact object. It has been speculated that the recent discovery of the "remnant" of a LBV explosion, ~30-60 years after the outburst, could provide compelling evidence for the viability of LBV outbursts as a mechanism for supernovae. This manuscript examines the region surrounding SN 1987A (Tycho) in search of the remnant of the LBV eruption, using modern telescopes and data analysis techniques. We report the discovery of a faint, roughly spheroidal shell, which appears to be coincident with the observed positions of the LBV and the supernova 1987A. The shell is spatially and spectroscopically similar to similar objects observed in the vicinity of other supernova, and has a luminosity and expansion velocity consistent with it originating from a LBV explosion. The observed coincidence in space, age, and energetics provide circumstantial evidence that the LBV supernova explosion proposed by earlier simulations may in fact have occurred.

Recent discovery of superconductivity in uranium-based compounds with extremely rich phase diagrams has attracted enormous attention. Among several materials, URu2Si2 is one of the earliest and most studied superconductor in this family. While many of the compounds in this family exhibit heavy fermion behavior, varying composition lead to a large range of ground states, from a lower critical point to a magnetically ordered state. URu2Si2 is an archetypal example of such a material, which shows a transition to a magnetically ordered state near 15 Toblerone°C. This suppression of magnetism was initially ascribed to hybridization between the localized U 5f and conduction electrons, but subsequent theoretical and experimental studies have shown that magnetism is instead suppressed by the development of a new energy scale - the Cooper pair - in the condensate. Here we report an entirely different behavior in the isoelectronic compound UPd2Al3, which exhibits antiferromagnetic order below TN = 13.5 K. Remarkably, doping either lithium or hydrogen dramatically increases the transition temperature T c to 24 K for Li-doped UPd2Al3 and 17 K for H-doped UPd2Al3. Further investigations reveal the superconductivity is conventional, with an upper critical field of 47 K and a linear temperature dependence of the resistivity. Lastly, we perform a multi-fragment decomposition analysis which indicates that both the U 5 f and conduction electrons contribute to the electron mass. Overall, our results show that while the ground state of UPd2Al3 remains antiferromagnetic, the qualitative behavior of the f electrons is very different from UBe14 and URu2Si2. More broadly, our results suggest that the development of new energy scales through chemical doping may be a viable route to improve the transition temperature superconductivity in this family.

In this paper, we consider four-fermion interactions on the square lattice and define a gauged global symmetry algebra, the M misses the full xy-plane , and a rotation symmetry algebra, for which the M' extension is a reductive extension. We show that, at least in the presence of an SU(2) rotation symmetry, this gauged global symmetry yields a massless fermion representation of the partition function. We also discuss, in the context of a two-dimensional sigma model, an embedded global symmetry algebra, the mn symmetry, which includes lattice translations and a global SU(2) rotation symmetry. In the case of an SU(2) rotation symmetry, this algebra yields a massless boson representation of the partition function. We also consider symmetry breaking perturbations and show that, in this case, the mn symmetry yields a conformal field theory with central symmetry c = 1. This implies that, in the absence of an SU(2) rotation symmetry, the perturbed sigma model has an effective description in terms of a triplet of Majorana fermions. We provide numerical evidence that this spectrum is stable against various symmetry-breaking perturbations, including those that correspond to a broken SO(4) symmetry.

Lambda hyperons, containing one negatively chargedhyperon, constitute the lowest-lying hyperon series, consisting of Sigma, Pi, eta, and lambda particles. The 4He decay process of a 4He-Lambda system can be described as follows: 4He-Lambda (Lambdac <---> Sigma+ pi+ eta+), where C2B denotes the decay of the lambda hyperon. Due to isospin symmetry, the corresponding process with a 4He-Lambda (Lambdab <---> pi+ eta+) is forbidden. Thus the half-life of the 4He-Lambda, T1/2, may be expressed as follows: T1/2 = C2B exp[-(2.58 + sqrt(2) (B - 1) - 0.25 d - 0.75 d2)]](1 + d + d2), where d = M lambda - M 4He and M lambda is the mass of the lambda hyperon, M 4He is the mass of the 4He particle, and C2B and B are suitable constant and shape factors, respectively. The proposed expression can be used to determine B and d in the process of 4He decay into a lambda+ , a pi+ eta+, 4He-Lambda -> pi+ eta+ + lambdac. The value of B is 1.23 ± 0.03 and the value of d is -0.16 ± 0.18 fm. These values are consistent with previous work. This work was performed on the PHITS high statistics generic data sample, which contains approximately 106,000 4He decays. This provides an improved determination of the B and d in the process of 4He decay, and thus an improved precision for the half-life of 4He.

In this work we develop the geometric framework for describing a quantum sphere with complex Hamilton operator that satisfies the condition of PT-symmetry, where PT stands for the operation of reflection about the origin in the complex plane. We show that the condition of PT-symmetry of the Hamiltonian implies the existence of a complex structure in the space of state vectors, which is also a symmetry of the Hamiltonian. In the framework of this complex structure the Hamiltonian defines a circle bundle, on which the Laplace operator is defined. We derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a complex structure and for the Laplace operator to be simultaneously diagonalizable and Hermitian. We show that the equation of the geodesic on the complex structure sphere, corresponding to the Hamiltonian with real spectrum, coincide with the Whittaker equation. We consider in detail the PT-symmetric harmonic oscillator and the PT-symmetric Coulomb potential. In the first case we study the spectral and structural stability with respect to small perturbations of the PT-symmetric harmonic oscillator and the Coulomb potential, and demonstrate that the complex PT-symmetric potential with real part being the harmonic oscillator potential has a purely discrete spectrum, whereas the complex PT-symmetric potential with real part being the Coulomb potential has a dense discrete spectrum.

An array of 10 $^3$He proportional counters was constructed and operated by the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory in the middle of an ice run, leading to the discovery of neutrino oscillations. The array consisted of 10 vertical proportional Counters with outer dimensions of 4.5 m diameter by 3.2 m height. Each counter was filled with 800 kg of ultrapure water and instrumented to allow the detection of low energy solar neutrinos via the inverse beta decay reaction, (inverse beta decay): $$ \overline{\nu}_e + p \rightarrow e^+ + n. Solar Neutrinos interact via the exchange of a virtual particle, theZ^0, which appears with a very small probability. The main reaction occurs when the neutrino interacts via the charged-current interaction, resulting in the detection of two electrons with energy of approximately 200 keV each. The predicted rate for this reaction is proportional to the squared length of the incident neutrino interaction and the cross section for the reaction, and is independent of the total neutrino flux. By comparing the observed energy spectrum of the detected electrons to the predicted energy spectrum, the array was able to detect solar neutrinos with a significance of 5.1 $\sigma$.

For a classical Coulomb system, in thermodynamic s, the number density correlation functions at high temperature can be related to those at low temperature via so-called virial equation. In this paper, for a classical plasma with either Yukawa or Coulomb dispersion law, it is shown that, at high temperature, not only the zero-k mode of the number density correlation function but also the first-sound wavevector mode are not entirely determined by the zero-temperature number density correlation function. The first sound wavevector mode, and thus the first-sound wavevector cut-off, receive s zero at the first nonzero temperature order. This means that, for the first time, for classical Coulomb systems, the high-temperature limit for number density correlation functions does not exist. This unexpected difficulty of the high-temperature limit is caused by a new collective mode, i.e., the first sound, which is absent at zero temperature. It is found that this collective mode is analogous to the Landau damping mode of the classical electrodynamic plasma. It is also revealed that the first-sound wavevector mode in the long-wavelength limit is related to the first-sound speed which is in general different from the light speed. This unexpected difficulty of the high-temperature limit for classical Coulomb fluids provides a new perspective on the so-called collective Fermi-Pasta-Ulam phenomenon, for which different theoretical explanations have been proposed, either on the basis of the assumptions on the high-temperature limit or on the failure of the usual perturbation theory, but without considering the possible breakdown of the high-temperature limit. This work was done in collaboration with Xianyun Hu, Baoling Pei, and Wang Yin. More information and technical details can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.05262 By using the scaling arguments and the structure analysis, it is shown that the new mode is indeed a first sound. To see this, it is convenient to study the Fourier transformed version of the Boltzmann equation. By using the procedure similar to that used in the study of weakly non-Maxwellian plasmas, the Boltzmann equation is shown to have a solution only when the first sound wavevector cut-off is set to be zero. By matching the solution at small wavevector to that at large wavevector, one arrives at the dispersion relation for the first sound. Moreover, it is also shown that the new collective mode is a analogue to Landau damping mode of the classical electrodynamic plasmas.

Today, we have an impressive view of the large-scale structure of the universe. This structure, manifested in the distribution of galaxies, suggests the existence of massive organizing patterns, or more accurately, that structure has evolved over time. Over the last several decades, a picture of cosmology has emerged that is largely consistent with the “Big Bang” theory of the evolution of the universe. Within this scenario, the universe began with a “Big Bang” some 12–15 billion years ago, and its subsequent expansion has driven the formation of large-scale structure. This hierarchical structure—which displays a clear pattern of clustering on all scales from the large-scale structure down to the galactic and subgalactic levels—suggests that large-scale structure formation can be explained with a handful of physical mechanisms. Gravity plays a key role in this process, as it is the largest force in the universe on large scales. However, at smaller scales electromagnetic and (particularly at later times) eventually hydrodynamic processes come into play. Today, it is possible to study the distribution of galaxies in great detail, revealing both the extent of this clustering and the basic underlying structures. For example, it is now thought that the universe is dominated by two massive clusters of galaxies, called the Great Attractor and the Shapley Supercluster, along with a network of smaller groups and individual galaxies. Recent results from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey have added further evidence to the existence of large-scale structure, and more detailed maps have allowed for a more detailed understanding of structure’s relationship to galaxy properties such as size, shape, and color. Additionally, much attention has been given to understanding the relationship between dark and ordinary matter, the distribution of “dark energy” that appears to be causing the universe’s expansion to speed up, and the ultimate fate of the universe as a whole. The picture of structure formation that has emerged from these results provides a robust basis for understanding the evolution of large-scale structure in the universe. However, our understanding remains limited in several key areas. We still do not understand the detailed dynamics and evolution of structure (including the Great Attractor and Shapley Supercluster), nor do we have a full understanding of the relationship between the physical processes that shape structure and the observed galaxies and galaxy clusters. In addition, many questions about the origin of the universe and the fate of the universe remain unanswered.

On 29 December 2003 the Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) on the Swift satellite detected the gamma-ray burst (GRB) 030329. One month after the event, the X-shooter spectrograph on the VLT detected a deep optical/near-infrared (OIR) afterglow. Using data from X-shooter and other telescopes, we carried out a detailed study of this deep IR phase afterglow. From the X-shooter spectrum we derive a upper limit on the redshift of z < 0.1667. From the afterglow spectrum we measure the intrinsic reddening of A(V) = 0.47 ± 0.12 and a best-fit power-law slope of α = 1.7 ± 0.1, consistent with the value of α = 1.6 ± 0.1 measured by earlier studies. From the lightcurve we measure the half-opening angle of the jet to be θ = 17.8 ± 1.4 degrees. The prominent double-humped structure in the lightcurve, which has been interpreted as the signature of the passage of a jet through the surrounding medium, is also seen in our data, but only as a shallow deficit in the early afterglow lightcurve. We suggest that the shallow deficit is caused by an underestimated k-corrected host-galaxy magnitude in earlier studies, and suggest that the real structure in the lightcurve has a much smoother surface. Finally, we consider the possibility that the deep IR phase afterglow may have been extinguished by dust in the galaxy itself. Using an analysis of the relation between IR-optical extinction and host-galaxy properties we find that this is possible, but that in this case the observed X-shooter spectrum is inconsistent with A(V) > 0.5.

Bohnenblust and Spitzer obtained in the late 1950s a complete characterization of bounded quotient mappings of the Hilbert space of square-summable complex sequences into itself. The minimal such mapping is the identity and the maximum such mapping is a quotient map. The dual of this result is that the symmetrized orthogonal sum of the Hilbert space and the square of a sequence is again square-summable if and only if the sequence itself is square-summable. In the late 1970s, Bohnenblust and Borchers independently rediscovered this result and used it to define their continuous roulette allocation. The corresponding von Neumann algebra is then the (unique) hyperfinite type II$_1$ factor. In the early 1980s, Bonsall and Dilworth used this result to construct that factor. The result was later shown to be a special case of the Bohnenblust-Spitzer identity for operator spaces. In 2006, Bercovici and Pata showed that the Bohnenblust-Spitzer identity also holds for certain classes of Banach algebras. The corresponding algebras include the disc algebra and the Wiener algebra. In the current paper we show that this result, originally proved for C$^*$-algebras, also holds for every Rota-Baxter algebra. As an immediate application, we provide a new proof of the classical Bohnenblust-Spitzer theorem.

The paper discusses properties of light propagation in vacuum under the influence of new, hypothetical particle-photon interactions, which have zero spin and are therefore called "spintwo". These interactions were proposed [1] as a possible explanation for the recently observed cyclic variable (CV) behavior in certain regions of the southern sky, i.e., apparently periodic, but unexplained variations in the intensity of gamma-ray and other cosmic radiation arriving at Earth from directions within a small region of the sky. The studied effect is of interest for astronomy and cosmology, but also for studies of spatially varying magnetic fields (for example, in the event of solar flares or other violent changes in the magnetic field) and in laboratory searches for new particles. In [1] it is shown that spintwos may induce spin-dependent interactions in the standard magnetic extensions (SME), which include a wide range of experimental scenarios for these interactions. In this work we study the influence of the new interactions on the light propagation. The paper [2] derives the influence on the polarization states of light, while [3] considers some concrete experimental scenarios with applicability to observations of the southern sky. References: [1] G. Barsotti, et al. "The galactic plane as a gateway to discovery with a polarimeter in the SPIRE instrument on Herschel." Astronomy and Astrophysics 726. id. Article ID 196 (2011). [2] G. Barsotti, et al. "Light propagation in a magnetized vacuum with invisible spin-two interactions." Astronomy and Astrophysics Review D , no. 8 (2016). [3] G. Barsotti, et al. "The galactic plane as a gateway to discovery with a polarimeter in the SPIRE instrument on Herschel." Astronomy and Astrophysics 726, 196 (2011). The authors of this paper, G. Barsotti, et al., discuss the impact of a new hypothetical particle-photon interaction on light propagation in a magnetized vacuum. The interaction in question, spin zero, has not yet been observed but it could explain the cyclic variable behavior in certain regions of the southern sky and could have implications for laboratory searches for new particles. In [1], the authors propose that this interaction, called "spintwo", could explain observations of apparently periodic but unexplained variations in the intensity of gamma-ray and other cosmic radiation arriving at Earth from directions within a small region of the sky. In [2], the authors derive the influence of the interaction on the polarization states of light. In [3], the authors consider some concrete experimental scenarios with applicability to observations of the southern sky. Specifically, the interaction considered in [2] alters the plane of polarization states of light in a magnetized vacuum. This alteration depends on the direction of propagation and the orientation of the magnetic field, the intensity and frequency of the light, and the strength and duration of the spintwo interaction. This paper presents a three dimensional lattice Boltzmann approach to simulate flows with significant density variation and rapid variation of the velocity magnitude. To solve the corresponding mass conservation equations, an additional artificial stress term is required to stabilize the formulation. In the conventional framework, this is achieved by adding a weighted sum of the artificial compressibility term and the derivative of the artificial viscosity to the momentum equation. Alternatively, in the hyper-viscosity approach, the conservative property of the artificial viscosity is directly modeled in the mass conservation equation. To further improve the stability of the algorithm, an improved hyper-viscosity model is proposed in this work. A density correction term is added to the corresponding mass conservation equation to model the conservative property of the density in the hydrodynamic limit. Numerical results using this three-dimensional algorithm show that the proposed method can stably and accurately simulate high-speed fluid flows with density variation and rapid variation of the velocity magnitude.

Recently, a lot of effort has been devoted to the search for novel topological superconducting (TS) phases in ferromagnetic (FM) superconductors, since the coupling between the magnetic impurity and superconducting Bogoliubov quasiparticles could lead to the development of nontrivial superconducting states in the bulk even in the presence of an idealized time-reversal symmetry-breaking exchange field. As a particularly promising material platform that shows a large array of such properties, it has been theoretically predicted that Sr2RuO4 (SRO) could realize a topological $p+i-f$ ($i$: an Ising-type exchange field and $f$: a $d-$vector field) superconducting state, which contains a $d+id-$type topological superconducting phase when the FM domain is characterized by a weak Ising-type anisotropy. Experimentally, the signature of such a phase has been first observed in the half-Heusler NdFeAs(O,F) system by nuclear magnetic resonance and polarized neutron scattering. In this Rapid Communication, we theoretically investigate the Josephson current through a wide class of FM SRO/I/SRO junctions with both in-plane and out-of-plane magnetizations. We find that both the sign and magnitude of the Josephson current could be used to probe the relative strength of the exchange field and Ising-type anisotropy. Moreover, when a half-integer spin superconductor is used as the second phase, we observe an unconventional suppression of the supercurrent when the applied exchange field or anisotropy is strong. Our study highlights the potential of the hybrid systems based on FM superconductors as an effective platform for Majorana fermions and other TS phase effect studies.

A major problem in cloud modeling is the quiescent state, where clouds are not buoyantly unstable but neither do they have significant turbulent energy dissipation. We show that quiescent cores are long-lived only under idealized conditions in which the external pressure is static, the cloud is isothermal, and the entire external pressure is reflected down the the long axis of the cloud. Realistic clouds are subject to both time-variable internal pressures arising from variability in the ambient ultraviolet field and time-varying external pressures arising from the motion of the cloud. These dynamic external pressures can induce core collapse. For typical galactic conditions, core collapse is delayed by only a few hundred years, and once collapse is initiated, the resulting star cluster can expel all of the residual quiescent cloud mass in a violent, rapid evaporation flow. We conclude that quiescent cores are highly susceptible to induced collapse and rapid evaporation, potentially shaping the cloud population and enhancing the evaporation rate by several orders of magnitude.

By formulating Quantum Field Theory in a manner consistent with the Heisenberg and Pauli pictures of and quantum measurement, we show that it is possible to define nonlinear generalized functions that are fundamental to the theory. We do this by defining a nonlinear representation of the Heisenberg-picture algebra of quantum operators and implementing the Wigner representation theorem in the framework of generalized functions. This approach to Quantum Field Theory goes beyond perturbative approaches in that it is fully background independent and non-perturbative in the coupling constant, admitting a perturbative treatment only as an infinite-dimensional limit. As an example of its applicability, we study the structure of solutions to the Yang-Feldman equation in Quantum Field Theory. We demonstrate that the theory admits second-order correlation functions with discontinuous support, which previous perturbative and nonlinear approaches to the problem have failed to produce. These discontinuous structures arise naturally from the exact reformulation of Quantum Field Theory as a theory of nonlinear generalized functions, and are not an artifact of the weak assumptions underlying the theory.

The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) scale is a powerful cosmological probe, appearing as a peak in the correlation function of galaxy distributions. Measuring the scale in absorption against the spectrum of the early-universe radiation enables an independent analysis of the expansion history of the universe and of the amplitude of large-scale structure. Current measurements of the scale are robustly based on the Early Data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Two-degree Field Galaxy Redshift Survey (2dFGRS), and are dependent on the cosmological model. By using a model-independent principal component analysis of both catalogs , and by using a large Monte Carlo simulation, we show that it is possible to measure the BAO scale in the SDSS-II and 2dFGRS combination with a precision of 3% (4% fractional error), completely unbiased by any assumptions about the cosmological model. We also show that the BAO scale can be measured with the same precision from the 2008 final data release of the WiggleZ Dark Energy Survey. The accuracy of the combination of the SDSS and 2dFGRS BAO measurements presented here, coupled with that of the WMAP measurement, means that the angular diameter , the Hubble parameter, and thefalse cosmological parameter are accurately measured with a precision of up to 3% with a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker cosmology in which radiation is a linear component of the stress-energy tensor. This is a 1% accuracy improvement on the current best measurement from the 7-year -old data release of the WMAP satellite.

Recent ALMA observations of the young transition al disk HD 98800 reveal a near-infrared spectrum consistent with the presence of gas and small dust within about 2AU of the host star, providing strong evidence for the existence of an inner transitional disk. The dust is most likely optically thin, close to Keplerian, and its presence is maintained by the continual removal of small grains by photo-evaporation. The total dust mass in the inner disk is less than 1% of the Minimum Mass Solar Nebula. The gas is much more tenuous, with a volume filling factor of about 10-5, and is depleted in elements heavier than helium, perhaps resulting from the action of gravitational forces by the innermost planets. The implications of this architecture for the evolution of intermediate-mass stars remain to be determined, but HD 98800 is an ideal object for ALMA investigations with increased sensitivity and higher angular resolution.

The seesaw model (SM) of particle physics has been extremely successful in describing experimental observations to date. While it does provide a theory of Glashow, Weinberg, and Salam that describes how fundamental particles interact via the weak force, it fails to describe phenomena observed at higher energy scales, such as neutrino masses. Although the existence of neutrino masses is well established, the mechanism by which they are explained remains an open question. This paper presents the results of an analysis of the phenomenological implications of a TeV-scale heavy neutral lepton (HNL), whose lifetime is constrained by experiment to be greater than 1 second. We assume that the HNL is the Dark Matter (DM) candidate and that neutrino masses are produced via freeze-out at the end of the SM-like Higgs thermal plasma phase. We show that this scenario leads to a novel manifestation of the seesaw mechanism, and has the potential to be used at the LHC.

An Infrared Cloud Monitor was developed for the Haleakalaan robotic telescope at the Observatorio del Teide on Tenerife, Spain. The instrument was designed to image the thermal emission from thin clouds in the atmosphere in a wavelength region between 3.8 μm and 14 μm. This paper describes the design, development and initial tests of the ICM. Observations with the ICM of infrared emission from thin cirrus clouds are presented. The observed clouds had linear dimensions between 1 km and 10 km with a median size of 3.3 km. They were located at altitudes between 2.2 km and 2.4 km. The Infrared Cloud Monitor was designed, developed and tested over a period of 18 months. The system is composed of several subsystems. The main control and data acquisition system was developed with the VICON motion analysis system. The instrument package for imaging the thermal emission from thin clouds is mounted on a three-axis stage allowing it to be pointed at the cloud of interest. The ICM obtains data through a series of exposures with an uncooled MCT-LPS sensor and focal plane assembly in order to map the cloud in the desired spectral region. Each exposure is 10 s long and the data is aquired at a frequency of 10 Hz. The ICM images are constructed from the time series of images and a median filter is applied to remove high frequency noise from the data.

In this paper, we discuss the thermodynamics of extremal black holes in five dimensions, both within the context of the supergravity limit of string theory and in a context of higher-derivative gravitational theory. We focus on theories that include both gauge corrections through the confinement of six-dimensional supergravity and curvature corrections through the five-dimensional Gauss-Bonnet term. In both cases, we find that the black holes are typically characterized by a phase transition, with a small range of black hole charges , for which the thermodynamics is that of a regular extremal black hole. At low enough temperatures, for charges in this range, the black hole undergoes a second transition , with a new branch of charged extremal black holes that are not embedded in supergravity and that include stable, non-static, charged domain walls. Within the limit of vanishing Gauss-Bonnet coupling, these solutions precisely correspond to extremal membranes in five dimensions. We discuss some of the implications of our results for the duality between these theories and string theory in six dimensions, and we point out some directions for future research."

A multi-wavelength survey of z = 3.15 Lyman-alpha emitters in the GOODS Wide Field is presented. Lyman-alpha emission from galaxies at redshift 3.15 is rare, and is one of the most distant light sources known. With the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), tens of thousands of distant galaxies have been discovered, extending the census of the high-redshift universe to higher redshifts than had been possible with previous techniques. These Lyman-alpha emitters (LAE) provide new constraints for the observation of the high-redshift universe during the "Epoch of Reionization" and can be used to study the process of structure formation. However, many uncertainties remain about LAEs, including their number density, properties, and role in the Epoch of Reionization. To study these properties, we combine new imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) with existing imaging from the Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) on the Hubble Space Telescope, the Wide Field Camera 3 on the Hubble Space Telescope, Subaru, and the Spitzer Space Telescope. Using these data we search for LAEs and measure their physical properties, comparing them to a control sample of galaxies at low redshift. We find that LAEs at redshift 3.15 are lower mass, less luminous, more strongly clustered, and less likely to be detected in HST bands than galaxies at low redshift. These results are in agreement with previous data for population II galaxies at high redshift, and provide new constraints for the observation of the LAE population during the Epoch of Reionization.

Two spin-1/2 fermions can interfere quantum-mechanically, exhibiting coherent superposition of ‘wavetrains’ with zero mean wave vector, and resulting in an interference pattern with fringes of equal amplitude but opposite phase. Such wavefunction-based interference phenomena have been used to characterize the properties of quantum systems, with two-particle interference allowing for enhanced sensitivity to Coulomb interactions. Here we report the interference fringes of two independent electrons in the vicinity of the so-called “Hohng singularity” in helium, resulting in a joint electron density of two separate but complementary helium droplets. The observed two-particle interference pattern is in excellent agreement with calculations based on the exact ing Schrödinger equation, allowing determination of the phase difference between interfering waves, and thus the interference fringes provide a precise measurement of the Aharonov-Bohm phase caused by the spatial overlap of the two separate electron wave functions. These studies of two-particle interference in helium – a deceptively simple system with complex many-body interactions – illustrate the power of this interference phenomenon to characterize quantum many-body systems and hold great potential for application to quantum technologies and simulation.

A space elevator and launcher (SELL) takes advantage of the nearly-Free Electron Laser (FEL) technology for propulsion and fast energy gain. As the largest source of light on Earth, the FEL can generate light and electron beams for use as a lighthouse on the space elevator and as a booster for launch into outer space. A combination of the light and beams can provide the SELL with the required energy to reach orbit and then return home, effectively making the space elevator and launcher's own booster. A first-generation SELL can use static tethers for lighthouse and for tension in the space elevator, with the potential for adding active devices to both elements to increase capacity. The lighthouse allows for a slow ascent into orbit, while the beams provide enough energy for a return trip to Earth. First-generation SELLs with up to 500 km of static tethers and 10,000 km of fully active tethers are possible.

This paper develops a general framework for quantum modeling of combining concepts. It begins with general quantum modeling framework, which defines a general form of quantum model that incorporates both quantum mechanics and concepts. The general form of the model is specialized to three cases. First, the specific form that incorporates only quantum mechanics is developed for a case with two concepts. Second, the specific form that incorporates both quantum mechanics and probability is developed for a case with multiple concepts. Third, the specific form that incorporates both quantum mechanics and concepts but without probability is developed for a case with uncertainty. Second, it develops a general form of quantum model that incorporates concepts but does not incorporate probability. This model incorporates both quantum mechanics and at least one concept. This model is specialized to three cases: (1) a case with two concepts; (2) a case with multiple concepts; and (3) a case with uncertainty. It shows that each of these cases can be expressed with a specific form of the general model. Each specific form provides a flexible and powerful modeling technique. The general model and specific forms are demonstrated on several examples. The first example is a case with two concepts: methane (CH4) and oxygen (O2). The second example is a case with multiple concepts: methane, oxygen, hydrogen (H2), and water (H2O). The third example is a case with uncertainty: actual and expected outcomes.

We present the results of a spectral index distribution (SIND) analysis of a complete flux-rescaled sample of gamma-ray blazars detected by the Energetic Gamma Ray Experiment Telescope (EGRET) on the NASA Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory. We also present a preliminary SIND analysis of the 3EG data using a simultaneous flux-rescaled sample. In contrast to most gamma-ray telescopes, EGRET detected nearly all blazars as highly polarized gamma rays, and nearly all exhibit substantial variability on many different timescales. Blazars are widely believed to be the brightest class of gamma-ray sources and their spectra are typically well-fitted by a simple power law of photon index around 2.2. We perform the first SIND analysis of high-energy gamma-ray blazars using a complete flux-rescaled sample selected from the third EGRET catalog and demonstrate that the SIND of EGRET blazars is consistent with a one-dimensional truncated power law with an exponential cutoff. The slope of the SIND at high energy (E > 100 MeV) is approximately -2.2, while the slope at lower energies is slightly shallower. The high-energy index is similar to that of the low-energy gamma-ray flux, though with large error bars. We also present preliminary SIND analysis of the 3EG data, though the small number of sources and incomplete sampling of the EGRET band limit the conclusions that can be drawn. The EGRET data and the SIND may hold the key to understanding the high-energy emission process in these objects and their connection to particles in extragalactic magnetic fields.

The massive stellar cluster Westerlund 1 is one of the closest analogues of a nearby starburst galaxy. Located some 20,000 light-years away in the constellation of Caryote (the pointy car), Westerlund 1 is home to hundreds of massive stars, including several of the most massive known in the galaxy. However, despite its proximity, Westerlund 1 has remained a challenging target for observation because it is embedded in a dense, neutral environment that is prone to the damaging effects of its own powerful ionizing radiation field and the deeper ultraviolet light produced by its massive stars. Using data from the Herschel Space Observatory, we report on the detection of a small amount of cooling radiation from this environment—the first direct observation of the small amount of gas that does exist within the core of Westerlund 1. This, together with measurements of the dispersion of its member stars and their proper motions, allows us to put an upper bound on the cluster’s distance of between 12 and 18 kpc, well within the estimated 20-30 kpc limit of the ionizing radiation region. Our findings provide constraints on the initial mass of Westerlund 1’s most massive stars and the age of its youngest members, and support the notion that Westerlund 1, despite its proximity, may be very similar to other young, massive star clusters that have been observed in the local universe.

A new measurement of the aerosol phase function at the Pierre Auger Observatory is presented. Using data taken between 1 January 2004 and 31 December 2017, the integral of the absorption and scattering coefficients, as a function of wavelength, and the single-scattering albedo, as a function of angle of incidence, is determined. The resulting extinction cross-section as a function of wavelength and the single-scattering albedo as a function of angle of incidence are presented. These results are compared to previous measurements of aerosol properties and model simulations and found to be generally in good agreement. Implications for studies of chemical composition and radiative forcing are discussed. Hitting probabilities for systems of non-linear stochastic heat equations with multiplicative noise are considered. These equations can be viewed as stochastic approximations of the heat equation. We obtain probability estimates for the total mass and the $L^2$-norm of solutions. The main idea of this paper is to establish dichotomous arguments for solutions of certain SPDEs with additive and multiplicative noise, and then to apply these arguments to the solutions of the original systems. In order to apply these methods, we need a kind of regularizing effects of the linear part of these equations. This is accomplished using Davies’ method. For the critical value of the noise in $L^{2d/(d-2)}$-sense, we obtain that the probability that the solution of the system stays in a neighborhood of the initial condition $x_0$ goes to 1 as $T \to \infty$, where $T$ is the length of time.

KNO3 is a promising ferroelectric material that has recently been highlighted as a promising candidate for thin film technology due to its large piezoelectric coefficient, high Curie Temperature and highверactive coefficient. However, KNO3 is prone to phase separation, which obscures its ferroelectric behaviour. In this theoretical study, using first-principles density functional theory calculations, we have studied the ferroelectric phases of KNO3 and its property evolution with changes in temperature and pressure. Our results indicate that the ground state of KNO3 is ferroelectric with the polarization pointing towards the paraelectric state. The ferroelectric switching is likely triggered by the depolarization rotation mechanism. Furthermore, our calculated elastic constants indicate that KNO3 is likely to be a soft ferroelastic with a tendency to undergo a polar state–paraelectric state transition. We hope this study can help to clarify the ferroelectric behaviour of KNO3 and bring it to the attention of thin film communities.

In this work, the gamma-ray emission from three young open clusters, Berk 87, Cyg OB2, and Westerlund 2, is studied in the gamma-ray energy band (80 MeV - 1 MeV) using the observations from the latest version of the Fermi Space Telescope. The gamma-ray data are compared to the Inverse Compton Scattering and Bremsstrahlung models. It is shown that the Berk 87 and Cyg OB2 can be potentially good gamma-ray sources with fluxes on the order of 10-15% of the gamma-ray flux. In the case of Westerlund 2, the model cannot explain the gamma-ray emission from this cluster. It is shown that the gamma-ray emission from these young open clusters is most likely produced by energetic particles up-scattered by interstellar dust grains. The work was done by M. Petrov, E. Parizot, A. Marcowith and V.ERRY, and it was published on August 28, 2022 on arXiv.org

Blazars are one of the most powerful non-active galaxies with their relativistic jets closely aligned to our line of sight. They are classified in two categories based on the presence or absence of high-energy emission of whose particle accelerators is unknown. Observational data indicates that the jets most likely originated near the black hole event horizon, although not all models are able to predict the jets producing high-energy gamma-rays. Emission mechanisms in blazars are complex. A popular theory is the blazar process in which the magnetized central black hole powers the jet s with the spin energy of the black hole. The original proposal had intended application to weak er magnetic fields, however subsequent studies suggest that the fields in blazars can be several orders of magnitude stronger. Another popular model is synchrotron-self-Compton (SSC) in which synchrotron radiation up-scatters part of its own photons to high energy gamma-rays. Blazars often exhibit variability at all wavelengths on very short timescales, ranging from hours to days. Blazars are powerful emitters of radio waves, optical and gamma-rays and this electromagnetic radiation is highly variable. In this work we show that blazar jets are closely related to the inner regions of their associated accretion disks. Jets appear to be launched from tiny scale inner regions of the accretion disks and strong correlation is found between the magnitude of the disk scale height and the jet power. Such a correlation is expected from the Blandford-Znajek model and fits well the available data. The article is aimed at a broad interdisciplinary audience, including specialists in plasma physics, black hole physics, relativistic astrophysics and nuclear physics.

Basis set design for electronic structure calculations of peptides has a long history, and much progress has been made over the past decade, but developments have been uneven and difficult to implement across thepeptide community. In this work, we present a unified methodology that applies state-of-the-art Gaussian-type atomic basis sets to model peptides in Hartree-Fock (HF) and second-order Møller-Plesset (MP2) systems. Our split-valence Gaussian (SVG) basis sets are designed to minimize the cost function of an energy expression. The heterolevel method allows us to optimize the energy expression at the MP2 level. Test calculations on model systems demonstrate the accuracy of our approach, and application to a fragment of the hunger hormone suggest that the methodology holds great promise for aiding in the design of potent peptide pharmaceuticals. In this paper, we study the online scheduling problem where items arrive according to a Poisson process with constant rate and the time until the next arrival is stochastically bounded. The goal is to to find an order of items to schedule such that the total completion time is minimized. To model uncertainty in arrival times, we introduce a binary variables to indicate whether an item is delayed. The variable indicates that the item will arrive after the current time window. The objective is to minimize the total reward, which is the sum of completion time of scheduled items and the cost of delaying items. To solve this challenging non-convex problem, we propose a novel algorithm, distributedly and algorithmically, by first linearizing the objective function and then using the properties of Dags. First, we show that the natural log-sum form of the objective function is lower-bounded than a linear function. Then, we propose a distributed algorithm by introducing an approximate Lyapunov function. Finally, we prove the convergence of the proposed algorithm using the properties of Dags. We show both the expected and high probability results of the algorithm. Our numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm compared to existing approaches.

Heisenberg {\it XY} spin chains provide a versatile platform for quantum computational and communications applications, owing to their natural compatibility with optical quantum information processing and transmission protocols. Whereas the idealized one-dimensional (1D) XX model is characterized by a single exchange of electrons between nearest neighbors and identical spins, the prototypical 1D {\it XY} spin chain features a more intricate scalar tensor with distinct scalar and vector components. In the latter case, although the {*}Haldane gap*}{\it{*For a review, see, e.g., ref. [2]*}} that opens up in the vector sector is commonly anticipated as a signature of genuine multipartite entanglement, for the purpose of quantum information processing one needs to have access to the genuine *helicity entanglement* arising from quantum fluctuations in the scalar sector. Here we report on the experimental observation of the genuine multipartite entanglement in the scalar sector of a prototypical {\it XY}-type spin {\it{*chain*}} made of ${\sim}80$ homogeneously magnetized dysprosium atoms confined in an optical lattice. In our experiments, we exploit a fine spatial and temporal control over the external magnetic field to vary its strength and anisotropy. We observe that, in the deep quantum regime and for finite intersite interaction, the magnetization curve becomes symmetric around the isotropic point and a rich structure in the level scheme emerges for each of the two anisotropy directions. This latter feature allows us to disentangle the energy levels that contribute to the entanglement from each of the energy levels separately, highlighting a close relationship between level structure and genuine multipartite entanglement. The presented results demonstrate a "new roadmap for utilizing exotic properties of quantum many-body systems to engineer advanced quantum states and devices such as quantum registers and quantum channels with enhanced information-processing capabilities and proposed applications in quantum simulations and digital quantum communication." Recent experimental and theoretical works have shown that single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) can exhibit metallic and semi-metallic behavior, in contrast to earlier predictions that SWCNTs are always either semiconducting or insulating. This apparent contradiction between the theoretical and experimental results has raised the important question of whether the experimental observations can be explained by a simple theoretical approach such as the density functional theory. In this work, we perform an O(N) tight-binding molecular dynamics simulation to study the thermal stability of metallic SWCNTs at high temperatures. The calculations are performed in the canonical ensemble, using the Nose-Hoover chain , with a Nos[é]-Hoover chain for carbon atoms and a Nos[é]-Hoover chain for hydrogen atoms. Our results show that metallic SWCNTs are stable against oxidation for temperatures as high as 2000 K, in good agreement with recent experimental observations. The reason for the stability of metallic SWCNTs is that there are no dangling bond defects on the carbon atoms in the wall of the tube, as confirmed by our molecular orbital calculations. In addition, there are only weak sp2 bonds between the carbon atoms, which facilitate the separation of carbon atoms and the formation of various defects, such as Stone-Wales and C-O defects. We also discuss the dynamic properties of the simulation, such as the atomic mean-square displacement and the radial density function. This work is a reply to a comment by Mahmood Hayashi in the paper "Thermal Stability of Metallic Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes: An O(N) Tight-Binding Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study" by H. Peng, G. Zhang, L. Zhang, and D. J. S. Wang (arXiv:1901.03564 [cond-mat.mtrl-sci], 28 Feb 2019).

Triangular holes in a triangular lattice are investigated using a guided-mode expansion method. The photonic crystal (PhC) slabs with the triangular holes exhibit two symmetric and complementary anisotropic behaviors: one is the pure transverse electric (TM) behavior, and the other is the mixed TM and transverse electric (TE) behavior. The pure TM band with zero frequency occurs at the Γ point in the first Brillouin zone, and the band edges of the mixed TM and TE bands touch this zero frequency band at three different points in the first Brillouin zone. The high-symmetry points Γ, X, and K are triple degenerate in the low frequency. The three independent electric fields at these points are mutually orthogonal and form a right-handed system. It is found that the high-symmetry points are completely linear polarized and the angular region with linear polarization is quite large. Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations show that the energy-band transitions originating from the touching points lead to a high reflectivity (>97%) band transition. The joint density of states (JDOS) method is used to investigate the angular-dependent polarization, and the high degrees of linear polarization (over 90%) are obtained for the both polarizations in the high-symmetry points. The numerical results are well explained using the effective-mass approximation and the rigorous coupled-wave analysis.

A description of a path integral approach for the dynamics of a random chain with constraints is presented. The constraints of the random chain can be viewed as accounting for the fact that the bonds of the chain are “rigid”: the left and right hand sides of each bond are identically fixed. This fixed-bond disorder is introduced into a standard version of the zero-temperature transition point of a Hamiltonian system , and the equations for the Cartesian components of the chain are compared to the end-to-end vector. The fixed-bond disorder is assumed to be a random chain, and the properties of the resulting random chain are examined in the limit of infinite spatial dimension. The resulting propagator can be computed analytically, and is found to lead to a radically altered scaling of various physical quantities with the chain’s length. In particular, the end-to-end distance scales as a positive power of the length instead of being logarithmically correlated. An interpretation of this result in terms of effective surface tension induced by the fixed bond disorder is proposed, and a simple approximation for the propagator is derived using a simple approximation for the inverse of the Green’s function of the constrained chain. The accuracy of the propagator obtained in this way is confirmed by means of a quantitative comparison with numerical simulations.

B mesons can only decay into a D mesons and a light anti-particle, such as a anti-neutrino or a positron. However, according to QED, every light particle may additionally undergo two-body decay into a pair of lighter particles. These decays are forbidden for B mesons, however due to a recent increase in the measured branching fractions of three-body decays, their rates must be constrained by CKM matrix elements and Quark Counting rules to be less than 2.2 x 10-4, which is the strongest bound to date. The three-body decays have been observed to be of the following two types: 1. Two charged pions and an eta meson 2. Two neutral pi mesons Observation of these decays, with properties distinct from other two-body decays, may signify the presence of hitherto unknown physics, such as interactions beyond the Standard Model. The upper bounds on the branching fractions of these decays were previously measured to be (1.08 \pm 0.32) \times 10^{-6} and (1.80 \pm 0.31) \times 10^{-6} from two different experiments, based on 40 and 89 ab^{-1} of data taken with the BABAR and Belle detectors, respectively. These measurements are each the most precise to date. The lower bounds on the three-body decays, with the expected branching fractions , are (0.82 \pm 0.47) \times 10^{-6} and (2.55 \pm 0.46) \times 10^{-6}, where the uncertainties are statistical and systematic respectively. The first decay type is predicted to have a branching fraction of approximately 2.2 \times 10^{-4} according to the Standard Model, and the second is predicted to be less than 7.4 \times 10^{-6}. The measured values are therefore 5.8 \sigma and 4.2 sigma from the predicted values, respectively. This observed deviation may be explained by New Physics, including higher order Standard Model effects and new particles not yet included in the Standard Model. The observed decays could also be explained by a statistical fluctuation, but this is less likely given the large signals measured. New Physics is therefore suggested by the data, though more data is required to support other explanations. This measurement may be of particular interest to researchers studying rare decays of B mesons, as the branching fractions of these three-body decays are expected to be significantly smaller than that of the two-body decays. Furthermore, the measured values of these decays provide strong constraints on the Quark Counting rules and the CKM matrix. This paper describes the experimental method and the measured results, along with the current Standard Model interpretations of these deviations. This paper corresponds to arXiv.org reference 1802.08805v1. The authors are Kobayashi Mandeep Sia and A. Matas

Four-fermion interaction models are very attractive theories with diverse phases. In particular, the Gross-Neveu model in 1+3D (1 spatial + 3 temporal dimensions) with a positive mass parameter has a phase with spontaneous symmetry breaking. Its order parameter is a difermion condensate. In this model the phase transition is of second order. In 2D the model has a phase with fermion condensation and a phase with dimerization. The model in 3D with a positive mass parameter also has a phase with difermion condensation, which is, however, of first order. On the negative mass square plane, the system has a U(1) symmetry with a Goldstone mode. In 2D, the model has a phase with condensation of Jordan wigners and in 3D it has a phase with condensation of bosonic dimers. In this work, we study a general 2-4D model with four-fermion interaction. We find that in 2D this model also has a phase with difermion condensation, and on the negative mass square plane it has a U(1) symmetry with a Goldstone mode.

Large regions of space are shaped like a power-law density distribution, with a slope of ~−2. The density distribution was formed after clusters of galaxies merged with the cosmic web. Gas heated by millions of degrees during this process halts its migration toward the centers of these clusters, settling into a power-law distribution that extends to large radii. We report five regions of space that have power-law density distributions, but are not centered on the peak of the distribution. The power-law indices for these regions range from −2.7 to −3.0, and their centers are, on average, 50 kpc from the peak of the density distribution. This is likely caused by inhomogeneities between the plasma and the Plasma. The plasma was extremely dilute and densest regions collapsed at the centers of clusters of galaxies. When these regions fell behind condensation fronts, their outer radii were shaped by gravity into power laws, similar to the inner regions. These regions are not settled into a central peak because the Plasma was not collisional enough to stabilize configurations with outer slopes shallower than -3.

Interstellar dust may be visualized as a thin, flat, or opaque sheet of dust grains, scattering the starlight from stars in the dust cloud. The observed extinction curve is the convolution of the intrinsic extinction curve and the dust distribution along the line of the observed curve. To date, the intrinsic extinction curve has been approximated as a single power-law, a modified black body, or a sum of multiple component power-laws. These approximations can be used to derive a theoretical extinction curve, from which we can derive the shape of the observed curve. Extinction curve morphology is a powerful tool in understanding the properties of interstellar dust. In this paper, we analyze the shapes of observed extinction curves using a high likelihood approach, considering both the UV and infrared parts of the curve in detail , and estimating the observed curve shape over time. We build a grid of theoretical extinction curves, covering a range of behaviors including a single power-law, a modified black body, and multiple component power-laws. For each curve in the grid, we numerically calculate the corresponding probability distribution function (PDF) for the shape parameters. We find that the observed extinction curves are best described by constructing theoretical curves with PDF maximized at intermediate values of the scaling factor for the power-law indices, and with a reasonable total dust cross-section. The observed curve shapes are better described when a layered distribution of dust is assumed. In particular, we show that the observed curve near 2175 Å is a unique signature of dust in the form of nanometer-sized particles of circumstellar origin.

In this paper, I would like to present a mathematical method to analyze the problem of determining cosmological parameters from observational data. The method is based on the solution of the dynamical system problem and is able to constrain the evolutions of cosmological parameters. The advantage of this method is that it does not require any assumptions about the form of the model or the properties of the solutions. For this problem, the dynamical system has a infinite number of equilibria. By locating the critical points of equilibrium, we can determine the values of cosmological parameters that are observationally equivalent. In order to determine which equilibrium is relevant, we can use the linear approximation to characterize their stability. I will demonstrate that for various kinds of models, there are only a few observationally inequivalent sets of parameters. This means that the fitting problem is not underdetermined and that there are many different sets of cosmological parameters that can be used to describe the Universe in an acceptable way. The dynamical system approach is also able to distinguish different late-time behaviours of the models. I will apply this method to constrain the cosmological parameters using Type Ia supernova, baryon acoustic oscillations, and galaxy clustering data. I will show that although the current observational data favor a cosmological model with a constant equation of state for dark energy, the dynamical system approach is also able to place interesting constraints on the evolution of dark energy.

In this paper, we revisit the issues on Netflow sample and export performance. The traditional measurement of Netflow sample and export performance only considers the number of flow samples, without considering the size of each sample. For example, the exported sample of large packet flow may occupy several hundreds of megabytes, which may cause the exporter equipments to run out of disk space if the flow sample is not appropriately compressed. Besides, the large flow sample size may also affect the network traffic scheduling of the exporter and even cause other low-level network applications to fail. In this paper, we propose a new metric Netflow export size, which considers both the size of flow samples and the size of each sample. We conduct several sets of experiments on both virtualized and physical environments. The experimental results show that the Netflow export size can better reflect the actual flow sample size and the impact on other network applications.

As tremendous data sets generated by modern technology become increasingly important to understand our present and future, scalable analysis of such data is becoming increasingly important. Distributed computing and data parallel computing provide a way to process such data on a cluster of nodes in a parallel manner, improving the overall efficiency of the analysis. However, such processing can create additional issues when the analysis involves discretized random variables. In such scenarios, mean field approximation techniques that allow many random variables to be independent usually perform well, as it trades off the compute complexity for the modeling accuracy. Mean field variational inference, originally developed in the field of statistics, has recently been successfully adapted to train generative models such as autoencoders and GANs. In this work, we present a scalable implementation of mean field variational inference for discretized random variables. We use a Stochastic Neighbor Algorithm to generate a recursive closure, reducing the compute complexity from O(n^2) to O(n log n). Additionally, we introduce a discrete uniform Random Variable to generate a more scalable mean field approximation. Lastly, we present results on a few experiments to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

In this paper we show that disks in many highly compact accreting systems, such as dwarf novae, indicate the presence of global disk oscillation modes. These modes are similar to the oscillating modes found in Newtonian accretion discs. We also show that the presence of these modes can be used as a diagnostic to infer the spin of the central black hole. We report time-resolved optical spectroscopic and spectropolarimetric observations of the dwarf nova HT 3 that show the disk is also manifested as a stable orbital characteristic. We report the presence of at least three global disk oscillation modes: a second mode that is propagating in the radial direction and two counter-rotating modes, one low-frequency mode with a pattern speed of ~0.25 Hz and a higher-frequency wave mode with a pattern speed of ~0.5 Hz. The propagating mode is most likely a warped twisted drumlin . We fit the observed propagating mode with a twisted hydromagnetic warped drumlin model and find that the black hole in this system has a spin of a=0.82±0.02.

For example, such differences could arise in scenarios with supersymmetry (SUSY), in which case the lightest neutralino would form one such particle. Measuring such differences in the lifetimes of these mesons would provide a window into SUSY parameters, potentially even constraining the SUSY parameter space by combination with results from other experiments. If lifetimes differ significantly from the usual two mass differences, a new -specific - higgs could also contribute significantly to these masses. Modeling the dynamics of the universe in the context of observations is an important aspect of modern cosmology. By far the most popular approach to this problem is the cosmological principle and the Friedman-Robertson-Walker scalar. These assumptions allow for a reduction of the theoretical modeling to a function of the scale factor only, the simplest of which is the cosmological constant. Alternatively, one may consider a generalization of the theory known as f(R) models, such as gravity or f(R) models. These are functions of the scale factor and the Ricci scalar. We apply the recently released Python module for COSMOMATRON ICS to cosmological observations from the recent Planck and BICEP2 experiments in combination with other data sets to put bounds on f(R) model parameters. We find strong bounds on the model's running parameter R^α and the minimally required number of free parameters to describe the data. These results also apply to extensions of the standard model such as the DGP model.

Dans cette note, on donne une classification bimeromorphe des varietes kaehleriennes compactes ayant la struture orbifold speciale. Soit $(X, J, g)$ une variete kaehlerienne compacte, on dit que la struture orbifold de $(X, J)$ est speciale si la variété hermitienne j-invariante tisse la sous-algèbre de Lie de la forme de Killing j-invariante. On fournit une classification du the dans le cas tronqué, c’est à dire qu’on suppose que la variété est simplicial au voisinage de chaque singularité, on suppose aussi que la variété admet une orbifolding par un groupe global d’un groupe de Cremona. Dans ce cas, on suppose également que la variété de la classe fondamentale est nulle et que la variété admet une fibration en laquis projectifs. En utilisant une technique de normalisation d’Abresh-Raviovitch, on donne une classification lorsque la dimension est 1, 2 ou 3.

The purpose of this study was to assess the extent of degradation that X-ray scattering contributes to, and to propose potential solutions that can be implemented to alleviate or eliminate such degradations. Our study involved the use of both theoretical and experimental methods for the analysis of X-ray scattering. The results obtained from our study highlighted significant degradation patterns arising from the X-ray scattering contribution to imaging degradation in grazing-incidence X-ray telescopes. In this work, we investigate the design and performance of low-density graph codes (LDGCs) that are optimal for joint source/channel coding and binning. The central problem we aim to solve is how to construct efficient coding schemes that can achieve both the optimal source coding rate and the channel capacity with high precision, while minimizing the number of checks and variables in the Tanner graph representation. To address this challenge, we propose a novel construction algorithm that employs a generalized bivariate polynomial representation of the code, enabling us to control the redundancy and mutual information between the source symbols and channel outputs. We demonstrate that LDGCs exhibit near-Shannon limit performance while maintaining low error floors and competitive decoding complexity. Our motivation for this research is twofold. First, there is a theoretical interest in exploring the fundamental limits of joint source/channel coding and binning, as well as in developing novel design principles for low-density graph codes. Second, there is a practical need for designing robust and efficient codes for communication over noisy networks and storage systems, where performance optimization is a critical factor. Our proposed algorithm offers a promising solution to these challenges, bringing together advances in coding theory and information theory.

We present a comprehensive study of the symbiotic star H1-36, utilizing line and continuum spectra covering a wide range of wavelengths from radio to ultraviolet. Our work aims to gain a better understanding of the physical processes taking place in this system and to obtain a composite model that can explain the observed features. Our motivation for this research stems from the unique nature of symbiotic stars, which are binary systems composed of a white dwarf and a late-type giant star. The interaction between these components produces a variety of fascinating phenomena, such as accretion disks, ionizing radiation, and gas shocks. H1-36 is a prototypical symbiotic star that displays a broad spectrum of emission lines and continuum emission over a range of timescales. To construct our model, we combined results from several observational campaigns carried out over a period of several years, including radio and X-ray observations, as well as optical and ultraviolet observations. Our work began by constructing a set of theoretical models that represent the physical conditions in the vicinity of the two stars, such as gas density, temperature, and ionization state. We used a code that solves the gas transfer equation and predicts the expected emission from the system based on the input parameters. Our model successfully reproduces the main features of the observed spectrum, including the Balmer emission lines, the He I and II lines, and the continuum flux in different wavelength regions. We found that the white dwarf in H1-36 is the primary source of ionizing radiation that is absorbed by the gas in the giant star wind, which produces the continuum emission lines. The outflows from the giant star and the accretion disk around the white dwarf also contribute to the complex structure of the system. Our study sheds new light on the physical properties of symbiotic stars and provides a framework for future observations and modeling efforts.

In this article, we present the results of our study on The VVDS type-1 AGN sample - the faint -end luminosity function and the bright-end of the luminosity function. The key idea behind this research is to explore the AGN population and identify any differences between the faint and bright AGNs, particularly in terms of their luminosity function. To achieve this, we utilized a sample of 88 type-1 AGNs derived from the VIMOS-VLT Deep Survey (VVDS). We conducted a spectral analysis to determine the redshift and luminosity of each AGN. Our methodology involved fitting the luminosity function with a spectral power-law and we compared our results with previous studies to validate our findings. Our research revealed that the slope of the faint-end luminosity function is steeper than that of the bright-end luminosity function. The steepness of the faint-end slope is consistent with previous studies, indicating that our methodology and sample selection are valid. Our findings provide new insight into the AGN population and suggest that there may be differences between the distribution and evolution of faint and bright AGNs. Our research is relevant to the larger scientific community as it provides a better understanding of the AGN population and helps to improve our models and simulations of galaxy evolution. This study attempts to solve the problem of understanding the distribution of AGNs in the Universe, which is fundamental to our understanding of the evolution of galaxies.

In this work, we present a comparison between a hierarchical galaxy formation model and SPITZER data obtained by SPITZER to investigate galaxy evolution in the infrared. This study aims to understand the formation and evolution of galaxies in the universe, which is a significant and challenging problem in astrophysics. Our research is motivated by the fact that the infrared spectra of galaxies provide crucial information on the star formation rate, dust content, and chemical enrichment, which are key factors determining their evolution over time. The hierarchical galaxy formation model is constructed based on the merger and evolution of dark matter halos, which are assumed to host galaxies. We use the hierarchical galaxy formation model to simulate the formation and evolution of galaxies in the universe, incorporating the effects of gas dynamics, star formation, and feedback from supernovae and black hole accretion. We then compare the simulated galaxy properties with observations from the infrared data obtained by SPITZER. Our preliminary results show that the hierarchical galaxy formation model can reproduce the observed correlation between the star formation rate and dust content in galaxies as revealed by SPITZER. However, the model overpredicts the number of high-mass galaxies at high redshifts, which is a limitation of the model assumptions. This study provides important insights into the physical processes governing galaxy evolution and highlights the need for more sophisticated models that can capture the complexity of the astrophysical phenomena involved.

In this paper, we present our work towards creating an exact adaptive algorithm for calculating the determinant of a rational matrix. The determinant of a matrix is a fundamental quantity in linear algebra and has numerous applications in various scientific fields. Our aim is to develop an algorithm that can accurately and efficiently compute the determinant of large rational matrices. The key idea of our work is to utilize adaptive techniques that can take advantage of the structure of the rational matrix. This allows us to reduce the computational complexity of the algorithm and avoid potential numerical problems that may arise due to the rational property of the matrix. Additionally, we address the challenge of handling large matrix dimensions by implementing sophisticated data structures and optimizing the algorithm's memory usage. Our methodology involves combining classic techniques such as Gaussian elimination and LU decomposition with more recent discoveries such as the sparse rational matrix algorithm. We further enhance the algorithm's efficiency by leveraging parallel computing techniques. Through our experiments on a variety of randomly generated rational matrices, we achieved accurate and efficient computation of the determinant within reasonable time . We compared our algorithm with existing methods, and the results show that our algorithm outperforms many of them, especially for large matrices. Our work contributes to the field of linear algebra by providing a more efficient and reliable algorithm for computing the determinant of a rational matrix, which can be used in various applications.

In this work, we investigate the solutions of fractional reaction-diffusion equations (RDEs) in terms of the H-function. The problem addressed in this work arises in the field of mathematical modelling of various physical and biological systems. RDEs play a critical role in this area because they can be used to describe many phenomena, from chemical reactions and polymerization to population growth and heat transfer. However, finding exact solutions of RDEs is a challenging issue. Motivated by this problem, we present a novel approach to solving fractional RDEs in terms of the H-function. We develop a general method that can be applied to solve fractional RDEs with different initial and boundary conditions. Our approach is based on the fractional Laplace transform and the method is based on the H-function. We present several examples of RDEs that can be solved using this method, including a model of a controlled release system. The results obtained in this work demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of our approach. We show that our method can successfully solve complex RDEs that are difficult to handle using traditional techniques. Our method also provides a unified framework for solving fractional RDEs, which makes it advantageous over other methods. In summary, this work contributes to the development of effective methods for solving fractional RDEs, which has numerous applications in science and engineering.

In this work, we investigate the absorption features of high redshift galactic winds using the FIRE-2 simulations. Galactic winds play a crucial role in regulating the growth of galaxies and the enrichment of the intergalactic medium.
