Our primary objective was to measure the current and voltage correlations between electrons in the fractional quantum Hall edge channels. In addition, we focused on the noise properties of the fractional edge states arising in the vicinity of the filling factor of 5/2. We aimed to solve the problem of understanding the underlying mechanisms responsible for the noise activity in these systems. To this end, our work involved detailed analysis of the measured data and comparison with theoretical models. Our results have provided insights into the dynamical processes and correlations between electrons in fractional quantum Hall effect systems. The understanding gained through our research has practical implications for the development of future electronic devices that are based on the fractional quantum Hall effect.

In this research work, we present a novel approach for the recursive calculation of effective resistances in distance-regular networks based on the Bose-Mesner algebra and Christoffel-Darboux identity. The motivation for this research is the necessity to efficiently calculate effective resistances, as they are fundamental in a variety of fields such as network design, control, and information theory. Current methods for effective resistance calculation are based on matrix inversion or Monte Carlo methods, which can be computationally expensive for large networks. The problem we attempt to solve is to provide a faster and more efficient method for calculating effective resistances in distance-regular networks. Our proposed approach combines the spectral properties of distance-regular graphs with the recursive relation obtained using the Bose-Mesner algebra and Christoffel-Darboux identity to obtain a compact and efficient algorithm for effective resistance computation. We apply our algorithm to a set of distance-regular graphs and compare our results with those obtained using matrix inversion and Monte Carlo methods. Our results show that our approach is significantly faster than existing methods for effective resistance computation and provides better results for calculating effective resistances in distance-regular graphs. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm based on Bose-Mesner algebra and Christoffel-Darboux identity provides an efficient and accurate method for calculating effective resistances in distance-regular networks. This research work contributes to the development of faster and more efficient algorithms for network analysis and will be useful in various fields where network design is concerned.

In this paper, we present our study on the observation of two-particle Aharonov-Bohm interference, which deals with the interference between two independent electrons. There is a growing interest in understanding the behavior of quantum systems that involve interactions between particles, as this has been a subject of intense interest in the field of quantum mechanics. Furthermore, exploring these interactions is crucial for the development of novel technologies, such as quantum computing and cryptography. With the help of a custom-built four-terminal electron microscope, we were able to observe the interference pattern created by two independent electrons as they pass through two different paths around a magnetic flux. This phenomenon, known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, is caused by the phase difference introduced to the electrons and the functions of the electrons due to their exposure to a magnetic field. Our results demonstrate the existence of two-particle interference within this system and provide insight into the nature of quantum mechanical interactions. Furthermore, our findings may have significant implications in the study of entangled states and the development of quantum-based technologies. Overall, this research emphasizes the importance of understanding the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to facilitate future advancements in the field.

In this study, we investigated the thermal stability of thin metallic single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) using O(N) tight-binding molecular dynamics simulations. The motivation for this research arises from the importance of understanding the behavior of SWCNTs under extreme temperature conditions, which could potentially limit their application in numerous fields. Our simulation study revealed that the melting temperature of SWCNTs is highly dependent on their diameter, with thinner nanotubes being more stable at higher temperatures. Additionally, our results suggest that the observed thermal stability behavior of SWCNTs is largely due to the pre-melting mode of atomic vibrations, rather than the diffusion of individual atoms. To perform the simulation study, we employed O(N) tight-binding molecular dynamics, which is a computationally efficient method suitable for simulating large systems. We used a combination of classical molecular dynamics techniques and Langevin dynamics simulations to investigate the thermal stability of SWCNTs. This study provides valuable insights into the thermal stability of SWCNTs under high-temperature conditions, which can have significant implications for their practical applications in materials science. The results suggest that thinner metallic SWCNTs may be more stable at extreme temperatures, indicating their potential for use in high-temperature applications.

In this paper, we present a novel hierarchical Markovian model for hyperspectral image segmentation. The main challenge in hyperspectral image segmentation is to extract meaningful information from a large number of spectral bands. The proposed model addresses this problem by incorporating both spectral and spatial information using a hierarchical approach. The model consists of two levels. The first level involves pixel-level segmentation using a Markov random field (MRF) model. The second level involves segment-level segmentation using a nested MRF model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model on a large number of hyperspectral datasets. The results obtained show that the proposed model outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy. The main motivation for this research is to improve the accuracy and efficiency of hyperspectral image segmentation, which is an important task in remote sensing, biomedical imaging, and other applications. The proposed model can be used to extract important information from hyperspectral data for various applications, such as land-use classification, crop monitoring, and disease diagnosis. The hierarchical Markovian model presented here is a significant contribution to the field of hyperspectral image analysis and paves the way for future research in this area.

In this study, we investigate the inner jet of radio galaxy NGC 315 using observations from Chandra and the VLA. Radio galaxies exhibit powerful radio jets, the origins of which are still not fully understood. NGC 315 is located approximately 51 million light-years away and is an ideal target to study relativistic jets due to its proximity and unique structure. Our research aims to determine the location and composition of the X-ray emitting gas associated with the inner jet of NGC 315, as well as investigate the possible existence of a shock front in the jet. We used data obtained from Chandra and the VLA to create X-ray and radio images of the galaxy, respectively, to study the jet structures and associated emission. Our results show a clear and distinct radio emission from the inner jet of NGC 315, which is too bright to be explained by synchrotron emission. We observe a sharp shift in the X-ray emission and identify this shift as a possible shock front in the jet. We also find that the radio emission is closely aligned with the X-ray emission, supporting the idea that the jet generates shocks as it propagates through the X-ray emitting gas. Overall, our study provides important insights into the structure and behavior of radio jets in AGN and the underlying physical processes that govern them.

In this research, we investigate the basis set convergence of post-CCSD (coupled cluster singles and doubles) contributions to molecular atomization energies. The motivation for this study is rooted in the importance of accurate prediction of molecular atomization energies and reactivity, which depends on the quality of the quantum chemical calculations used for the calculations. However, these calculations can be computationally expensive, and convergence of the basis set is important to obtain reliable results. The problem we attempt to solve is determining the minimum basis set needed to obtain accurate results for post-CCSD contributions to atomization energies. We employ the perturbation theory approach to estimate these contributions, and the coupled cluster method with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations to compute canonical CCSD(T) energies. To evaluate the basis set convergence, we used a series of augmented correlation-consistent basis sets up to quintuple zeta quality, and further apply the extrapolation technique. Our findings suggest that the convergence depends on the system under study, and the completeness of the basis set is critical for accurate predictions. These results have the potential to impact the design of experiments in a variety of fields ranging from materials science to molecular biology. Therefore, our research contributes to the fundamental understanding of the basis set convergence of post-CCSD contributions, providing a basis for the selection of appropriate basis sets for future computational studies.

In this work, we report the detection of a rare supersoft outburst event during a Suzaku observation of the supernova remnant 1E0102.2-7219. This remnant is known to have been formed by the explosion of a massive star, which likely left behind a compact object such as a neutron star or a black hole. We were interested in studying the X-ray emission from the remnant, particularly at energies of less than 1 keV, where the emission is expected to be dominated by soft X-rays. During our Suzaku observation, we discovered a transient source that appeared to be coincident with the remnant. The source displayed a soft X-ray spectrum and a rapid rise and decline in X-ray flux over a timescale of a few days. These observations are consistent with the signature of a supersoft outburst event, which is a rare phenomenon thought to be caused by a thermonuclear runaway on the surface of a white dwarf or a neutron star. Our discovery of this event in connection with 1E0102.2-7219 provides new insights into the nature of the compact object in the remnant, as well as the physical conditions in the surrounding medium. Our results represent a significant step forward in understanding the complex processes that drive supernova explosions and the subsequent evolution of the remnants they leave behind. This work highlights the potential of Suzaku and other observatories to detect and study rare astronomical events, and underscores the importance of continued exploration of our dynamic universe.

we investigate convolutions on compact groups and Fourier algebras of coset spaces in this work. Our primary goal is to determine which coset spaces can be realized as Fourier algebras of compact groups. We attempt to solve this problem by studying the essential ideals of Fourier algebras and the properties of convolution operators. Our methodology involves examining the properties of harmonic functions and the Fourier transform on compact groups. We also use the theory of Banach algebras to study commutative function algebras and their representations. By combining these techniques, we establish conditions under which a Fourier algebra of a coset space is isomorphic to a Fourier algebra of a compact group. Our investigation is motivated by the desire to better understand the structure of Fourier algebras on compact groups and to classify the coset spaces that can be realized as such algebras. This research has applications in several areas of mathematics, including representation theory, harmonic analysis, and operator algebras. In conclusion, through our work on convolutions on compact groups and Fourier algebras of coset spaces, we have developed a deeper understanding of the structure and properties of Fourier algebras, essential ideals, and convolution operators. Our findings have important implications in the fields of representation theory and harmonic analysis, and we expect them to spark future research in these areas.

In this work, we present a comparison of two popular methods used for out-of-equilibrium simulations of polymeric systems, namely dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) and Langevin thermostats. The aim of this study is to identify the strengths and weaknesses of each method, and to identify the most appropriate approach for simulating polymeric systems in a non-equilibrium state. To achieve this goal, we performed a series of simulations on a model polymeric system using DPD and Langevin thermostats. The simulations were carried out under two different non-equilibrium conditions, namely shear flow and uniaxial elongation. Our findings reveal that DPD and Langevin thermostats yield comparable results under equilibrium conditions. However, in non-equilibrium simulations, the two methods exhibit significant differences in their ability to reproduce the physical behavior of polymer chains. Specifically, we find that DPD is better suited for simulations of complex and large-scale systems subjected to non-equilibrium conditions. On the other hand, Langevin thermostats prove to be more effective at reproducing the physical behavior of polymeric systems. Our study suggests that the choice of simulation method depends on the specific polymeric system under simulation and the non-equilibrium conditions it is subjected to.

In this study, our aim was to develop high order convergent multigrid methods on domains containing holes for black hole physics data. The problem we aimed to solve was the inaccuracy and high computational cost of existing methods when solving partial differential equations (PDEs) on domains with complicated geometries like those containing holes. These domains pose a challenge to existing numerical schemes since standard methods like finite differences are slowing down in such cases. To address this problem, we developed a new approach that employs the multigrid method, which has proven to be effective in solving PDEs on domains containing holes. Our method successfully overcomes the difficulty of singularities in domains containing holes, allowing us to apply our multigrid method to domains of arbitrary complexity. Our results demonstrate that the accuracy and computational cost of our method are superior to existing techniques and converge to the correct underlying solution. The main motivation for our research was to provide a practical solution to the numerical challenges in studying black hole physics, one of the major frontiers of theoretical physics. The results of our work hold promise for accelerating progress on simulations of gravitational wave signals from black hole binary mergers, critical for exploring the properties of gravity at strong field regimes and testing general relativity.

In this work, we present the Anderson-Yuval-Hamann (AYH) representation of the nonequilibrium two -dimensional quantum system (TLS) in the Coulomb gas framework. The problem we attempt to solve is the description of the dynamics of a TLS driven out of equilibrium by a time-dependent electric field. The key idea behind our approach is to represent the TLS as a four-dimensional complex based on the Keldysh contour, which allows us to map the problem to a two-dimensional Coulomb gas framework in imaginary time. Our methodology involves the application of the functional integral formalism, where we derive the partition function of the system and obtain an effective Lagrangian describing the dynamics of the AYH field. We then perform a saddle point approximation to compute the expectation value of the field and obtain the occupation probability of the TLS. The motivation for our research lies in the need to better understand the nonequilibrium dynamics of quantum systems, which play a crucial role in modern technology such as quantum computing and sensing. Our work provides a rigorous numerical description of the TLS under time-dependent driving, which can be further extended to more complex systems. Overall, our results contribute to the development of a better understanding of the nonequilibrium quantum mechanics and its potential applications in quantum computing.

In this work, we present polarization observations of the supernova remnant G156.2+5.7 at a wavelength of 6 cm. Our aim is to understand the morphology and magnetic field structure of this remnant. We used the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array to obtain high sensitivity polarization observations, and we compared the results with previous measurements made at different wavelengths. The polarization analysis reveals that the magnetic field orientation in the western part of the remnant is perpendicular to the remnant's shell, while in the eastern part, it is parallel. These results suggest that the magnetic field in the western part is strong and has managed to push away the plasma, while in the eastern part, the magnetic field is weak and tangled. Furthermore, we observe a clear magnetic field in the shell surrounding the remnant's shell, which indicates the presence of an ordered magnetic field. The motivation for this work is to gain a better understanding of supernova remnants and their magnetic field structures. Such knowledge will not only help us understand the evolution of supernova remnants but also provide useful information for studying other astrophysical phenomena such as cosmic ray acceleration and the interstellar medium. Overall, our observations contribute to the growing body of knowledge regarding the magnetic field structures of supernova remnants and their role in shaping their evolution.

In this paper, we present WHAM, a high-order, General Relativistic (GR) numerical scheme for solving hydrodynamical problems. Our scheme utilizes the Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO) technique, which allows for sharp interfaces and high accuracy. We also use a modified version of the moving puncture method in order to evolve the GR field equations. The main objective of our work is to solve hydrodynamic problems in a GR setting, which is crucial for a number of important astrophysical phenomena, such as compact binary mergers and supernovae explosions. These calculations require a high level of accuracy, since small errors can lead to significant changes in the outcome of the system. To test the accuracy and stability of WHAM, we perform simulations of a number of standard hydrodynamic test problems. Our results show that our scheme maintains both high accuracy and stability, even under conditions of strong shocks and gravitational waves. We also compare our results to other numerical techniques in the same settings, and show that our method outperforms them in both accuracy and stability. Overall, we believe that WHAM is a valuable numerical tool in the field of computational astrophysics. Future work includes upgrading the scheme to include magnetohydrodynamics and other more complex systems.

In this research, we investigate the demographics of transition objects, which have been proposed as a new class of astronomical objects. Our study aims to provide a better understanding of the properties of these objects, especially their age and how they are formed. We used data from the SDSS and UKIDSS surveys to analyze the spectral energy distributions of transition objects and to compare them with evolutionary models. Our results indicate that these objects are likely to be intermediate-age stars with ages ranging from 5 to 10 billion years, although we cannot rule out the possibility of them being very young stars. Additionally, our analysis showed a significant correlation between the ages of transition objects and their metallicity, suggesting that their formation may be influenced by the metal content of the local environment. The motivation for our research is driven by the importance of understanding the evolution of galaxies and the role that transition objects play in it. These objects are thought to represent a transitional phase between young and old stars, and they provide crucial information about the formation and evolution of galaxies. Furthermore, transition objects have been proposed as potential progenitors of some types of supernovae, making them important objects to study for their role in the production of heavy elements in the universe. Our findings will help to refine our understanding of the demographics of transition objects, improving our ability to interpret their properties and extract meaningful information about the history of galaxies.

We present a novel statistical approach to classify extrasolar planets based on their measurable properties. Our methodology relies on a hierarchical clustering algorithm that groups similar planets based on their mass, radius, temperature, and orbital parameters. We tested our method on a sample of more than 1500 planets and found that it yields a more robust taxonomy than previous methods based on planet mass and radius alone, as it takes into account a larger set of variables. We also identified several groups of planets that share similar properties, such as rocky planets with small radii and short orbital periods, which are likely to be terrestrial in nature. The motivation for this research stems from the need to develop a more comprehensive classification scheme for extrasolar planets that reflects the diversity of their physical and chemical properties. The current understanding of planetary formation processes suggests that a planet's composition is determined by a variety of factors, including its distance from the central star, the amount of gas and dust in the protoplanetary disk, and the presence of nearby planets. Our approach aims to capture this diversity by quantifying the influence of each of these factors on the observed properties of extrasolar planets. In conclusion, our methodology offers a new way of organizing and understanding the population of extrasolar planets, which will help to guide future studies of their formation and evolution.

In this paper, we examine confinement in N=1 SQCD, focusing on the one-step beyond Seiberg's duality. This research seeks to understand the mechanisms behind confinement in supersymmetric theories by investigating the behavior of confinement in supersymmetric theories. Our key goal is to utilize generalized orbifolds to gain insight into the confining properties of SQCD. We introduce a new gauge coupling for the orbifold which is related to the original theory, and we show that this new gauge coupling gives rise to confinement. Using this technique, we derive an effective theory for low-energy bound ing of quarks and gluons under confinement. Our methodology relies on a detailed analysis of the tensor product of SU(n) gauge groups, identifying a new gauge symmetry. Applying this symmetry to SQCD, we obtain an S-dual theory, which leads to the new understanding of confinement in the generalized orbifold. The problem this work attempts to solve is to bridge the gap between the supersymmetric and non-supersymmetric theories, to unravel the moduli spaces and find a concrete mechanism for four-dimensional confinement. Our findings contribute to the ongoing effort to better understand the nature of confinement in supersymmetric theories, and can be extended to other gauge theories beyond SQCD.

In this work, we present phase-resolved measurements of stimulated emission in an optically pumped laser system. The problem we aim to solve is to investigate the dynamics of stimulated emission with high temporal resolution, which is crucial for understanding the underlying physical and chemical processes that govern laser operation. Stimulated emission is a fundamental phenomenon in laser science and technology, and its precise measurement is essential for the development of new laser sources and applications. Our methodology involves using a fast photo-detector to perform time-resolved measurements of the laser output signal, along with a phase-locked loop detector to extract the phase information of the signal. This allows us to obtain phase-resolved data of the stimulated emission in a laser system, which provides insights into the dynamics of the laser cavity and the mode of operation of the laser process. The motivation for this research stems from the importance of developing novel laser systems for applications ranging from material processing to bioimaging. By refining our understanding of the stimulated emission , we can improve the efficiency and stability of laser sources, enabling better performance and wider application of laser technology. Our results provide valuable insights into the dynamics of stimulated emission, paving the way for the development of advanced laser systems.

In this work, we provide evidence for the evolution of early-type galaxies in the GOODS/CDF-S field. Our study focuses on the analysis of the rest-frame colors and masses of galaxies, obtained through deep optical and near-infrared imaging. We investigate the redshift evolution of the population of early-type galaxies, and its influence on mass and environment. Our methodology involves the use of a large sample of high-quality photometric redshifts and a well-defined selection of early-type systems based on structural parameters. Our motivation for this study is to shed light on the formation and evolution of massive galaxies, a fundamental question in modern astrophysics. Early-type galaxies represent a crucial piece in this puzzle, as they are typically old, quiescent systems with prominent bulges, and are thought to have formed through a combination of in-situ and merger-driven processes. By probing the evolution of these systems as a function of redshift and mass, we can test theoretical models and gain insights into the physical mechanisms driving the observed trends. Our results indicate that the number density of early-type galaxies increases significantly with redshift, and that this evolution is more pronounced for lower-mass systems. We also find that the fraction of early-type galaxies in overdense environments is higher than in the field, suggesting that environmental processes may play a role in shaping the morphological properties of galaxies. Our results are consistent with a scenario where early-type galaxies grow mainly through dry mergers, and their star formation process is quenched over time.

In this work titled "Lyman Break Galaxies at z~5: Rest-frame UV Spectra, Part II," we present an analysis of 35 Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) at redshift z~5 using high-resolution spectroscopy obtained with the Keck telescope. The problem our work attempts to solve is the characterization of the physical properties and evolution of early galaxy populations during the cosmic reionization epoch, which is a critical period in the evolution of the Universe. The motivation for our research is to understand the emergence and evolution of early galaxies and their contribution to the reionization of the Universe. Our work addresses this by studying the ionizing properties and dust content of high-redshift galaxies. We use data from the Keck telescope to extract the rest-frame UV spectra of the LBGs. We then measure the equivalent widths of spectral features, such as Lyman-alpha and SiIV lines. Our key findings suggest that LBGs at z~5 have dust attenuation levels similar to those of local star-forming galaxies. Furthermore, we find evidence for the presence of ionizing outflows in the young galaxies, implying that they could be potential sources of ionizing radiation and metal enrichment in the early Universe. Our methodology involves a combination of spectral analysis and comparison with local galaxy templates. Overall, our work sheds light on the physical properties and evolution of early galaxy populations, contributing to our understanding of the Universe's history and the crucial role of galaxies in driving cosmic reionization.

In this work, we investigate model-independent constraints on reionization using large-scale CMB polarization. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that reionization is an important epoch in the evolution of the Universe, and understanding it can shed light on a variety of astrophysical and cosmological phenomena. In particular, the process of reionization has implications for the formation and properties of the first galaxies, as well as the overall ionization state of the intergalactic medium. To achieve our objectives, we use observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation obtained by the Planck satellite, as well as measurements of the large-scale polarization of the CMB. We focus on a range of CMB multipoles that are related to the reionization process of the Universe, and use a Bayesian framework to place constraints on the timing and duration of reionization, as well as its optical depth and mean electron scattering optical depth. Our results show that our methodology allows us to place robust and reliable constraints on the timing and duration of reionization, without invoking any specific model or assumptions about the astrophysical processes involved. These constraints are in good agreement with previous estimates from the Planck probes, and provide further validation for the standard cosmological model. Our work demonstrates the potential for large-scale CMB polarization measurements to provide important insights into the astrophysics of the early Universe.

In this work, we investigate the driving mechanism of the jets and outflows in the process of star formation. Star formation is a complex phenomenon that involves the collapse of dense molecular clouds, the formation of protostars, and the ejection of jets and outflows. Understanding the driving mechanism of these jets and outflows is crucial for comprehending the overall physics of star formation. To address this issue, we perform hydrodynamic simulations of jets and outflows using the adaptive mesh refinement technique. Our simulations reveal that the jets and outflows are formed as a result of the interaction between the protostar and its accretion disk. As the protostar accretes gas from the disk, it launches bipolar outflows that clear the surrounding gas and dust. Meanwhile, the accretion disk also generates a collimated jet that propagates along the rotational axis. Furthermore, we find that the morphology and velocity of the jets and outflows depend on the interaction of the protostar and its environment. Our results provide new insights into the driving mechanism of jets and outflows and shed light on the early stages of star formation.

In this paper, we present a Non-Gaussianity analysis on local morphological measures of WMAP data. The study aims to investigate the statistical properties of the primordial density perturbations that were created during the inflationary phase of the early universe, using local morphological measures in a Non-Gaussianity framework. The main problem that this work attempts to address is the detection of deviation from the Gaussian distribution of the initial conditions of the universe. While the inflationary theory is well supported by observations, the assumption of the Gaussianity of the primordial perturbations may be challenged by possible mechanisms operating during or after inflation. If detected, these non-Gaussian signatures may reveal important information about the physics of the early universe. In this study, we perform a Non-Gaussianity analysis on local geometric quantities derived from the WMAP data of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropies. Our analysis involves the calculation of the local skewness and kurtosis of the geometric measures on different scales, and testing their consistency with a Gaussian distribution. Our results reveal that the local geometric measures display significant deviations from the Gaussian distribution, indicating the presence of non-Gaussian signatures in the primordial perturbations that may provide insights into early universe physics.

In this paper, we investigate a problem of Yamabe type on compact spinorial manifolds. Our main objective is to investigate the conformal geometry of such manifolds by analyzing their spinorial structure and curvature. We establish several important results that shed light on the behavior of the Yamabe constant on these manifolds and on the existence of extremal metrics in certain cases. Our motivation for this research is twofold. On one hand, Yamabe-type problems have been a central topic in geometry for several decades, with applications ranging from topology to physics. On the other hand, compact spinorial manifolds are of great interest in the study of spin geometry, with important implications in theoretical physics. To tackle this problem, we use a combination of geometric and perturbation methods. We first establish some necessary conditions for the existence of extremal metrics on compact spinorial manifolds, based on a careful analysis of their spinorial curvature. We then develop a perturbation argument to construct extremal metrics in certain cases. Our results shed light on the conformal geometry of compact spinorial manifolds and provide new insights into the interplay between spinor geometry and the Yamabe problem. Overall, our work represents an important contribution to the study of Yamabe-type problems on compact spinorial manifolds, with potential applications in theoretical physics and other areas of mathematics.

In this work, we explore the astrophysical and cosmological implications of large volume string compactifications. The key idea underlying our research is that string theory, a theoretical framework that aims to unify all known physical laws, predicts the existence of extra dimensions beyond the three spatial and one temporal dimension we observe in our everyday lives. These extra dimensions are typically compactified or curled up in a tiny space, making them invisible to our senses. We employ a modern mathematical tool called the Large Volume Scenario (LVS) to construct compactifications of string theory that give rise to a large volume of space in the extra dimensions. This scenario has far-reaching implications for cosmology and astrophysics, as it opens up the possibility of extra dimensions playing a role in phenomena such as dark matter and inflation. Our analysis focuses on the impact of large volume string compactifications on the evolution of the Universe, the formation of galaxies, and the properties of dark matter. Specifically, we investigate the effects of the compactification on the spectrum of primordial gravitational waves, the abundance of dark matter particles, and the formation of baryonic structures. We show that the LVS generates a rich phenomenology that can be tested with current and future observations, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, large scale cosmological surveys, and particle accelerator experiments. Our research provides a new avenue for exploring the interplay between fundamental physics and cosmology, and may ultimately lead to the discovery of new physical laws and phenomena.

In this work, we investigate the shock and release temperatures of molybdenum. The motivation for this research stems from the importance of understanding the dynamic response of materials to high-velocity impact events. Among the refractory metals, molybdenum is of particular interest due to its unique mechanical and thermal properties. Hence, there is a need for accurate measurements of its shock and release temperatures. We employ a high-pressure gas gun to generate high-pressure shock waves on molybdenum samples. We monitor the pressure and temperature evolution of the shocked states using a suite of diagnostics, including VISAR, X-ray, and impedance matching techniques. Our main objective is to investigate the Hugoniot curve and the release adiabat of molybdenum. The results obtained show that the Hugoniot curve of molybdenum is steeper than that of other refractory metals, and its release adiabat has a unique shape. These findings provide new insights into the dynamic behavior of molybdenum under extreme conditions, which are crucial for understanding its applications in materials science and engineering. Additionally, the experimental data presented in this work can be used to improve existing equations of state for molybdenum, which are essential for modeling and simulating high-velocity impact events.

In this work, we present the results of a Fourier resolved spectroscopy analysis of the low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1728-34. Our investigation focused on deciphering the spectral and temporal properties of the binary system using high-resolution X-ray spectra obtained by the Reflection Grating Spectrometer on board the XMM-Newton satellite. The primary objective of our study was to investigate the possible presence of a high-frequency QPO (HFQPO) in the power spectrum of 4U 1728-34. Our methodology involved the use of Fourier analysis to resolve the X-ray spectrum into narrow frequency bands and investigate the properties of the corresponding power spectra. Our analysis revealed the presence of a broad bump centered around 30 Hz in the power spectral density distribution. Contrary to our expectations, we did not find evidence for the existence of a coherent bump in the frequency range of 30-100 Hz. Furthermore, our results suggest that the observed variability is likely due to the combination of several incoherent frequency components. Overall, this study provides new insights into the spectral and temporal properties of low-mass X-ray binaries and reveals that the HFQPO phenomenon might be more elusive than previously thought. Our findings contribute to advancing the field of low-mass X-ray astronomy and have implications for the interpretation of similar systems.

In this work, we examine the electron heating mechanisms in black hole accretion disks during low and high states. The heating mechanisms are crucial for understanding the spectral energy distribution of the disk and the emission from the corona, both of which are important quantities for observing black holes. Our motivation for studying electron heating in black hole accretion disks during low states is twofold. First, the observed spectra during low states of black hole binaries are different from those during high states, indicative of a different accretion geometry. Second, previous models do not provide a physical explanation for this difference. Therefore, we aim to understand the electron heating mechanism responsible for these spectral differences. We use magneto-hydrodynamic s simulations to model the accretion disk in low state. Our simulations show that magnetic reconnection is the dominant heating mechanism in the corona and drives the observed differences in the spectral energy distribution between low and high states. The implications of our results suggest that magnetic reconnection is not only key to understanding electron heating in black hole accretion disks, but also provides insight into the energetics of the corona and its interaction with the black hole disk.

In this study, we investigate the occurrence of resonant Kelvin-Helmholtz modes in sheared relativistic flows, which results in the instability of these flows. Such instability can lead to significant changes in the physical properties of the medium and has important implications for several astrophysical phenomena. Our work attempts to solve the challenge of characterizing Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities in highly unstable relativistic fluids, which have been widely observed in a variety of astrophysical phenomena, such as black hole accretion disks, neutron explosions, and gamma-ray bursts. We employ a numerical simulation approach to solve the equations governing the relativistic fluid dynamics, and we examine the conditions under which the medium is more prone to resonant Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. Our results demonstrate that the properties of sheared flows, such as their Lorentz factor, the angle of shear, and the perturbation wavelength, play an important role in determining the onset of instability. Overall, our study provides an important theoretical foundation for understanding the behavior of relativistic fluids in the presence of sheared flows. Our findings may have important implications for a variety of astrophysical phenomena, and our methodology may be used to simulate and model a range of unstable systems in the universe.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for modeling the three-point correlation function (3PCF) in astronomical data. The 3PCF is a cosmological measure that provides information about the clustering behavior of galaxies, and its accurate estimation is crucial to gain insights into the large-scale structure of the universe. Our proposed approach attempts to address the limitations of previous methods, which primarily rely on computational simulations and traditional perturbation theory, by introducing a new hybrid model that combines perturbation theory and machine learning techniques. We show that our model outperforms existing approaches in accurately predicting the 3PCF for a range of galaxy datasets, with an average improvement of up to 20% in accuracy. Our method addresses challenges such as the non-Gaussianity of the 3PCF, uncertainty in the observational data, and high computational demands. Moreover, our approach is generalizable to a broader range of cosmological data and applications. The key idea in our hybrid approach is to learn the mapping between the 3PCF and a set of perturbative features by training a neural network. Our methodology involves first using perturbation theory to compute the power spectra, bispectra, and other relevant features that capture the spatial distribution of galaxies. Subsequently, we use these features as inputs to a neural network, which predicts the 3PCF. The proposed approach provides an efficient and accurate framework for predicting the 3PCF in complex cosmological datasets, and can significantly enhance our understanding of the universe's large-scale structure.

In our experimental study, we investigated the effects of varying optical properties of boundary surfaces on the Casimir force. This force, initially observed as an attractive force between two metal plates, emerges due to quantum fluctuations in the vacuum. The Casimir force plays a significant role in several areas of physics, such as nanotechnology and fundamental physics. Our work aims to address the issue of disparate Casimir forces encountered in various systems that are due to different optical properties of their boundary surfaces. This problem arises because the boundary surface's optical characteristics affect how electromagnetic fields interact with it. To address this issue, we performed experimental studies on boundary surfaces by creating microfabricated surfaces with varying optical properties. Our results show that by altering the surface's optical properties, we could control and manipulate the Casimir force to decrease or increase its magnitude. Our work highlights the importance of the boundary surface's optical properties in determining the Casimir force. This insight can inspire advancements in nanotechnology and also provide new insights into the fundamental aspects of quantum field theory and the vacuum's fluctuations. Our experimental methods provide a potential approach for studying the influence of other surface properties on the Casimir force in future research projects. We hope that our results will be useful in the field of nanotechnology.

In our research study, we present DWEB, a Data Warehouse Engineering Benchmark. Our motivation was to develop a benchmark that can evaluate the performance of data warehousing tools across different stages of the data warehouse lifecycle such as design, implementation, and maintenance. Data warehousing has become a critical aspect of modern decision-making processes, and it requires robust data management solutions. Therefore, there is a need to identify and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of data warehousing tools in terms of their ability to manage and process large datasets, ensure data quality, and provide effective visualization and reporting capabilities. We conducted experiments on two competing data warehousing tools: Apache Kylo and Apache Nifi, using the DWEB benchmark framework. Our results indicated that the framework is useful for identifying performance bottlenecks in data warehousing tools. Specifically, we found that Apache Kylo outperforms Apache Nifi in most stages of the data warehouse lifecycle, including data extraction, transformation and loading, and implementing data quality checks. Our research study seeks to solve the challenge of assessing data warehousing tools' performance comprehensively. By presenting DWEB, we provide the foundation for a standard benchmark system that evaluators, developers, and researchers can use to compare the performance of competing data warehousing tools. Additionally, our study can also help data warehouse professionals to identify the strengths and weaknesses of their current data warehousing tools, allowing for a more informed decision-making process.

In this work, we investigate the sensitivity of stellar evolution models to individual element abundances in order to improve our understanding of how stars evolve. We employ a series of stellar population models utilizing the MESA code that vary in initial element abundance s to test how the evolution of stars changes depending on the ratio of individual elements. Our methodology involves using a set of evolutionary tracks to compare how different stars evolve when different individual element abundances are present. We determine that elements such as oxygen, carbon, and nitrogen have a significant impact on the evolutionary tracks of stars. Notably, models with higher oxygen abundances have a longer main sequence and develop larger helium core sizes, while lower oxygen abundances result in shorter main sequences and smaller helium core sizes. These findings enable us to better understand the variability in the observed properties of different stars. Specifically, by examining the influence of individual element abundances on stellar evolution, our work has the potential to provide insight into the historical composition of stars and the role that different elements play in the life cycle of stars. Ultimately, this research represents a key aspect of our understanding of stellar evolution, and provides crucial information for those studying the formation and behavior of galaxies and the universe as a whole.

In this work, we investigate the role of dipolar order in enhancing dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP). We demonstrate that rapid diffusion of dipolar order leads to more efficient transfer of polarization from electrons to nuclei in DNP, resulting in significant increases in the efficiency of NMR signals. Our experiments utilize biradical polarizing agents for DNP, where the rate of nuclear polarization transfer is controlled by manipulating the distance between the polarizing electron spins. By tuning this distance to achieve optimal dipolar order, we show that DNP enhancements in excess of 500 are achievable by using polarizing agents at room temperature. The motivation for this research lies in the challenges of NMR spectroscopy, particularly in studies of biological macromolecules, which require high resolution and resolution. DNP has emerged as a powerful technique for amplifying NMR signals, but its efficiency and applicability remain limited by various factors. Our work addresses a key challenge of DNP by showing that dipolar order can be exploited to improve the efficiency of nuclear polarization transfer. Our results represent a significant advance in the field of DNP, where dipolar order has long been recognized as a critical factor but its role has not been fully understood. We expect that our findings will lead to the design of new polarizing agents and improved DNP protocols for applications in a wide range of fields, including materials science and drug discovery.

In this work, we present the results of the SAURON project, an observational survey of 24 early-type spiral galaxies that we studied using IFU spectroscopy at the William Herschel Telescope. We reconstruct the stellar populations of these galaxies using absorption line strength maps for a wide range of spectral features, including Mg and Fe. The main idea behind our work is to use a spatially resolved approach to probe the age, metallicity, and alpha-element abundance of the stellar populations in these galaxies. By extracting this information, we aim to investigate the formation and evolution of galaxies and the role of different physical processes in shaping their stellar content. Our methodology involves using a combination of spectral synthesis models and pixel-fitting techniques to derive the relevant physical parameters from the observed spectra. We examine the radial variation of these stellar populations as a function of the galaxy's structural properties, such as its bulge-to-disk ratio and the presence of bars. We find a diverse range of stellar population gradients among the galaxies, with some showing a significant age or metallicity gradient, while others show no significant variation. Thus, the main problem that our work attempts to solve is to provide a comprehensive , spatially resolved analysis of the stellar populations in early-type spiral galaxies. Our results shed light on the formation and evolution of these galaxies and highlight the importance of spatially resolved spectroscopy in understanding the physical mechanisms that drive their evolution.

In this study, we present the results of a comprehensive investigation on the spatially resolved kinematics and stellar populations of the brightest cluster and group galaxies. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that these galaxies are the most massive and luminous members of galaxy clusters and are critical to understanding the formation and evolution of their host structures. Using data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at the International Space Station (MaNGA) data set, we analyzed the kinematics and stellar populations of 113 brightest cluster galaxies and 64 brightest group galaxies, spanning a range of redshifts and environments. Our study revealed that both cluster and group brightest galaxies exhibit complex kinematic structures, including rotation, dispersion, and stellar motions. Furthermore, we found that the stellar populations of these galaxies exhibit clear gradients in age, metallicity, and abundance ratios, with the central regions being more metal-rich and dominated with alpha-elements. The key idea behind this study is to understand the formation and evolution of brightest cluster and group galaxies by exploring their kinematic and stellar properties in detail. To achieve this, we employed a state-of-the-art kinematic model, combined with spectral fitting techniques, to extract the relevant parameters from the MaNGA data. Our results were compared with the analysis of galaxy spectra at different spatial locations to obtain detailed kinematic, stellar , and metallicity maps, which provide insight into the physical processes responsible for galaxy formation and evolution. Overall, our study sheds light on the complex nature of brightest cluster and group galaxies, and highlights the importance of kinematics and stellar populations in understanding their properties and formation mechanisms.

In this study, we developed a hybrid cellular automaton model to investigate the dynamics and stability of cell colony growth. The model incorporates both the stochasticity and spatial dependency of cell proliferation, movement, and death within the colony. Our simulations showed that the model can exhibit a variety of growth patterns, including colony expansion, contraction, and coexistence of multiple subcolonies. We also demonstrated that the model's outcome was influenced by the initial cell density, division rate, and movement probability. The key idea behind the model is to bridge the gap between continuous and discrete models by using the cellular automaton framework. We developed a set of rules that govern the behavior of cells within the colony, which can be modified to reflect different biological contexts. To test the model's validity, we compared the simulation results with those from well-established models for single-cell and colony growth and found good correlations. Our work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the impact of stochasticity and spatial dependency on cell colony growth. By developing a hybrid model that captures both of these features, we offer a novel approach for investigating the dynamics and stability of cell populations. Our findings suggest that the model can be useful in studying the factors that lead to tumor formation and progression and in designing strategies for cancer treatment.

In this study, we examine two gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), GRB 050410 and GRB 050412, to determine if they are truly "dark," meaning that they have no detectable afterglow emission at longer wavelengths. To achieve this goal, we analyzed multiwavelength observations from different instruments, including the Swift, Chandra, and XMM-Newton telescopes, as well as ground-based optical and radio telescopes. Our analysis reveals that both GRBs have faint afterglows in the X-ray and radio bands, indicating that they are not completely dark. This observation challenges the prevailing theory that dark GRBs are due to a lack of a collimated jet that produces an afterglow. To explain the observed faint emission, we propose a model where the jet is narrow but has a low kinetic energy and an isotropic equivalent energy of less than 10^50 erg, which is lower than most typical GRBs. The low energy of the collimated jet would cause the emission to be faint, and the narrow opening angle would make it difficult to observe from Earth. Our work attempts to solve the puzzling nature of dark GRBs and contributes to our understanding of the physics of GRBs and their afterglows. As our survey of afterglows improves, we expect to see more low-energy and faint collimated bursts. Our results suggest that our understanding of these essential phenomena is far from complete.

We present a mathematical model for a copolymer in an emulsion system. Our research focuses on understanding the behavior of copolymers in emulsion as a function of molecular weight and composition. Although copolymers are widely used in various industrial applications, their behavior in emulsion remains largely unexplored. As a result, we aim to develop a rigorous mathematical framework that accurately predicts the behavior of copolymers in emulsion. In our work, we use statistical mechanics to derive a model that considers the chain length and composition of copolymers in emulsion. We then numerically solve the resulting equations for several different scenarios and compare the results with experimental data. Our results show that our model is able to successfully predict the behavior of copolymers in emulsion for a broad range of molecular weights and compositions. In particular, we find that the behavior of copolymers in emulsion is strongly influenced by the chain length distribution of the copolymer chains. Our work has significant implications for the design and optimization of copolymer-based materials for use in a variety of industrial systems. By developing a mathematical framework that accurately predicts the behavior of copolymers in emulsion, we provide a valuable tool for scientists and engineers to optimize the properties of these materials for specific applications.

In this work, we investigate the isospin violation in the decays $\phi, J/\psi, \psi^\prime \to \omega \pi^0$ via hadronic loops. The investigation is motivated by the goal of understanding the symmetry violation in hadronic interactions, which plays a crucial role in various theoretical models and experimental studies. The aim of this research is to provide a quantitative prediction for the isospin violation in the hadronic decays using chiral symmetry theory and dispersion relations. Our analysis is based on the effective Lagrangian approach, which allows us to calculate the decay amplitudes in terms of the relevant low-energy constants and hadronic loops. The hadronic loops contribute significantly to the amplitude, and our analysis includes the contributions from the $\rho$ and $f_2$ resonances. We find that the isospin violation in the studied decays is relatively small, with the branching ratio for the isospin-violating mode being below 1%. Our results are in good agreement with the existing experimental data and provide insights into the symmetry breaking in hadronic interactions. In conclusion, our work contributes to the understanding of isospin violation in hadronic decays and provides a quantitative prediction for the isospin violation in $\phi, J/\psi, \psi^\prime \to <unk>omega \pi^0$ via hadronic loops.

In our work titled “Is diversity in the workplace good?”, we address the question of whether diversity in the workplace is beneficial or harmful. As society becomes increasingly diverse, the concept of diversity has gained widespread acceptance, but its effects remain unclear. The problem our work seeks to resolve is the inconclusive nature of research on the subject, which has led to conflicting viewpoints among researchers, policymakers, and practitioners. To address the issue, we draw upon literature from various disciplines, including sociology, psychology, and business management. Our key idea argues that diversity is beneficial in certain situations but can also pose challenges if not managed effectively. Specifically, we posit that properly managed diversity results in better decision-making, increased creativity, and greater productivity, which can lead to positive outcomes for both employees and organizations. However, poorly managed diversity can lead to conflict, stress, and reduced job satisfaction, which may ultimately harm the organization. Our methodology involves reviewing and synthesizing existing research on the topic, including empirical studies, theoretical models, and case studies. Through this literature review, we aim to provide a comprehensive and comprehensive understanding of the effects of diversity in the workplace. The motivation for our work is to contribute to the ongoing debate on the merits of diversity in the workplace. By clarifying when diversity is harmful and how diversity is beneficial, we hope to inform both policymakers and organizations about the importance of diversity management and its potential benefits for employees and organizations.

In this work, we investigate the hidden symmetry underlying the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix and the neutrino mixing matrix. We introduce the concept of a “neutrino mapping matrix” which relates the mixing matrices of neutrinos in different generations. Our analysis reveals a significant correlation between the CKM matrix and the neutrino mixing matrices, indicating a deeper structure in the Standard Model flavor sector. We explore the consequences of this symmetric relation on the physical parameters of the matrices including the Dirac and Majorana CP phases, which are essential to understanding neutrino oscillations and studies of CP violation. The problem our work attempts to solve is the lack of a fundamental explanation for the observed patterns in the CKM and neutrino mixing matrices. Our results reveal a hidden symmetry not widely appreciated in the literature and suggest a possible pathway to a more fundamental understanding of neutrino physics and CP violation. We employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods to demonstrate the existence and properties of the hidden symmetry. We also investigate the implications of the symmetry for the neutrino mass hierarchy and the possibility of a common origin for quark and lepton mixing. Our approach provides a fresh perspective on the flavor sector of the Standard Model and its extensions.

In this research, we attempt to predict the response of structural systems under earthquake motions using artificial neural network (ANN). The main objective of this work is to provide accurate and efficient prediction of the structural response to improve the resilience and safety of buildings subjected to seismic events. The main problem this work attempts to solve is the difficulty of accurately predicting the behavior of complex structures due to the nonlinear and highly dynamic nature of earthquakes. Current analysis methods are expensive and computationally intensive, making them impractical for predicting structural responses in earthquake scenarios. We propose using a trained ANN to predict the response of the structural system subject to ground motions generated via an earthquake simulator. Our approach involves developing a comprehensive database of seismic response from numerical simulations of a three-story reinforced concrete building under various ground motion and structural parameter combinations to be used for training and testing the ANN. The results indicate that the ANN can predict the structural response with high accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional methods. The proposed methodology eliminates the need for complex modeling and parameter calibration and therefore provides a practical tool for real-time prediction of structural responses. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the potential of artificial neural networks as a novel approach in predicting the response of structural systems under earthquake motions, which can be used to improve safety and resilience in built environments.

In this study, we present the results of our asteroseismic analysis of the bright star alpha Cen A, using data from the TESS space mission. Our aim is to investigate the rotational behavior of the bright star, and in particular to detect the signature of rotational splitting in the frequency spectrum of the oscillation modes. The detection of such splitting would provide important information about the internal structure and dynamics of the star, and would also have implications for the study of exoplanetary systems that orbit alpha Cen A. Our analysis is based on a combination of time-series measurements, which allows us to measure the oscillations of the star, and theoretical modeling, which allows us to interpret these measurements in terms of the star's interior properties. We apply several techniques to identify the signature of rotational splitting in the frequency spectrum of the oscillations, and we find clear evidence for such splitting at low rotational frequencies. These results are consistent with previous studies of alpha Cen A and support the current understanding of this star as a strong candidate for asteroseismic modeling and further investigation of exoplanetary systems in its vicinity. Overall, our work provides new insights into the rotational behavior of alpha Cen A and highlights the importance of asteroseismology in the study of stellar physics and exoplanetary systems. Our findings contribute to ongoing efforts to improve our understanding of the properties and evolution of stars, and have implications for the search for life beyond our solar system.

We investigated the behavior of Supergiant Fast X-ray Transients (SFXTs) to better understand their origin and whether they represent a class of objects defined by common characteristics. These high-energy astronomical transients exhibit sudden, intense X-ray bursts lasting minutes to hours, typically originating from the vicinity of a blue supergiant star. Though rare, they have been observed around the Milky Way and in other galaxies. The primary motivation for studying SFXTs is to shed light on the fundamental questions of their physical origin and the astrophysical processes accompanying their emission. To address these questions, we analyzed data from the Swift satellite, which monitored the X-ray sky and provided a comprehensive picture of the SFXT phenomenon. Our approach included observing the long-term X-ray properties of a sample of objects and searching for common patterns. We found that there were similar properties and behavior shared among the studied SFXTs and that they could be classified as a distinct class of objects. Our results suggest that SFXTs may be the product of a complex physical mechanism, making them a unique and important object within the wider field of high-energy astrophysics. Our study opens up new avenues for further investigation of this fascinating class of objects and the physics responsible for their unique behavior.

In this study, we investigate the mid-infrared fine structure line ratios in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) observed with Spitzer IRS and examine the evidence for extinction by the torus. The torus is a hypothesized dusty structure surrounding the central engine of an AGN. Its line-of-sight obscuration can affect the observed properties of AGNs, including their mid-infrared line ratios, which are considered to be powerful diagnostics of their physical conditions. We have analyzed a sample of 92 AGNs spanning a range of luminosities and spectral properties and find that their mid-infrared fine structure line ratios are consistent with photoionization models, but they also show a dependence on AGN luminosity. Furthermore, we observe a significant correlation between the ionic line ratios and the silicate absorption depth, which suggests the presence of dusty material along the line-of-sight. We interpret this observation as evidence for the torus as the responsible structure. Our results suggest that extinction by the torus is a crucial factor that must be taken into account in the interpretation of AGN spectra. The methodology we have employed involves modeling the AGN spectra with photoionization models and analyzing the correlations between the mid-infrared line ratios and the silicate absorption depth.

In this work, we investigate capillary ordering and layering transitions in two-dimensional hard-rod fluids. The problem we attempt to solve is understanding the fundamental behavior of hard rods in the presence of attractive forces. Specifically, we investigate the mechanism by which the hard rods self-assemble and are ordered , due to capillary interactions and layering transitions. Our research is motivated by the importance of understanding the behavior of simple model systems in materials science, soft matter physics and engineering applications. The key idea of our study is that we utilize molecular dynamics simulations to explore the systematics of capillary ordering in two-dimensional fluids of hard rods with long-range attractive forces. We investigate the behavior of the system as the size and temperature are varied, and we analyze the resulting structures using statistical measures such as radial distribution functions and orientational correlation s. Additionally, we investigate the role of the size distribution of the rods on the formation of the capillary ordering transition. Our methodology involves a combination of simulations and numerical analysis to probe the behavior of the system. We utilize a self-consistent field approach to verify the results of our simulations and to elucidate the role of the attractive forces in the ordering behavior. Our findings suggest that the capillary ordering transition is sensitive to the size distribution of rods, and that this ordering can be tuned by adjusting the attractive forces. Overall, our work provides a detailed understanding of capillary ordering and layering transitions in two-dimensional hard-rod fluids and could have implications in fields such as materials science and soft matter physics.

In this research, we investigate the presence of magnetic dead layers in La2/3Ca1/3MnO3 thin films using X-ray magnetic circular dichroism in reflection. The issue of the presence of magnetic dead layers in thin film magnetic materials is well known, with the existence of non-magnetic layers at the surface of a magnetic film causing a reduction in the magnetic moment and thereby affecting the magnetic performance of the material. We present X-ray magnetic circular dichroism in reflection that investigates the presence of a magnetic dead layer at the surface of La2/3Ca1/3MnO3 thin films with thicknesses in the range of 7-23 nm. The results show that the dead layer thickness increases as the thickness of the film decreases, reaching a maximum thickness of around 2.8nm. Our findings have significant implications for the understanding and characterization of magnetic properties of thin films, particularly in understanding how the presence of magnetic dead layers affects their behavior. Moreover, our research contributes to developments in the field of spintronics, where the understanding of magnetic thin films is crucial for the future of computing technology. The methodology of our research involved the deposition of La2/3Ca1/3MnO3 thin films using pulsed laser deposition, and the characterization of their magnetic properties using X-ray magnetic circular dichroism in reflection at the Soft X-ray Materials Science beamline. Our work provides fundamental insights into the magnetic behavior of thin films with practical applications in spintronics, nanoelectronics, and data storage.

In this study, we investigated the collisions between equal-sized agglomerates of ice grains. The purpose of the study was to explore the fundamental mechanics of ice agglomerate collisions, which are important for understanding the formation and evolution of planetary systems and icy comets. Our experimental methodology involved launching two agglomerates towards each other and recording their impact using high-speed cameras. We measured the initial speed and angle of the agglomerates and observed the resulting collision characteristics. Our results showed that collisions between equal-sized agglomerates of ice grains can be classified into three types: sticking, bouncing, and fragmentation. We also found that the outcome of a collision depended on the initial conditions, such as the impact angle and velocity. The sticking collisions were more likely to occur at lower impact angles, while fragmentation was more common at higher velocities. The study explores the fundamental mechanics of ice agglomerate collisions, which is essential for understanding the processes that form and shape our solar system's planets and icy comets. Furthermore, the study provides essential data for the future development of numerical models and computational simulations of these types of collisions. We believe that utilizing a better understanding of how ice agglomerates interact may lead to a more profound understanding of the formation and evolution of planetary systems, including our own solar system.

In this study, we present a new approach to Orbital-Free Density Functional Theory that utilizes kinetic potentials and ab-initio local pseudopotentials. Our research aims to address the limitations of existing theories by providing a more accurate and efficient method for modeling complex systems such as metals, semiconductors, and molecules. Using our approach, we generated results that demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional DFT methods. We applied our methodology to a range of systems and found that our approach yielded results that are in good agreement with experimental data. Our work is motivated by the need for accurate and efficient computational methods to better model complex systems. By providing a more accurate and efficient method for modeling complex systems, our research offers significant potential applications in materials science and engineering. Our key ideas and methodology involve the development of composite kinetic potentials that are derived from the Taylor expansion of the density, and local pseudopotentials that capture the non-local ization of the potential. We implemented these ideas using the KEDF scheme and found that our methodology provided accurate results while requiring significantly less computational resources than existing methods. In summary, our study provides a new approach to Orbital-Free Density Functional Theory that has the potential to significantly impact materials science and engineering. Our approach offers improved accuracy and computational efficiency, making it a valuable tool for researchers and engineers alike.

In this work, we investigate the hot QCD equations of state in the context of relativistic heavy ion collisions. Our motivation for this research arises from the need to better understand the nature of the high-temperature and high-density matter formed in these collisions. Despite extensive experimental studies, there still remain several unanswered questions regarding the nature of this matter, especially its equation of state. The problem we aim to solve is to determine the equation of state of the quark-gluon plasma phase, the quark-gluon plasma phase that exists at high temperatures and how it relates to the hadronic phase at low temperatures. We use the lattice QCD technique to calculate the equation of state for pure gluon as well as 2 + 1 flavor QCD ensembles. These calculations are performed at finite temperature and non-zero baryon chemical potential. We also use the Polyakov-Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model to apply these calculations to chemical freezeout points. Furthermore, we explore the consequences of these equations of states for the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma in heavy ion collisions by implementing them in hydrodynamic simulations. Our results show that the equation of state of the quark-gluon plasma significantly affects the final state of the collision, particularly in terms of the collective flow and the emission spectra. This work provides valuable insight into the behavior of the quark-gluon plasma and can be used in future experimental studies of relativistic heavy ion collisions.

In this study, we investigate the intercalation of potassium into graphite using a van der Waals density-functional-based method. The main goal of our research is to understand how the interaction between potassium and the graphite layers can be tuned by adding a voltage to the system, which could have implications for the design of better electrical energy storage devices. The methodology involved performing density-functional calculations on different potassium concentrations in graphite, in order to obtain the optimal voltage at which intercalation occurs. We found that the optimal voltage for intercalation is around 2.5V, and that potassium exhibits stronger interlayer adsorption than graphite. Analysis of the electronic properties revealed that potassium intercalation enhances the electronic properties of graphite and induces charge transfer from the potassium atoms to the graphite layers. Furthermore, our results show that the interaction between potassium and the graphite layers is strongly dependent on the orientation of the potassium atoms, with the (001) orientation inducing the strongest adsorption. Overall, our study provides new insights into the intercalation process in graphite, highlighting the potential of van der Waals density-functional-based calculations for the design of new materials for energy storage applications.

In this work, we introduce a new hybrid inflationary model with a smooth transition from inflation to the reheating epoch without the use of an extra scalar field. The model is based on a non-canonical kinetic term and a potential with a shifting parameter. We calculate the slow-roll potential and find that it can satisfy the kinetic term for inflation. We also derive the cosmological observables, such as the scalar and tensor power spectra, the scalar spectral index, and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. The results are consistent with the current observational data from the Planck satellite. The main goal of this work is to address some of the issues present in the standard hybrid inflation models, such as the need for an extra scalar field to obtain a smooth transition from inflation to reheating. With our proposed model, we avoid the complications associated with the introduction of a second scalar field without sacrificing the smoothness of the transition. Finally, we explore the constraints on the model's parameters and find that it is consistent with the current data. Our approach offers a novel way of constructing hybrid inflation models, which could have implications for early universe cosmology. The proposed model can be tested by future experiments and could provide a new avenue for understanding the early universe dynamics.

In this work, we present a study on the Single Transverse-Spin Asymmetry (STSA) in Hadronic Dijet Production. The aim of this study is to investigate the asymmetry in the production of dijets and how it changes under single transverse spin. The results obtained highlight that the STSA is measurable and significant in dijet production. This implies that there is an apparent effect of transverse spin on dijet production. The methodology employed involves Monte Carlo simulations, where we simulate the scattering of polarized protons by unpolarized protons in the center-of-mass frame. We then use the generated data to calculate the spin-dependent cross-section asymmetry. The key idea behind this study is to reveal the extent to which a single transverse spin affects dijet production. The problem that this work aims to solve is to gain insight into how single transverse spin asymmetry affects hadronic dijet production. This is an essential step in advancing our understanding of the spin structure of hadrons. This work contributes to the improvement of our knowledge of the spin-dependent mechanisms and dynamics in hadronic processes. We hope that this study serves as a stepping stone for further research into spin-dependent asymmetries in other hadronic processes.

In this study, we investigate the frequency distribution of semi-major axis of wide binaries, which play a crucial role in the cosmogony and dynamical evolution of planetary systems. The primary goal of our research is to reveal the frequency distribution of these binaries and to explore the implications of this distribution on the theories of star formation and the formation and evolution of planetary systems. The method used in this study involves analyzing data from the Gaia-DR2 survey, which provides accurate astrometric measurements of stars in our galaxy. We focus on wide binaries with separations greater than 1000 AU and use Monte Carlo simulations to estimate the completeness and reliability of our sample. We then fit several theoretical models to the observed distribution of semi-major axis of wide binaries and examine the goodness of fit of each model using statistical tools. Our results show that the frequency distribution of semi-major axis of wide binaries exhibits a power-law behavior, which is consistent with previous studies.
