Interestingly, we find that the slope of the power-law distribution changes for binaries with separations greater than 10,000 AU. We discuss the implications of this result for the formation and evolution of planetary systems, including the possibility of multiple-population scenarios. The motivation for this research stems from the need to better understand the formation and evolution of planetary systems, which are intimately connected to the properties of wide binaries. Our findings provide new insights into the dynamics of stellar systems and contribute to a deeper understanding of the processes that shape the structure of our galaxy. We hope to contribute to the understanding of star formation and the evolution of planetary systems.

In this work, we present two results related to homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomials. Our main motivation is to explore the theory of Hessian polynomials in the context of nilpotent polynomials. The key idea of our research is to study the relationship between the Hessian matrix and the nilpotency of the polynomial. In the first result, we show that if a homogeneous polynomial of degree d is Hessian nilpotent, then so is the polynomial obtained by removing any monomial of degree less than d from the initial polynomial. The proof of this result relies on the algebraic manipulation of the Hessian matrix and the application of some basic linear algebra tools. In the second result, we give an explicit construction of a homogeneous family of Hessian nilpotent polynomials. Specifically, we show that a homogeneous polynomial of degree 2d-2 whose Hessian matrix has rank less than or equal to d-1 is Hessian nilpotent. The construction of this family involves a systematic iteration process that results in a classical result in algebraic geometry known as the "determinantal representation." Our results contribute to the theory of nilpotent polynomials and provide new insights into the interplay between the Hessian matrix and the nilpotency of polynomials. The techniques presented in this work could also be used to study other families of polynomials and matrices.

In this study, our goal was to investigate the evolution of the dust attenuation in the star-forming galaxies with the redshift. We focused specifically on Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) at redshift z~1. Our motivation was to understand the impact of dust attenuation on the observed properties of high-redshift galaxies, which is essential for interpreting their physical properties accurately. We selected a sample of 141 LBGs that were detected in the Central Deep Field South (CDF-S) and used multi-wavelength data to estimate their physical properties, such as stellar mass, star formation rate, and dust attenuation. We compared our results with previous studies on LBGs at lower redshifts. Our analysis showed that the average dust content in the selected sample at z~1 is significantly lower than that at lower redshifts. This implies that the dust content of galaxies decreases with increasing redshift, consistent with previous studies. We also found that the evolution of the dust attenuation is stronger in massive galaxies than in low-mass galaxies. This result suggests that mass plays an important role in the evolution of the dust attenuation in star-forming galaxies. Our research methodology involved a statistical analysis of a large sample of galaxies using multi-wavelength data. Overall, our study provides new insights into the evolution of the dust attenuation in star-forming galaxies and sheds light on the physical processes that govern this evolution.

In this study, we investigate the galaxies hosting strong CaII QSO absorption systems at redshifts lower than 0.5. These systems are characterized by a strong absorption feature in their spectra, which allows us to infer the presence of a dense, cool gas surrounding the absorber. While previous studies suggest that these gas clouds are often associated with massive galaxies, it is still unclear what properties of these galaxies may be responsible for the observed absorption features. We use data from images and spectra obtained with the Keck telescope and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey to identify the host galaxies of 17 strong CaII QSO absorbers. We measure the properties of the host galaxies, such as their stellar masses, star formation rates, and position relative to the absorber line-of-sight. In addition, we investigate the morphology of the galaxies, using an expert-based classification system. Our results suggest that the majority of the strong CaII absorbers are associated with galaxies that are massive and actively star-forming. We also find evidence for a spatial correlation between the absorbers and the galaxies, suggesting the importance of proximity to the absorbers in determining the gas clouds and triggering the absorption phenomena. In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the nature of strong CaI I QSO absorption systems, shedding light on the key role played by the host galaxies in shaping the properties of these gas clouds.

In this study, we investigate the spectral properties of accretion-powered X-ray pulsars using Comptonization models. The key idea is to understand the physical mechanisms that produce the X-ray spectra emitted by these astrophysical systems. Comptonization is a process where the energy of photons is increased through the interaction with high-energy electrons. We compare different Comptonization models with the observed spectra of several X-ray pulsars and derive their spectral properties, such as the temperature and optical depth of the Comptonizing plasma. The motivation for this research is to improve our understanding of the nature of X-ray pulsars and the physics of accretion processes around compact objects. Accretion-powered X-ray pulsars are sources of high-energy radiation and are believed to be powered by the accretion of gas from a companion star onto a neutron star or a black hole. However, the detailed mechanisms that produce their spectra are not well understood and require theoretical modeling. The main problem this work attempts to solve is to identify the physical processes that dominate the X-ray emission of accretion-powered pulsars. Our analysis of Comptonization models provides insights into the properties of the Comptonizing plasma and its relation to the observed spectra. The results shed light on the nature of these astrophysical systems and can be used to improve our models of accretion processes and high-energy radiative transfer.

In this study, we present the results of gas and dust spectra analysis of the D' type symbiotic star HD330036, which is the second brightest in the sky in the 1-5 keV energy range. The aim for this research was to investigate the properties of the hot gas and dust in HD330036, as well as to explore the possibility of searching for exotic objects such as intermediate mass black holes in symbiotic stars. We obtained spectra of the star using the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories, as well as the Keck telescope and Spitzer Space Telescope in the near - and mid-infrared regions. Our analysis of the X-ray spectra revealed the presence of strong, broad emission lines from highly ionized elements such as Fe and Ca, indicating the existence of a hot plasma in the symbiotic environment. Furthermore, we detected a strong dust continuum in the infrared spectra, suggesting that the dust component of this symbiotic system is substantial, which is consistent with previous models. Our results suggest that HD330036 is an exciting system for further investigation into the physics of symbiotic stars and their potential links to black hole formation. This study highlights the importance of the multiwavelength approach for understanding the complex nature of symbiotic star systems.

In this paper, we explore the notion of squashed entanglement for multipartite states and entanglement measures based on the mixed convex roof. The motivation for our research is to deepen our understanding of entanglement, a crucial concept in quantum information theory. Our focus is on the squashed entanglement, which quantifies the correlation between two parts of a quantum state after performing a measurement and discarding one of the outcomes. We extend this notion to multipartite systems and propose a new entanglement measure based on a mixed convex roof construction. This measure is shown to satisfy many desirable properties, including strong additivity. To achieve our results, we use tools from convex optimization and linear algebra, as well as concepts from quantum information theory. Our main contributions are two-fold. First, we establish a framework for multipartite squashed entanglement and propose a new entanglement measure that satisfies key properties. Second, we demonstrate the usefulness of our measure for quantifying entanglement in different quantum scenarios, including those involving hidden non-locality and quantum error correction codes. Overall, our work sheds light on the complex structures of entanglement in multipartite systems and opens new possibilities for future research in quantum information theory.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of the physics of the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) G328.4+0.2, its neutron star, and the progenitor supernova explosion. The main goal of this research is to investigate the connection between the properties of PWNs, their associated neutron stars, and the supernova explosions that formed them. To achieve this, we carried out a multi-wavelength study of the PWN, combining radio, X-ray, and hydrodynamics data. Using the Australia Telescope Compact Array, we obtained high-resolution radio images that reveal the morphology and spectral index of the PWN. We also used data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory to investigate the properties of the X-ray emission from the nebula and its central neutron star. Finally, we performed numerical simulations of the supernova explosion that gave rise to G328.4+0.2, using the FLASH code. Our results provide new insights into the physics of PWNs and their associated neutron stars. We find that the morphology and spectral index of G328.4+0.2 are consistent with a PWN that is expanding into a lower-density environment. The X-ray emission from the PWN and its central neutron star is highly variable and exhibits complex morphological features that reflect the non-thermal nature of the emission. Our supernova simulations suggest that the progenitor star was a massive, rapidly rotating star with a high magnetic field. Overall, our study highlights the importance of multi-wavelength observations and numerical simulations in understanding the complex physics of PWNs, their associated neutron stars, and the supernova explosions that formed them.

In this work, we investigate bond formation and heterogeneous dynamics in adhesive spheres with long-ranged repulsion by conducting a quantitative test of Mode Coupling Theory. The motivation for this work stems from the significant practical applications of adhesion—ranging from biomedical devices to microfluidics—yet the underlying mechanisms of adhesion dynamics remain unclear. Through experimental experiments and numerical simulations, we probe the effects of various system parameters, including adhesive strength, repulsion range, and concentration, on the formation and relaxation of bonds between particles. Our results show that the presence of a long-range repulsion can dramatically affect the bond strength and dynamics, leading to asymmetric bond behavior in some cases. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of adhesion in complex systems and offer a starting point for optimizing design parameters in practical applications. Our investigation also represents a quantitative test of Mode Coupling Theory, highlighting the method's capacity to predict complex non-equilibrium dynamics in adhesive spheres undergoing structural relaxation. Overall, our research sheds light on a crucial aspect of adhesive behavior and offers insights into the broader field of non-equilibrium physics.

We present a study on the diversity of rise times of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) using a decline-rate corrected analysis. One of the main problems in studying SNe Ia is the fact that their light sources appear to be largely homogenous, thus leading to a limited understanding of their underlying physical mechanisms. However, recent studies have suggested that the rise times of SNe Ia may reveal important information about these supernovae. In particular, it has been proposed that SNe Ia rise times exhibit bimodality, with one cluster of SNe having fast rise times and the other having slow rise times. In this work, we investigate whether this bimodality is real or merely an artifact of the analysis methodology. To do so, we use a sample of well-observed low-redshift SNe Ia and employ a decline-rate correction technique that is more robust than existing methods. Our preliminary results suggest that the observed bimodality is likely to be real, and further analysis may help shed light on the physical mechanisms that govern SNe Ia. This work is motivated by the need to better understand the nature of SNe Ia, which are important cosmological probes and play a crucial role in the understanding of dark energy.

In this study, we investigate preferred frame effects in relativistic binary pulsars by analyzing a large set of observational data. We find a characteristic observable signature that indicates the presence of these effects, which could have important implications for the understanding of gravity and the nature of spacetime. Specifically, we find a strong correlation between the apparent spin and orbital periods of the pulsar, which can be explained by the rotation of the binary system in a preferred direction defined by the local environment. Our work aims to solve the problem of identifying and quantifying preferred frame effects in binary pulsar systems, which have been studied extensively for over four decades. Previous attempts to detect these effects have been inconclusive, and their existence has been a subject of debate in the scientific community. By using a novel statistical approach and a more comprehensive dataset, we are able to identify a robust and consistent pattern of preferred frame effects. The motivation for this research is two-fold. Firstly, it is an important test of the theory of general relativity, which predicts the absence of preferred frames and has been validated in many other experiments. Secondly, it provides a unique insight into the geometry and dynamics of binary pulsar systems, which are among the most fascinating and extreme astrophysical objects in the universe. Our results open up new avenues for exploring the nature of gravity and the properties of spacetime, and may ultimately lead to a better understanding of the fundamental laws of nature.

In this study, we aim to determine the optimal window for the 2MASS dipole. The 2MASS dipole is a variation in the cosmic microwave background that is used to measure the velocity of the Sun with respect to the reference frame of the Universe. This measurement is essential for accurately determining the cosmic microwave background spectrum and allowing for deviations from the standard model of cosmology. However, determining the optimal window for the 2MASS dipole is a non-trivial task. Our key idea is to use a Bayesian approach to estimate the optimal window. This method involves creating a model for the dipole signal and comparing it to observed data. We use a Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach to sample the posterior distribution of the model parameters, which allows us to estimate the optimal window on the basis of the evidence. Our methodology involved analyzing the data from the WMAP and Planck missions and comparing it to our model for the dipole signal. We found that the optimal window for the 2MASS dipole is between 50 and 80 degrees, which is consistent with previous studies. In conclusion, our study presents a Bayesian approach for determining the optimal window for the 2MASS dipole. Our model for the dipole signal allowed us to estimate the optimal window on the basis of the evidence. Our results will assist us in refining measurements of the cosmic microwave background spectrum and testing the standard model of cosmology.

In this work, we investigate the accretion origin of the Milky Way's stellar halo. Our aim is to understand the formation of the Milky Way's halo through various accreted systems. We analyze the GAIA data, and investigate the kinematics and metallicity of the accreted stellar systems. Our key idea is to explore the possibility of multiple accretion events forming the Milky Way's halo. We propose a theoretical model based on hierarchical merging of dwarf galaxies to describe the Milky Way's halo's formation. Our methodology includes statistical analysis of the observed data sets and simulations using N-body models. The results of our analysis support the hypothesis that the Milky Way's stellar halo has an accretion origin. We find that the accreted stellar systems contributed significantly to the halo and that their contribution increased gradually over time. Our research provides a new understanding of the formation of galaxy halos, which has essential implications for the study of the Milky Way and the formation of other galaxies in the universe. This work establishes the necessity of including multiple accretion histories in the formation of any galactic halo.

In this study, we investigate "hidden" Seyfert 2 galaxies, i.e., those that are not easily detected using conventional methods, in the Chandra Deep Field North. We employ an X-ray stacking analysis to reveal these elusive objects, using data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, optical/near-infrared spectroscopy, and multi-wavelength observations. Our objective is to understand the role of these obscured active galactic nuclei (AGN) in galaxy evolution and their contribution to the cosmic X-ray background radiation. Motivated by the fact that more than half of the universe's AGN activity is obscured by gas and dust, we attempt to identify these hidden Seyfert 2 galaxies and study their properties. We utilize X-ray stacking analysis since it helps to increase the signal-to-noise ratio of faint sources and recover information from undetected sources. We confirm the existence of "hidden" Seyfert 2 galaxies in the Chandra Deep Field North by detecting their high-energy emission, which is a useful diagnostic of AGN activity. This work attempts to contribute to a better understanding of the AGN population and their significance in galaxy evolution, as well as to provide insight into the origin of the cosmic X-ray background. Our results highlight the importance of X-ray observations in detecting obscured AGN activity, and contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the nature of the observed cosmic X-ray background radiation.

In this work, we revisit the outbursts of EX Hydrae, a cataclysmic variable system exhibiting frequent outbursts. Our study is motivated by the recent observations made by other researchers which led to the discovery of an unusual outburst pattern in this system. We hypothesize that the observed outburst pattern can be explained by the existence of different accretion regimes that are triggered when the luminosity increases over a certain threshold. To test our hypothesis, we analyzed new observations made with the Chandra X-ray Observatory during the 2015/2016 outburst of EX Hydrae. We used spectral and timing analyses to study the evolution of the system during the outburst. Our results confirm the presence of two accretion regimes during the outburst, supporting our initial hypothesis. We find that the transition between the two regimes occurs at a luminosity of ~10^34 erg/s. Moreover, we show that the properties of the two regimes are consistent with the disk instability model. We also report on the detection of a hard X-ray emission component in the system, which may be related to non-thermal plasma emission powered by magnetic fields. Our findings shed new light on the physical mechanisms underlying the outburst behaviour of cataclysmic variable systems.

In this study, we investigate the evolution of the giant planets in the solar system, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, during the formation of the solar system. We explore the relationship between the initial locations of the proto-planets in the gaseous protoplanetary disk and their current orbital architectures. Our methodology is based on numerical simulations, using a combination of theoretical and experimental simulations, and an analytical model of the migration of the proto-planets in the gaseous disk. Our results show that the giant planets did not form in their current orbits, but migrated to their initial positions in the protoplanetary disk. The process of migration was caused by interactions with the gas disk , which resulted in the reshaping of the early solar system environment. We find that the initial evolution of the giant planets was chaotic and unpredictable, with the gas disk playing a crucial role in shaping their final orbits. The study aims to solve the problem of understanding the formation and evolution of the solar system, and in particular, the giant planets' current orbital configuration. By investigating their initial positions and migration paths, our study provides insights into the early history of the solar system and its formation. The results have implications for exoplanet studies and provide a better understanding of the evolution of exoplanetary systems.

In this paper, we present optimal bounds for the Green function of half-spaces for the relativistic $\alpha$-stable process. The goal of this work is to develop an understanding of the behavior of the Green function of the half-space for this particular type of process. The motivation behind this research stems from the fact that the Green function is a fundamental quantity in the statistical analysis of stochastic processes, and understanding its properties is central in harmonizing various areas of mathematical analysis. In addition, the $\alpha$-stable process is a well-known stochastic process in signal processing, finance, and physics, and developing optimal bounds for its Green function has the potential to shed new light on its statistical and spatial properties. A key idea in our work is to construct two-sided bounds for the Green function using refined methods for potentials of signed measures. These bounds provide a more precise estimate of the behavior of the Green function close to the boundary and reveal important new asymptotic regimes. Our methodology involves delicate analysis of positive and negative potentials of suitable measures and careful control of the constants arising from the estimates. Overall, our work is a significant contribution to the study of $\alpha$-stable processes and has the potential to impact a wide range of fields where these processes arise.

In this study, we investigated the magnetism and thermodynamics of spin-1/2 Heisenberg diamond chains in a magnetic field. Our aim was to solve the problem of understanding the fundamental properties of these chains and how they behave under a magnetic field. We utilized a variety of techniques such as the Bethe ansatz and Quantum Monte Carlo simulations to numerically model the system. Our results showed that the magnetic field strongly influences the magnetization of the diamond chain. Specifically, we found that when the magnetic field is perpendicular to the chain, the magnetization displays a plateau at a value close to the saturation magnetization. On the other hand, when the magnetic field is parallel to the chain, the magnetization exhibits a linear dependence on the field. Moreover, we found that the thermodynamics of the diamond chain can be evaluated via the study of entanglement entropy. Our calculations showed that the entanglement entropy scales logarithmically with the length of the chain, highlighting the chain’s topological properties. In conclusion, our study sheds light on the magnetism and thermodynamic properties of spin-1/2 Heisenberg diamond chains, and demonstrates the versatility of these chains for future research in areas such as quantum computing and condensed matter physics.

In this study, we investigate the origin of collimated outflows in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) using the magnetar-driven bubble mechanism. Our motivation lies in the fact that despite extensive research, the exact cause of collimated outflows in GRBs remains unclear. To understand this phenomenon, we performed numerical simulations of the jet formation from a magnetar-driven wind bubble and compared our results with those from previous studies. Our approach included simulations of the magnetar's outflow interacting with the surrounding medium in a 3D space to simulate the formation and evolution of a jet. Our simulations revealed the development of a jet, which was accompanied by a dominant non-thermal emission and a noticeable afterglow. Our findings indicate that the magnetar-driven bubble mechanism is a plausible explanation for the formation of collimated outflows in GRBs. The mechanism suggests that the jet formation is driven by the magnetar's wind, which forms a bubble around it. The bubble interacts with dense material surrounding the bubble, creating a jet that emerges along the region of the weakest magnetar outflow. In conclusion, our study provides evidence supporting the magnetar-driven wind bubble as a significant mechanism responsible for the collimated outflows in GRBs. Additionally, our findings can be useful in explaining other astrophysical phenomena that involve collimated outflows.

The motivation for our research work is to explore and further understand critical phenomena and the behavior of phase transition in Ising meanfield dynamics. More specifically, we are interested in investigating the manifestation of tricritical points in the dynamic phase boundary. Our work is concerned with identifying inflection points as a form of tricritical points, which we believe can provide insight into the nature of dynamic phase transitions. The key idea behind our work is to apply a rigorous mathematical and computational methodology to model Ising models and explore their behavior under changing external conditions. The methodology we employ includes numerical simulations and statistical analysis of the model's behavior. By studying the manifestation of tricritical points in the dynamic phase boundary of Ising meanfield dynamics, our research aims to solve the problem of understanding the nature and behavior of phase transition in complex systems. Our findings may provide new insights into the underlying mechanisms of critical phenomena, and have potential applications in diverse fields such as materials science, condensed matter physics, and information theory. In summary, our research aims to contribute to the scientific understanding of complex phenomena by investigating the manifestation of tricritical points in the dynamic phase boundary of Ising meanfield dynamics, utilizing numerical simulations and statistical analysis to analyze the behavior and transition of phases under changing external conditions.

In this study, we present an improved version of the quantum hard-sphere ground-state equation of state (EOS) that accurately describes both the low-density and high-density regimes. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that the current hard-sphere EOS is known to be inadequate in describing certain aspects of materials such as dense uranium and other simple metals. Previous attempts have focused on improving subsets of the EOS rather than the whole EOS, which has led to inconsistencies and limitations in predicting the thermodynamic properties of these materials. The key idea behind our improved EOS is to incorporate a more accurate description of quantum mechanical effects. Specifically, we utilize a new analytical expression for the quantum correction factor, which accounts for the wave nature of the particles. To test the validity and accuracy of our improved EOS, we carry out a series of Monte Carlo simulations of hard-sphere -like interactions with varying densities. Our results show that our improved EOS is in excellent agreement with the simulation data over a wide range of densities. Overall, our study has provided an effective theoretical tool that can accurately predict the structural and thermodynamic behavior of complex systems such as dense metals. Our analytical expression for the quantum correction factor has enabled us to create a more accurate and predictable EOS, which is a significant step towards improving the quantitative description of the thermodynamic properties of many materials that have hard-sphere-like interactions.

In this work, we construct a family of vector-valued modular functions for the modular group and the hypergeometric equation. Our main motivation is to provide a new perspective on the theory of modular forms and their application to hypergeometric equations. Our approach is based on the theory of representations of Lie groups and Lie algebras. We derive a family of vector-valued modular forms of weight one-half with respect to the action of the modular group. These functions are solutions of a set of first-order linear differential equations with polynomial coefficients that are in involution with the modular group. We also construct a family of vector-valued modular forms of arbitrary weight one-half to satisfy a second-order differential equation that is a linear combination of the hypergeometric equation and its dual. Our key contribution is the development of a methodology for constructing vector-valued modular forms as solutions to linear differential equations with polynomial coefficients. This methodology allows us to obtain explicit expressions for the vector-valued modular forms in terms of hypergeometric functions. We also provide a connection between our results and the classical theory of modular forms and their applications in number theory and algebraic geometry. In summary, our work provides a new approach for understanding the relationship between modular forms and hypergeometric equations. Our results have potential applications in the study of automorphic forms, algebraic geometry and combinatorics.

In this study, we investigate the properties of a five-quark hadronic molecule using lattice QCD simulations. The five-quark state consists of two positively charged quarks, two negatively charged quarks, and one neutral quark. We find that this hadronic molecule has a binding energy of approximately 25 MeV and a radius of 0.8 fm. Additionally, studying the meson-meson scattering data, we found that this state is a possible candidate for a resonance structure near the D*D* threshold. The methodology is based on lattice QCD simulations, where the space-time is discretized and the QCD equations are solved numerically. We use a fine lattice spacing and large volumes to ensure good control over the systematic errors. By studying various correlation functions and their energies, we extract the low-lying spectrum of the hadronic molecule and estimate the error bars by using jackknife re-sampling methods. The motivation for this work is that despite several years of experimental investigations involving meson-meson interactions, relatively little is known concerning the existence of states that are composed of more than three quarks. This work can help to shed light on the properties of five-quark hadrons and their possible resonances. Furthermore, our findings have important implications in the context of multiquark states and their role in the hadron spectrum.

We present here the results of our research on the determination of the form factors for the semileptonic B0 -> D*- l+ nu_l decay and of the CKM matrix element |V_cb|. This work is motivated by the need to constrain theories and models on the weak interaction in the Standard Model of particle physics, as well as to contribute to the measurement of fundamental parameters of the universe. In order to carry out this investigation, we used data obtained from the Belle II experiment, which records collisions between electron-positron beams. The B0 mesons and leptons involved in these events decay into D*- mesons and leptons, which can be detected and measured by the experiment. We applied a method based on the Heavy Quark Effective Theory to extract the form factors by analyzing the distribution of the invariant mass of the D*-lepton system. We then combined these results with a precise measurement of the B0 lifetimes, and applied the theoretical framework of the relativistic corrections to the decay rate equation, to obtain a value of |V_cb| for the CKM matrix element |V_cb|. This analysis yielded a significant improvement in the precision of the form factors determination, which represents an important contribution to the state-of-the-art in experimental particle physics. The value of |V_cb| obtained is consistent with the results obtained by other experiments, and represents a valuable contribution for the ongoing effort to determine the parameters of the weak interaction in the Standard Model with greater accuracy.

We present a study on the X-ray properties of the most-luminous quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Quasars with high luminosity provide an opportunity to study the physics of the accretion disk around a supermassive black hole, and their X-ray properties are essential for understanding the emission mechanisms and the interaction between the disk and the surrounding environment. Using the archival data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, we analyzed the X-ray spectra of 36 most-luminous quasars at z>2.5. We found that most of the quasars in our sample have X-ray luminosities exceeding 10^45 ergs s^-1, with a peak at ~10^46 ergs s^-1. We also found that the majority of the quasars in our sample have a power-law spectrum, with a photon index ranging from 1.5 to 2.5. Our study attempts to address the following questions: How does the accretion disk produce the high X-ray luminosity in the most-luminous quasars? What is the spectral distribution of the X-ray emission? Are there any differences between the X-ray properties of the most-luminous quasars and those of less-luminous ones? Our key methodology involved X-ray spectral fitting using XSPEC, a widely used X-ray spectral analysis package. Our results show that the X-ray properties of the most-luminous quasars are consistent with the standard accretion disk model, implying that the disk is the dominant source of X-ray emission. The power-law spectrum suggests that the Comptonization process is important in the X-ray production. Our findings provide important constraints on the physical processes in the accretion disk of the most-luminous quasars and give insights into the evolution of supermassive black holes in the early universe.

In this paper, we present a passivity-based stability criterion for a class of interconnected systems and apply it to biochemical reaction networks. The motivation for this research stems from the need to better understand the dynamics of complex systems, particularly those found in biological processes. The past decade has seen an increase in the study of biochemical reaction networks, due to its relevance to many important biological functions, such as metabolic processes and regulatory systems. We begin our analysis with a brief survey of the literature on the stability of interconnected systems, highlighting the importance of passivity-based approaches. We then introduce our passivity-based stability criterion for interconnected systems and demonstrate its effectiveness in two different applications to biochemical reaction networks. The results obtained show that our approach is capable of better characterizing the stability properties of such networks compared to existing approaches. Our key idea is to leverage passivity -based stability criterion to better understand the dynamics of interconnected systems by extending the notion of Lyapunov functions. Our methodology consists of a combination of analytical and computational tools, including Lyapunov function construction and simulation-based methods. We believe that the passivity-based stability criterion presented in this work has the potential to be applied to a wider range of systems beyond biochemical reaction networks, and thus contribute to the broader understanding of complex interconnected systems.

We present our findings on IIB backgrounds with five-form flux, which have important implications for string theory and its compactifications. Our work provides a deeper understanding of the structure and properties of IIB backgrounds with the five-form flux and its impact on the geometry and physics of these backgrounds. At the core of our research is the identification of a new class of solutions that exhibit supersymmetry and are supported by the five-form flux. We find that these backgrounds have non-vanishing flux and satisfy the conditions required for a non-trivial background geometry to be consistent with supergravity. In particular, we observe that the geometry of these backgrounds is characterized by a singular metric that is, however, regular in its near-horizon limit. Our work addresses a fundamental problem in the study of IIB backgrounds with flux, namely the lack of a comprehensive understanding of their properties and their significance in the context of string theory. By providing a more detailed and comprehensive analysis of these backgrounds, we aim to fill this gap and contribute to the ongoing efforts to develop a more complete and unified theory of string theory. Our investigation combines a range of analytical and numerical techniques, including the use of differential geometry, algebraic topology, and computer simulations. We employ a variety of mathematical tools and concepts, such as the analysis of moduli spaces and the analysis of spectral properties, to derive and validate our results. Overall, we provide important insight into the structure and properties of IIB backgrounds with five-form flux, which have important implications for the understanding of string theory and the nature of the universe.

In this work, we present a theoretical resolution of magnetic reconnection in high energy plasmas. Our study focuses on understanding the underlying mechanisms that govern magnetic reconnection, which is one of the most fundamental phenomena in astrophysical and space plasmas. To achieve this goal, we applied analytical and numerical methods based on the principles of plasma physics and magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). We used these methods to investigate the influence of magnetic fields on particle transport, energy dissipation, and plasma flow dynamics. Our study demonstrated that current sheet thinning and instability in high-energy plasmas are the key factors that trigger magnetic reconnection. We also discovered that the interaction between plasma flows and magnetic fields plays a significant role in the reconnection process. We further demonstrated that the efficiency of magnetic reconnection is proportional to the magnetic field intensity and the plasma flow velocity. These findings have significant implications for understanding the dynamics of plasma systems in a variety of astrophysical and space environments. Our work contributes significantly to the ongoing efforts in developing a comprehensive theory of magnetic reconnection in high-energy plasmas.

In this study, we investigated the impact of dimensionless numbers on the efficiency of MRI-induced turbulent transport in a fluid system. The fundamental goal of our research was to understand the nature of the turbulent transport process and identify the key factors that dictate its efficiency. We employed numerical simulations and analytical calculations to quantify the effects of magnetic Reynolds number and Prandtl number on the transport properties of MRI-induced turbulent transport systems. Our results showed that the magnetic Reynolds number played a significant role in the turbulent transport process. Specifically, we found that higher magnetic Reynolds numbers promoted more efficient transport behavior, while lower magnetic Reynolds numbers exhibited more stable and less turbulent fluid behavior. Additionally, the Prandtl number had an even stronger impact on the transport properties, with lower Prandtl numbers resulting in highly efficient transport behavior. The key idea behind our research was to understand the underlying physics behind the MRI-induced transport process and identify the key parameters that govern its efficiency. By investigating the effects of dimensionless numbers on the transport properties, we were able to provide valuable insights into the fundamental behavior of the system. Overall, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the MRI-induced turbulent transport process and highlights the importance of dimensionless numbers in controlling its efficiency. Our work will serve as a valuable foundation for future studies aimed at optimizing the efficiency of MRI-induced transport systems in a variety of applications.

In this work, we present molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to study the spatial scale of low energy excitations in a simple polymer system. Our study is motivated by the interest in understanding the fundamental mechanisms underlying energy transfer in molecular systems. The potential applications of this knowledge range from energy harvesting to the design of future materials with desired functionalities. To achieve our goal, we employ the MD technique to analyze the motions of chains under low energy excitations at low temperatures. Key ideas of the study involve quantification of the mobility of polymer chains in response to thermal perturbations, identification of characteristic length scales for the energy transfer in the system, and the analysis of the correlation between chain dynamics and the local environment of molecules. Our results show a clear dependence of the mobility of chains on the local molecular packing density, indicating that the spatial scale of the energy transfer is a function of the local packing density. We observe that chain motions are hindered in densely packed regions and are rather free in regions where molecules are less packed. Our study provides new insights into the correlation between local structure and energy transfer in polymer systems. Our results may be useful in designing materials that are capable of controlled energy transfer, for example, in thermoelectric materials.

In this study, we aimed to explore the question of whether there is evidence for a Hubble bubble by examining the nature of Type Ia supernova colors and dust in external galaxies. The idea of a Hubble bubble, a hypothetical feature of our universe consisting of an underdensity on very large scales, has been proposed as an explanation for the observed acceleration of the universe. Our research seeks to provide additional insight and understanding about this possible phenomenon. To do so, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the nature of Type Ia supernova colors and dust in a sample of external galaxies. Our methodology involved using multi-color observations obtained from multiple telescopes to assess the reddening of light by dust in order to obtain a better understanding of the properties and distribution of dust. Our results suggest that there may be evidence for a Hubble bubble, as the properties of dust in the external galaxies show a similar degree of reddening as dust in our own galaxy. We also found that the colors of Type Ia supernovae vary significantly across different galaxies, indicating the presence of varying degrees of dust. Overall, our study provides important insights into the nature of Type Ia supernova colors and dust in external galaxies. Our findings suggest that further research is needed to fully understand the nature of a Hubble bubble, and may have important implications for our understanding of the larger structure of the universe.

Our research on energy conditions and current acceleration of the universe aimed to investigate the validity of the energy conditions in light of the current accelerating expansion rate of the universe. The accelerating expansion of the universe is one of the biggest challenges in modern cosmology and is generally attributed to dark energy. The accelerating expansion prompts a thoughtful reconsideration of the validity of the energy conditions, which are the set of constraints on the energy-momentum tensor that are required to ensure the validity of general relativity. Our work attempted to advance the understanding of the connection between the energy conditions and the acceleration of the universe by introducing a new class of energy conditions called quasi-average energy conditions. The quasi-average energy conditions are an extension of the averaged energy condition that are based on the assumption that the cosmic expansion can be considered locally homogeneous and isotropic. We found that, compared to the averaged energy conditions, the quasi-average energy conditions are valid for a wider range of matter contents that lead to accelerated expansion. Moreover, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the transformation rules of energy conditions under conformal transformations, which was essential in our study of dark energy' behavior. Our findings provide new insights into the validity of the energy conditions and their relationship with the acceleration of the universe, and would facilitate more accurate predictions of the behavior of dark energy.

In this work, we propose a scheme for continuous quantum error correction (CQEC) in the presence of non-Markovian decoherence. Our main goal is to improve the resilience of quantum systems to environmental fluctuations, minimizing the likelihood of decoherence propagation and maximizing the fidelity of quantum information processing. Our approach is based on a hybrid approach combining Hamiltonian evolution and quantum measurement, where the evolution is driven by a feedback control that monitors the environment and corrects the quantum state accordingly. We first motivate our research by highlighting the need to overcome the limitations of traditional quantum error correction (QEC) methods, which are based on discrete measurements and short time intervals. In contrast, CQEC provides a continuous quantum error correction that enhances the stability and prolongs the coherence time of the quantum system, enabling real-time error detection and correction with minimal disruption to the computational process. However, the non-Markovian nature of decoherence poses a challenge due to the indefinite memory of the quantum system and the complex correlations between the system and its surroundings. Our methodology employs a master equation approach, where we derive a stochastic master equation for the quantum system in the presence of non-Markovian noise. We then use a feedback control loop that acts on the system based on the information provided by the measurement outcomes to actively correct the quantum state. Our results show that the proposed CQEC scheme can achieve better error suppression rates and higher fidelity compared to standard QEC methods, especially in the case of non-Markovian decoherence. This has important implications for practical quantum computing and other quantum information processing tasks, where reliability and longevity are crucial.

We present the results of our investigation into transit-selected exoplanet candidates from the MACHO survey. The MACHO survey detected microlensing events that may indicate the presence of exoplanets orbiting their host stars. Our study aimed to identify and characterize these exoplanet candidates by searching for transit signals in their light source. By using the photometric data from the MACHO survey and transit-fitting techniques, we were able to confirm six exoplanet candidates out of 34 that were initially detected by microlensing. Our analysis revealed that three of the confirmed exoplanets are Jupiter-like planets and two are Saturn-like giants, while the remaining three are Neptune-like planets. The purpose of our study was to contribute to the growing body of knowledge regarding the diversity of exoplanets and provide insight into the formation and evolution of these systems. The study also aimed to demonstrate the importance of combining different observational methods to discover and confirm exoplanets. Our methodology involved the use of the Transit Analysis Package, which employs MCMC algorithms to model the transit events and estimate the parameters of the exoplanets, such as their radii and periods. We also conducted a comparative analysis to compare the properties of the confirmed exoplanets with those of other known exoplanets. In conclusion, our investigation of transit-selected exoplanets from the MACHO survey has resulted in the confirmation of six exoplanet candidates, providing valuable information about the diversity of exoplanets and the methods used to detect them. Our study highlights the importance of utilizing multiple observational techniques to expand our understanding of exoplanetary systems and their properties.

In this study, we investigate the behavior of Na I D resonance lines in main sequence late-type stars, which can provide crucial information about stellar atmospheres and chemical abundances. Our approach involves analyzing high-resolution spectra of a sample of 14 main sequence late-type stars covering a range of atmospheric properties, including effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity. By employing a spectroscopic modeling technique, we aimed to extract accurate line parameters, such as equivalent widths, central wavelength, and line depth, from the spectra. We also assessed the impact of various atmospheric parameters on the Na I D line strength. The main problem that this work attempts to solve is the lack of a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of Na I D resonance lines in main sequence late-type stars and their variations with atmospheric conditions. This, in turn, limits our ability to determine accurate stellar parameters and chemical abundances from these spectral features. Our results show that the Na I D lines are highly sensitive to effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity, with a complex interplay between these parameters. We also found that the line profiles exhibit deviations from the classical Voigt model due to the presence of non-thermal motions in the photosphere. Our study provides crucial insights into the behavior of Na I D resonance lines in main sequence late-type stars , with implications for spectroscopic analysis and stellar astrophysics.

In this work, we investigate the behavior of spherically symmetric spacetimes in the context of f(R) gravity theory. We aim to understand the implications of the modified gravity equations in the presence of a spherically symmetric solution, which is a highly non-trivial problem. Our approach consists of analyzing two distinct cases: a Schwarzschild black hole and a general spherically symmetric solution. Using standard methods from general relativity, we derive the modified Einstein equations and analyze the resulting equations of motion for each case. Our results demonstrate that f(R) gravity can have important consequences for spherically symmetric spacetimes. Specifically, we find that while the Schwarzschild metric remains a vacuum solution, the general spherically symmetric solution is significantly affected by the gravitational modifications. Overall, our work provides a new understanding of the behavior of spherically symmetric spacetimes in modified gravity theories, filling a gap in the literature and contributing to the ongoing study of gravitational theories beyond general relativity.

Our research delves into the phenomenon of geometry-induced asymmetric diffusion, where the geometry of a medium can cause particles to exhibit directional preference in their movement. We aim to understand the fundamental mechanisms of this phenomenon and explore its potential applications in various fields. The motivation behind our research stems from the ubiquitous presence of geometry in the natural world, ranging from complex biological systems to simple physical environments. The ability to predict and control particle behavior in these geometries can have far-reaching implications in fields such as drug delivery, microfluidics, and environmental science. The problem we aim to solve is to develop a comprehensive model of asymmetric diffusion in complex geometries. Previous work in this area has focused on simple geometries and has relied on simplifying assumptions, limiting its applicability. We utilize a combination of analytical and computational techniques to derive a generalized model that can account for various geometrical features. Our key idea is to consider the effects of both geometric confinement and asymmetry simultaneously, rather than treating them as two distinct phenomena. Our model takes into account the non-uniform density of particles in the confined space and the interplay between particle-particle and particle-boundary interactions. Our methodology involves mathematical analysis and simulations to test our model's predictions against experiments and previous findings. We anticipate that our work will provide insights into the fundamental physics of geometry-induced asymmetric diffusion and pave the way for designing novel applications in various fields.

In this work, we explore the cosmological applications of a wavelet analysis on the sphere. Prior to our analysis, spatial data on the sphere had to be projected onto a planar grid, leading to loss of valuable information and introducing distortions. However, wavelets provide an orthogonal solution that permit the analysis of non-periodic data without the loss of resolution. By using wavelets on the sphere, we aim to reduce the loss of information and improve the accuracy of cosmological observational data analysis. Our research involved the application of wavelet transforms on temperature maps of the cosmic microwave background radiation, a field of study that allows us to understand the early universe's origin and evolution. We obtained highly detailed maps of anisotropies and other features in regions with unexpected temperature variations. Our results show that wavelet analysis on the sphere is a powerful tool for detecting local features in the cosmic microwave background radiation and studying their potential non-Gaussianity, which could reveal crucial information about the early universe's inflationary phase. The motivation behind this research is to advance our understanding of the universe's evolution from its early stages by using the most robust statistical techniques to analyze cosmological observational data. By introducing wavelet analysis on the sphere, we can access more information and significantly improve the quality of data analysis, leading to more detailed and accurate cosmological studies.

In this work, we investigate the emergence of Cooper pairs, d-wave duality, and their impact on the phase diagram of cuprate superconductors. These superconductors are known for their unconventional superconductivity, which deviates from the standard BCS theory. Our motivation for this research is to gain a deeper understanding of the phenomena involved in high-temperature superconductivity. Based on extensive theoretical and experimental studies, we find that the d-wave symmetry of the superconducting gap is crucial for the unconventional behavior of cuprate superconductors. This leads us to propose a model for the formation of Cooper pairs in these materials, incorporating both spin and charge density waves. Our calculations show that these fluctuations create a favorable environment for the emergence of Cooper pairs with d-wave symmetry, which stabilizes the superconducting state. Moreover, we investigate the interplay between superconductivity and other competing phases, such as magnetism and charge density waves. Our results demonstrate that the d-wave duality plays a critical role in the phase diagram, leading to complex interactions between these various phases and the superconductivity. In summary, our work sheds light on the emergence of Cooper pairs with d-wave symmetry and their impact on the unconventional superconductivity in cuprate superconductors. This research has critical implications for the development of new materials with improved superconducting properties. We look forward to sharing our findings with others.

In this study, we investigate the influence of the cylindrical shape of the nucleosomes and H1 defects on the properties of chromatin. The motivation for this work stems from the fact that chromatin plays a crucial role in DNA replication and gene expression, and any alteration in its properties can have significant consequences on various cellular processes. Previous research has established that the cylindrical shape of nucleosomes is important for the formation of compact chromatin fibers and the efficiency of transcription. Furthermore, H1 linker histones have been shown to regulate chromatin structure and accessibility to transcription factors. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these phenomena remain poorly understood. In our study, we employed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the effects of cylindrical shape and H1 defects on chromatin properties. Our results show that cylindrical nucleosomes favor the formation of regular chromatin fibers and promote compaction, while H1 defects promote the formation of compact chromatin fibers and decrease fiber density. We also observed that H1 defects induce local chromatin unfolding, leading to enhanced accessibility to transcription factors. In conclusion, our study sheds light on the important role of cylindrical nucleosomes and H1 linker histones in chromatin structure and accessibility to transcription factors. These findings may have important implications for understanding the regulation of chromatin and gene expression and its role in various cellular processes.

In this study, we investigate the locomotor activity rhythms of two sympatric parasitoid insects, Eupelmus orientalis and Eupelmus vuilleti. These Hymenopterans belong to the family Eupelmidae and are known to be natural enemies of several insect species, such as the xylophagous beetles. The main aim of this study is to compare the daily activity patterns of these two species, and to explore the possibility of their temporal partition, which may help them avoid competition and reduce mortality risks. To achieve this goal, we use a combination of techniques, including video recording, image analysis, and statistical analyses. Our results show that both species exhibit diurnal behavior, with a peak activity in the early morning. However, whereas the Eupelmus vuilleti activity level is homogeneous throughout the day, E. orientalis presents a significant decrease in activity during the hottest hours of the day. This difference in temporal partitioning could be the outcome of differences in their feeding habits and habitat s. Overall, this study provides new insights into the behavioral ecology of parasitoid wasps and may contribute to the development of more efficient biocontrol strategies against xylophagous insect pests.

In this work, we focus on the study of supersymmetric Q solitons of arbitrary genus. The main motivation of this research is to better understand non-perturbative effects in quantum field theory. Specifically, we investigate soliton solutions in the context of four-dimensional super Yang-Mills theory and explore their properties in depth. Our methodology is based on using techniques from algebraic geometry and complex analysis to construct a moduli space of solitons that are bound to certain differential equations, known as the ADHM equations. By studying the geometry of this moduli space, we are able to extract information about the solitons, including their mass, charge, and stability properties. Our key idea is to generalize previous work on soliton solutions of genus zero to arbitrary genus, allowing us to explore a wider range of possibilities and more complex topological structures. This provides a deeper understanding of soliton dynamics and their physical implications. The main result of this work is the construction of a family of supersymmetric Q solitons of arbitrary genus that are stable and non-trivial. These solitons have interesting properties, such as confinement of mass and charge and mutual non-locality, and provide insight into the rich dynamics of supersymmetric field theories. Our work thus contributes to the broader understanding of non-perturbative phenomena, which has important implications for various fields of physics.

In this work, we investigate the statistical properties of giant pulses from the Crab pulsar, with the aim of understanding their origin and mechanisms of production. Giant pulses are rare, extremely bright pulses that occur sporadically among the hundreds of regular pulses emitted by the Crab. Due to their brightness, they provide a unique opportunity to study the inner workings of the pulsar and its surrounding environment. Our research attempts to address several key questions: What are the statistical properties of giant pulses? What fraction of the total emission does their contribution represent? Are they a result of a different physical mechanism than regular pulses? We use high-time-resolution data from the Crab pulsar observed with the Parkes radio telescope in Australia. We analyze nearly all of the individual giant pulses to study their statistical properties, such as pulse intensity and duration. In addition, we perform a detailed comparison of regular and giant pulses in order to identify any differences in their characteristics. The motivation for this research arises from the need to gain a better understanding of the Crab pulsar, one of the most studied pulsars in the sky. Furthermore, giant pulses have recently been shown to be a useful tool for testing theories of pulsar emission and structure. A better understanding of their statistical properties could provide important insights into the mechanisms responsible for these fascinating phenomena.

In this work, we investigate the possibility of the production of magnetic energy through macroscopic turbulence in afterglows of Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs). We propose that the turbulent motions triggered by the interaction between the GRB outflow and the surrounding medium can generate significant amounts of magnetic energy. To explore this concept, we perform magnetohydrodynamic simulations of a relativistic outflow propagating through an ambient medium. Our results show that the turbulence induced by the interaction triggers a dynamo mechanism that amplifies magnetic fields, leading to the production of magnetic energy. The strength of the magnetic field produced is found to be proportional to the level of turbulence, implying that larger turbulence translates to higher magnetic energy production. Our work provides a potential resolution to the long-standing problem of how magnetic fields are generated in turbulent astrophysical environments. By introducing the idea that turbulence can trigger the dynamo mechanism, we suggest that magnetic energy production could be a significant player in GRB afterglows. Our methodology involves the use of numerical simulations to investigate the physical mechanisms governing the turbulent interactions. The results of this study shed light on the complex interplay between hydrodynamics and magnetic fields in astrophysical systems. Overall, this study contributes to the advancement of our understanding of the physics of GRBs and magnetic field generation in turbulent systems.

We present the discovery and characterization of XO-2b, a transiting hot Jupiter exoplanet orbiting a metal-rich common star in a low motion binary system. Our study is motivated by the need to understand the formation and evolution of hot Jupiters in metal-rich environments and the role of binary companions in the evolution of exoplanetary systems. The XO-2b planet was detected using the transit method, and its parameters were derived from a joint analysis of radial velocity and photometric data. The host binary star has a separation of 6,700 AU and a mass of [Fe/H]=+0.27, making XO-2b one of the most metal-rich exoplanets discovered to date. We find that XO-2b has a radius of 1.06 ± 0.03 R_J and a mass of 0.597 <unk> 0.025 M_J, resulting in a density of 0.76 ± 0.05 g cm^-3. Its host star has a mass of 1.16 ± 0.04 M_sun and a radius of 1.09 ± 0.04 R_sun. Our work adds to the growing body of evidence that metal-rich environments are favorable for the formation of hot Jupiters. Additionally, the presence of the binary companion at a large separation suggests that hot Jupiters may have migrated inward due to planet-planet -planet interactions or Kozai-Lidov oscillations. Our study provides a unique opportunity to further understand the diversity of exoplanetary systems in binary star environments and their formation and evolution processes.

We present an experimental study on the controlled collisions of a single atom and ion, whereby the relative velocities, impact parameters, and scattering angles are precisely controlled by movable trapping potentials. This novel trapping architecture allows for the precise control of the ion-atom interaction and collisional dynamics to an unprecedented level of accuracy, providing a robust experimental platform for exploring ion-atom interactions and quantum dynamics. We use a combination of ion cooling and trapping techniques coupled with electrostatic potentials to guide and trap the ion and atom, respectively. By adjusting the relative positions of these potentials, we generate controlled collisions between the two particles. The time-of-flight of the scattered particles is recorded and analyzed to reveal the collision dynamics. Our experimental results demonstrate the ability to finely tune the impact parameters and scattering angles in the collision process, which can be exploited for a wide range of applications, from quantum information processing to the study of fundamental physics. Our research is motivated by the need to develop experimental platforms for exploring ion-atom interactions and quantum dynamics in a controlled manner. Overall, the ability to control and manipulate the collisional dynamics of ions and atoms provides a powerful tool for both fundamental investigations and practical applications. Our results show promising potential for understanding the behavior of interacting systems and developing new technologies for quantum information processing. We look forward to sharing our results with others.

We present an empirical study of the internal structure of the Indian financial market by analyzing the cross-correlation behavior between stocks listed on the National Stock Exchange (NSE). Our main aim is to uncover the hidden structure and relationships in the complex network of financial instruments and investigate the underlying drivers of market dynamics. The analysis is based on daily closing prices of 50 stocks from different sectors, covering a period of 5 years from January 2018 to December 2019. We apply cross-correlation matrix and minimum spanning tree methods to identify the most correlated stocks and their clusters, as well as to study the evolution of the market structure over time. Our results show the emergence of well-defined clusters that correspond to the sector composition of the market, revealing the interdependence of stocks in each sector. Moreover, we find evidence of changing correlations and network topology during periods of high volatility, which suggest the presence of contagion effects and interdependence of crises. Our work contributes to the understanding of the internal structure and behavior of the Indian financial market and has implications for risk management and portfolio diversification strategies.

In this work, we investigate the uniqueness of $\bf C^*$- and $\bf C_+$-actions on Gizatullin surfaces, which are a particular class of complex surfaces. The main question we address is whether two such actions are necessarily equivalent, meaning that one can be obtained from the other by a change of coordinates. We prove that these actions are, in fact, unique up to certain transformations, which we describe explicitly in the paper. Our approach is based on the use of algebraic and geometric techniques, such as the analysis of linear systems of equations and the analysis of rational curves on the surface. Our research result is of great interest in several areas of mathematics, including algebraic geometry and group theory, where it has applications in the study of symmetries of complex surfaces and their classification. Furthermore, our work provides a new insight into the geometry of Gizatullin surfaces, which are an important and much-studied class of algebraic varieties. Overall, our investigation sheds light on the structure of $\bf C^*$- and $\bf C_+$-actions on Gizatullin surfaces and opens up new avenues for further research in this exciting area of mathematics.

In this work, we investigate the relativistic effects in extreme mass ratio gravitational wave bursts. The problem that we attempt to solve is the accurate prediction of gravitational wave signals emitted by low mass compact objects such as neutron stars or black holes orbiting around a supermassive black hole, or a supermassive black hole. The relativistic effects in such systems are significant, and they affect the waveform in a way that can be observed with future gravitational wave detectors. We present the results obtained through numerical simulations of extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) using a fully relativistic code. Our simulations consider different initial conditions for the small compact object, which effectively represent the distribution of stars in the galactic center. We show that relativistic effects such as frame-dragging and gravitational redshift have a significant impact on the signal waveform, and they must be taken into account for accurate detection and parameter estimation in future gravitational wave observations. The key ideas in this work are to investigate the importance of relativistic effects in EMRIs, and to provide a better understanding of the predictions for gravitational wave signals from low mass compact objects orbiting black hole binaries. We employ a rigorous method based on fully relativistic numerical simulations of EMRIs, which are then compared to analytical predictions using Post-Newtonian theory. Overall, our work shows that relativistic effects cannot be ignored in the analysis of low mass compact objects around supermassive black holes. Understanding these effects is essential for the success of future gravitational wave observations, and for the advancement of our understanding of the astrophysical processes taking place in the galactic center.

In this study, we investigate the lensing, reddening, and extinction effects of MgII absorbers at redshifts from z=0.4 to z=2. Our motivation for this research lies in the need to understand the impact of MgII absorbers on the evolution of the intervening galaxies and quasars at different redshifts. We aim to solve the problem of the variability in the MgII absorption properties of intervening galaxies and quasars at different redshifts, which is crucial for understanding the nature and evolution of these galaxies and quasars. To achieve this aim, we employ a large sample of MgII absorption systems and their associated galaxies and quasars, obtained from the Sloan e Space Telescope and the National Sky Survey Data Release 7. We use gravitational lensing measurements to estimate the mass of the MgII absorbers, and combine these with the observed extinction and reddening properties to investigate the relationship between the absorption, galaxy properties, and quasar activity. Our key idea is that the MgII absorbers are associated with intervening galaxies, and the properties of the absorbers vary with redshift due to the evolution of these intervening galaxies. We use a combination of statistical methods and physical modeling to test this idea, and to investigate the dominant physical processes that drive the evolution of MgII absorbers and their associated galaxies and quasars. Our findings shed light on the nature and evolution of galaxies and quases, and improve our understanding of the impact of MgII absorbers on their evolution.

In this study, we investigate the phase behavior of the dilute magnet LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4. The motivation for this research stems from the desire to understand the complex magnetic interactions present in this system and to further our understanding of magnetic ordering in rare earth-containing compounds. To study the phase behavior, we performed high-resolution neutron diffraction experiments on single crystals of LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 with x ranging from 0.1 to 0.5. Our results indicate that as x is increased, the magnetic ordering transitions from the well-known spiral magnetic structure of pure LiHoF_4 to a more complex incommensurate structure. Furthermore, we find that there is a critical concentration of Ho ions at which the incommensurate magnetic structure disappears entirely, leading to a non-magnetic ground state. Overall, our findings shed light on the rich magnetic behavior present in LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4, and suggest that this system may be a promising candidate for future studies of magnetic ordering in rare earth-containing systems. These results may also have implications for the design and optimization of novel magnetic materials for technological applications.

In this study, we investigate the X-ray luminosity functions (XLFs) of normal galaxies in the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey (GOODS), with the aim of shedding light on their X-ray emission properties. This work builds on previous studies which focused on the X-ray emission of AGNs and star-forming galaxies, yet largely overlooked the contribution of normal galaxies to the overall X-ray emission in the GOODS. Our motivation stems from the fact that X-ray emission can provide valuable insights into the composition and physical properties of galaxies. We employ data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Hubble Space Telescope to construct the XLFs of normal galaxies in the GOODS. Our results show that the XLF of normal galaxies can be reliably estimated and modeled by a single power law, in contrast to the more complicated XLFs found in AGN and star-forming galaxies. Furthermore, we find that normal galaxies contribute significantly to the overall X-ray emission in the GOODS, making up a significant fraction of the X-ray luminosity "gap" between AGNs and star-forming galaxies. This work suggests that normal galaxies should not be overlooked in future X-ray studies and XLF modeling.

In this study, we investigate the concept of dark matter in the context of gauge mediation from emergent supersymmetry. This approach is motivated by the fact that standard models of particle physics fail to explain the presence and behavior of dark matter in the universe. Dark matter is believed to comprise a significant portion of the universe’s total mass, yet is entirely invisible due to its lack of interaction with light. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of emergent supersymmetry, which arises due to the collective behavior of particles in a given system, rather than from a specific underlying theory. This approach enables us to explore the interactions between dark matter and other particles, such as neutralinos, which may be responsible for its creation and stability. Our methodology involves the use of computer simulation and statistical analysis to model the behavior of particles at the microscopic level. We examine the scenarios and parameter spaces that influence the mass and coupling values of the neutralino and gauge boson, and their respective interactions with dark matter. Our results show that the emergent supersymmetry approach leads to a significant enhancement in the neutralino dark matter abundance, making it an appealing candidate for the elusive material. Our study findings highlight the importance of incorporating emergent supersymmetry concepts in future research to provide a better understanding of dark matter in the universe.

In this paper, we investigate the generalization of entropy measures and pathways in complex systems. The main objective of this work is to introduce a novel approach to characterize and analyze the dynamics and behavior of complex systems in terms of a generalized entropy measure and pathways. We aim to formulate an extended framework for the analysis of non-equilibrium systems that enables us to elucidate not only the macroscopic quantities but also the micro-level dynamics of the system. To achieve this goal, we start by defining the concept of a generalized entropy measure that considers the distinct ways in which the system evolves over time. We then utilize a graph-theoretic formalism to represent the system's pathways, which allows us to examine how the evolution of the system gives rise to different possible states. Through our analysis, we investigate the effects of perturbations on the entropy measures and pathways of the system. Our research provides new insights into the dynamics of complex systems and their response to perturbations. We demonstrate the potential of the generalized entropy measure and pathways formalism as a powerful tool for quantifying and characterizing complex systems in a variety of fields, including biology, physics, mathematics, and economics. This work provides the foundation for future research aiming to develop more efficient approaches to analyze and predict the behavior of complex systems.

In this work, we investigate the direct CP violation of CP symmetry in the decay $\bar{B}^0 \to \rho^0(\omega)\rho^0(\omega) \to \pi^+\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-$. This decay is a rare process that involves the decay of a $\bar{B}^0$ meson to two vector mesons $\rho^0(\omega)$, followed by the decay of each of these mesons to two charged pions. The study of this process is of great interest because it allows us to study the violation of CP symmetry directly, which is a key ingredient of the Standard Model of particle physics. We perform our analysis using data collected by the LHCb detector at CERN using the standard model of particle collisions. We employ time-dependent amplitude analysis techniques to extract the necessary parameters to study CP violation in the decay. Our analysis shows significant evidence for direct CP violation in the decay, with a statistical significance of 5.3 standard deviations. The results of our study are consistent with the results from the Standard Model, but there is still room for improvement in the precision of our measurements.
