Our work is an important step towards a better understanding of the fundamental interactions in nature and could potentially provide clues for the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

In this work, we present an analysis of heavy quarkonia transitions with pion emission, in terms of the QCD multipole expansion. Additionally, we determine the mass spectra of hybrids using the same approach. The motivation for this research lies in the need to better understand the properties of quarkonia and hybrids, which are essential to the study of heavy ion collisions, strong interactions, and the formation of the quark-gluon plasma. The problem that this work attempts to solve is twofold. Firstly, there is a need for a more precise and comprehensive analysis of quarkonia transitions with pion emission, which have received less attention in the literature compared to transitions with photon emission. Secondly, the mass spectra of hybrids are not well understood, and their experimental observation is challenging due to their relatively long lifetimes. The key ideas of this work are based on the QCD multipole expansion, a powerful tool for the analysis of transitions involving hadrons. We apply this approach to heavy quarkonia transitions with pion emission and hybrids, and calculate their mass spectra systematically. The methodology involves a combination of theoretical , experimental, and numerical simulations. In summary, our work provides a comprehensive analysis of heavy quarkonia transitions with pion emission and determination of mass spectra of hybrids, which will contribute to the further understanding of QCD and the properties of hadronic systems.

We present an analysis of inhomogeneities in the universe and the fitting problem. The motivation for our work is to explore the distribution of matter in the universe and determine the nature of dark energy. We use numerical simulations and observational data to study the large-scale structure of the universe based on cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB) and bounded acoustic oscillations (BAO) measurements. We aim to develop a comprehensive understanding of the universe by designing models that fit both CMB and BAO data, as well as constrain cosmic parameters. Our work shows a significant improvement in model fit by utilizing a more sophisticated form of dark energy, which is able to better accommodate specific physical phenomena. Our results indicate that a non-flat universe with additional curvature significantly improves the model fit, and also supports the existence of dark energy acting as a cosmological constant. Our findings signify a promising step towards characterizing the behavior of dark energy and understanding the evolution of the universe. These results have significant implications for future models, cosmology, and the potential to unlock new insights into our universe.

Our work on Two-photon transitions in hydrogen and cosmological recombination investigates the intricate details of atomic physics in the early universe. The study is motivated by the need to understand the recombination process that occurred when the early Universe was approximately 300,000 years old. During the recombination epoch, the primordial plasma of free electrons combined with atomic nuclei to form neutral atoms, marking the beginning of the opaque epoch. The recombination era produced the cosmic rays and background radiation that we observe today. Our research focuses on the two-photon transitions of hydrogen atoms, which play a significant role in the recombination process. By carefully examining the two-photon transition processes, we aim to develop a more precise understanding of the recombination era, and consequently, to improve our understanding of the early universe. We employ a combination of theoretical and computational methods to simulate the behavior of hydrogen atoms under different environmental conditions. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a completely accurate model of hydrogen's two-photon transitions and its impact on the recombination process. Through our work, we aim to contribute to the broader field of cosmology by filling in critical knowledge gaps about the early universe's evolution. Our findings will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the recombination epoch and the early universe's formation and evolution.

In this paper, we derive a Non-Markovian Scalar Liouville Equation (NSLE) and its Markovian representation. The motivation for this work stems from the growing need for understanding the dynamics of open quantum physical systems that exhibit non-Markovian behavior. The NSLE is a generalization of the well-known Markovian Liouville equation, and it is essential in understanding the dynamics of open quantum systems. We propose an implementation of the Continuous Time Random Walk (CTRW) approach to study the non-Markovian behavior, which results in a memory kernel that is dependent on the distribution of jump s. We apply our methodology to various systems, including a two-level system subject to a thermal bath and a quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to a bath of harmonic oscillators. Our key idea is to utilize tools from the theory of stochastic processes to study the non-Markovian behavior of open quantum systems. We employ the Laplace transform to solve the Markovian representation of the NSLE and obtain analytical expressions for the reduced density matrix. The obtained results yield new insights into the non-Markovian behavior of open quantum systems. For instance, in the case of the two-level system, we show that the memory kernel exhibits a power-law decay, indicating long-term quantum coherence. In conclusion, our work opens up new avenues for modeling and simulating non-Markovian systems and provides a platform for investigating the dynamics of open quantum systems.

In this research, we investigate the stellar population and origin of the high-latitude star-forming cloud CG 12. This cloud is located at a high galactic latitude of ~70° and has puzzled astronomers due to its unusual location and properties. To better understand this cloud's nature, we obtained deep space and infrared spectral data using the CTIO/MOSAIC-II camera and the Spitzer Space Telescope. These observations allowed us to conduct a detailed analysis of the population, age, and distribution of the stars in this region. Our findings reveal that CG 12 is composed of at least two distinct, young stellar populations, which differ in age and spatial distribution. These populations exhibit a remarkably anomalous mass function, indicating extreme star formation conditions. Additionally, we find that the cloud is surrounded by a large, low-density shell, suggesting that the cloud has undergone a violent encounter with a nearby massive star. The results of this study provide important insights into the formation and evolution of high-latitude star-forming clouds and highlight the need for further investigations of these enigmatic systems. By shedding light on the origin and properties of CG 12, we can better understand the broader context of star formation in the Milky Way and other galaxies.

In this study, we report on our search for gravitational-wave bursts in data collected by LIGO during its fourth science run. The main problem we aim to address is the detection of short-lived, high-frequency gravitational-wave signals that are challenging to detect using traditional techniques. These signals may originate from a range of astrophysical events, such as black hole mergers or supernova explosions, and may provide important information about the dynamics of the universe. To address this problem, we employed a novel search algorithm that is based on a suite of time-frequency methods designed to identify coherent signals above the detector noise. The methodology involves the detection and characterization of short-lived transient events in the data using wavelet transforms and matched filtering. We also implemented a robust follow-up procedure to reduce the number of false positives detected. The motivation for this research stems from the desire to deepen our understanding of the universe and the physical processes that drive it. The detection of gravitational waves has opened up new avenues of exploration and has the potential to improve our understanding of fundamental physics. Our search for gravitational-wave bursts in LIGO data from the fourth science run represents a significant step forward in the ongoing quest to detect and characterize these elusive signals.

In this paper, we present the measurement of the top-quark mass using missing $E_T$+jets events with secondary vertex $b$-tagging at the CDF II detector located at the Fermilab Tevatron collider. The top-quark is the heaviest known elementary particle , and its mass is a fundamental parameter in the Standard Model of particle physics. Precise measurement of the top-quark mass is crucial to test the consistency of the Standard Model and to search for new physics beyond it. Our goal was to measure the top-quark mass using a novel method consisting of selecting events that have missing transverse electrons (MET) and at least one jet that contains a secondary vertex identified as a $b$-jet. We analyzed data collected in proton-antiproton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 1.96$ TeV by the CDF II detector, located at the Fermilab Tevatron accelerator. The key idea of our analysis was to construct a template of the top-quark mass distribution by fitting the MET distribution in data and comparing it to the prediction from simulation. We used a Bayesian approach to extract the top-quark mass distribution and its uncertainty. Our method has the advantage of being less sensitive to the jet energy scale and resolution uncertainties, compared to traditional top-quark mass measurements. Our result for the top-quark mass is $172.8 <unk> 2.2 \mathrm{(stat.)} \pm 1.5 \mathrm{(syst.)}$ GeV/$c^2$, which is one of the most precise measurements to date. This measurement contributes to the global effort to improve the knowledge of the top-quark mass and to search for new physics phenomena.

In our work entitled "Grand minima and maxima of solar activity: New observational constraints," we present the results of our investigation of the behavior of the Sun's magnetic activity over timescales exceeding a century. Our motivation for conducting this study stems from the need to better understand the inherent variability of solar activity, which is crucial for many applications ranging from space weather forecasting to the interpretation of climate records. Specifically, we are interested in identifying the occurrence of "Grand minima" and "Grand maxima" - periods of low quiescence and high activity, respectively - which have been observed in the past. However, previous studies have relied on indirect proxies of solar activity, which may not accurately reflect the true behavior of the Sun's magnetic field. Our work uses direct measurements of solar magnetic activity from the last 150 years to analyze the occurrence of extreme episodes, and we find that the Sun's behavior over this timescale is much more stable than previously thought. We show that the occurrence of Grand minima can occur with a highly probabilistic probability, while Grand maxima can occur, but with a low probability. Our results have important implications for future space weather and climate predictions, and provide valuable observational constraints for models of solar dynamo and variability.

We present the results of our study on the mass and temperature of the TWA -type debris disk. The main goal of this work was to improve our understanding of the dynamics and physical properties of circumstellar disks, which play a crucial role in the formation and evolution of planetary systems. We combined ALMA and GPI observations to model the disk structure and constrain its dust properties. Our model revealed a circumstellar disk with a radius of about 35 AU and a mass of 0.02 M_sol. We also found evidence of significant dust grain growth and radial expansion, which suggests that the disk is in the late stages of its evolution. In addition, we estimated the disk temperature profile using a radiative transfer model, and found that it is consistent with a power law surface density distribution of dust. Our results provide important insights into the relationship between disk properties and the formation and evolution of planetary systems. They also highlight the importance of high-resolution observations and detailed modeling in the study of circumstellar disks. Overall, this work contributes to a deeper understanding of the potential properties of exoplanetary systems and the processes that govern their formation and evolution.

In this work, we investigate the implications of the Hagedorn temperature in string theory and the correspondence principle in Anti-de Sitter space (AdS) 3 dimensions. Our main objective is to understand the behavior of the Hagedorn transition in AdS3 space through the study of free strings. We use the formalism of a light-cone gauge and the Polyakov action to determine the thermal partition function of the strings. We obtain an explicit expression for the Hagedorn temperature as a function of the AdS3 radius and curvature. Additionally, we study the behavior of the density of the energy of the strings in the large temperature regime. Our results suggest that the Hagedorn transition in AdS3 is closely related to the Brown-Henneaux central temperature. Specifically, the Hagedorn transition can be interpreted as a phase transition that separates a regime of high energy density, where the string behaves as a thermal ensemble, from a low energy density regime, where the string behaves as a coherent state. Our work contributes to the understanding of the Hagedorn transition in AdS3 and its relation to the correspondence principle. Additionally, our work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the behavior of free strings in AdS3 space and its relationship to the correspondence principle by the Hagedorn temperature.

In our work, we investigated the phenomenon of entanglement in a Jaynes-Cummings model with two atoms and two photon modes. The problem this work attempts to solve is to better understand the dynamics of entanglement in a multi-atom quantum system. This is an important area of research as entanglement is a key feature of quantum mechanics and plays a crucial role in quantum computation and communication. Our approach was to use the Jaynes-Cummings model, which describes the interaction between a two-level atom and a single mode of an electromagnetic field, in combination with two identical atoms and two photon modes. We then used the concept of the concurrence to determine the amount of entanglement in the system. The main idea behind our work was to explore the role that different parameters, such as the atomic detuning and the coupling strength between the atoms, play in the entanglement dynamics. Our methodology involved theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of the model. Our results show that entanglement can persist in the system for a long time, provided the atoms are initially prepared in an entangled state. We found that the degree of entanglement in the system is highly sensitive to the initial conditions and the parameters of the model. Our work provides insights into the complex dynamics of entanglement in multi-atom Jaynes-Cummings models, which could be useful in the development of future quantum technologies.

In our work, we explore the possibility of effectively cleaning a dirty floor using probabilistic potential theory and the Dobrushin uniqueness theorem. Our research is driven by the fact that cleaning floors is an essential task for maintaining hygiene and the health of the occupants of a space. However, traditional cleaning methods may not be effective in removing dirt and germs from certain types of floors, particularly those with complex surface geometries. Our key approach is to model the floor-cleaning process as a stochastic process, where the floor's state changes over time according to a probabilistic transition mechanism. We utilize the Dobrushin uniqueness theorem, a powerful tool from probability theory, to establish conditions for the existence of a unique stationary distribution for the stochastic process. We then propose an optimal cleaning method that maximizes the probability of achieving the desired clean state. Our methodology involves numerical simulations and analytical results that validate the effectiveness of our approach under different conditions. We show that our method outperforms standard cleaning practices in terms of both cleaning efficiency and time. Therefore, our research provides a promising theoretical framework for developing smart, automated cleaning systems that are capable of responding to variable surface geometries and dirt levels. Ultimately, our work has real-world applications in reducing the spread of infectious diseases, improving indoor air quality, and promoting a healthier living environment.

In this work, we explore the phenomenology of Light Heavy (LH) Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) Higgs bosons at large tanβ. Large tanβ can significantly alter the production and decay of the MSSM Higgs bosons. We investigate the existing constraints on the LH MSSM Higgs bosons from various experiments, such as LEP, Tevatron, and LHC. We carry out a comprehensive analysis of the phenomenology of LH MSSM Higgs bosons and investigate their possible signatures, such as the production cross-sections, branching ratios, and the decay modes, under the constraints from the existing experimental data. Our results show that the LH MSSM Higgs bosons could provide an interesting target for the experimental searches at the LHC. In particular, for the large values of tanβ, we observed that the decay modes of LH MSSM Higgs bosons into the final state of a τ-lepton pair can significantly enhance the sensitivity of the search for these bosons. We also found that the production cross-section for the LH MSSM Higgs bosons in the decay processes of heavier <unk>-lepton pairs can be greatly enhanced by the large value of tanβ. Therefore, the results of our study offer concrete predictions for the experimental searches of LH MSSM Higgs bosons at the LHC, which can be important for the ongoing efforts of the LHC to detect new physics beyond the Standard Model.

In this paper, we investigate the computational complexity of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)-based estimators in large-dimensional samples. The main motivation for this research is to understand the performance limitations of MCMC-based methods and provide insight into the practical limitations of these techniques. We focus on Bayesian inference problems where the posterior distribution of the parameters is high-dimensional and complex, making standard inference techniques intractable. We first introduce the concept of the spectral gap for MCMC chains and show how it is related to the mixing properties of the parameters. We then examine how the number of parameters and the sample size influence the computational complexity of MCMC-based estimators. We consider both Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling algorithms and show that the computational complexity of these methods can vary widely depending on the chosen parameters. Our results provide practical guidance for researchers who use MCMC-based methods for Bayesian inference in large-dimensional problems. Specifically, we find that the optimal values of the MCMC algorithm can depend strongly on the problem at hand, and that convergence to the stationary distribution can be slow in these problems. Our work also highlights the importance of considering spectral gap when choosing the parameters of the MCMC algorithm in order to achieve reliable and efficient inference in complex models.

In this study, we investigate satellite galaxies and fossil groups in the Millennium Simulation - a state-of-the-art N-body cosmological simulation. The motivation for this work is rooted in understanding the evolution of the largest bound structures in the universe - galaxy groups and clusters. In particular, we focus on the unique case of fossil groups, as they offer a glimpse into the formation and evolution of galaxy groups with massive central galaxies, surrounded by a complement of smaller satellites. We aim to study the spatial distribution and properties of satellites in contrast to the fossil group, to gain insight into their dynamical evolution and potential role in shaping the central galaxy. Our results show that satellite galaxies display a preferential distribution in the fossil group halo, with a steeper radial dependence than the dark matter. We find that the stellar mass and age of satellites in the fossil group halo are significantly lower than those in the outer halo, indicating a possible stripping of material. In addition, we observe black hole feedback to be more efficient in the central galaxy, explaining its exceptionally high mass. These findings highlight the role of satellite galaxies in the assembly of massive galaxies and provide a new aspect of the study of fossil groups. Overall, this work contributes to our understanding of the nature of galaxy groups and fossil groups, and provides new insights into the processes shaping the largest structures in the universe.

In the field of cosmology, only a small portion of the universe is directly observable. Dark Energy is a hypothetical form of energy that is believed to exist in the vast and largely unobservable space between galaxies. However, this concept does more harm than good to the study of the cosmos. This work investigates the implications of this theoretical construct on our understanding of the universe and how it can be detrimental to the advancement of astronomy. Our study shows that the concept of Dark Energy is problematic because its introduction conflicts with fundamental physics principles. The hypothesis of Dark Energy requires a negative pressure that drives the universe's expansion, but such pressure would contradict the fundamental concepts of thermodynamics and quantum field theory. Additionally, we argue that varying the concept of Dark Energy in the currently accepted physical equations can have potentially harmful theoretical consequences. The methodology employed involved evaluating critical literature pertaining to cosmology and physics. We identified and analyzed possible theoretical inconsistencies regarding the concept of Dark Energy and examined its implications on key physical concepts such as causality and energy conservation. Our findings suggest that the adoption of alternative theories, such as Modified Gravity, could lead to a more profound comprehension of the universe. This study also underscores the importance of theoretical consistency when studying phenomena that remain beyond the bounds of direct experimental observation. The study concludes with a discussion of the implications of Dark Energy for astronomy.

We present the design and imaging performance of the Infrared Camera (IRC) on the AKARI satellite. The IRC was designed to cover the 1.7-26 μm wavelength range with three channels: NIR (1.7-5.5 μm), MIR-S (4-13 μm), and MIR-L (12-26 μm). The IRC has a 9.4'×10.1' field of view and uses Si:As IBC detector arrays with 40-mas pixels. We report on the sensitivity, stability, and spatial resolution of the IRC based on the on-orbit pointed observation data of standard stars and galaxies. The observations show that the IRC has a sensitivity of 0.056, 0.41, 3.8, and 310 mJy (5σ, 1 <unk> , and 1<unk> integration) in the NIR, MIR-S, MIR-L, and FIR bands, respectively. The absolute photometric calibration of the IRC is accurate to 5%-10% depending on the band and processing method. The IRC also has a point source spatial resolution of 1.3-3.6'', depending on the band and the observing mode. The excellent imaging performance of the IRC enables us to study a wide range of astronomical objects, from nearby Solar System bodies to high-redshift quasars and galaxies. Our research was motivated by the need to advance our understanding of the universe through high-quality observations in the infrared regime. The IRC is an essential instrument for achieving this goal, with unprecedented sensitivity, spatial resolution, and wavelength coverage. This work provides a thorough characterization of the IRC design and performance, demonstrating its scientific potential and setting the foundation for future research in infrared astronomy.

In this work, we study substructures in the nearby clusters from the WIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS) dataset. Our motivation is to investigate the properties and formation mechanisms of galaxies and galaxy clusters, which are closely related to the evolution of the universe. We adopt a novel approach to detect substructures using the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) method on the projected phase-space data. We find that more than half of the clusters in our sample show evidence for substructures, which are often associated with ongoing or past mergers. These substructures exhibit a wide range of properties, including different levels of spatial segregation, velocity dispersion, and mass ratio. We also investigate the impact of the mergers on the dynamical properties of the clusters, such as the velocity dispersion and the mass estimates. Our study highlights the importance of substructures in understanding the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. The GMM method we employ provides a powerful tool for detecting substructures, which can be applied to a broader range of datasets beyond WINGS. Our results support the idea that galaxy clusters are not static systems, but rather complex and dynamic entities that evolve over cosmic time.

In this study, we aimed to simulate heme using the Density Functional Theory plus Hubbard U approach (DFT+U) and investigate the accuracy of spin-state energetics. Heme is an essential protein in many biological processes, including oxygen transport and electron transfer. The accurate determination of its spin-state energetics is crucial for understanding its cellular mechanism. However, the spin-state energetics of heme are a challenging problem because of the strong electron correlation effects. In this study, we first validated the DFT+U approach by comparing our results with experimental data. We then compared our calculations with those from the DFT approach, which neglects electron correlation effects, and found that the DFT+U approach significantly gave a lower energy prediction for the high-spin state than the DFT+U approach. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the inclusion of U significantly improves the accuracy of the energy predictions by taking into account the electron correlation effects. These findings reveal the importance of including electron correlation effects in simulating spin-state energetics of heme, and the DFT+U approach provides a reliable method for such simulations. This work paves the way for more accurate simulations of heme and other proteins with strong electron correlation effects, and thus contributes to the advancement of computational chemistry and materials science.

In this work, we revisit the role of allovalency in multisite phosphorylation and substrate rebinding. Our analysis sheds new light on the complex mechanisms of regulatory protein interactions and provides insight into the cellular processes that underlie cellular signaling pathways. Our research was motivated by the desire to better understand the complex interactions between regulatory proteins and the impact they have on cellular function. We sought to investigate the role of allovalency – the ability of one ligand binding event to affect the binding behavior of another – in the context of multisite phosphorylation and substrate rebinding. Using a combination of theoretical and computational methods, we analyzed the impact of allovalency on complex multisite phosphorylation pathways. Our results reveal that allovalency can dramatically alter the kinetic and thermodynamic properties of these pathways, leading to significant changes in the binding behavior of the regulatory proteins involved. Overall, our work represents an important step forward in our understanding of cellular signaling pathways and the mechanisms behind multisite phosphorylation. By exploring the role of allovalency, we hope to provide new avenues for future research in this exciting and rapidly growing field.

In this work, we investigate the influence of spatial dispersion on the shape of a Gaussian light pulse in a quantum well. The motivation for this research stems from the need to better understand the behavior of light in materials with varied properties. By studying the behavior of light in quantum wells, we can gain insight into the dynamics of quantum systems and potentially find new applications for them. We conducted simulations of a Gaussian pulse propagating through a quantum well and found that the dispersion parameter affects the shape of the pulse. Specifically, increasing the dispersion parameter causes the pulse to change in shape over time. This phenomenon is due to the fact that the dispersion parameter influences the group velocity of the pulse, which in turn modifies the spatial localization of the pulse. Our research aims to provide a more detailed understanding of the behavior of light in quantum wells and to contribute to the development of novel quantum technologies. The results obtained in this work demonstrate the importance of considering spatial dispersion when modeling light propagation in quantum wells, and suggest that controlling the dispersion parameter may be a useful tool for manipulating light in these systems.

In this work, we present a hierarchy of N=8 mechanics models and analyze their properties. The primary objective of this study is to provide a systematic approach to the study of mechanical systems with eight degrees of freedom. We address the problem of characterizing the behavior of a wide range of physical systems, including mechanical and biological systems. To achieve this goal, we introduce a framework to generalize the Euler-Lagrange equations for mechanical systems with N degrees of freedom. Our methodology involves defining a set of Lagrangian models with increasing complexity and introducing a hierarchy of mathematical tools to analyze their behavior. Starting from the simplest N=2 model (a particle in a plane), we incrementally develop more complex models, including a system of three pendulums, a spherical pendulum, and a planar double pendulum. Finally, we analyze the general N=8 case. We obtain several results, including the solutions to the equations of motion for each model, the stability of equilibrium points, and the classification of the models based on their symmetries. Our approach provides a systematic and efficient way to study mechanical systems with eight degrees of freedom and has important applications in fields such as robotics, biomechanics, and aerospace engineering.

In this study, we investigate the effects of turbulent diffusion on the chemistry of diffuse clouds. Diffuse clouds are a type of interstellar medium characterized by low density and low temperature, which makes their chemistry highly sensitive to environmental changes. Turbulent diffusion is known to play a key role in mixing different populations of molecules and atoms in the interstellar medium, but its impact on the chemical evolution of diffuse clouds is not well understood yet. With this goal in mind, we use a combination of numerical simulations and analytical modeling to study the diffusion of hydrogen, helium, oxygen, and other species in a diffuse cloud with different turbulence levels. Our results show that turbulent diffusion has a significant influence on the abundances of molecular and atomic species in diffuse clouds. In particular, we find that small-scale turbulence enhances the mixing of different atomic species, leading to higher levels of molecular formation and fragmentation. On the other hand, large-scale turbulence promotes the diffusion of heavy elements, such as carbon and oxygen, which can trigger complex chemical pathways involving ion-molecule reactions. Our findings suggest that turbulent diffusion is a key factor in shaping the chemical diversity of the interstellar medium and should be taken into account in models of Galactic chemical evolution.

In this work, we investigate the non-perturbative corrections and modularity in N=1 Type IIB compactifications. Our research aims to address the problem of understanding the non-perturbative corrections to the effective superpotential in four-dimensional N=1 supergravity models with Type IIB string compactifications. We seek to explore how supergravity invariance and modularity effects are related in these models and how this relationship can be used to gain insights into the underlying physics of compactifications. The key idea of our research is to use the framework of mirror symmetry to study the non-perturbative corrections in Type IIB compactifications. We show how these non-perturbative corrections can be understood in terms of modular forms, which are functions that transform in a specific way under modular transformations. Our methodology involves a combination of mirror symmetry, modular forms, and supergravity computations. Our research is motivated by the desire to deepen our understanding of the physics of string compactifications and to explore the relationship between different areas of mathematics and physics. We aim to shed light on the role of modularity in string theory and to uncover the symmetries underlying the non-perturbative effects that appear in string compactifications. Our research has important implications for the study of supersymmetric field functions and their applications in high-energy physics.

In this research article, we investigate the critical behavior of irreversible reaction systems. Our primary objective is to understand the fundamental mechanisms that govern the dynamics and stability of such systems. We explore a theoretical framework to study the critical phenomena arising in the reaction-diffusion systems under various conditions. Our approach involves the development of mathematical models that describe the dynamics of these systems, followed by numerical simulations to investigate their critical behavior. Our findings reveal that these irreversible reaction systems exhibit critical behavior under specific conditions, such as the presence of strong fluctuations and non-linearities. We demonstrate that the critical behavior of these systems depends on the coupling strength between the reactants and the diffusion rates. Additionally, we observe that the critical behavior of these systems are characterized by power-law behavior. Our methodology consists of a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, including linear stability analysis, bifurcation analysis, and numerical simulations. We use these techniques to identify the critical phenomena in the system and identify the relevant parameters that govern them. Our work aims to contribute to the understanding of the critical behavior of irreversible reaction systems, which has significant implications for the design and implementation of such systems in industrial processes, environmental remediation, and biological systems. Our research provides insights into the mechanisms that govern the stability and dynamics of these systems under various conditions, which can inform the design and implementation of such systems in practical applications.

In this study, we investigate the mass assembly history of spheroidal galaxies, specifically focusing on whether newly-formed systems arise via major mergers. The main problem this study attempts to solve is understanding the dominant formation mechanism of spheroidal galaxies and its relation to the merging history of these systems. Using a sample of 88 spheroidal galaxies at redshifts between z = 1.6 and 0.3, we examine their mass assembly histories through galaxy stellar mass growth rates. We also employ high-resolution simulations to compare with these observations. Our results reveal that the majority of these galaxies attained half of their stellar mass by redshift z = 1.6, through a quiescent mode of star formation. We find evidence for both minor and major mergers contributing to the mass assembly histories of these spheroidal galaxies, but major mergers do not appear to be the dominant contributors. Overall, our findings suggest that a combination of a number of physical processes, such as cold gas accretion and minor mergers, likely produce spheroidal galaxies and that major mergers play a significant role in spheroidal galaxy formation. This work provides crucial insight into the formation mechanisms of spheroidal galaxies and sets the stage for further studies aiming to comprehensively investigate their mass assembly histories.

In this work, we investigate the possibility of obtaining an almost supersymmetric model of the Standard Model from intersecting D6-branes on the Z_6' orientifold. We focus on the compactification of type IIA string theory on a toroidal orientifold with orientifold planes. We consider a six-dimensional orbifold obtained by dividing a six-dimensional torus by a Z_6' orientation, which has orientifold planes and D6-branes at fixed points. We study the low-energy effective theory of the D6-branes and analyze the spectrum of chiral matter under the Standard Model gauge group. We find that the resulting spectrum contains all the particles of the Standard Model, except for the right-handed neutrinos, and that the Yukawa couplings are generated by instanton effects. Our work aims to address the problem of obtaining a realistic model of particle physics from string theory. The success of the Standard Model of particle physics in explaining the experimental data leaves little room for new physics beyond the Standard Model at low energies. String theory provides a consistent framework for quantum gravity that unifies all fundamental forces, but constructing a realistic model of particle physics from string theory is a challenging task. Our approach involves the use of intersecting D6-branes and the Z_6' orientifold, which is a particularly interesting model due to its rich phenomenology. Intersecting branes provide a geometric realization of the chiral matter , while the orientifold projection allows for the cancellation of tadpoles and the breaking of supersymmetry. Our methodology involves a detailed analysis of the low-energy effective theory of the D6-branes and the computation of instanton-generated Yukawa couplings. Our results show that a realistic model of the Standard Model can be obtained from string theory using the use of intersecting branes and orientifolds.

In 2005, we conducted a simultaneous monitoring campaign of the blazar PKS0537-441 using the Swift and REM telescopes. The motivation for this research is to study the variability of the blazar at different wavelengths, as it is known to exhibit highly variable emission across the electromagnetic spectrum. We aimed to investigate the correlation between the synchrotron and inverse Compton components of the blazar's emission, by simultaneously observing it in the optical/UV and X-ray bands. Our methodology involved collecting data from the Swift XRT and UVOT, and the REM optical telescope, over a period of 13 hours. We utilized various analysis techniques, including spectral fitting and cross-correlation analysis, to study the variability of the emission. This work addresses the challenge of understanding the physical mechanisms responsible for the blazar's variability, and the connection between the different components of its emission. The simultaneous multi-wavelength monitoring allows us to explore the relationship between the synchrotron and inverse Compton emission in a single observation campaign. Our findings suggest that a simple , synchrotron self-Compton model is inadequate to explain the observed variability. The results thus contribute to our understanding of blazar emission patterns and the mechanisms that drive their variability.

In this work, we investigate the relationship between two-dimensional twisted sigma models and the mirror chiral de Rham complex, with a particular focus on twisted generalized mirror symmetry. Our motivation for this research stems from the desire to better understand the correspondence between two-dimensional sigma models and algebraic geometry, as well as to uncover new tools for studying mirror symmetry phenomena. To achieve our goals, we perform a detailed analysis of twisted sigma models and their associated chiral de Rham complexes, including their cohomology and relationships to other mathematical structures. In particular, we show how twisted sigma models with a certain type of symmetry correspond to specific objects in the mirror chiral de Rham complex. We then use these results to obtain a twisted version of the classical generalized mirror symmetry theorem, which relates the topology of two mirror manifolds through their de Rham cohomology structures. Our research not only contributes to our understanding of the relationship between sigma models and algebraic geometry, but also provides a new avenue for studying mirror symmetry phenomena. In addition, our work highlights the importance of considering twisted symmetries and incorporating them into our mathematical models. Overall, we hope our findings will inspire further research in this area and shed light on new connections between seemingly disparate mathematical concepts.

In this work, we investigate the multijet production at low $x_{\rm Bj}$ in deep inelastic scattering at HERA, aiming to elucidate the underlying dynamics of the strong interaction at small distances. The difficulty in probing this regime stems from the limited reach of the current accelerator technologies, leading to a lack of experimental data in this domain. Our study utilizes the next-to-leading order perturbative QCD calculations, which have been shown to provide accurate descriptions of various hard-scattering processes observed at HERA. We present our predictions for the differential cross sections of jet production and compare them to the available data, showing reasonable differences between the two. We also examine the sensitivity of the results to variations in the parton distribution functions, exploring the impact of uncertainties on our knowledge of the proton structure. The motivation for this research comes from the desire to deepen our understanding of the fundamental interactions of matter and the strong force, as well as to test the validity of QCD in a previously unexplored kinematic region. Our analysis represents a step towards a comprehensive description of the subatomic interactions, facilitating future investigations of the high-energy phenomena.

In this paper, we delve into the question of how popularity shapes the formation of pop culture phenomena and how a “hit” is born. Using the collective choice framework, we construct a model that describes the dynamics of collective choice and the emergence of popularity. Our model considers the influence of individual preferences, the structure of social networks, and the properties of the item being evaluated. We analyze the trade-off between popularity and quality and show that popularity is a self-reinforcing process that can lead to the emergence of a hit. Moreover, we demonstrate that the properties of the item being evaluated, such as its intrinsic quality, can play a significant role in determining the likelihood of hitting. To test our model, we use data from a popular culture recommendation system, and we show that our model provides an accurate description of the data. Our findings indicate that collective choice mechanisms and network structure can significantly affect the emergence of popularity. Our results provide insights into the mechanisms underlying the emergence of popular culture and can help us understand the factors that contribute to the creation of a hit. The motivation for our research is to better understand the dynamics of collective choice and how they shape the formation of pop culture phenomena. This work aims to solve the problem of explaining how and why certain products and cultural artifacts become hits, while others fail to gain traction. In doing so, our model provides a comprehensive framework that can be applied to a wide range of contexts, from music to fashion and beyond.

In this work, we explore a new methodology for modeling complex materials via two-point correlation functions. The problem we attempt to solve is the difficulty of accurately characterizing complex materials with varying microstructures. Traditional methods such as finite element analysis often require significant computational resources and may not capture the full range of microstructural features. Our approach relies on the statistical analysis of material properties, as described by two-point correlation functions. These functions quantify the probability that two points in a material are of the same phase, allowing us to develop realistic microstructural models that generate accurate material properties. To implement this methodology, we begin with a review of the basic principles of two-point correlation functions. We provide a thorough explanation of the mathematical foundation behind these functions, as well as their significance in characterizing complex materials. Next, we apply the methodology to a set of heterogeneous materials, utilizing computational simulations to evaluate the accuracy of our developed models. Our results demonstrate the significant potential of two-point correlation functions in modeling complex materials. The methodology presented in this work will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in various fields, including materials science, engineering, and physics.

In this work, we explore 2-frame flow dynamics and hyperbolic rank rigidity in nonpositive curvature. The main problem we attempt to solve is the study of nonpositive curvature spaces and how the hyperbolic rank rigidity, which is a well-known combinatorial condition, affects the dynamics of the 2-frame flow. We aim to provide a better understanding of the relationship between the two by exploring how the 2-frame flow behaves in terms of its trajectories and dynamics as we vary the hyperbolic rank. Our key idea is to use the dynamical behavior of the 2-frame flow as a means to characterize the geometric structure of the nonpositive curvature space. We use a combination of techniques, including graph ing and combinatorics, to characterize the behavior of the flow. Through our methodology, we prove that the hyperbolic rank rigidity plays a crucial role in determining the behavior of the flow and its trajectories. Specifically, we show that the flow dynamics exhibit a significant difference depending on the hyperbolic rank. In conclusion, this work sheds light on the 2-frame flow dynamics and hyperbolic rank rigidity in nonpositive curvature spaces. Our findings show that the dynamics of the 2-frame flow can provide insights into the geometric structure of the space and that the hyperbolic rank rigidity plays a crucial role in determining the behavior of the flow. Our work contributes to the understanding of these important concepts and opens up new avenues for further exploration.

In this work, we perform a systematic scan for 7-colourings of the grid, aiming to find all possible ways to colour a rectangular grid of size m×n using seven distinct colours. We use a divide-and-conquer approach, where we decompose the grid into smaller sub-grids and find all possible 7-colourings for each sub-grid, and then combine them to form a single 7-colouring for the entire grid. The motivation for this research lies in the need to understand the colouring properties of grids, which have applications in various fields such as graph theory, computer vision, and telecommunications. By presenting an exhaustive list of 7-colourings of the grid, we contribute to the development of methods for optimising grid colourings in these fields. Our results show that the number of distinct 7-colourings of the grid increases rapidly as the size of the grid increases. For example, we found 8,065,328 distinct 7-colourings for a 4x4 grid, while for a 5x5 grid, we found 630,880,211 distinct 7-colourings. Furthermore, we observed that there exist symmetrical 7-colourings that are invariant under certain reflections, rotations, or translations. In conclusion, our systematic scan for 7-colourings of the grid provides a comprehensive list of all possible ways to colour rectangular grids using seven colours and offers insights into the colouring properties of grids.

In this study, we investigate the correlation between X-ray and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich X-ray and SZ scaling relations in galaxy clusters. Our key objective is to understand the underlying physical mechanism governing the scatter in the observed X-ray and SZ signals. For this purpose, we have analyzed the observational data obtained from the Chandra and Hubble telescopes on a sample of 40 galaxy clusters spanning a wide range of masses. Our analysis is based on the scaling relations between the integrated Compton parameter (Ysz) and the X-ray luminosity (Lx), temperature (Tx), and gas mass (Mgas) of the galaxy clusters. Our methodology involves developing a statistical model that accounts for the scatter in the observed X-ray and SZ scaling relations. We used Bayesian inference techniques to constrain the validity of our model and infer the intrinsic scatter in the scaling relations. Our results indicate that the intrinsic scatter in the Lx-Ysz and Tx-Ysz scaling relations are consistent with the scatter expected from the underlying physical processes, while the Mgas-Ysz scaling relation shows a higher scatter than expected. Overall, our findings suggest that the X-ray and SZ signals in galaxy clusters are governed by a complex interplay between underlying physical processes such as gas cooling, heating, and feedback. Our results provide valuable insights into the underlying physics of galaxy clusters and have important implications for cosmological studies using galaxy clusters as probes of the universe's large-scale structure.

In this work, we present a first-principles study on the coupling between the magnetic ordering and structural instabilities in perovskite biferroics. The ability to control magnetic properties with electric fields makes biferroics highly sought after for applications ranging from data storage to spintronics. However, in order to fully utilize their capabilities, a fundamental understanding of the coupling between magnetic order and structural instability is needed. Our research attempts to address this gap in knowledge by using density functional theory to study the effects of magnetic ordering and structural distortions on the electronic structure and magnetic properties of perovskite biferroics. We specifically investigate the cases of BiFeO₃ and BiFeO3 and find that coupled structural and magnetic instabilities arise in both materials at zero pressure. We also show that the electronic and magnetic properties of biferroics can be manipulated by applying external pressure or strain. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of understanding the interplay between magnetic ordering and structural instabilities in designing functional ly stable materials. Our work provides valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of magnetoelectric coupling and the potential of biferroic s for future technological applications.

In this work, we present further evidence that the redshifts of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) galaxies may have intrinsic components. The problem we attempt to solve is the discrepancy between the redshifts of AGN galaxies and their host galaxies. It has been observed that AGN galaxies tend to have higher redshifts than their surrounding galaxies, and this has been attributed to the expansion of the Universe. However, recent studies have suggested that part of this redshift may be intrinsic ally related to the expansion of the Universe and the activity itself. Our key ideas are based on a detailed statistical analysis of a large sample of AGN galaxies using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) data. We focus on the correlation between the redshifts of the AGN galaxies and the properties of their host galaxies, such as their color, luminosity, and morphological type. We also explore the impact of different systematic effects on our results, such as peculiar velocities and selection biases. The motivation for our research lies in the need to better understand the physical mechanisms that determine the observed redshifts of AGN galaxies. This is important because redshifts are commonly used as proxies for the evolution of the universe and can affect our understanding of the large-scale structure and evolution of the Universe. Our findings support the idea of intrinsic redshifts in AGN galaxies, which could have important implications for cosmological studies and the development of theories of gravity.

In this work, we investigate the origin of which-way information and its connection with the Born rule, which is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics. We propose a new methodology to study the relationship between these two concepts by introducing a generalization of the Born rule, which considers the role of which-way information in quantum measurements. Our approach is based on a set of experiments with two-path interferometers, where the presence of which-way information is controlled. We use a statistical analysis to compare the data obtained in these experiments with different theoretical predictions. Our study reveals that the Born rule is tightly related to the presence of which-way information in quantum measurements, and that the generalization of the Born rule provides a consistent description of the experimental results. The motivation for this work comes from the need to understand the nature of quantum mechanics, which still faces several fundamental challenges. The origin of which-way information and its relationship with the Born rule are key aspects of this theory, and their study can shed new light onto its fundamental properties. Our results highlight the importance of considering the role of which-way information in quantum measurements, and can have important implications for the future development of quantum technologies.

In this work, we investigate the Interior Point Decoding (IPD) method for Linear Vector Channels (LVCs). The IPD is a methodology used for solving optimization problems. It has been shown to perform well in various applications such as signal processing, control, and communication systems. Our research focuses on examining the performance of the IPD method in decoding information transmitted through LVCs. Our motivation stems from the increasing popularity of wireless communication and the need for efficient decoding methods. The LVC is a widely used model for wireless communication channels. It is a generalization of the scalar channel model to one in which the input is a scalar vector and the output is a noisy vector. The main advantage of using LVCs over scalar channels is the increased diversity gain, which can significantly improve the performance of communication systems. Our results show that the IPD method outperforms other decoding methods for LVCs, such as Maximum Likelihood and Minimum Mean Square Error, in terms of decoding accuracy and computation time. Specifically, the IPD method is shown to achieve near-optimal decoding performance at a significantly lower computational cost, making it a promising candidate for practical implementation in wireless communication systems. Overall, our work contributes to the ongoing effort to improve the performance and efficiency of decoding methods in wireless communication systems, with potential implications for various real-world applications.

In this paper, we present our analysis of the Norma Cluster (ACO 3627), the largest and most massive cluster in the Great Attractor. The motivation behind our research was the need to understand the dynamical properties of this massive cluster, which is essential for understanding the large-scale structure of the universe. Our study is based on data acquired through spectroscopic observations of 311 cluster members using the AAOmega instrument on the Anglo-Australian Telescope. Our key idea is to use the radial velocity distribution of cluster members to determine the dynamical state of the cluster, including its virial mass, velocity dispersion, and substructure. We employ various analysis techniques, including the biweight scale estimator, the Dressler-Shectman test, and the maximum-likelihood method, to determine the cluster's properties. Our results show that the cluster has a virial mass of M_vir=1.87×10^15 km s<unk>-1 and a velocity dispersion of σ_v=1219±49 km s^-1. We also found significant substructure within the cluster, indicating that it is still in the process of formation and is not yet virialized. In conclusion, our study provides a detailed analysis of the dynamical properties of the Norma Cluster, emphasizing its significance as the most massive cluster in the Great Attractor and its potential impact on the large-scale structure of the universe. Our results and methodology can be extended to other massive clusters in the Great Attractor and have significant implications for our overall understanding of the universe's dynamics.

In this work, we investigate the adiabatic quantum dynamics of a random Ising chain crossing the quantum critical point, motivated by the need to understand better the behavior of random quantum systems at criticality. Specifically, we study the time evolution of the system under a slowly varying transverse field, which drives the ground state from the ordered phase, through the quantum critical point, to the disordered phase. We use a combination of numerical techniques, including quantum diagonalization and quantum product state simulations, to explore the properties of the system during the adiabatic evolution. Our main results show that the quantum critical point manifests as a smooth but rapid change in the dynamics, driven by a scaling of the adiabatic energy gap, as well as universal critical exponents governing the scaling of the entanglement entropy and fidelity susceptibility. Furthermore, we observe that the random disorder induces strong finite-size effects, causing the transition to occur at a non-universal value of the transverse field. Overall, our work provides insight into the behavior of random quantum systems at criticality, highlighting the importance of finite-size effects and offering potential applications in quantum information and computation.

In this research, we aim to explore the possible relations between Negative Matter, Repulsion Force, Dark Matter, Phantom and Theoretical Tests, and their impact on the Inflation Cosmos and the Universe's Evolutionary Mechanism. The motivation behind this study is to investigate the fundamental concepts of the universe and clarify the nature of these mysterious particles. Furthermore, understanding the interrelation between these particles can unlock the secrets of dark energy that shape the universe. One of the key objectives of this research is to examine the effects of Negative Matter in the universe. Negative Matter is a theoretical construct that has the ability to repel gravitational force. It is also known as exotic matter that violates the conventional laws of physics. We will explore how Negative Matter can contribute to the repulsion force that drives the universe's expansion. Additionally, we will investigate how Dark Matter and Phantom particles can interact with Negative Matter to influence the universe's evolution. Our methodology involves theoretical tests that use numerical simulations and mathematical models. We will use theoretical models such as the Standard Model and Grand Unified Model to explore the potential interaction between these particles. We will also examine available experimental data to validate our theory. The problem this research attempts to solve is to explain the source of dark energy, the mysterious force that drives the universe's expansion. We hope that our findings can help us find an explanation, and ultimately lead to a better understanding of the fundamental nature of the universe.

In this paper, we propose a novel tool for seismologists, the Cumulative Spectral Power (CSP). Our motivation for this research stems from the inadequacy of current methods for identifying small earthquakes buried within noise and larger earthquakes. The CSP is designed to assist in readjusting a dataset in such a way that it reduces the frequency content of small earthquakes and at the same time dampens the frequency content of larger earthquakes and noise. The key idea of this new tool is that it enforces the idea that small earthquakes within a given frequency band can reveal substantive information about the subsurface structure of the Earth. The CSP is created using a single time window and a cumulative distribution function of the spectral power. Our primary methodology for testing the effectiveness of the CSP is through numerical simulations and field data analysis, which shows that CSP can significantly improve the detection of small earthquakes. We anticipate that this new tool will be critical in unraveling the Earth's subsurface structures and aid seismologists in image reconstruction and monitoring earthquake activity.

Our work focuses on investigating the free energy of activation for the Comorosan Effect, a phenomenon where a low-mass object exhibits a sudden increase in its weight when brought in close proximity to another object. This effect has been attributed to the interaction of gravitational forces between the objects, but the exact mechanism and the magnitude of the energy required for this transformation are not well understood. Motivated by the lack of experimental data on the Comorosan Effect, we have used a combination of experimental and theoretical methods to determine the free energy of activation required for this phenomenon. Our study uses a setup where two small metal spheres are suspended from a torsion balance and brought into close proximity to one another. The balance detects even small changes in their gravitational interaction as their separation distance is varied. Our results show a sudden increase in weight as the spheres approach each other, which we attribute to the Comorosan Effect. We have also calculated the free energy of activation associated with this effect by using statistical mechanics tools. Our values suggest that for small masses, the energy required is much smaller than the one predicted by common gravitational theories. The findings of this work contribute to our understanding of the Comorosan Effect and open up new avenues for further research, including the development of new models consistent with our experimental observations.

In this research, we investigate the capacity of sparse multipath channels in the ultra-wideband (UWB) regime. The motivation for our study is the growing demand for high-capacity wireless communication systems that can support various applications, including high-speed data, multimedia streaming, and internet of things (IoT) devices. However, sparse multipath UWB channels pose significant challenges due to their multipath propagation, which results in severe signal attenuation and interference. To solve this problem, we propose a novel approach for estimating the channel capacity of UWB channels with sparse multipath. Our method is based on the principle of compressed sensing, which exploits the sparsity of the multipath channel impulse response. We show that our approach can significantly improve the channel capacity compared to traditional methods. Our results demonstrate that sparse multipath channels have a significant potential for providing high-capacity wireless communication systems in the UWB regime. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to other wireless communication systems that use sparse multipath channels. Overall, our research provides valuable insights into the capacity analysis of sparse multipath channels, which can contribute to the development of efficient and reliable wireless systems that can support various applications.

In this work, we explore the properties of isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter in the framework of chiral mean-field models (RMF) with chiral limits. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a consistent and well-established equation of state (EoS) for isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter, which is crucial for understanding various astrophysical phenomena such as the structure and dynamics of neutron stars, supernova explosions, and heavy-ion collisions. Our key ideas involve incorporating the chiral symmetry of QCD and the interaction between nucleons and mesons into the RMF models to obtain a more accurate and realistic representation of the nuclear matter. Our methodology involves implementing the chiral limits in the RMF models and solving the equations of motion self-consistently . We calculate the EoS for isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter properties such as energy density, pressure, symmetry energy, and isospin asymmetry. We also determine the behavior of the EoS at high densities and isospin asymmetries and compare our results with previous theoretical predictions and experimental data. Our results indicate a significant enhancement of the symmetry energy and its slope parameter in the chiral RMF models, which is consistent with recent experimental observations. Moreover, our EoS calculations show a stiffer dependence on the isospin asymmetry, particularly at high densities, which may have implications for the maximum mass and radius of neutron stars and the dynamics of heavy-ion collisions. Overall, our work provides a new framework for the study of isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter and its role in astrophysical phenomena.

In this work, we explore the possibility of Feynman-Weinberg quantum gravity and the extended standard model as a theory of everything. The fundamental aspect is to find the unification of the four fundamental forces in nature: Gravity, Light, Weak and Strong forces. We have methodically examined the key elements of the standard model of particle physics, which comprise gauge symmetry and the Higgs boson. The work has focused on unifying gravity with the current established laws of particle physics. We present a comprehensive analysis of the Feynman-Weinberg quantum gravity theory, which provides a framework to unify the gravitational force with the existing particle physics theories. We review the key concepts related to the formalization of quantum gravity theory and its application to the standard model. Our methodology has been to examine the various approaches and techniques in developing the Feynman-Weinberg quantum gravity model, including the use of perturbation theory and the gravitational path integral together with the standard model, as well as, string theory. We attempt to solve the problem of finding a complete quantum theory that can be used to describe the unification of fundamental particles Overall, our investigation has concluded that Feynman-Weinberg quantum gravity and the extended standard model method are a plausible theory of everything that could provide a unified description of the four fundamental forces, which would extend the current achievements in particle physics and theoretical physics.

In this extended review, we analyze and critique the work presented in "One-Range Addition Theorems for Coulomb Interaction Potential and Its Derivatives" by I. I. Guseinov , published in the journal of Chemical Physics. The article discusses the one-range addition theorems, which aim to provide an analytical expression for the integral of the Coulomb interaction potential and its derivatives. The author uses a recursive method to derive these formulas, allowing for the computation of molecular properties in an efficient and straightforward manner. However, we identify several shortcomings in the article, including the lack of clarity in the methodology and the inconsistency in the notation. Additionally, we point out the limited application of the formulas and the need for further research to extend them to other types of molecular interactions. Despite these limitations, we acknowledge the valuable contribution of the author in providing a mathematical framework for calculating molecular properties based on Coulomb interaction potentials. We encourage future work in this field to address the issues we raised and build upon this foundational research.

In this work, we explore the quantum limits for physical implementations of the quantum NOT gate induced by the conservation laws. We demonstrate that the conservation laws, such as energy conservation and charge conservation, impose fundamental bounds on the accuracy of the gate operation, which can be characterized by the gate fidelity and the gate error probability. Our analysis is based on the quantum Zeno effect, which arises from the repeated measurement of the quantum system during the gate operation, and leads to the stabilization of the system if the measurement rate is sufficiently high. However, we show that the conservation laws limit the quantum measurement rate, which in turn limits the achievable gate fidelity and increases the gate error probability. The key idea behind our results is that physical implementations of the quantum NOT gate require the transfer of quantum information between different quantum systems, which inevitably involves the exchange of energy and charges, leading to the conservation laws-induced quantum limits. We formalize our analysis using the theory of quantum measurement and the theory of open quantum systems. Our work provides a new perspective on the design and optimization of quantum gates and highlights the importance of taking into account the conservation laws and the corresponding quantum limits.

In this study, we explore the Josephson current in a SFS junction with in-plane ferromagnetic domains. The problem we attempt to solve is an investigation of the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism, which are two fundamental concepts in condensed matter physics. Ferromagnetic domains in an SFS junction alter the density of states available for Andreev reflection, which in turn modifies the Josephson current across the junction. Our motivation for the research is to understand how the Josephson current is affected by ferromagnetic domains and to explore the potential applications of this phenomenon in quantum computing and information processing. The key idea behind this work is to use a theoretical model to investigate the impact of ferromagnetic domains on the Josephson current in an SFS junction. Our methodology involves using the Usadel equations to numerically solve for the superconducting density of states and the self-consistent magnetization of the ferromagnetic layer. We also use the quasiclassical Green's function formalism to calculate the Josephson current across the SFS junction. Our results show that ferromagnetic domains significantly affect the Josephson current, leading to a reduction in its magnitude and a modulation of its phase. Our work contributes to the understanding of the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism, and provides insight into the design of hybrid quantum devices based on SFS junctions.

In this study, we present an investigation on sulphur abundances in stars using the SI near-infrared triplet at 1045 nm. The motivation for this research stems from the lack of reliable measurements of sulphur abundances in stars, which is a crucial element for galactic evolution and nucleosynthesis models. The problem we aim to solve is the inconsistency between the abundances obtained through previously used optical lines and the S I triplet in the near-infrared region. To overcome this problem, we employed the S I triplet at 1045 nm to analyze the optical spectra of a sample of 30 evolved stars and derived their sulphur abundances using equivalent width and spectrum measurement techniques. We also compared the obtained results with the atmospheric parameters and iron abundances of the stars. Our key findings reveal that the sulphur abundances derived using the SI triplet in the near-infrared region are in good agreement with the optical results for dwarfs, giants, and some giants. However, significant discrepancies are observed for certain giants, indicating that the triplet might be affected by non-LTE, 3D hydrodynamic effects, or other uncertainties. Overall, our study highlights the importance of using the S I triplet in the near-infrared region to obtain reliable measurements of sulphur abundances in stars and the need for further investigation on giants to determine the root cause of the discrepancies.

In this research, we investigate the properties of cosmic rays with GeV gamma rays. Cosmic rays are highly charged particles that originate from sources in the universe and reach Earth's atmosphere. One of the ways to study cosmic rays is by detecting gamma rays produced in their interactions with the interstellar medium. The use of GeV gamma rays as a probe provides a unique opportunity to study cosmic rays in greater detail. This work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the origin and acceleration mechanisms of cosmic rays. Despite decades of research, the sources and acceleration processes of cosmic rays remain elusive. By studying GeV gamma rays, we aim to shed light on this long-standing mystery. Specifically, the study focuses on the detection of gamma-rays in the Galactic plane, which is a region of potential sources of cosmic rays. The results show that the study of cosmic ray emission with GeV gamma rays provides complementary information to other cosmic ray detectors. By analyzing the gamma-ray flux and acceleration mechanisms, we were able to constrain the properties of the cosmic ray sources and acceleration mechanisms. Furthermore, we found that the detection of gamma rays in the Galactic plane is consistent with the prediction of a diffuse gamma-ray emission originating from interactions of cosmic rays with the interstellar medium. The motivation for this research comes from the desire to deepen our understanding of the most energetic particles in the universe. The study of cosmic rays with GeV gamma rays has the potential to provide crucial insights into the workings of cosmic accelerators and the physical processes that govern the evolution of the universe.

We present our work on pairing based cooling of Fermi gases. The motivation for this research arises from the need to achieve lower temperatures and higher density in ultracold atomic gases. This field aims to study the behavior of gases at temperatures close to absolute zero, where classical physics can no longer accurately explain their behaviors. Studies have shown that Fermi gases can be cooled below their Fermi temperature by pairing fermions into composite bosons. The key idea behind our work is to make use of this pairing mechanism to cool the Fermi gas even further. We propose to control the interaction between the fermions and the composite bosons by tuning external magnetic fields. Our methodology involves using numerical simulations to study the thermalization time scale of the Bose-Fermi mixture, as well as the overall cooling efficiency. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of efficient cooling methods for Fermi gases. Our pairing-based cooling scheme offers a new avenue to achieve this goal. By using composite bosons to reduce the number of fermions, we can increase the density of the gas for a lower temperature. Our results show that this method is more efficient in cooling a Fermi gas to lower temperatures than traditional cooling methods. We believe that our work has the potential to contribute to the development of more efficient cooling methods for ultracold atomic gases.

In this work, we explore the estimation of the unconditional distribution of post-model-selection estimators. Post-model-selection estimators have become increasingly popular in statistics due to their ability to deal with high-dimensional data. However, the selection of models can lead to biased estimators, and the uncertainty associated with this selection process is often ignored. Our aim is to develop a method to estimate the unconditional distribution of post-model-selection estimators. We propose a new approach based on empirical characteristic functions. Using this method, we obtain an estimator of the characteristic function of the unconditional distribution. We show that this estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal under mild conditions. Furthermore, we derive a consistent estimator of the unconditional distribution by inverting the characteristic function. We also use numerical simulations to support the effectiveness of our proposed method. The main theme for our research is the importance of having accurate estimators for data analysis. Considering that post-model-selection estimators are widely used, it is essential to have a method that allows for the uncertainty associated with model selection to be accounted for. Our proposed method offers a robust solution to this issue, enabling us to draw more accurate and reliable inferences. Overall, our work contributes to the development of statistical theory for high-dimensional data analysis.

In our research, we explore the connection between cosmological symmetry breaking, pseudo-scale invariance, and dark energy within the context of the standard model of physics. Our work aims to address the issue of dark energy, which remains an enigma in the field of modern cosmology. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that dark energy makes up approximately 70% of the energy content of the universe, yet its properties and origins remain unclear. We put forth the idea that the observed pseudo-scale invariance of the universe at large scales is a consequence of the breaking of a primordial symmetry during the early universe, which also gives rise to dark energy. This symmetry breaking is driven by the Higgs mechanism, a key aspect of the standard model. We analyze this mechanism through the use of theoretical calculations and simulations, as well as comparison to observational data. Our findings indicate that the breaking of this symmetry during the early universe is responsible for the observed cosmic acceleration attributed to dark energy. The pseudo-scale invariance observed at large scales is a result of this symmetry breaking and holds important implications for the evolution of the universe. In conclusion, our work provides insight into the origins of dark energy and sheds light on the fundamental mechanisms driving the evolution of the universe.

In this work, we investigate the phenomenon of Multiple Parton Scattering (MPS) in atomic nuclei, specifically focusing on quark-quark scattering.
