Our motivation for this research is rooted in the fact that the traditional interpretation of the energy gap does not provide a comprehensive understanding of the superconducting phenomenon. We aim to provide a more comprehensive explanation of the energy gap that takes into account the physics that governs the behavior of the electrons. Our key idea is to interpret the energy gap as the amount of energy required to excite a bound electron pair. We accomplish this by introducing a new mathematical framework that is based on the concept of excitation energy. We then use this framework to develop a new methodology for calculating the energy gap in the BCS theory of superconductivity. Our approach differs from previous attempts to interpret the energy gap in the cut-off approximation. Previous work has typically focused on the mathematical properties of the energy gap rather than the physical properties of the quantity. Our work seeks to bridge this gap by providing a more physical interpretation of the energy gap. Overall, our work aims to solve the problem of understanding the energy gap in the BCS theory of superconductivity by providing a more comprehensive and physically motivated interpretation. We believe that our approach has the potential to greatly deepen our understanding of the superconducting phenomenon and pave the way for new breakthroughs in superconductivity research.

We present a research study on inductively coupled circuits with spin wave bus for information processing. The motivation behind this work is to address the need for faster and more effective communication between different components in quantum computers and other electronic devices. Our methodology involves inductively coupling spin wave bus circuits as a means of transmitting and processing information. We investigate key ideas such as the spin wave propagation, coupling between circuits, and the use of magnetic fields to propagate the spin waves. Our results included successful transmission of information between coupled circuits with low loss, high coherence and connectivity, which can be useful for the development of quantum computing and other advanced electronic devices. Furthermore, we demonstrated that inductively coupled circuits with spin wave bus could be used to implement a universal set of quantum gates. In conclusion, our study highlights the potential of inductively coupled spin wave circuits as a promising approach to increase the speed and efficiency of information processing in electronic devices. The coupling of such circuits provides a versatile and flexible platform for realizing complex information processing circuits, and we strongly believe that our findings will pave the way for future work in this area.

We present a methodology for the secure sharing of random bits over the Internet. Our approach leverages the properties of Shamir's Secret Sharing Scheme, where a secret is divided into multiple shares and distributed among participants, such that only a minimum threshold of shares is required to reconstruct the secret. To ensure the security of the shared random bits, we employ information-theoretic techniques that guarantee that any subset of shares imparts no information about the secret to an eavesdropper. Additionally, we use a cryptographic hash function to enhance the confidentiality of the secret by encrypting it beyond recognition. Our methodology can securely share random bits among any arbitrary number of participants and any threshold of minimum number of participants required for secret reconstruction. Our motivation for this research stems from the need to securely share random bits among multiple parties over the Internet. The need for such a protocol arises in numerous applications, including secure multiparty cryptographic computations, secure polls and elections, and secure key management systems. We aim to provide a viable solution that retains the confidentiality and integrity of the random bits throughout the sharing process. Our work seeks to solve the problem of securely sharing random bits over a public and insecure network (the Internet), where attackers can potentially eavesdrop on communication between parties and compromise the confidentiality of shared bits. The proposed methodology ensures the security of the shared bits while accommodating both the privacy and scalability requirements necessary for modern applications. We believe that our results hold significant promise for enhancing security in several domains and can provide a foundation for future developments in related areas.

In this work, we present a factorization analysis of fragmentation functions in hadrons that contain a heavy quark. Our motivation is twofold. Firstly, fragmentation functions are an essential ingredient in the description of high-energy collisions involving hadrons at collider experiments. Secondly, the presence of a heavy quark in the hadron introduces a new scaling variable that modifies the fragmentation functions, making a factorization formula more difficult to obtain than in the case of light hadrons. We address this problem by applying the framework of Soft-Collinear Effective Theory (SCET), which allows us to systematically separate hard and soft contributions to the fragmentation process. We show that, in the case of heavy quark hadrons, the structure of the factorization formula changes due to the presence of new classes of soft modes that are not present for light hadrons. In particular, we find that the factorization formula involves the convolution of a hard coefficient function with two separate soft functions, one of which is specific to heavy quark hadrons. Our results provide a new understanding of the fragmentation process in heavy quark hadrons and provide an essential tool for precision measurements at collider experiments. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to other processes involving heavy quarks, providing a more general understanding of the interplay between hard and soft dynamics in QCD.

In this present study, we explore the universality of mixed action extrapolation formulae in the context of lattice QCD simulations. Our main focus is to understand the effectiveness of mixed action simulations in obtaining reliable estimates of physical observables. The methodology involves using partially quenched theories with different actions for the valence and sea quarks, with the aim of taking the continuum limit while keeping the quark masses physical. This allows us to study nonperturbative effects and perform a variety of simulation procedures, and we verify our results with three different sets of gauge ensembles generated by the MILC collaboration. The motivation behind this research stems from the need to obtain accurate results for observables that are poorly known , such as the proton charge radius or the CKM matrix elements. The results obtained from these simulations can provide valuable information about the underlying physics and test the validity of the Standard Model. In our study, we investigate mixed action simulations with different lattice spacings, quark masses and volumes, and show that the mixed action extrapolation formulae can be used reliably to estimate the physical values of the observables under investigation. The main outcomes of our study highlight the importance of mixed action simulations for the precise determination of the physical properties of hadronic observables. The universality of the extrapolation formulae confirms their robustness and applicability to different types of gauge ensembles, thus making them valuable tools for current and future lattice QCD calculations. These results can potentially provide new insights into the physics of the strong interaction.

In this work, we investigate the hydrogen 2p--2s transition signals from the epochs of recombination and reionization. Our study aims to solve the problem of understanding the role of the hydrogen 2p--2s transition in the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB) and the reionization of the universe. The motivation for our research arises from the fact that the 2p--2s transition plays a significant role in shaping the CMB due to its resonant nature. Another motivation is that the 2p--2s transition is a probe of the gas temperature and density during reionization. Our main findings show that the 2p--2s transition is indeed a powerful probe of the free electron fraction during reionization. We also find that the 2p--2s absorption feature does not significantly impact the CMB power spectrum but can leave an imprint on the CMB polarization spectrum. In addition, we show that the large-scale anisotropy due to the 2p--2s transition cannot be neglected in the context of precision cosmology, especially in the epoch of reionization. In summary, our work highlights the importance of the hydrogen 2p--2s transition in understanding the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB) and the reionization of the universe. Our findings provide useful insights for future observations and cosmological simulations aiming to constrain the epoch of reionization.

In this work, we investigate the shortcomings of the Schiff theorem and its corrections concerning atomic electric dipole moments. These dipole moments arise due to the presence of an electric field and lead to phenomena such as the violation of time-reversal symmetry and the search for particle physics beyond the standard model. The Schiff theorem predicts the electric dipole moment of an atom to be zero at the first order in perturbation theory. However, higher-order corrections can lead to non-zero values, making the theorem not entirely accurate. Our motivation for this research stems from the importance of accurately predicting atomic electric dipole moments in experiments. These dipole moments play a crucial role in the search for CP-violation of time-reversal symmetry and in the search for new physics beyond the standard model. Hence, addressing the shortcomings of the Schiff theorem and its corrections is of critical importance. We present three main ideas in this work. First, we review the current state of the Schiff theorem and its corrections. Second, we summarize the significant theoretical and experimental advancements in the field. Finally, we discuss the implications of the recent observations and suggest possible future directions of research. We use a formal academic and scientific writing voice throughout the work, employing the first plural person form to emphasize the collaborative nature of research in the field. We also use the active voice to highlight the agency in our research and findings. Overall, this work contributes to our collective understanding of atomic electric dipole moments and their role in uncovering the mysteries of the universe.

Our research aimed to enhance the lifetime of wireless sensor networks (WSNs) with the collaborative beamforming and cooperative transmission (CBCT) approach. WSNs have a limited lifespan due to their energy consumption constraints, and in many cases, replacing them is not practical. Therefore, extending the lifetime of WSN is of great importance. We proposed a novel CBCT approach that combines two techniques, collaboration among sensor nodes and beamforming. The proposed approach optimizes the energy consumption of the network by reducing the energy consumption of each node. The CBCT approach also makes the transmission more reliable and resilient against interferences and obstacles. Our experimental simulations showed that the proposed CBCT method could improve the network's lifetime by nearly 20% compared to traditional techniques. Additionally, our results showed that our approach outperformed existing solutions in terms of reliability, energy consumption, and network lifetime. In conclusion, this work demonstrates the effectiveness of the CBCT in improving the lifetime of WSNs. The innovative approach combines the benefits of beamforming and cooperative transmission to optimize the energy consumption and enhance the lifetime of the WSN. The CBCT has the potential to enable efficient and reliable wireless sensor networks for numerous applications in which WSNs play a vital role.

In this study, we present statistical evidence for the existence of three distinct classes of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) using a sample of 1746 GRBs observed by the Swift satellite over a span of 15 years. The detection of different types of GRBs has been a long-standing problem in astrophysics, as understanding their nature can provide crucial insights into the physics of extreme astrophysical events and the evolution of the Universe. We employ a machine learning approach to classify GRBs into one of three groups based on their spectral and temporal properties. We find that the three classes have distinct properties in terms of their spectral peak , duration, and hardness ratios. One class is characterized by short-duration, hard spectra that are commonly associated with neutron star mergers, while another class exhibits longer -duration and softer spectra often associated with the collapse of massive stars. The third class is composed of intermediate-duration GRBs that exhibit different properties from the other two classes. Our results provide compelling statistical evidence for three different GRB classes, which could have significant implications for our understanding of the mechanisms that produce these high-energy events, their progenitors, and the large-scale structure of the Universe.

In this work, we analyze the quark loop contributions to the electric dipole s (EDMs) of the neutron, deuteron, and mercury in the context of supersymmetry without R parity. Our investigation aims to provide a deeper understanding of the particle physics models that could potentially explain the observed value of the EDMs. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a clear explanation for the EDMs, which cannot be explained within the Standard Model of particle physics. The key idea is to study the effect of supersymmetric particles, including squarks and charginos, on the quark loop contributions to the EDMs. We use the One-Loop RGE-Improved Effective Lagrangian framework to calculate the quark loop contributions to the EDMs and take into account the constraints on the supersymmetric parameter space from various experimental and theoretical considerations. We find that the contributions from squarks and charginos can significantly enhance the quark loop contributions to the EDMs, leading to potentially observable effects in future EDM s. Our results emphasize the need for more precise measurements of the EDMs of the neutron, deuteron, and mercury, which can aid in guiding the search for physics beyond the Standard Model.

In this work, we aim to investigate the collective modes in two-band superconductors. The motivation for our research stems from an increasing interest in the physics of multi-band superconductors. Multi-band superconductors have been shown to exhibit novel properties compared with their single-band counterparts, including the possibility of an unconventional pairing mechanism. Understanding the collective modes in these materials is therefore crucial for unraveling their complex physical properties. Our work attempts to solve the problem of identifying the collective modes which describe the low-energy excitations in two-band superconductors. To achieve this, we use a variety of theoretical methods, including the Green's function formalism and the Eliashberg theory. By employing these techniques, we investigate the impact of interband couplings on the collective modes in two-band superconductors. The key ideas of our research are to identify the collective modes that emerge in the two-band superconducting state, and to understand how these modes are affected by the interplay between the pairing mechanisms of each band. Our results will contribute to a better understanding of the physics of multi-band superconductors as well as provide insights into the design of new devices based on these materials.

In this paper, we present a study of the far-infrared cosmic background radiation using data obtained from the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) and Wilhowsky H Alpha Mapping (WHAM) experiments. The far-infrared spectrum occupies a crucial region of the electromagnetic spectrum, as it enables us to probe the early universe and study the formation and evolution of galaxies and large-scale structures. Our objective is to employ the COBE/DIRBE and WHAM observations to determine the intensity and spectral energy distribution of the cosmic background radiation at frequencies around 100 microns. We first present an analysis of the COBE/DIRBE data, which provides the most precise detection of the cosmic background in the far-infrared region. We then use the WHAM data to correct for the weak foreground emission due to the presence of dust and gas in our Milky Way Galaxy, which can contaminate the cosmic background . A significant challenge in this study is to distinguish the faint cosmic signal from the much stronger foreground emission, which requires careful modeling and data analysis. Our results show a clear detection of the far-infrared cosmic background at 100 microns, with an intensity of 14.6 +/- 1.8 nanowatts per square meter per steradian and a spectral energy distribution consistent with a blackbody at a temperature of 18.5 +/- 1.3 Kelvin. Our analysis provides an important contribution to our understanding of the early universe, and has broad implications for cosmology and astrophysics.

The present work offers a detailed optical and X-ray analysis of the cooling flow cluster Z3146, named ARCRAIDER I. Our analysis confirms a strong cD galaxy at the center of the cluster, surrounded by a cooling flow of gas. The spatially resolved spectral analysis shows that the intra-cluster cooling flow (ICM) is hot in the cluster's center and cools down radially, with temperatures of around 2 keV at the edge. We also found a clear correlation between temperature and metallicity, showing that the central ICM is enriched in heavy elements, while the outskirts hold a higher concentration of lighter elements. This research provides essential information about the complex mechanisms involved in the cooling flow mechanism, which is vital for further understanding the evolution of galaxy clusters. Such analyses are necessary to comprehend the cooling flows' physical properties and their connection to the evolution of cluster properties. Additionally, studying the metallicity distribution in the ICM not only provides crucial information about the elemental abundances but also helps trace the history of star formation in the cluster. The results obtained in this work serve as a significant contribution to the ever-growing body of knowledge on cluster evolution and can serve as a launching point for further research in this field. The analysis presented here attempts to solve the problem of shedding light on the nature of cooling flows and metallicity distribution, which has been a long-standing source of debate and research in the cosmological community.

In this study, we present annotations to a certain passage of Descartes' work that aims to provide a solution for finding a formula that can calculate the quadrature of the circle. The key idea behind Descartes' work is to use geometry to find a formula that can calculate the area of a circle. In doing so, he utilized his analytical geometry skills to solve this problem, which was considered a famous challenge at the time. Our research aims to provide annotations to this specific passage that will help interpret the methodology and ideas behind Descartes' work. Our motivation for this study is rooted in the fact that Descartes' work was a significant advancement in the field of mathematics. We hope that our annotations will help readers understand the problem as it was presented by Descartes, and contribute to the development of the field by providing valuable insights into the methodology used to solve this particular mathematical problem. The problem our work attempts to solve is to provide a comprehensive interpretation of a certain portion of Descartes' work, which is considered one of the most important contributions to the field of mathematics. Our annotations reveal the key concepts, ideas, and techniques used by Descartes to analyze the problem and develop a solution. They also help to contextualize the work and provide a deeper understanding of the significance and contribution of Descartes' work to the history of mathematics.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of triple stars with and without pulsar in star clusters. The aim of our research is to make predictions related to the formation and distribution of triple systems in star clusters and to provide insights into the mechanisms that govern the behavior of such systems in star clusters. We approached this problem by employing a numerical simulation that incorporates the dynamics of gravitational interactions between stars in a cluster. Our model takes into account the effects of gravitational forces, as well as other factors such as mass loss and tidal interactions. The results of our simulations show that triple systems with pulsars have shorter lifetimes, due to the perturbations caused by the pulsar, as compared to those without pulsars. Moreover, we found that the number of triple systems with pulsars in a cluster is lower than that of triple systems without pulsars. Furthermore, our study indicates that there is a strong correlation between the presence of pulsars and the distribution of triple systems in clusters. Overall, this study shed light on the dynamics of triple stars in star clusters and helped us understand the mechanisms that govern the behavior of such systems. Our predictions could also help future observational studies to unravel the mysteries of triple systems in star clusters.

In this study, we determine the iron abundances of two B-type post-Asymptotic Giant Branch (post-AGB) stars located in two globular clusters: ROA 29 in M 13 and ROA 5701 in Omega Cen. The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the chemical evolution of these clusters, which are among the oldest and most metal-poor stellar systems in the Milky Way. Furthermore, post-AGB stars are excellent probes for studying the late-stages of stellar evolution and can reveal important information about the nucleosynthesis processes that occur in these stars. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of accurate iron abundances for B-type post-AGB stars in globular clusters. We employ high-resolution spectroscopy to obtain the iron abundances and other chemical abundances for our targets. Our results show that both post-AGB stars in our sample are enriched in sub-solar iron abundances, confirming the metal-poor nature of these globular clusters. Additionally, we find that ROA 5701 is enriched in s-process elements, which is consistent with its previous classification as a barium star. Overall, our work enhances our understanding of the chemical composition of globular clusters and sheds light on the nucleosynthesis processes that govern the late stages of stellar evolution.

In this article, we present a comprehensive set of elemental abundances in Damped Lyman-α systems (DLAs) to investigate their star formation histories. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that DLAs provide an excellent opportunity to study the properties of high-redshift galaxies, as they are the primary reservoirs of quasar gas that can be traced by the absorption of quasar spectra. By doing so, understanding the elemental abundances in DLAs can shed light on the chemical evolution of galaxies and how these systems have formed over time. To achieve this goal, we have compiled a catalogue of DLAs detected in quasar spectra and analyzed their elemental abundances. We have looked at the abundances of alpha, iron-peak, and neutron-capture elements and analyzed their correlations, which provide insights into the enrichment processes of these systems. Additionally, we have also calculated stellar masses and star formation rates for the host galaxies of DLAs to characterize their star formation histories. The key idea behind this work is to build a comprehensive dataset of the elemental abundances in DLAs to gain a better understanding of how galaxies evolve over time. By doing so, we hope to fill in the gaps in our knowledge about the formation and evolution of galaxies, which will ultimately help us to unravel the mysteries of the universe.

In this paper, we present a study of the non-linear period-luminosity (P-L) relation of LMC Cepheids. We utilize two powerful statistical tools, Testimator and Schwarz information criterion (SIC), to investigate the deviation from linearity in the P-L relation. Our motivation is to improve the accuracy of distance measurements using Cepheids and ultimately shed light on the cosmic distance ladder and the expansion and contraction of the Universe. We employ the OGLE-III LMC Cepheid data set as our sample, spanning a period range of 1 to 100 days. We fit the P-L relation with a linear model and a quadratic model using maximum likelihood estimation. We then apply Testimator, a model selection criterion that compares the log-likelihoods of the models to select the best-fit model. Finally, we use SIC to penalize overfitting and select the model that provides the best trade-off between goodness-of-fit and complexity. Our analysis reveals significant evidence for non-linearity in the P-L relation of LMC Cepheids, with the quadratic model providing a superior fit over the linear model. The results indicate that the non-linearity is not merely a result of statistical fluctuation but reflects the astrophysical physics of the Cepheids. Our study highlights the importance of utilizing non-linear models in the analysis of Cepheid data and provides valuable insights into the astrophysical properties of these important standard candles.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to information retrieval within collaborative development context. The problem we aim to solve is the information asymmetry that often occurs in collaborative development projects due to the different perspectives and expertise of members involved in the project. This asymmetry makes it difficult to retrieve relevant information from multiple sources of knowledge. The key idea of our approach is to leverage the multiple viewpoints of the members to enhance the retrieval of information. Our methodology involves the development of a collaborative knowledge management system that captures the multiple viewpoints of members through a combination of metadata, tags, and feedback mechanisms. The system also utilizes natural language processing (NLP) to identify and extract relevant information from multiple sources. Our results indicate that our approach is effective in enhancing the retrieval of relevant information in collaborative development projects. We conducted a case study in a software development project and found that the system was able to retrieve relevant information with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, the members reported that the system was beneficial in supporting their collaboration and decision-making processes. In conclusion, our approach of leveraging multiple viewpoints to enhance information retrieval in collaborative development projects is a promising solution to the problem of information asymmetry commonly faced by collaborative development teams. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and suggest further exploration into its potential applications in other contexts.

In this study, we aimed to explore the properties of four large-resolution (WR) stars that might have triggered gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) or core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe). We specifically focused on circumstellar absorption lasers (CSALs) in the spectra of the stars. Such spectra can provide crucial information about the composition and kinematics of the winds blown by the stars, and thus, help us understand their evolution and ultimate fate. We analyzed high-resolution optical spectra of the four WR stars to identify and measure the properties of their CSALs. We found that the CSALs exhibit a wide range of velocities, ranging from a few hundred to several thousand kilometers per second, as well as complex line shapes due to the overlapping of multiple components. The properties of the CSALs suggest that the stars are undergoing significant mass loss and likely have very high initial masses. Our results suggest that the stars have important constraints on the GRB and CCSN progenitors. The detection and proper interpretation of the properties of CSALs in the spectra of massive stars can help us identify their evolutionary stage and predict their final outcome. This study serves as a step forward in understanding the complex and intricate processes that govern the evolution of massive stars in the Universe.

In this paper, we present a novel experimental setup to demonstrate frequency upshifting through relativistic tennis ball with photons. Our methodology involves colliding two probe laser pulses with orthogonal polarization to create a relativistic flying mirror, which reflects a separate probe laser pulse. The probe pulse experiences frequency upshifting due to the Doppler effect resulting from the relativistic motion of the flying mirror. Our setup also utilizes a spectral interferometer to measure the frequency upshifted signal with high accuracy. The motivation for this research is to explore the fundamental principles of special relativity and their potential application in the field of optics. Frequency upshifting is a significant phenomenon that can be applied in various fields such as nonlinear optics, laser-plasma interactions, and astrophysics. Our work attempts to solve the problem of experimental verification of frequency upshifting through relativistic effects, which has not been effectively demonstrated before. Our results show a clear demonstration of frequency upshifting through relativistic flying mirror with photons. We have achieved a maximum frequency upshift of 2.5 times and measured the frequency upshifted signal through spectral interferogram modulation with a visibility of 0.6. The successful demonstration of this phenomenon opens up the possibility of developing new technologies in various fields such as ultrafast laser pulse generation and medical imaging.

In this study, we report the discovery of four quasars with redshifts above six from the Canada-France High-z Quasar Survey (CFHQS). These objects were selected based on their broad emission and redshift spectra and were subsequently confirmed using ground-based spectroscopy. The motivation for this research lies in the importance of high-redshift quasars for understanding the early Universe. Quasars are the most luminous and long-lived objects in the early Universe, and as such, they provide a unique probe of the cosmic environment and the growth of supermassive black holes. The results of our study reveal that these four quasars have redshifts ranging from 6.3 to 6.5, corresponding to a time when the Universe was less than one billion years old. These quasars have black hole masses ranging from 1 to 5 billion solar masses, indicating that the formation of supermassive black holes occurred early in the Universe's history. We also find that the quasar luminosity function at z ~ 6 is consistent with previous measurements from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, suggesting that the growth of black holes near the end of the reionization epoch was not significantly impacted by radiation feedback from these sources. The key methodology in this study involves the use of the wide-field imaging capabilities of the CFHQS to identify the four quasar candidates. Follow-up spectroscopy with ground-based telescopes allowed us to confirm the redshifts of these objects. These new discoveries add to our growing sample of high-redshift quasars and provide important insights into the early Universe and the growth of black holes.

In this study, we investigate the micro and macrorheological properties of highly cross-linked actin networks. Actin is an essential cytoskeletal protein that plays an essential role in cell structure and movement. It is a crucial component of many biological processes, including cell division, migration, and signaling. The aim of this research is to gain a better understanding of the mechanical properties of actin networks and their response to external forces. We conducted rheological experiments on highly cross-linked actin networks with varying degrees of cross-linking using optical trapping, micropipette aspiration, and passive microrheology. We found that the elastic moduli of the networks increased with cross-linking , indicating that cross-linking enhances the strength of the actin network. Additionally, we observed that the frequency dependence of the elastic shear modulus was higher in more highly cross-linked networks, indicating that cross-linking alters the mechanical response of the network. The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the mechanical properties of actin networks in various physiological conditions. This knowledge will aid in developing new therapies and treatments for diseases that affect the cytoskeleton, such as cancer and muscular dystrophy. Our research sheds light on the molecular mechanisms behind cellular mechanics, providing a better understanding of the fundamental processes that dictate cellular behavior.

In this work, we investigate the role of massive perturbers in enabling the efficient merger of binary massive black holes (BHs). We identify that close interactions with these perturbers, such as massive stars and gas clouds, can alter the binary BH's orbit and facilitate the merger. We perform numerical simulations of binary BHs with and without perturbers, varying the mass and velocity of the perturber as well as the initial conditions of the binary BH. We find that the presence of a perturber can significantly decrease the time to merger for the binary BH, with some cases resulting in mergers occurring within only a few million years. Our work aims to answer the long-standing question of how binary BHs, which are initially separated by a large distance, can merge within the lifetime of a universe. The ubiquitous presence of massive perturbers in most galaxies suggest that this mechanism is fundamentally essential for the formation and evolution of massive BHs. Our results suggest that massive perturbers are highly efficient in facilitating the merger of binary BHs that would otherwise not merge on a cosmological timescale. Our methodology involves using state-of-the-art numerical simulations to model the dynamics of the binary BH-perturber interactions and analyze the resulting merger times. The key idea of our work is to demonstrate the importance of massive perturbers in facilitating the merging of binary BHs. Our findings shed light on the broader understanding of the role of massive perturbers in BH physics.

In our work, we investigate a problem that has remained unsolved in the field of theoretical physics: the existence of forbidden territories within the string landscape. The string landscape encompasses all possible configurations of strings within a theoretical space. Our research aims to identify areas within this landscape where the laws of physics break down, rendering them forbidden to explore. To tackle this issue, we have employed mathematical models that allow us to map the landscape with greater accuracy. Through careful analysis of these models, we were able to identify and explore forbidden territories that had not previously been detected by other researchers. Our findings confirm that such territories do indeed exist, and suggest that they may be more prevalent than previously believed. The motivation for our research stems from the desire to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying principles that govern the universe. We believe that by identifying and exploring these forbidden territories, we may be able to uncover new insights into the nature of the universe and the fundamental laws that govern it. Ultimately, our work has the potential to contribute to the ongoing quest to develop a unified theory of the universe, and to provide a foundation for further research in the world of theoretical physics.

In this work, we explore the problem of gravitational instability in binary protoplanetary disks, which arises due to the mutual gravitational interaction between the disks and the stars. Binary systems are common in the universe, and the study of binary protoplanetary disks has become increasingly important in understanding how planets form and evolve. Our work aims to solve the problem of how gravitational instability affects the dynamics and structure of binary protoplanetary disks. Key ideas that emerge from our study include the analysis of linear growth of binary protoplanetary disks and non-linear evolution of the disks. We have used numerical simulations to investigate instabilities in disks with various parameters, such as mass ratio, disk aspect ratio, and binary separation. The results of our simulations highlight the importance of the disk's aspect ratio and show a crucial role in enhancing instability and evolution of binary protoplanetary disks. Our study has significant implications for the formation and evolution of planets in binary systems. It provides insights into how multiple planets can form and interact in binary star systems and how their orbits may evolve over time. This work offers new avenues for research into the structure and dynamics of binary protoplanetary disks and improves our understanding of the formation and evolution of planetary systems in the universe.

Our research addresses the issue of the information rate of multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems with finite rate channel state feedback (CSF) and power on/off strategy. The motivation behind this work is the need to improve the information transfer in wireless communication systems, particularly in the MIMO system where multiple antennas enable higher data rates in the fading channel. The power on/off strategy, which optimizes the transmit power , is used to decrease the interference caused by CSF. However, the use of CSF with limited feedback rates can restrict the amount of information that can be transferred. Our key idea is to determine the information rate of MIMO systems with finite rate channel state feedback (CSF) and power on/off strategy. We propose a novel methodology by developing an optimal power allocation algorithm using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) condition. We also derive the mutual information rate of finite rate CSF MIMO systems using the Bayesian lower bound approach. The problem we attempt to solve is to find the optimal power allocation algorithm and the fundamental limits of information rates in the presence of CSF and power on/off strategy. Our research provides insights into the effect of limited feedback on the information rate and provides a framework for optimal power allocation in MIMO systems with finite rate CSF and power on/off strategy. Our innovative approach and results offer significant advancements in wireless communication systems, paving the way for further improvements in the performance of future wireless systems.

In this work, we present a methodology for generating a detailed simulation of a radio telescope using both ray-tracing and physical-optics analysis. Our goal is to investigate the aperture efficiency of the telescope's system, which represents a crucial parameter for assessing its overall performance. Using this approach, we investigated both the geometrical configuration of the telescope and the electromagnetic behavior of the reflector. Our results show that the aperture efficiency of the telescope is significantly affected by various factors, including the alignment accuracy of the reflector, the size and shape of the aperture, and the accuracy of the wavefront . In particular, we found that the alignment of the reflector plays a significant role in the overall performance of the telescope. We also investigated the impact of different shapes of the aperture on the aperture efficiency. Our work contributes to the improvement of radio telescopes by providing insight into the factors that may degrade their performance. Moreover, our work may be extended to assess the aperture efficiency of other systems involving electromagnetic waves.

. Our research aims to develop a new type of instrumentation for ultra-low-field magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based on Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices (SQUIDs). The motivation behind this work is to enhance the sensitivity of MRI studies to allow for imaging of materials with extremely low magnetic fields, such as biological tissues and polymers. The current methods for ultra-low-field MRI use bulky and expensive equipment that often require cryogenic storage. To overcome these limitations, our proposed SQUID-based instrumentation offers a novel and practical solution. SQUIDs have proven to be extremely sensitive in detecting weak magnetic fields, and we believe that this property can be harnessed to develop highly sensitive and cost-effective ultra-low-field MRI systems. Our work focuses on the development of a custom SQUID-based sensor assembly, which can operate at room temperature for high-resolution tomography. We have developed a setup that allows us to achieve magnetic field sensitivities in the order of microtesla, which is at least two orders of magnitude greater than the state-of-the-art MRI systems. Overall, our results indicate that SQUID-based MRI can provide high spatial resolution and superior contrast for a wide range of applications. We believe that this work represents a significant step towards developing efficient and cost-effective ultra-low-field MRI that can benefit a broad range of scientific and industrial areas.

In this study, we investigate the predictive power of the bulge properties of host galaxies for the masses of their supermassive black holes (SMBHs). The motivation for this work lies in the fundamental question of how SMBHs evolve and grow within their galaxies. We hypothesize that the bulge properties, specifically the mass and luminosity, are closely linked to the growth of SMBHs. Using a sample of 50 galaxies with measured SMBH masses, we obtain bulge luminosities and masses from archival data. We also extract morphological properties of host galaxies, such as their brightness to light ratio (B/T). We find a strong correlation between the host galaxies mass and the bulge mass, with a scatter of only 0.3 dex. Furthermore, the B/T ratio is a powerful predictor of the SMBH mass and luminosity. We also provide insight into the bulge formation history. Our results support the idea that SMBH growth is closely linked to the formation and evolution of galaxy bulges. This study highlights the importance of understanding the co-evolution of SMBHs and their host galaxies. Our methodology and findings provide a foundation for future studies of SMBHs and their properties in various types of galaxy.

In this study, we investigate the effective anisotropies and energy barriers of magnetic nanoparticles with Neel surface anisotropy. Magnetic nanoparticles are widely used in various fields, including biomedicine, information storage, and energy conversion. Understanding the magnetic properties of these nanoparticles is crucial for optimizing their applications. Our work attempts to solve the problem of accurately predicting the effective anisotropies and energy barriers of magnetic nanoparticles with Neel surface anisotropy, which have received less attention compared to other types of magnetic nanoparticles. We use a combination of analytical calculations and numerical simulations to obtain the magnetic energy landscape of these nanoparticles. The results show that the effective anisotropy depends on the size and shape of the nanoparticles, and the energy barrier to magnetization reversal varies with the orientation of the external magnetic field. We also demonstrate that the Neel surface anisotropy can enhance the magnetization stability of magnetic nanoparticles, which is promising for their potential applications in magnetic storage and biomedical imaging. This study provides a deeper understanding of the magnetic properties of nanoparticles with Neel surface anisotropy and paves the way for the design and optimization of magnetic nanomaterials for various applications.

In this work, we present the X-ray spectral analysis of two Seyfert galaxies, NGC 2992 and NGC 3081, utilizing data from XMM-Newton observations. Seyfert galaxies are known for their active galactic nuclei (AGN), where intense radiation is generated by supermassive black holes at their centers. Our motivation for this study is to investigate the spectral variability and thermal properties of the AGN in these galaxies, with particular emphasis on the Fe Kα emission line. The Fe Kα line has been observed extensively across various Seyfert galaxies and is thought to originate from the vicinity of the black hole. Our analysis reveals significant differences in the spectral properties of NGC 2992 and NGC 3081, which can be attributed to differences in their AGN accretion rates and geometries. NGC 2992 exhibits a prominent Fe Kα line, indicating the presence of dense, optically thick gas, whereas NGC 3081 shows a weak Fe Kα line, consistent with a lower accretion rate and less dense gas. The spectral variability across different epochs is also analyzed, showing only marginal variations in the Fe Kα line. This work aims to improve our understanding of Seyfert galaxies and their AGN by investigating their X-ray spectra and the properties of the Fe Kα line. These results can provide valuable insights into the thermal processes and thermal feedback mechanisms between the AGN and the surrounding interstellar matter.

In our work, we present ab initio wavefunction-based methods to predict the excited states in solids, with a particular focus on ionic oxides. The problem we aim to solve is the underestimation of the band gaps of these materials when using conventional density functional theory (DFT), which can lead to inaccurate predictions of their electronic and optical properties. To address this issue, we incorporate correlation corrections to the band structure using Coupled Cluster theory (CC) and evaluate their impact on the electronic structure and optical spectra of representative oxides, such as MgO and CaO. Our methodology involves calculating the ground and excited state energies using CC theory, which allows us to capture the electron correlation effects that are beyond the reach of standard DFT. We also use time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) to obtain the optical spectra of representative oxides and compare them with experimental measurements. Our results show that the inclusion of correlation corrections significantly improves the agreement with experimental measurements and leads to a better understanding of the electronic and optical properties of ionic oxides. In summary, our work demonstrates the importance of considering correlation corrections in the calculation of excited states in solids and provides a reliable theoretical framework to predict the properties of ionic oxides with a high degree of accuracy.

In this study, we investigate the properties of off-center HII regions in power-law density distributions in order to better understand the mechanisms behind star formation in their surrounding environments. Our methodology involves performing numerical simulations using the adaptive mesh refinement code FLASH, which accounts for the effects of radiative transfer and gas dynamics on the evolution of HII regions. We explore the effects of various initial conditions such as the shape, position and power-law slope of the density peak as well as the strength of the ionizing radiation source. Our results suggest that off-center HII regions tend to have longer lifetimes and more complex gas dynamics compared to their centered counterparts. We also find that the shape and position of the HII region can have a significant impact on the surrounding gas distribution, leading to the formation of secondary dense clumps and filaments. Our analysis sheds light on the potential role of off-center HII regions in the dynamics of star formation in their surroundings, highlighting the importance of accounting for the effects of off-center ionization sources in simulations of dynamic star-forming regions. This research contributes to our understanding of the complex interplay between radiation and gas dynamics within dynamic star-forming regions.

In this study, we propose a novel approach to identify the presence of dark matter burners in the Galactic center. Our methodology relies on the analysis of the energy distributions of the different astrophysical objects that populate the region, including galaxies, pulsars, and black holes. The goal is to detect the emission of high-energy gamma rays that could be the signature of dark matter that is decaying or annihilating. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that dark matter is one of the most crucial unknowns in modern physics. Understanding its properties and interactions with other particles could shed light on its nature and provide clues to the more fundamental laws of the universe. Moreover, the Galactic center is a particularly promising target for dark matter searches due to its high concentration of matter, including dark matter. Our results show that several of the detected gamma-ray sources in the region, such as the gamma-ray excess observed by the Fermi-LAT telescope, could be explained by the presence of dark matter burners. We discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of the nature and distribution of dark matter in the Galaxy. Overall, our approach provides a valuable new avenue for identifying the elusive dark matter particles and furthering our knowledge of the fundamental nature of the universe.

In this article, we present the first study of the gluon-quark-antiquark static potential in SU(3) lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Our aim is to provide a deeper understanding of the confining force that binds quarks and anti-quarks in hadrons. The confinement problem in QCD remains one of the main challenges in particle physics, and our study represents an important step towards solving it. To achieve this goal, we employ numerical simulations using the Wilson gauge action model and domain-wall fermions. Our simulations are carried out on a large lattice with a volume of 24³ × 48, and we use multiple lattice spacings to ensure that our results are free from finite lattice spacing effects. Our main result is a precise determination of the gluon-quark-antiquark static potential in SU(3) QCD. We find that the potential is well-described by a Cornell-like potential, with a linearly rising term at long distances and a Coulomb-like term at short distances. We also observe that the string tension, which characterizes the linearly rising term, is consistent with previous lattice QCD studies. In conclusion, our study provides important insights into the confining force in SU(3) QCD and establishes a solid foundation for future studies of the static potential in SU(3) lattice QCD.

In this work, we present the results of an imaging survey for extrasolar planets around 45 close, young stars using SDI techniques from the VLT and MMT. The main motivation behind this research was to detect and characterize potential young exoplanets in the early stages of formation while still embedded in their natal disks. Our survey covered a total of 45 stars, all within approximately 100 light-years from Earth, with a detection sensitivity of less than 10 Jupiter masses at separations ranging from 0.1 to 5 arcseconds. The results obtained from our imaging survey revealed no undiscovered planets around our target stars, but a total of seven previously known companions were re-detected. In addition, we estimated the mass limits for any undetected planets around our target stars. Our primary methodology involved using the SDI technique to filter out the bloated point-spread-function of the central stars, allowing us to detect fainter companion objects. While this technique is not a perfect solution, we have achieved a significant improvement over traditional imaging. Overall, our imaging survey has provided valuable new data on young exoplanets and their environments, adding to the growing body of research in this field. Our results are also relevant to future direct imaging missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

In this study, we investigate the extended structure of the remote cluster B514 in M31 by detecting extra-tidal stars. Our key objective is to understand the nature of the cluster and determine whether it is a disrupted satellite or a distant object. The methodology of this work involved multi-band imaging with the Subaru telescope, which enabled us to identify and isolate extra-tidal stars from the background. We also used the deep optical data from the Hubble Space Telescope to confirm the existence of the extra-tidal stars and to determine the cluster's size and luminosity function. The main problem that our work attempts to solve is clarifying the origin and evolution of the remote cluster B514. Our results confirm the presence of the extra-tidal stars, and their spatial and kinematic distribution suggests that the cluster is a disrupted satellite. We also find that B514 has a large half-light radius and is more than ten times as massive as previously thought, which indicates that it might be a member of the undiscovered population of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies. Our findings demonstrate the importance of studying the extended structures of remote clusters, which can provide essential information about the galaxy's mass, history and structure.

In this work, we investigate the statistical mechanics of nonlinear on-line , nonlinear ensemble learning. Our motivation lies in developing a better understanding of machine learning algorithms that leverage the advantages of ensemble learning and operate in an on-line, non-stationary setting where the input data distribution and task may change over time. We utilize a statistical mechanics approach to analyze the asymptotic performance of a class of on-line, ensemble learning algorithms based on gradient descent with soft committee s. By considering the large ensemble limit and assuming a sparsely connected network of teachers modeled by random graphs, we derive expressions for the steady state free energy landscape of the system. We then employ replica theory and ensemble learning algorithms to analyze the generalization error and the effect of noise and perturbations on the performance of the algorithm. Our results show that the ensemble learning algorithm can improve generalization and robustness, but the performance is highly dependent on the connectivity of the teacher network and the strength of the coupling among the teachers. Moreover, we find that the replica symmetry is broken in the system, leading to an intricate phase space structure with multiple competing solutions. This work aims to provide theoretical insights into the statistical mechanics of on-line, nonlinear ensemble learning and may have implications for the design and optimization of machine learning algorithms in non-stationary environments.

In this work, we investigate the valley-dependent optoelectronics originating from inversion symmetry breaking in two-dimensional materials. The main problem that we aim to address is the lack of understanding of charge and spin dynamics in such materials. The motivation for this research stems from the potential application of valleytronics in quantum computing and communication technologies. Our approach involves designing models for two-dimensional materials with broken inversion symmetry, calculating the electronic band structures, and analyzing the valley-dependent optical and magnetic properties of the materials. We explore the effects of various perturbations, such as the polarization direction of the incident light, electric field, and magnetic field, on the valley polarization and spin lifetime of the materials. Our findings show that valley polarization and spin lifetime can be manipulated in the presence of these perturbations. We observe that the valley polarization is highly dependent on the polarization direction of the incident light and can be efficiently tuned by external perturbations. We also note that the spin lifetime is sensitive to the scattering mechanisms in the materials and can be greatly extended under proper conditions. Our work enhances our understanding of the fundamental properties of two-dimensional materials and opens up exciting opportunities for future applications in valleytronics. We anticipate that our findings will inspire further exploration in this field and contribute to the advancement of technological innovation.

In this study, we use a multiphysics modeling approach to understand the behavior of a carbon nanotube thin film field-emitting diode (CNTFED). The motivation for this work stems from the need to develop high-performance field-emission devices for applications in vacuum electronics, flat-panel displays, and advanced medical devices. CNTFEDs have attracted significant attention due to their extraordinary electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties, making them an ideal candidate for field-emission applications. The key idea of this work is to understand the complex interaction between multiple physical phenomena that occur in CNTFEDs during field -emission applications. The multiphysics approach involves the coupling of mechanical, thermal, electrical, and transport models to simulate the complete field-emission process, including the generation, transport, and collision of electrons in the carbon nanotube thin film. Our approach provides a comprehensive understanding of the CNTFED system and its key operating parameters, such as the field enhancement factor, current density, and emission properties. This understanding can lead to the development of new designs and optimization strategies for high-performance CNTFEDs. The work attempts to solve the problem of predicting the emission characteristics of CNTFEDs, which is crucial for their practical implementation. Overall, our study provides insights into the fundamental physics governing the behavior of CNTFEDs and serves as a guide for understanding the emission and transport phenomena in these systems.

In this study, we present evidence for the existence of a massive protocluster in the S255 molecular cloud complex. The motivation for this research is driven by a desire to better understand the processes of massive star formation and their role in the evolution of galaxies. The S255 complex has long been known as a site of high-mass star formation, and our study sets out to investigate the possibility of a protocluster in the region. Our research is focused on high-density molecular gas traced by the ammonia molecule (NH3) and radio continuum emission, which we analyzed using the Very Large Array (VLA) and the Green Bank Telescope (GBT), respectively. We identified a region of enhanced ammonia emission which we interpret as a massive, high-mass protocluster. This region coincides with the location of several high-mass young stellar objects and radio continuum emission. Our methodology involved analyzing the properties of the molecular gas, such as the kinematics and density distribution, and comparing them to numerical simulations of protoclusters. We also performed spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling to estimate the masses of the young stellar objects. Our findings provide strong evidence for the existence of a massive protocluster in the S255 molecular cloud complex, which could have important implications for our understanding of the formation, evolution, and evolution of high-mass stars in clusters.

In this study, we investigate the process of planetesimal accretion onto growing proto-gas-giant planets, which is crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of gas-giant planets in the early stages of the planetary system. The problem we attempt to solve is to address the complex mechanisms of planetesimal accretion onto gas giants, such as their scattering in the presence of gas or gravitational instability. The motivation for this research is to improve our understanding of the complex mechanisms that lead to the formation of gas giants, especially in light of the growing body of observational data on exoplanets. Our work proposes a new model for planetesimal accretion onto proto-gas-giants, which considers the dynamics of planetesimal orbits and gas accretion rates. We employ numerical simulations to investigate the impact of gas density on planetesimal accretion and the role of planetesimal eccentricity in disrupting the gravitational stability of gas giants' disks. The model considers the effects of gas drag, planetesimal accretion, and scattering off planets on the formation of the gas giants. The results of this study enable us to gain insights into the viability of current theories about the formation of gas giants. Our work highlights the importance of understanding planetesimal accretion in the formation of gas giants, elucidating key factors that shape the initial conditions of growing proto-gas-giants and resulting planetary architectures. In conclusion, our study offers a valuable contribution to the current understanding of the formation of gas giants by revising assumptions and providing new models that account for the challenges that arise in planetesimal accretion. The implications of this work extend beyond our planetary system and provide insight into the formation of exoplanets.

In this paper, we present a Dynamics-Controlled Truncation (DCT) scheme for nonlinear dynamics in semiconductor microcavities. The motivation behind this research is the growing need for accurate and efficient modeling of the nonlinear dynamics in microcavity systems, which play an essential role in many optoelectronic applications. In particular, the DCT scheme is designed to address the challenge of efficiently modeling and analyzing the nonlinear dynamics in semiconductor microcavities while minimizing the growth of numerical errors resulting from the long simulation times required for analyzing the nonlinear dynamics of these systems. The key idea behind the DCT scheme is to exploit the dynamic nature of the system to make informed decisions on the level of details needed in the simulation at each time step. This is achieved by controlling the truncation of higher-order terms in the system's equations of motion at specific time intervals, guided by the behavior of the system's variables. The DCT scheme is implemented using a split-step Fourier method, which allows for efficient computation of the system's evolution. The problem that this work attempts to solve is the challenge of efficiently modeling and analyzing the nonlinear dynamics in microcavity systems with high accuracy and long simulation times. We demonstrate the efficacy of the DCT scheme by applying it to the study of the nonlinear dynamics of a semiconductor microcavity system and comparing the results against those obtained using conventional numerical methods. Our results show that the DCT scheme can significantly reduce the computational cost of simulating nonlinear dynamics in semiconductor microcavities while retaining high accuracy.

In this study, we examined the transition zone in Balmer-dominated shocks, which is a crucial region in astrophysical plasmas where the kinetic energy generated by shock waves is converted into thermal energy. Understanding the complex physical mechanisms occurring in this zone is essential for interpreting numerous astrophysical phenomena, including supernova remnants, pulsar wind nebulae, and active galactic nuclei. Using state-of-the-art numerical simulations, we investigated the impact of various parameters, such as shock velocity, magnetic field strength, and particle acceleration, on the ionization state and temperature distribution of the transition zone. Our results demonstrate that the width and heating efficiency of the transition zone strongly depend on these parameters and that they significantly affect the observed emission properties of astrophysical sources. We also identified two key physical processes that play a crucial role in shaping the properties of the transition zone: ionization enhancement due to electron heating and ionization enhancement due to charge exchange with neutral hydrogen . These processes provide a new insight into the microphysics of astrophysical shocks and open up new avenues for interpreting observational data. Overall, our work highlights the importance of the transition zone in shaping the observable features of astrophysical plasmas and provides a theoretical framework for interpreting observational data using the latest numerical simulations.

In this work, we present a theoretical framework based on density functional description of thermostatted inhomogeneous granular fluids. The study of granular materials has gained a lot of attention due to their relevance in a wide range of natural and industrial processes. Although granular materials have been widely studied at the nanoscale and macroscopic level, there is still a fundamental gap in the description of nonequilibrium states. Our work aims to fill this gap by proposing a theoretical framework based on density functional theory to describe the nonequilibrium behavior of inhomogeneous granular fluids. We focus on thermostatted systems, in which an external energy source is added to balance the energy dissipation due to collisions. The main challenge of our work lies in tackling the complex interplay between energy dissipation and flow in non-uniform systems. Our methodology involves the derivation of a set of self-consistent equations to describe the particle density profiles, temperature, and pressure of the system. We additionally investigate the properties of the system, such as phase behavior and transport coefficients, using these equations. Our results show that the proposed framework is effective in describing the behavior of inhomogeneous granular fluids under the influence of an external thermostat, providing insights into the energy dissipation and transport properties of these materials. Overall, this work contributes to the understanding of the fundamental properties of granular materials, paving the way for further studies on nonequilibrium states in these materials.
command-xlarge-nightly: We present a detailed analysis of the four greatest X-ray flares ever observed from the magnetar CXOU J164710.2-455216 in Westerlund 1. These extraordinary flares were discovered in a one-week monitoring campaign in April 2018. The observed energy distribution in the flares is well described by an exponentially cut-off power law with a cutoff energy of 2.2 kJ. This energy distribution is consistent with the temperature distribution in the flaring magnetosphere, suggesting that the flares were produced by magnetic reconnection in the magnetosphere. We show that the energy released in the flares is much larger than the spin-down power of the magnetar, indicating that the magnetic energy in the magnetosphere is deposited by the magnetic field of the companion star. We find that the occurrence of such flares is a rare event in magnetars with a well-developed magnetosphere, and that the probability of occurrence decreases with increasing magnetic field and volume of the magnetosphere. Our results suggest that magnetic reconnection is an important process in the magnetosphere of the companion star, and can lead to the occurrence of flares with an energy content of up to 80% of the stellar mass of our Sun.

Classical and quantum randomness and the financial market. We investigate the role of classical and quantum randomness in the financial market, by means of a simple model in which agents are influenced by random news. We show that the probability distribution of the random news has a significant impact on the resulting dynamics of the financial variables. In particular, we find that the possibility of extreme events, which is characterized by the existence of tail events of large magnitude, has a crucial effect on the stability of the market. This finding provides a possible explanation for the prevalence of crashes in financial markets, even in the absence of obvious systemic risk. Our results suggest that the role of randomness, and the possibility of extreme events, should be taken into account in financial risk management. We investigate the role of classical and quantum randomness in the financial market, by means of a simple model of the financial market in which agents are influenced by random news. We assume that the random news is generated by a random walk, and that the impact of the news on the dynamics of financial variables is described by a vector autoregression. We analyze the model in the presence of a wide class of probability distributions, including both classical and quantum distributions. We show that the dynamics of the financial variables can be either stable or unstable, depending on the probability distribution of the random news. In particular, we find that the existence of tail events of large magnitude has a crucial effect on the stability of the market. This finding provides a possible explanation for the prevalence of crashes in financial markets, even in the absence of obvious systemic risk. Our results suggest that the role of randomness, and the possibility of extreme events, should be taken into account in financial risk management.

We present photometric and spectroscopic observations of the Type Ic supernova (SN 2002ap), made since its discovery in 2002. Our high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio spectra show a stripped-down stellar emission line, indicating that the progenitor star is still present. The observations needed to independently verify this interpretation, however, have been made only recently. We show that the observations are consistent with a free-free absorption model with an expansion velocity of 6,000 km s$^{-1}$, and that this model explains the changes in the SN 2002ap spectrum as observed between 2002 and 2014. We show that the un restricted stellar emission line explains the evolution of the supernova. If the observed progenitor star is a member of the stripped-down stellarator (a stripped-down Wolf-Rayet star), then its initial mass must have been at least $25M_{\odot}$. If, instead, the progenitor was a member of a massive convective envelope around a neutron star (or black hole), then its initial mass must have been at least $50M_{\odot}$. We discuss the properties of the stripped-down stellarator, and compare them to the stellar emission properties of SNe 2002ap and 2008ha.

We present an analysis of the optical and X-ray properties of the cooling flow cluster Z3146. We find that the cluster contains a large number of cool detached clumps, and that the clumps and the intracluster medium can be distinguished on the basis of their X-ray temperatures. We estimate the temperatures of the intracluster gas and the detached clumps, and find that they differ by about 2.5 kK. We argue that the cool detached clumps have been formed through the collapse of large detached clumps, and that the intracluster gas has been compressed by the infall ibility of these clumps. We find that the surface brightness of the cluster is not uniform, but has a correlation with the local X-ray temperature. We interpret this correlation in terms of the contribution of the detached clamps to the total surface brightness. We find that the cool detached clumps have a mean mass of 4.3 kM⋅ pc−2, and that they are responsible for 17% of the total surface brightness. The highest surface brightness is found in the regions with the highest X-ray temperatures, where the contribution from detached clumps is small. We conclude that the intracluster gas is responsible for the majority of the cluster's surface brightness, while the cool detached clumps give rise to the peaks and the high surface brightness in the outskirts of the cluster.

Node-based interactions are central to a wide range of networks, including collaboration networks, protein interaction networks, and communication networks. We consider a specific class of node-based interactions, namely encounter-based interactions, in which the activity of each node depends only on its current neighbors. We propose a simple model in which each node keeps track of the number of its neighbors and the sum of their activities. Each node then uses these quantities to determine its own activity. We show that this model is capable of producing a wide range of complex behavior, such as power-law degree distributions and small-world properties, while remaining analytically tractable. We use this model to analyze two real-world networks, namely the collaboration network of scientific papers and the calling network of mobile phones, and show that our model is able to reproduce a variety of features present in these networks. We also use our model to analyze a synthetic network in which the node attributes are generated according to a probability distribution, and show that our model is able to extract meaningful information about this distribution from the activity of the nodes. Our work suggests that encounter-based interactions can be a powerful and analytically tractable abstraction of node-based interactions.

The purpose of this investigation was to determine if a gravimetrical method could be designed to revive the corpuscular theory of light. The idea for this method was inspired by the double-slit pattern of light. The basic setup for this method consisted of a light source, a double-slit aperture, and a photoelectric detector. The intensity of the light that hit the photoelectric detector was measured and recorded. The photoelectric detector was adjusted so that the brightest spot in the double-slit pattern was at the center. Then, the gravitational field was applied to the light by placing a mass directly above the light source. The mass was allowed to fall freely and it passed between the two slits. The falling mass changed the path of the light, which in turn changed the position of the bright spot on the photoelectric detector. After the mass passed the double-slit aperture, the bright spot was back in the center of the photoelectric detector. The photoelectric detector measured the intensity of the light, which should have decreased while the mass was passing in front of the double-slit aperture. The data showed that the intensity of the light decreased while the mass was passing in front of the double-slit aperture. This result suggests that the corpuscular theory of light may be revived using a gravimetrical method.

We consider the Marcus-Lushnikov processes, Smoluchowski's and Flory's models. We show that the Smoluchowski and Flory models are special cases of the Marcus-Lushnikov processes. The Marcus-Lushnikov processes are generalization of the conservative processes to the case of drivenDissipative systems. The processes are defined by the system of balance laws which conserve the energy only in the thermodynamic sense. The special cases of the Marcus-Lushnikov processes are the conservative processes, the Smoluchowski and Flory models. The difference between the conservative and Marcus-Lushnikov processes is that the conservative processes have the additional condition: the change of the total probability of the state $\Phi$ in the infinitesimal time $dt$ is equal to zero: $\dot \Phi=0$, and the Marcus-Lushnikov processes have the additional condition: the change of the total probability of the state $\Phi$ in the infinitesimal time $dt$ is equal to the total probability of the state $\Phi$: $\dot \Phi=\Phi$ . The general form of the Marcus-Lushnikov processes is the combination of the additional conditions: the change of the total probability of the state $\Phi$ in the infinitesimal time $dt$ is equal to zero: $\dot \Phi=0$ and the change of the total probability of the state $\Phi$ in the infinitesimal time $dt$ is equal to the total probability of the state $\Phi$: $\dot \Phi=\Phi$ .

We present a method to obtain spatially and temporally resolved dynamics of penumbral filaments in solar flares. We have developed a technique that utilizes the correlation between the magnetic field and the temperature to extract the p-mode dynamics in penumbral filaments. To apply this method, we have developed an automated algorithm to identify penumbral filaments in solar flares. Once the penumbral filaments are identified, we use the correlation between the magnetic field and the temperature to extract the p-mode dynamics. We have applied this method to several solar flares and found that the p-mode dynamics in penumbral filaments can be very different from one flare to another. For example, in some flares the p-mode dynamics is very stable, while in other flares the p-mode dynamics is very chaotic. We have also found that in some flares the penumbral filaments can exhibit a different type of dynamics, which we call modified p-mode dynamics. In these cases, the period of the p-mode dynamics is much longer than the typical periods of tens of seconds. These long-period p-mode dynamics can be very stable, or they can be very chaotic. This new type of dynamics could be due to the interaction between the penumbral filaments and the surrounding magnetic field. Our results suggest that the dynamics of penumbral filaments can be very complex, and can be different in different flares. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC, grant No. 2017YFC0100299), the Ministry of Science and Technology of China (grant No. 2017XFC010100293), and the National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2017YFC0100299).

Electro-optically tunable microring resonators in lithium niobate A high-Q optical resonator can be formed by confining light in a microring structure, which can be implemented in a semiconductor microcavity or in a crystalline resonator. One advantage of the crystalline resonator is that it can provide strong light confinement in a tiny core while achieving a high quality factor, and therefore it can be integrated with various optical and photonic devices. In this article, we demonstrate a tunable microring resonator in lithium niobate (LN), a ferroelectric crystal, which can be used for optical switching and cavity quantum electro-optics. The resonator has a high-Q factor of 0.3 in the absence of a perturbation, and its free-spectral range is 4.3 nm. By utilizing the electro-optic effect in LN, the resonator can be tuned by an electrical signal, and the tuning range can be as large as 70 nm. Our results show that the tunable microring resonator in LN can be applied to optical switching and that it has potential for use in cavity quantum electro-optics.
